News.title: Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86
News.content:
Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him."

Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer".

James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer.

Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company."

Michael Grade, who produced the TV adaptation of Archer's Kane and Abel, told BBC Breakfast he "was a consummate storyteller in real life as as well as on on the page".

"That was his greatest skill. But his greatest regret, I'm sure, was that he wasn't able to fulfil his political ambitions. I think he always secretly wanted to be - not necessarily so secretly - to be prime minister.

"But because of the mistakes he made in his life, it wasn't for me. But he loved politics more than anything," Lord Grade said.

Kate Elton, CEO of Archer's publisher HarperCollins, told BBC's Radio 4 Today programme: "He was curious about everybody and everything and he was just enormous fun."

Last week, Archer returned to his former school to promote his last book.

"It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School.

Archer had been due to attend the Cheltenham Literature Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel.

He and his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said.

The couple have two sons and five grandchildren.

News.title: Rise in babies in care proceedings raises fears of unnecessary adoptions, experts tell BBC
News.content:
Broadhurst acknowledges that term is "politically loaded" and the modern care system is very different from the coercive practices that took place mainly between 1949 and 1976 - and for which the government recently apologised for cases in England.

But she says it "is actually what's happening because parents do not agree".

"They want to continue to be in contact with a child," she says. "Even parents who feel they couldn't look after a child at that point find it particularly brutal that they're going to have no contact, or very little contact, with that child until they're 18."

One birth mother, Jean, tells us she never wanted to give up her daughter, Tye, for adoption - and describes it as "forced". Her local council says it followed a lawful process.

Jean was separated from her daughter for 16 years, after Tye was taken into care at 11 weeks' old and then adopted at the age of two.

Now, with Tye an adult, they are reunited. When she turned 18, having struggled with adoption and questions about her identity, Tye looked for her mother on social media.

"I knew I had a mum somewhere and it wasn't the people I was growing up with," she says - describing her adoption as something that had left her "completely alone" without a "whole chunk of heritage".

When Jean became pregnant, she was looking forward to being a mother. But she had concerns too: "The only thing I knew for certain was that I was disabled, I couldn't look after myself properly, so I wasn't sure how I was going to be able to look after a baby, so I needed help."

Her local authority at the time, Newham Council in east London, told her such help was not available, she says. Tye was put into foster care, but Jean was able to see her often.

There had been multiple assessments and residential placements as Jean tried to keep Tye. But professionals, including doctors and social workers, ultimately advised the court that Tye needed a stable, permanent family and that Jean could not provide it.

Jean says she fought and "gave it my all" through years of court proceedings. She even asked if she could have visiting rights, in a similar way to a parent in a divorce. "I was told that was an unrealistic expectation," she says.

News.title: MPs call for investigation after Lutnick-Epstein whistleblower dies
News.content:
The treatment of whistleblowers by the UK's financial watchdog must be investigated following the death of a British trader who exposed evidence of links between US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Jeffrey Epstein, MPs have said.

Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners - the international firm of financial brokers founded and run by Lutnick before his appointment by US President Donald Trump - died last month in Thailand.

Earlier this year, Andriesz raised concerns with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the FBI and other watchdogs about evidence he had uncovered of business links between Epstein and Lutnick. It cast doubt on Lutnick's public statements about his associations with the late sex offender.

A group of UK MPs have now said his death raises "deeply troubling questions" about the way whistleblowers can be treated when they approach the FCA - the financial regulator - with concerns about wrongdoing and subsequent retaliation.

Andriesz's family said he had taken his own life on 23 September, and that there was no suggestion of foul play.

News.title: Europe is pouring billions into space. Can Glasgow's satellite industry keep up?
News.content:
In 2005, a young space engineer called Craig Clark moved back to his home city of Glasgow. He'd graduated from university just over a decade before, but the only jobs he could find were south of the border. Now Craig wanted to start a company of his own. He called it Clyde Space.

I went to school not far from the River Clyde, where Glasgow's shipbuilding industry earned a global reputation for craftsmanship and engineering excellence. There was a saying that I grew up with: "The Clyde made Glasgow and Glasgow made the Clyde."

What I hadn't realised until recently was that, in a different guise, that tradition is still alive. Two decades later, Glasgow is a European leader in building small satellites.

Many of those built here are known as CubeSats. Their basic building block measures just 10cm by 10cm by 10cm - think of something about the size of a Rubik's Cube. They are much smaller, cheaper and quicker to develop than the huge contraptions that you might picture when you think of satellites.

News.title: Man charged over Gosport migrant protest
News.content:
A man has been charged after a protest over migrant arrivals in a Hampshire town.

The Home Office said 149 migrants were picked up on Sunday in a mid-Channel rescue operation by the RNLI, alongside a French vessel, and were brought ashore at Gosport.

Flares were set off and there were scuffles with police during a stand-off involving about 150 anti-migrant demonstrators.

Jamie Bennett has been charged with failing to comply with a prohibited assembly direction. The 38-year-old, of Thyme Avenue in Whiteley, Fareham, has been bailed to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates' Court on 26 November.

Police made 12 arrests following the protest on Haslar Road, 11 men aged between 22 and 59, and a 57-year-old woman.

Suspected offences included assaulting police officers, affray and racially aggravated public order.

The remaining 10 men and one woman have been bailed pending further inquiries.

Police said a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries but none were seriously hurt.

Some demonstrators stopped police vans from advancing by standing in front of them and chanting "shame on you" and "deport the lot".

News.title: Children brave snipers and mortars to go to school near Yemen front line
News.content:
Every morning at 6am, 10-year-old Rafeef and her younger brother get ready for school, putting on their cream and brown uniforms.

She always looks forward to seeing her friends and learning about everything from maths to Arabic and Islamic studies. She can't wait to start studying English next year.

But for Rafeef, the journey to school involves far greater risks than crossing roads or missing the bus.

Her school in Taiz, south-western Yemen, stands on a mountain at the edge of a valley known as no-man's land - a heavily contested front line in the civil war between forces supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Iran-backed Houthis.

On one side of the school is government-held territory, on the other are Houthi sniper positions.

Rafeef's home is further down the mountain.

Every time she goes to school, she has to walk uphill with her back towards the snipers. "I'm afraid," she says.

News.title: UK oil refinery broke toxic pollution limits dozens of times, documents reveal
News.content:
One of the UK's biggest oil refineries spilled pollution into local rivers and the Mersey Estuary on dozens of occasions in 2023 and 2024, documents shared exclusively with the BBC suggest.

EET Fuels, formerly known as Essar, which runs Stanlow refinery, pleaded guilty this year to 12 charges of breaching environmental law between 2018 and 2020.

But documents obtained by investigative journalists from SourceMaterial describe other breaches from the refinery in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, with toxic chemicals and oil regularly spilled into the waterways and even groundwater.

EET Fuels said it "takes its environmental responsibilities extremely seriously".

The Environment Agency (EA) has confirmed that it is investigating the breaches.

The Stanlow oil refinery is one of only four remaining refineries in the UK and processes 10 million tonnes of crude oil each year - producing around 18% of the country's fuel for road transport like cars and trucks.

EET Fuels, which bought the refinery from Shell in 2011 for Â£842m, holds a permit to operate the site.

This says it can discharge controlled amounts of oil and chemicals into the air and waterways. However, it must make efforts to limit pollution to the environment and harm to humans.

But reports from the EA into activities at the refinery, uncovered by environmental journalists SourceMaterial, show that in 2023 and 2024 the permitted levels for chemical releases were exceeded hundreds of times.

The regulator has determined this meant EET Fuels broke its permit conditions 58 times over the two-year period - which could amount to an offence.

The documents show the spills included toxic chemicals such as cyanide, benzene, and heavy oils - into the air and local waterways like Thornton Brook and the River Gowy which connect onto the River Mersey Estuary.

The estuary is a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and home to endangered species including dolphins and a breeding ground for rare birds.

"Species like dunlin, black-tailed godwit and redshank will travel all around the world to feed and roost in the land around the River Mersey," explained Charlotte Harris, chief executive of Cheshire Wildlife Trust.

Harris said this has only been possible because organisations, including the Wildlife Trusts, have undertaken years of pollution clean up from legacy industry in the area.

"We've seen the Atlantic salmon return to the river and also the critically endangered European eel makes its way up the Mersey and into the River Gowy to breed each year as well," she said.

News.title: I won't accept exclusion within Green Party, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion
News.content:
Nine Labour MPs have also referred the party to Sussex Police, asking the force to investigate whether alleged "possible antisemitic offences" at the conference merit a criminal investigation.

A spokesperson for Sussex Police said: "We can confirm we have received a letter and are reviewing its contents to determine the appropriate next steps."

It is the latest development in a backlash to the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton and endorsed by 1,022 votes to 813.

"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it said.

The motion has exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.

Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday and four of the party's five MPs opposed it.

Israel's foreign ministry responded by banning Polanski from entering the country, while some Jewish groups have described it as an "attack on the Jewish community".

In his first comments since the motion was passed, having declined interviews on Monday, Polanski released a lengthy statement saying he "take[s] seriously my responsibility to make sure everyone feels safe and welcome in our party".

He added: "As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of."

He said his party and its leadership stood for "deeply held values of compassion, fairness and equality for all".

Polanski, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".

News.title: I had to crawl on my hands and knees to get off train, says disabled woman
News.content:
A wheelchair user was left in tears as she crawled on her "hands and knees" through a train after being told a ramp could not be used to help her off.

Phoebe Tesoriere, 24, who lived in Caerphilly at the time, was on a Great Western Railway (GWR) train from London Paddington to Bath Spa when it happened.

Her family spoke to the assistance desk and were taken to the only designated wheelchair space on the train. Phoebe said she was assured a ramp and assistance would be waiting, but was told she was in a carriage beyond the platform and could not get off.

GWR said it was "really sorry" and admitted "we let her down, both when we helped her board and at several points during her journey".

Former Cardiff University student Phoebe, who has hereditary spastic paraplegia, external which causes weakness and stiffness in the leg muscles, said: "My mum specifically asked if a ramp and assistance would be waiting at Bath Spa. We were assured it would be."

While on the train, staff checked which station she would be getting off at numerous times during the incident in December 2025, she added.

Despite this, Phoebe was not told the carriage she was directed to would stop beyond the platform, leaving her unable to use a ramp to get off.

News.title: Lego fraudster among last year's most high-profile insurance scammers
News.content:
A scammer jailed for making false home insurance claims about supposedly stolen Lego has been listed as one of last year's most high-profile insurance fraudsters.

The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, insurance trade body the ABI said.

Other insurance fraud cases flagged by the ABI include someone who staged car crashes with people they met online and a complex travel insurance scam involving multiple fake identities and documents.

The average value of a fraudulent claim reached Â£14,300 last year, the second-highest level on record, the ABI said.

There was Â£1.34bn worth of fraudulent claims in 2025, a 14% increase on the Â£1.18bn detected the previous year.

At the same time, the number of detected fraudulent claims fell slightly to 93,900, down 2.7% on 2024.

Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the ABI, said: "Although the rate of detected insurance fraud fell slightly last year, our data shows that fraudsters areâ¯targeting much bigger payouts.

"As emerging technologies such as AI become more widely available, fraudsters will continue to look for new ways to exploit them."

Det Ch Insp Simon Klust, head of the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) at the City of London Police, said: "Insurance fraud is not a victimless crime and those who commit it increase the cost of premiums for honest customers."

He added that the 250 cases a day detected by the ABI last year were "unfortunately likely to be just the tip of the iceberg".

News.title: Scotland's first AI subject teacher warns pupils: Don't trust everything it tells you
News.content:
Some teenagers are already using artificial intelligence to tackle homework, revise for exams and sharpen coursework.

Others are steering clear of it completely.

At one Scottish school, staff have decided that pretending AI doesn't exist is not an option.

Mearns Castle High School in East Renfrewshire is believed to be the first school in the UK to appoint a dedicated principal teacher of AI literacy, creating a role focused entirely on helping pupils and staff understand the risks and benefits of the powerful new technology.

The job has gone to Jamie Laycock, a former principal teacher of biology, who says schools must help youngsters understand both the opportunities and dangers of AI.

The message underpinning the new role is: "We can't just hope AI goes away".

But rather than teaching pupils to embrace AI, Laycock's mission is to ensure they can question it, challenge it and use it responsibly.

News.title: Ofcom investigates Meta over Instagram Instants feature
News.content:
Ofcom is investigating whether Meta breached its duties under the UK's online safety laws with the launch of its "Instants" feature on Instagram.

The tool - allowing users to take and share an instant image with close friends, that disappears once viewed - was launched on Meta's photo-sharing app in May as "a new way to share photos in the moment".

But the regulator said the social media giant had not properly assessed risks posed by the feature prior to launching it - something it is required to do under the UK's Online Safety Act (OSA).

A Meta spokesperson said in a statement that it "takes its regulatory obligations under the Online Safety Act seriously".

"We conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom about this feature on a number of occasions before launching it," they said.

"We will of course co-operate with Ofcom during this investigation."

Ofcom said its probe would examine whether Meta breached OSA duties by not carrying out "a suitable and sufficient illegal content risk assessment and children's risk assessment before the launch of Instants".

Under the UK's sweeping online safety rules, platforms including Meta must carry out and update risk assessments to comply with a range of duties, including to tackle illegal content.

They must also show how they prevent children permitted to use their services from encountering content deemed harmful for them.

This spans material relating to pornography, or promoting self-harm or suicide - as "priority primary content" - alongside things like abusive, hateful or bullying content.

"Our online safety laws are clear â significant changes to platforms must be risk assessed before they're launched," said Ofcom enforcement director George Lusty.

"This is a vital step that tech firms must take to protect their users," he added.

"You wouldn't launch a new car without testing it properly, and it's the same for online services."

News.title: Temperatures set to fall as rain and cloud sweep across UK
News.content:
After weeks of unusually warm weather, autumn is finally set to make its presence felt on Tuesday as cooler air sweeps across the UK from the north-west.

Temperatures will plunge from the low 20s to the mid-teens. Wednesday could be the first day since June when temperatures stay below 20C across the whole of the country.

A spell of rain and stronger winds will accompany the colder air, adding to the autumnal feel.

But the cooler spell is not expected to last, with temperatures set to rise towards average over the weekend.

News.title: King's funding for Andrew not to be used for legal action against police
News.content:
Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.

The former Prince Andrew is not a working royal - so Buckingham Palace no longer speaks on his behalf and is not involved in his legal battle.

But a royal source said the King's financial support for his brother should not be directed towards paying for the judicial review that Mountbatten-Windsor is seeking.

It's not been disclosed how much the King gives to Mountbatten-Windsor, but the funding for his brother was part of the arrangement when the former Prince Andrew was moved from his previous home at Royal Lodge in Windsor.

This allowance for Mountbatten-Windsor is not from the Sovereign Grant, which is the Â£138m in public funding for the monarchy.

It is drawn from the King's private money, which includes his income from the Duchy of Lancaster, private estates and his own investments and inheritances.

At the time of Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest, the King said the "law must take its course", and the Palace is now distancing itself from the former Duke of York's legal pushback.

Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are understood to be challenging Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court over the lawfulness of warrants used for searches of Sandringham and Royal Lodge - in what has been Andrew's first public response since his arrest earlier this year.

Thames Valley Police has confirmed it is "engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court".

It added: "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."

Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants.

A court hearing on Thursday afternoon will be part of Mountbatten-Windsor's bid to quash the warrants.

News.title: Prisoner took his own life after terror order had 'substantial impact' on mental state, inquest finds
News.content:
Prior to being jailed in February 2020 for breaching the TPIM order, Uddin had served a sentence for racially or religiously aggravated harassment.

TPIMs allow the authorities to control people whom the government believes are involved in terrorism, but who are not facing criminal charges. The home secretary acts on advice from MI5 when imposing TPIMs.

Subjects of TPIMs face measures such as wearing an electronic tag, curfews, relocation to a different part of the country, bans on internet use, controls on finances, and limits on who they can meet and where they can go.

Breaches can result in a terrorism conviction and prison sentence. TPIMs can currently last up to five years, up from a maximum of two years when Uddin was under one.

Uddin breached the measures 12 times by withdrawing more money than he was permitted. The inquest heard he largely spent it on drugs. He had over 20 previous criminal convictions - none of which were for terrorism offences.

The inquest, which was the first ever to consider the impact of TPIMs, heard that Uddin believed the order was originally imposed because he had made reckless statements while under the influence of drugs, but that he insisted he was not a terrorist.

It is understood he was alleged to have made verbal threats and associated with people regarded by MI5 as being involved in terrorist activity.

Coroner Bernard Richmond KC said Uddin was "loved and loving" but was "not someone without his troubles" and these revolved around his drug use.

The coroner said he will be issuing a report to the government out of concern about a risk to other people under the terrorism control measures.

When the TPIM was first imposed on Uddin in January 2020, he was forcibly relocated to the West Midlands after being arrested at the prison gates in front of his sister who had come to meet him on release.

The full reasons for a person being on a TPIM are typically kept secret, even from the person subject to the TPIM, because they are based on MI5 intelligence.

The inquest heard that Uddin feared the TPIM would be re-imposed when he left prison early in 2022, and that he would again breach it due to drugs.

Today the inquest jury concluded the following:

"We are satisfied that the imposition of the original TPIM and its unusually restrictive nature had a substantial impact on the mental state of Akhtar Uddin."

"We are satisfied that the fear of a likely reimposition of such a restrictive TPIM, and its possibly never-ending nature, had a significant impact on the mental state of Akhtar in prison."

"We are satisfied, as a result of the consistent evidence that prison services were unaware of TPIM restrictions and their likely impact on Akhtar, there was a failure to provide support most suitably targeted to Akhtar's specific needs and situations."

A governor at HMP Wandsworth accepted in evidence that lack of knowledge of TPIMs by prison staff had resulted in "unintentionally cruel" treatment of Uddin.

Giving evidence, Uddin's sister Jasmine said that, in the weeks before his death, he had described "counter terrorism officers" questioning him in prison and saying he would never get off the TPIM.

A statement from Uddin's family, issued by their solicitors Birnberg Peirce, said they welcomed the inquest's findings.

"Although nothing can bring back their loving son, brother and uncle, they hope that this will make a real difference to those who are currently at the mercy of this inhumane regime."

His former solicitor, Amer Ahmad, had told Uddin in autumn 2021 there were "highly limited prospects" that he would succeed in having the TPIM legally overturned, the inquest heard.

Dr Richard Latham, an NHS consultant forensic psychiatrist, appeared as an expert witness for the coroner and concluded that Uddin had an undiagnosed "personality disorder", associated "psychological problems and vulnerabilities", and this resulted in impulsiveness, grievance and paranoia.

He said Uddin probably assumed the worst about the TPIM in future, and that this prospect would have created "distress and a sense of hopelessness".

Dr Latham added TPIMs are intended to create a "degree of isolation," but that plays on psychological vulnerability and can create "emotional isolation".

Questioned by Jesse Nicholls, representing the bereaved family, Dr Latham said Uddin "felt a sense of injustice" about being branded a terrorist.

The inquest heard there was little or no awareness by staff in HMP Wandsworth of TPIMs. The coroner said "very few people, if any" knew about Uddin's TPIM, the revocation, or potential re-imposition.

In the absence of jurors, the coroner said there was much assessment by the state of Uddin's potential risk to others, but he had seen "nothing" showing any assessment of risks to him. He said there is a "paucity of support for people subject to TPIMs" and there is a potential risk to other people subjected to them.

For this reason, he added, he would be writing a preventing future deaths report.

There has been a trend towards TPIM subjects having mental health issues.

The independent reviewer of terrorism legislation, Jonathan Hall KC, has noted in previous reports that the "Home Office recognises poor mental health as a dominant feature amongst recent TPIM subjects" and that "poor mental health and neurodivergence (autism)" as being in evidence amongst them.

A government spokesperson said TPIMs were "a last resort to manage the risk posed by terrorists who cannot be prosecuted or deported" and are "carefully considered and strictly focused" on stopping a person's "involvement in terrorist activity".

The government was dealing with a prison crisis it "inherited", the spokesperson added, and was improving training to help staff "manage risks of self-harm and suicide".

This article contains details some readers may have found upsetting. If you, or someone you know, are struggling with the issues raised in this article, support and information is available at BBC Action Line.

News.title: British Museum boss 'sorry' for Bayeux Tapestry visitor issues
News.content:
The head of the British Museum has apologised for the experience some visitors have had at its blockbuster Bayeux Tapestry exhibition.

The London institution has announced changes to how visitors see the historic work over concerns of overcrowding.

"Anyone that doesn't have a good experience, we're really sorry about that and we want to put it right," Nicholas Cullinan told the BBC's culture and media editor Katie Razzall.

The new plans include longer opening hours, an audio guide, additional seating and clearer signage.

Some people reported waits of up to two hours. Last week, hundreds of ticket holders were reportedly turned away due to backlogs when the museum closed early for a private event.

"You don't want anyone that comes to see it to have a bad experience, so our focus is very much on getting it right and learning lessons," Cullinan said.

"Obviously we want everyone that comes to have a fantastic experience. To put it into context, we're three weeks into the exhibition run. Next week, we'll hit our 100,000th visitor, which is a pretty extraordinary statistic. The vast number of visitors report having a very good experience."

Asked if the museum team had asked the embroidery's home museum in Bayeux for advice on queue management and timings, Cullinan said they had.

He also denied the museum had let too many people book tickets and said that the issues arose because visitors want to spend more time with the work than expected.

The problem "isn't just the interest, it's that people want to spend more time than anticipated. And that's a good thing. We want people to come and enjoy it, but it means we have to adjust accordingly and that's what we're doing," Cullinan said.

Some visitors have been spending longer than their allocated 40-minute slot viewing the tapestry, meaning others have to move through more quickly, he said.

News.title: Asos hacked latest: Customers sent bizarre, threatening notification by shopping app
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Asos appears to have been hacked, with customers sent a bizarre, threatening notification.

Users of the app received a message on Tuesday morning indicating that the company’s systems had been compromised.

“Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance,” it reads. “Engage with us, or we will leak it,” it continues, before linking out to a Telegram chat.

DPO refers to the data protection officer, the appointed person in a company who takes responsibility for safeguarding customers’ information. Snowflake is an online data platform used by a wide array of companies.

Asos did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It is not clear how many customers the notification was sent to. But it appears to have been delivered to at least a large number of the app’s customers.

More follows

News.title: Tory minister criticised for claiming Luton has ‘no go zones’ where ‘white people won’t go’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A Tory minister has sparked backlash after branding areas of Luton as “no-go zones” where “white people won’t go”.

Shadow home office minister Blake Stephenson claimed that some areas of Luton are “ghettos” as he called for parts of the UK to be “for all of us not just certain communities”.

The comments, made at a fringe event at the Conservative Party conference have prompted criticism from Labour MP for Luton North, Sarah Owens, who said they were “deeply irresponsible”. She accused Mr Stephenson of peddling “the same rightwing nonsense” as far-right activist Tommy Robinson and Reform UK.

Speaking at a Centre for Policy Studies meeting in Birmingham, Mr Stephenson described his experience of living in a village near to the area.

“I know Luton reasonably well because I live 10, 15 minutes away and represent Mid Bedfordshire, I live in a village just over the border,” he said according to the Guardian.

open image in gallery Shadow home office minister Blake Stephenson claimed that some areas of Luton are “ghettos” as he called for parts of the UK to be “for all of us not just certain communities” ( UK Parliament )

“I think the town is a shadow of its former self. There are parts of that town – and unfortunately the police will tell you this – it can be a very dangerous place. There are parts where white people won’t go. They are like no-go zones. It is not alone, there are other towns across the country in a similar situation. It is dreadful where we have got to.”

The comments echo sentiments voiced by Mr Robinson, real name Thomas Yaxley-Lennon. Yaxley-Lennon, who grew up in Luton, has repeatedly claimed the town is divided and cited some areas as supposed ‘no-go zones’ for white people.

Speaking at a fringe event called From Boriswave to Brain Drain: How Can We Fix Migration? Mr Stephenson said: “But we can move on from it but it requires deep levels of integration and we need to break apart these, erm… this is where it gets icky, but we need to make sure we don’t have ghettoes where there are no-go zones for anybody. The country is for all of us not just certain communities,” he said.

open image in gallery The comments echo sentiments voiced by far-right activist Tommy Robinson, real name Thomas Yaxley-Lennon. ( AFP/Getty )

“But we can move on from it but it requires deep levels of integration and we need to break apart these, erm … this is where it gets icky, but we need to make sure we don’t have ghettoes where there are no-go zones for anybody. The country is for all of us not just certain communities,” he said.

Sarah Owen, the Labour MP for Luton North, hit back at the comments. She said: “It is deeply irresponsible for any politician, let alone a senior Conservative, to peddle the same rightwing nonsense about Luton that we see from the likes of Yaxley-Lennon and Reform,” she told the Guardian.

“It is simply untrue and the shadow Home Office minister should get off social media and get to know the fantastic Lutonians I’m proud to represent and call my neighbours. I’d also call on the new Lib Dem/Tory/Green coalition-run council in Luton to disown these comments from their colleague.”

News.title: Ex-German spy chief detained on suspicion of espionage and treason – report
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Germany’s former foreign intelligence chief has been detained on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, Bild newspaper is reporting.

The newspaper said that prosecutors allege August Hanning, whose tenure ended in 2005, bought secret information from a former employee of the foreign intelligence agency BND and intended to sell it on as part of his consulting activities.

The BND and the office of Germany's federal prosecutor did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

Bild said that the investigation was launched after the discovery of an alleged leak of intelligence reports intended for the chancellery.

News.title: GP found dead in home near Sandringham Estate named locally as murder investigation continues
News.content:

A woman who was found dead at a property near the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk has been named locally as a GP.

Dr Hannah Terry was found at an address in Fern Hill, Dersingham, just over one mile from Sandringham House, in the early hours of Sunday.

A notice on the website of Grimston Medical Centre, where Dr Terry is listed as a member of the practice team, says it is “temporarily closed due to extremely difficult circumstances affecting our practice team”.

Dr Terry, who is also known by her married name Hannah Cain, has not been officially identified.

Norfolk Police said officers found the body of a woman in her 40s after they were called by the ambulance service shortly after 2.20am on Sunday.

A man in his 40s was arrested on suspicion of murder and taken to King’s Lynn police investigation centre for questioning, the force added.

open image in gallery Fern Hill in Dersingham ( Goolge )

Police said on Monday that officers had applied to Great Yarmouth Magistrates’ Court for a warrant of further detention, which would allow them an additional 32 hours to question the man.

A cordon remains in place at the address as inquiries continue.

Detective Inspector Alix Wright, of the Norfolk and Suffolk major investigation team, said on Sunday: “We are in the very early stages of this investigation, working to establish the exact circumstances surrounding the woman’s death.

“I’d ask anyone who believes they may have information that could help our investigation to please share this with us.”

Anyone with information can contact police on 101 or through the force’s website, quoting incident number 27 of Sunday, 4 October.

News.title: UK construction industry declines at slowest rate for eight months
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The UK’s construction sector declined at its slowest pace since January last month as it edged closer to recovery, according to new figures.

The closely-followed S&P Global UK construction PMI showed a reading of 46.1 in September, improving from 44.3 in August.

It marked the strongest industry performance for eight months.

Any reading above the 50.0 threshold indicates activity in the industry is increasing, while anything below means it is contracting.

The latest figures show the industry remained firmly in the contraction territory having been declining since January 2025, but at a slower pace than in recent months.

It was also significantly stronger than the 44.9 level expected by a consensus of economists.

Experts said the reduced downturn was linked to improvements across all parts of the sector.

Tim Moore, economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said: “All three construction sub-sectors have seen a degree of stabilisation relative to the rapid declines reported in the second quarter of 2026.

“In September, commercial building work saw its smallest fall in activity since May 2025.

“House building was again the weakest performer as rising borrowing costs and unfavourable market conditions weighed on output.”

Mr Moore said new orders were however “relatively subdued” for the month as clients deferred decision-making on major projects.

This was largely linked to subdued demand and geopolitical tensions.

Firms also highlighted some inflationary pressure, with around 25% of those surveyed reporting a rise in their purchasing costs, with fuel surcharges, higher freight costs and rising raw material prices all noted.

Reduced workloads also resulted in another month of job cuts, with employment reducing each month since January 2025.

Carly Thorpe, construction and engineering partner at Walker Morris, said: “The modest improvement in September’s PMI reflects a combination of stronger civil engineering activity and favourable operating conditions, with a drier-than-average September likely helping to maintain productivity on site.

“The figures also reinforce the ongoing shift in market activity away from residential development and towards infrastructure-led sectors, including transport, energy and data centres, where investment and project pipelines remain stronger.”

News.title: Lionel Messi is leaving international football with grace. Cristiano Ronaldo could never
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

In boxing, some say the classiest way to go out is on your back, staring at the lights. Everyone loves a fairytale ending, but there is a certain closure that comes with bowing out in defeat.

Regardless of what happens in Buenos Aires on Tuesday night, in a friendly against Benin, Lionel Messi will end his Argentina career in a similar vein. The final, overriding taste will be one of loss.

The eight-time Ballon d’Or winner, 39, announced his retirement from international football following the 2026 World Cup. His designated farewell match will be held at the the iconic Estadio Monumental, home of River Plate.

open image in gallery Lionel Messi will play his final game for Argentina on Tuesday night ( Getty Images )

Widely regarded as the greatest footballer of all time, Messi goes out having seen his stock rise even further in the summer. He completely outperformed expectation, even for him, at the World Cup to show that he could still run the show while pushing 40. Eight goals, four assists and, briefly, the tournament’s all-time top scorer - before golden boot winner Kylian Mbappe snatched that accolade - represented a truly remarkable output for the Argentinian magician, even if it all came to nothing.

After guiding the defending champions to a second successive World Cup final, he was unable to repeat his heroics of Qatar to end on the highest of highs. In fact, it was the lowest of lows. Argentina’s post-match brawl sparked by Leandro Paredes and co. cast a cloud of shame over him and an entire nation, though Messi was not an innocent party in Argentina’s performance of disgrace.

In the aftermath of Enzo Fernandez ragdolling Pau Cubarsi to get himself sent off in second-half stoppage time, he tried to level the playing field after Marc Cucurella spoke while covering his mouth, appealing to the referee to produce a red under the “Vinicius law” - something that had been written into the game courtesy of compatriot Gianluca Prestianni’s alleged racism. It was a desperate abandonment of sporting integrity from a footballing marvel made out to be immune to mistakes.

open image in gallery Messi was part of the shame that was Argentina's World Cup final loss in the summer ( Getty Images )

His efforts both in this regard and with the football at his feet proved fruitless. Spain ran out deserving winners against Argentina’s anti-football in extra time.

Messi’s tears on New Jersey shores spoke to an inevitability. Though with less individual ignominy than Diego Maradona before him, whose international retirement followed a failed drug test at the 1994 World Cup, Messi was similarly hurtling towards the end of his tenure as Argentina’s heroic figurehead. That was rubber stamped by the passing of his father and agent, Jorge, at the age of 68 after a long illness.

Six weeks after the final, Messi confirmed his retirement. “There isn’t much time left, chapters come to a close, and this is one that hurts me deeply,” he wrote on Instagram. “I love, have loved, and will always love being part of the national team. I've given it my all, I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are some really great young players coming through behind me who deserve their chance."

It felt right. After 21 years, 207 appearances, 125 goals and 68 assists, there will be just one more game. An international career categorised by pain and perseverance, he bows out with a World Cup, two Copa Americas and an Olympic gold medal to his name; though in contrast to his club success, he more often fell at the final hurdle. Runners-up medals at two World Cups and three Copa Americas, heartbreak regularly prevailed during the Messi era - something that eventually became the rocket fuel for the current crop of players, dedicated to deliver him those titles before it was too late. Lionel Scaloni built a team that would first and foremost die for Messi; that team won Argentina’s first World Cup since Mexico ‘86 and third overall.

He retires having achieved what he wanted, and he retires an undisputed hero. The same cannot be said for his “GOAT debate” counterpart, if you can even call him that anymore, with Cristiano Ronaldo’s international career at risk of coming to the most pathetic of ends thanks to his latest strop.

open image in gallery Cristiano Ronaldo's latest strop for Portugal puts his international career at risk of coming to the most pathetic of ends ( Getty )

After at least two years of being a hinderance to the team’s efforts, taking up a starting spot that should be going to someone younger and more deserving, Ronaldo opted against using the natural end of the World Cup cycle to hang up his international boots and instead remained in the fold. That was until he quit the squad after being an unused substitute for the first time in 18 years for a Nations League clash with Norway; one Portugal won, with his replacement Goncalo Ramos scoring the winner. “In due time, I will tell the truth to all Portuguese people about the reasons that motivated my departure from the national team,” he wrote on social media. Cue a fourth Piers Morgan interview.

The thing is, nobody actually cares anymore. Ronaldo is like that self-important wet flannel you kind of know that posts: “Deleting my social media, had enough of fake people. If you need me, text me.” Except he’s not 14, he’s 41. It’s for that reason we don’t want to give him anymore attention because, like a problematic child, it only encourages this behaviour.

Instead, we look to his rival, who has watched silently as Ronaldo hammered another nail into the coffin that is his “GOAT” argument. Ronaldo’s legacy is growing damaged by the month. Messi’s continues to glisten, despite being fresh off failure on the grandest of stages, both on an individual and team level. He has more than enough credit in the bank for that to be forgiven.

open image in gallery Messi’s legacy continues to glisten despite failure to win a second World Cup ( Getty Images )

In Buenos Aires, more tears will be shed; overflowing gratitude, pride and immense sadness. But there will be no anger, no disappointment, no ill-feeling. Messi has defined an era of football to a point of deification in his homeland. He leaves at the right time, with dignity and his head held high.

News.title: Average sum owed by people seeking debt help passes £10,000 – Citizens Advice
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The average debt among people across England and Wales going to Citizens Advice for support has passed £10,000 for the first time on the charity’s records.

The service said the increase is being driven by essential bills such as energy, council tax and housing debts.

Average debt has been above £10,000 since June and the trend has persisted for around a quarter of a year.

Citizens Advice has been tracking average debt among the people it helps with debt advice since the pre-coronavirus era of 2019, when the figure was around £7,000.

On average more than 48,000 people across England and Wales per month have sought help with debt from Citizens Advice so far this year – a 37% increase compared with 2022.

Half (51%) of those asking for debt support are in a negative budget, meaning their essential costs outstrip their income.

These households face an average monthly shortfall of £254, which the charity said could be nearly equivalent to a full week’s rent.

Among the people Citizens Advice sees who have some money left at the end of each month and so could potentially pay off debts, a third (33%) are likely to take more than a decade to clear them, the charity said, excluding any interest or fees.

Tom MacInnes, director of policy at Citizens Advice, described debt as “the elephant in the room” and said ways out of debt are needed “for those who simply can’t repay”.

He said: “Every day our advisers are helping people with increasingly complex debt across multiple essential bills.

“People are doing all they can but are building up levels of debt that decades of repayments won’t touch. This leaves families at breaking point and trapped in the red.

“When every spare penny gets spent on trying to clear debts built up due to the cost-of-living crisis, higher wages or lower bills don’t lead to people feeling better off.”

News.title: Tories promise to scrap Labour’s mansion tax
News.content:
The Tories have pledged to scrap Labour’s “mansion tax” on homes worth more than £2m.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, pledged to abolish the “vindictive levy” in his keynote speech to the Conservative Party conference, warning it would hit people living in “ordinary homes”.

Under the tax, which was announced by Labour last year, properties valued at more than £2m face an extra levy on their council tax from 2028.

The shadow chancellor said: “They pretend it’s a mansion tax, but it will hit people here in Birmingham, in Manchester, and those living in ordinary homes making long commutes to our capital city. For many, it will be simply unaffordable.”

He pledged to follow in the footsteps of Nigel Lawson, Margaret Thatcher’s chancellor, and cut one tax at every Budget if the his party returns to power.

Elsewhere in his speech, Mr Griffith promised to scrap a net zero “grocery tax” which pushes up the cost of the weekly shop and cut the cost of a new build by £50,000.

The shadow chancellor also accused previous Tory leaders of failing to govern as free market conservatives, and said Andy Burnham and John Healey want to take Britain back to a “socialist fever dream of the 1970s”.

News.title: How worried should we be about the Russian plague lab leak?
News.content:
Russian media says 200 people are being quarantined. How likely is it that the disease could now spread?

Experts say the risk from this particular bacterium is low.

It can be treated with antibiotics and – although its possible others have been exposed – it seems unlikely it will spread far. The pneumonic form of the disease is spread by droplets and prolonged direct and close contact is required for the disease to spread.

Brendan Wren, professor of microbial pathogenesis at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said the disease was less transmissible than Covid.

“Plague is still endemic in many parts the world, including western parts of the US, so there shouldn’t be too much concern as the transmission of Yersinia pestis between humans is generally poor.”

The incubation period of pneumonic plague is short – just a day in some cases – so if no one else falls in within the next week, the likelihood of sustained transmission is low.

What is plague exactly?

Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and is transmitted via rats and other small rodents.

The bubonic form of the disease – known as the Black Death when it spread throughout Europe in the Middle Ages – is characterised by swollen nymph nodes and has a 30 to 60 per cent mortality rate. This is the more common form of plague.

The pneumonic form of the disease is almost always fatal if left untreated. However, antibiotics are effective against it so early diagnosis and treatment is essential. But drug resistant forms of the disease are emerging.

Plague is endemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar, and is also present in some parts of the United States, including Arizona and New Mexico, where according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention there are an average of seven cases a year.

News.title: Extreme heat is increasing risks for pregnant women and babies, experts warn
News.content:
Soaring temperatures are increasing birth complications and defects in newborns, a new report has warned.

The report, which surveyed 1,000 doctors and midwives, found that at least 73 per cent of healthcare workers across Australia, Brazil, Britain, India and Zimbabwe had seen an uptick in heat-related complications in pregnancy and birth.

High temperatures can cause surface-level blood vessels to dilate, which in pregnant women can significantly decrease blood flow to the placenta and reduce oxygen and nutrients reaching the foetus.

This phenomenon can increase the risk of stillbirth, premature births, and low birth weight, the report, released by the Wellcome Trust, said.

Heat can also make it hard for newborn babies, whose bodies are already extremely fragile, to regulate their internal temperatures – which can significantly impact both their ability to breathe properly and feed from their mothers.

Extreme heat can also severely affect the health of a pregnant woman, placing heavy demands on the cardiovascular system and inadvertently increasing the risk of gestational diabetes, dangerously high blood pressure, and pre-eclampsia.

The effects are more severe on women who live in places where temperatures are newly or rapidly increasing, as opposed to women who have always lived in hot climates and whose bodies have acclimatised to the heat over time.

Insufferable heat can also impact women’s access to critical healthcare during pregnancy.

More than a quarter of healthcare workers surveyed by Wellcome said they had seen first-hand how fewer women travel to hospitals and clinics during heat waves, particularly in the developing world where millions access healthcare on foot.

The world experienced its hottest August on record in 2026, when the average global surface air temperature reached 16.96 degrees Celsius – roughly 1.65 degrees above pre-industrial levels.

Britain also saw its hottest summer since records began, with five heatwaves recorded over the course of just 40 days, and temperatures reaching 38 degrees in some parts of the country.

A Wellcome-funded project studying pregnant women in Wales, known as MAGENTA, has found that women in the UK have experienced negative birth outcomes as a result of the persistent heat.

Initial research has linked exposure to elevated temperatures exceeding 25 degrees with higher rates of premature births and stillbirths. A 1-degree increase in heat exposure can boost the chances of a preterm birth by around 5 per cent, the research found.

Climate change has been identified by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the greatest threat to global public health.

Between 2030 and 2050, experts project climate change will cause an additional 250,000 deaths every year.

The deaths will be due mostly to heat stress, malnutrition, and an increase in the prevalence of infectious diseases like malaria, which is spreading into new areas where mosquitoes can now more easily survive and spread disease, according to the WHO.

Dr Madeline Thomson, head of climate impacts and adaptation at Wellcome, said: “Extreme heat, fuelled by climate change, is impacting our way of life and our health - and yet many countries are not prepared. With El Niño pushing temperatures higher, the failure to act is costing lives.

“We already know many of the solutions to protect people - from early warning systems to cooler buildings.

“But the challenge is providing solutions to those who need them most, including pregnant women and newborns, who face serious risks but often receive inadequate information and support.”

News.title: ‘The dogs were eating their bodies’: Thousands of Yemenis flee war across the sea
News.content:
The Houthi militiamen had barely chased the government forces out of Alia Mohammad’s coastal village when the bombing began in a Saudi-backed attempt to recapture it.

Caught in the middle were Ms Mohammad, her family and their neighbours near the town of Dhubab, overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb strait, or ‘Gate of Tears’.

As the roar of planes split the sky over their heads and explosions shook their village, it took little time for them to decide what to do.

Born from generations of fishermen, they resolved to take to the sea and flee their homes in Yemen, to seek refuge across the strait in Djibouti.

More than 4,000 Yemeni refugees have arrived in the coastal Djibouti town of Obock in the past month, fleeing an offensive which has redrawn Yemen’s battle lines and strengthened Tehran’s hand in the Middle East energy crisis.

The offensive last month saw the Iranian-backed Houthi advance around 90 miles along the Red Sea coast in a 48-hour blitz that delivered what analysts have called the most consequential shift in Yemen’s front lines in years.

News.title: This is when to upgrade your tech (and when not to bother)
News.content:
The tech giants’ attempts to persuade people to upgrade to new gadgets every two years are proving less and less effective. According to YouGov polling, Brits are increasingly deciding to stick with the devices they have for longer, and it isn’t altogether surprising.

As well as the inherent wastefulness of the bi-annual upgrade cycle, year-on-year improvements are less dramatic than they used to be, and tech prices are sky-rocketing thanks to the growing needs of AI data centres.

Inevitably, however, there will come a time when you need to bite the bullet and buy a new model. These are the questions to ask yourself to decide whether that should be today, or whether you can kick the can a little further down the road.

How’s the performance?

A good place to start is to evaluate how your device functions day-to-day versus the day you bought it. Tech inevitably slows down over time, but the drop isn’t equal among devices: a five-year-old flagship smartphone may still outperform a budget model from last year.

If it’s still running smoothly enough, and isn’t broken in an unfixable way, then it probably pays to wait until it no longer passes this test. The longer you wait, the more appealing the upgrade choices will be.

The exception to this is if you’re bumping up against storage problems. If there’s no way to add more, and cloud storage isn’t cutting it, then you may need to upgrade early.

News.title: Jibulu emerges as England World Cup bolter in Sale defeat of Saracens
News.content:
Could Nathan Jibulu, the Sale Sharks hooker, emerge as a bolter for England’s World Cup squad? With Steve Borthwick, the England head coach, watching from the stands, the 23-year-old produced the kind of “wrecking-ball” performance in this surprise victory for the North West side that suggested he is on course to do so.

After their tame defeat by Bristol Bears in the opening round, few had predicted that Alex Sanderson’s side had much hope against Saracens, who were looking to back up their impressive win at Welford Road last weekend. But Jibulu’s powerhouse display on either side of the ball typified their stout and physical resistance, backed up by a masterly display by George Ford.

Given the age and injury profile of England hookers Jamie George and Luke Cowan-Dickie, who both missed this contest, and the fact that Theo Dan has yet to make a forceful challenge for the position in the national side, Sanderson is in no doubt that Jibulu has the X factor required to break into Borthwick’s squad this season.

“This is the player that any time you watch him play, he impacts – he takes metres either side of the ball – and we knew that he had that in him,” Sanderson said.

“It shows he’s of international class. He nailed his line-outs, on the back of that he was a wrecking-ball runner causing havoc around the field.

“This is the person that we knew, this is the player that we knew we had in him. It could be the year where he explodes onto the international scene. I hope it is, but it’s early days.

“He’s that quality, he’s that kind of an athlete. You can get away with being fast and skilful in the Prem, but it’s another level again in terms of the power that’s required at international level. And he’s got that ability, he’s immensely strong.”

Borthwick will have left the StoneX Stadium on Sunday evening with a full notebook. Ben Bamber, Sale’s 6ft 9ins lock, has also been attracting his interest and it was Bamber who crossed for the decisive try, Sale’s third, hitting a great line off Ford to finish like an outside centre.

News.title: Brilliant Hamilton storms to podium despite another Ferrari blunder
News.content:
One of the big talking points heading into the weekend has been the cooling vests drivers wear under their overalls (as opposed to the jacket-like ones they wear when they’re out of their cars). Russell told us in our Brits media session on Thursday that Mercedes had decided to forego the vests here, since the technology was not yet refined. The system works by pumping a coolant through thin tubes stitched into the vest.

Drivers have complained that the connecting valve to the pump, which was originally placed on the side of the vest, proved uncomfortable when combined with the high G-forces experienced in an F1 car. On some vests the connector has been moved to find a more comfortable position, but the thick material and tubing have also proved cumbersome under the driver’s fireproof overalls. There are also concerns over the reliability of some systems and the possibility that a failure will mean the vest will have the opposite effect and work as a heat insulator.preferring to spend that money instead on car upgrades. The money to develop the vests comes out of the budget cap.

But Russell added that the FIA should make the tech mandatory and develop it themselves, describing this race as like being in a “sauna”.The Briton’s comments prompted a sarcastic response from Verstappen - who doesn’t wear the vests either, out of choice - who said Russell “shouldn’t make a fuss”.

“I don’t need it,” Verstappen said. “Maybe I suffer a bit less from the heat.. I find a Finnish sauna at 85 degrees a lot hotter... You shouldn’t make a fuss. Yes, it is hot, but that’s part of it. You have to train for that.”

The Dutchman added: “When I was 18, I had a bit more trouble with these conditions. But after that, I started training more in the heat, such as in the sauna and a steam room, so that I can handle the sweating better and the fact that your head gets very hot. Maybe I should take him (Russell) to the sauna a few times.”

These two have history, of course. They’ve sniped at each other for years. In 2024, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, it reached a peak when Verstappen described Russell as being “two-faced” and said he had lost all respect for him. Russell responded by saying Verstappen was “a bully”. Earlier this year, the Mercedes driver said Verstappen could always retire from the sport and drive sports cars if he didn’t like the regs.

News.title: Rees-Zammit taunts Pollock as Bristol outplay Northampton
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Bristol Bears vs Northampton Saints from the Gallagher Prem, with both teams looking to build on winning starts following the opening weekend of action.

Last season’s champions Northampton kicked off their title defence with an emphatic 59-26 victory over a new-look Newcastle Red Bulls outfit at Franklin’s Gardens.

While Henry Pollock’s new cornrow hairstyle was the centre of attention at kick-off, the limelight was soon stolen by Tommy Freeman and James Pater, who both notched hat-tricks for Phil Dowson’s side.

Of 19-year-old full-back Pater, who starts on the bench today, Dowson said afterwards: “He doesn’t let the occasion get to him. He has an incredible skill set, great speed and ability to manoeuvre away from defenders.”

Bristol, meanwhile, began their season with an impressive 34-24 victory away at Sale Sharks, with Pat Lam’s side ensuring Courtney Lawes’s return to the English game was a disappointing one.

Louis Rees-Zammit was operating in his favoured wing position and got Bristol off to a strong start with two tries in the opening 23 minutes, offering Lam hope of a fruitful campaign from the Welshman.

“When you look at our wingers in the past, they scored a lot of tries and Louis is a world-class finisher,” the Bristol director of rugby said. “You get the ball to him in space and you create the opportunity, there’s a good chance he’ll finish it.”

Northampton will be hoping for a repeat of the meeting between the sides at Franklin Gardens in May when they thumped Bristol 94-33, but they have not won at Ashton Gate since 2021.

Both teams have made a pair of changes following their opening-weekend victories, with England international Ellis Genge among the players to drop out after spraining his wrist against Sale.

Sports.title: Mass brawl erupts at end of international clash as riot police forced to rush to scene
Sports.content:

A HEATED Nations League clash between Guatemala and Suriname descended into chaos after the two teams sparked such an intense brawl that riot police had to intervene.

The two Concacaf nations battled it out in their final fixture of their group in League A with high stakes on the line on Monday at the Cementos Progreso Stadium in Guatemala City.



The hosts won 1-0 thanks to a late, long-range stunner by Matthew Evans in the sixth minute of stoppage time against ten-man Suriname.

The visitors lost Richonell Margaret on 63 minutes after he was embroiled in a sensational scrap with fans at the stands.



That is when tempers flared as both benches got up in arms after the direct red card.

Following the full-time whistle, the two teams found themselves back at it and that led to a heated brawl on the pitch.



Cameras caught players and subs getting physical and exchanging blows with fans roaring from the stands.

Things got so out of hand that riot police had to get involved and separate the two sides.



Guatemala sealed their place in the CONCACAF Nations League A quarter-finals.

Luis Fernando Tena’s men will face Canada next month after winning Group B.

Sports.title: Dream Team managers fretting after Erling Haaland requests substitution during Norway’s loss to Portugal
Sports.content:

DREAM TEAM managers are on high alert after Erling Haaland (£8.8m) asked to come off during Norway’s defeat to Portugal on Sunday.

The prolific striker appeared to be limping in the moments before he was replaced by Jorgen Strand Larsen (£3.4m) in the 67th minute at Estadio do Dragao in Porto.

Norway head coach Stale Solbakken eased concerns after his side’s 2-1 loss in the Nations League, telling reporters that Haaland’s removal was pre-planned.



“We had hopes of 60 minutes after the conversation we had yesterday,” he told TV 2. “And he managed 65 minutes.



“There are a whole bunch of people who are leaving now. They need a breather.”

Indeed, Haaland has already made his way back to Manchester City, where he will be assessed ahead of Sunday’s trip to Anfield.

Enzo Maresca will be desperate for his star striker to be available for Gameweek 6 as PSG are due at the Etihad three days after City’s game against Liverpool.

Solbakken’s revelation that Haaland was only supposed to play an hour against Portugal comes as partial comfort for Dream Team bosses but the manner of his substitution doesn’t align with the official party line.

If the 26-year-old was supposed to be replaced at 60 minutes, why did he need to prompt the change with a clear gesture (and some grimacing) in the 67th minute?

Thankfully, gaffers can expect an availability update from Maresca prior to Saturday’s 11am deadline.



Needless to say, Haaland being ruled out of Gameweek 6 would turn Dream Team upside down.

Not only is he the game’s top performer at this moment in time having earned 68 points via seven goals, he is also the most popular player by a huge margin.

PIERS MORGAN has branded Cole Palmer a “bottle job” following his withdrawal from the England squad.

Palmer was recalled by Three Lions head coach Thomas Tuchel last month ahead of the extended international break.



However, the 24-year-old, who did not get called up for the World Cup this summer, pulled out of the squad due to load management.

Morgan has now criticised Palmer, claiming he is “squandering” his ability and “lacking” dedication to his country.



Speaking on his YouTube show, Football Uncensored, he said: “I think he’s a bottle job, Palmer. I think he’s a bottle job.

“The fact that he is so apparently lacking in dedication and commitment to his country…

“I think any player who doesn’t give 100 per cent to his country, which is clearly what Tuchel is saying about Palmer, you’ve got to just think, what’s wrong with them?”

Studio guests Kaveh Solhekol and Simon Jordan went on to question why Morgan used the term “bottle job” to describe the Chelsea star.

The presenter continued: “He’s not putting in a shift mentally, which I think is extraordinary, why wouldn’t you?

Sports.title: Inside story of Beckham’s Greece free-kick on 25th anniversary including team-mate who took mick out of him before it
Sports.content:
Next

IT IS 25 years since David Beckham scored THAT stunning free-kick against Greece to send England to the 2002 World Cup finals.

The Manchester United superstar came to the Three Lions’ rescue in the 93rd minute as they trailed 2-1 at Old Trafford – a result that would have dumped them into the play-offs.



We spoke with key witnesses to the moment that helped restore Goldenballs’ reputation with fans following his sending-off at the 1998 finals.

Talking exclusively to SunSport via Hajper, we start with the man who scored England’s first that day and who was fouled for the free-kick…





TEDDY SHERINGHAM

HOW can you go straight to Beckham’s free-kick when I scored the first equaliser? You can’t just gloss over that!

First of all, we were 1–0 down and thinking we’d shot ourselves in the foot.

We were playing at home, at Old Trafford rather than Wembley at the time, where you’re expected to win, but it didn’t quite go according to plan in the first half. We were quite bad that day.

I remember sitting with Gareth Southgate expecting a big speech from boss Sven-Goran Eriksson, but he was quite chilled at half-time despite us being behind.



There was nothing over the top to kickstart us for the second half but he made the substitution and I scored after six seconds. What a great substitution that was!
