"The kind of player he is, is ridiculous. He's on a whole other level right now. For a 19-year-old to be doing what he's doing is crazy.”

He added: “But if we were talking off last season, H [Kane] has got as big of an argument as anybody because his season was historic.



“The amount of goals he scored, the things he's done for us within the World Cup, they both have large arguments. So I wish them both the best of luck."

Sports.title: Gary Lineker criticises Suella Braverman for saying she is not an 'English person' as he claims her comments aimed to 'divide and rule'
Sports.content:
Gary Lineker has restarted his feud with Suella Braverman by criticising her claim that she is not English despite being born in Britain.

The former Match of the Day presenter said Reform UK's education spokesperson was wrong despite her justification that her parents were born abroad.

Lineker, 65, said such comments 'depress me a little bit' and were part of a plan by some to 'divide and rule', adding that he thought it was 'worth calling out'.

It comes after Mrs Braverman told the BBC's Question Time that she is 'British of Asian ethnicity' rather than English, because of her family's Asian heritage.

The former Conservative home secretary was then accused by a black member of the audience of being 'racist against herself' and 'reinforcing the racist argument'.

Now, Lineker has spoken out after Germany football manager Jürgen Klopp was asked last week whether his team were 'not German enough' or 'not white enough'.

In yesterday's edition of The Rest is Football podcast, Lineker said: 'I raise it because obviously we've had the thing with one of the Reforms, Suella Braverman, saying the same sort of stuff that, if you've got a different skin colour, you're not English.'

Lineker then quoted the response from Klopp, who said: 'There is absolutely no reason to pay attention to these people. You won't get my thoughts on this.

Gary Lineker spoke about Suella Braverman during his The Rest Is Football podcast yesterday

Reform UK's education spokesperson Suella Braverman on the BBC's Question Time in north London last Thursday when she said she is not English despite being born in Britain

'I have little time in everyday life for idiocy and even less on social media. The great crux of our lives is that everyone is allowed to express their opinion.

'It's insane when something like that exists. The world would learn a thing or two from a sports changing room. There, everyone is respected based on the facts and not discredited based on false opinions.'

Lineker then said: 'And I would also say by skin colour. It's a scary time, I don't really want to move into politics because I'm always a bit nervous about talking about politics but when it shows itself in football like that…

'Football for me is great about human beings – we all get on together. In the dressing room, no one's thinking about what the colour of someone's skin is, they're just thinking about whether they can get a cross in or a through ball.

'We focus sometimes on a racist chant or something at a football game or the occasional problems we have. But in the actual dressing rooms themselves, the harmony, whether, you know, you can be a Christian, a Catholic, a Muslim, any kind of ethnicity, you can be black, you can be brown, you can be white.

'But it just all comes together and it's so harmonious. And, yet, politicians and people speaking out in that way, it just depresses me a little bit. I saw someone put a graphic up of all the players of various colours that have played and represented England over the years.'

He concluded: 'I mean, come on. I know it's done to divide and rule. That's the whole plan. But it's worth calling out occasionally. I really do think that.'

It follows Question Time host Fiona Bruce asking Mrs Braverman last Thursday for her views about what it meant to be English, after an audience member cited how cited how former prime minister Rishi Sunak recently spoke about the subject.

Germany manager Jurgen Klopp at a press conference in Herzogenaurach on September 30, when he was asked whether the football team are 'not German enough' or 'not white enough'

Mrs Braverman responded: 'Doesn't sound very controversial to me but suddenly it has become debatable. I was born in London, north London actually, in 1980.

'My parents came as immigrants themselves to this country with nothing. Very grateful to Britain for the hand of friendship that Britain extended to them.

'I've always considered myself British of Asian ethnicity and that's never been something that I would question. Of course I'm not English. I'm not an English person.

'I am of Asian origin and in my book, I track some of my ancestry. Some of my ancestors come from India via Mauritius and Kenya all over the world but they're not English. So it would be misrepresentative of me to co-opt Englishness as an ethnicity.'

The row comes three years after Lineker compared Mrs Braverman's language around the Conservative Government's immigration policy to that of Nazi Germany.

He had responded on social media to a Home Office video in which Mrs Braverman unveiled plans to stop migrants crossing the English Channel on small boats.

The former England striker tweeted in March 2023: 'There is no huge influx. We take far fewer refugees than other major European countries.

'This is just an immeasurably cruel policy directed at the most vulnerable people in language that is not dissimilar to that used by Germany in the '30s.'

The BBC temporarily took Lineker off air before other presenters also walked out in solidarity, causing major disruption to sports coverage before he was reinstated.

Meanwhile Kemi Badenoch today rejected the suggestion that only white people can be English.

Asked about Mrs Braverman's recent comments, the Conservative leader told ITV's Good Morning Britain: 'I don't understand why all of a sudden some people are policing other people's identity.

'I think identity is something very personal. If that's how she feels about herself, I think that's fine. But what I'm worried about is, you know, politicians running around telling some people that they are not English.'

She added: 'I think that we need we need to be very careful with this sort of conversation. What are my children hearing when they're listening to things like that?'

Mrs Badenoch said: 'My children, they are half white and half black. We are a multiracial country. I think we should be proud of that.

'I think politicians should be talking about how we bring people together. I am tired of identity politics, where people keep putting other people into boxes.

'I think it just creates more division. That's not what the Conservative Party is about. The Conservative Party is about uniting people.'

Sports.title: Formula One star snubs private jets to CYCLE remarkable 350km journey from Malaysia to Singapore for Grand Prix this weekend
Sports.content:
Formula One star snubs private jets to CYCLE remarkable 350km journey from Malaysia to Singapore for Grand Prix this weekend

Formula One star Valtteri Bottas has taken the unique decision to cycle to the Singapore Grand Prix this weekend.

The majority of drivers tend to travel to races on private jets, but Bottas, 37, has snubbed that option to take his own route across Asia.

The Finnish driver crashed out of Sunday's chaotic Bahrain Grand Prix, which was held in Malaysia due to security concerns in the Middle East, and he will have to make up 350km (217 miles) to get to Singapore.

Bottas began his odyssey shortly after the race finished in Malaysia, and he has been documenting it on social media.

The 37-year-old has shared several videos and snaps, including one which was captioned: 'Taking the path less travelled (and maybe a bit longer).'

In another post on X, Bottas posted a video of him cycling at night and added: 'Yea I'm riding to Singapore.

Yea I’m riding to Singapore 🚲



On the gravel roads less travelled with my new @canyon_bikes Grail CFR.



See you there 🇸🇬 pic.twitter.com/jFKZCM6Vnq — Valtteri Bottas (@ValtteriBottas) October 5, 2026

Valtteri Bottas has taken the unique decision to cycle to the Singapore Grand Prix this weekend

'On the gravel roads less travelled with my new @canyon_bikes Grail CFR. See you there.'

Bottas is travelling alongside his partner Tiffany Cromwell, who is a professional cyclist from Australia, and needs to make it there by Thursday to fulfil his media commitments.

The journey is off-road and on gravel, and on Monday, during the second day of Bottas' cycle, he covered 161.91km across nearly six hours.

It is an unusual way to travel to a race for an F1 driver, yet it is perhaps no surprise that Bottas is undertaking it given he has history of completing cycling-related endeavours, often with Cromwell.

This included him qualifying for the Gravel World Championships after coming fifth in an off-road qualifying event in the Czech Republic during the summer.

However, given that event comes this weekend, he will be unable to compete.

In the past, he has also taken part in gravel races, while he is known to be involved with FNLD GRVL, a yearly race in his native Finland.

Bottas has ten wins in his F1 career, but he has endured a difficult 2026 season with Cadillac after spending last year as Mercedes' reserve driver.

After 16 races, the 37-year-old is yet to score a point and he has failed to finish eight of those.

Sports.title: The 'mess' that Harlequins can't escape: Too many yes men, fears Marcus Smith could leave, pressure mounting on Jason Gilmore and Robbie Deans, recruitment errors and Quins legends' anguish at 'turning from a rugby club to a brand'
Sports.content:
The 'mess' that Harlequins can't escape: Too many yes men, fears Marcus Smith could leave, pressure mounting on Jason Gilmore and Robbie Deans, recruitment errors and Quins legends' anguish at 'turning from a rugby club to a brand'

The vacant look on George Furbank’s face after Gloucester scored their fifth try of eight on Saturday said absolutely everything about Harlequins’ horror start to the season. Perhaps he was debating whether he could tear up his new contract and run back to Franklin’s Gardens.

After winning two of the last three PREM Rugby titles with Northampton, Furbank’s summer move to London was supposed to herald a fresh start for his new team, who have gradually slid down the league since winning the league themselves in 2021.

It hasn’t happened. A home defeat by Bath and a 48-0 humiliation at Kingsholm have seen Harlequins’ poor form from last term – where they finished second bottom – continue.

That’s not what Furbank has been used to. You had to feel for him as Harlequins capitulated to what was their worst league defeat in 26 years and their third biggest of all time.

With nothing to show in terms of points from their opening two matches, Harlequins already look in real trouble, even if it is still early days. It is tough to see how they can turn the corner with a trip to a resurgent Sale to come in round three.

‘I didn’t expect last year to be as bad as it was, but I did expect it to get worse before it was going to improve,’ former Harlequins and England scrum-half Danny Care told Daily Mail Sport, before this season began. ‘They've got to be harder to beat. It can literally only get better.’

George Furbank (centre) was Harlequins' marquee signing this summer. He may already be wondering whether he made the right decision

Gloucester showed Harlequins exactly where they've gone wrong - they only finished a point above them last season but thumped them 48-0 on Saturday

Harlequins won six of 18 league games last season and the decision to hand head coach Jason Gilmore a contract extension raised plenty of questions.

There are issues everywhere you look at Harlequins. The club’s recruitment – led by Ed Spokes – has been questionable at best. Furbank is a fine player and he should still be England’s first-choice full-back when fit. But on a salary of more than £300,000-a-year, it is impossible to get away from the fact Harlequins' priority should have been investing in fresh grunt in the forward pack.

Gloucester, who finished just a point and a place above Quins last season, have evidently done a better job of recruitment - to the tune of a 48-0 thumping between the two teams last weekend.

With Quins slowly slipping down the PREM table ever since their 2021 title, finishing third, sixth, sixth, seventh and ninth since then, big questions are rightly being asked of Laurie Dalrymple, who has been chief executive since 2019.

One former Harlequins player, who asked not to be named, described Dalrymple as a ‘massive problem.’ He added: ‘There needs to be accountability for an underperforming rugby department. Harlequins have turned from a rugby club into a brand.’

The club’s problems were laid out in plain terms at Gloucester last weekend. Over the summer the Cherry and Whites added significant heft, bringing in Wales co-captains Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan and South Africa World Cup winner Jean Kleyn for a harder edge.

It has clearly worked, Gloucester badly exposing Harlequins’ shortcomings in that area. It added insult to injury for the capital club that two of Gloucester’s best players were former Harlequins Will Joseph and Will Trenholm.

Quins do hope to have their star No10 Marcus Smith and his fellow England international Fin Baxter back on the field in the coming weeks. Both have been on the sidelines so far with finger and foot injuries respectively and their team’s struggles must be analysed within the context of their absence. However, it is clear the problems at Harlequins run far deeper than just playing personnel.

Harlequins won six of 18 league games last season and the decision to hand head coach Jason Gilmore a contract extension raised plenty of questions

With Quins slowly slipping down the PREM table ever since their 2021 title, big questions are rightly being asked of chief executive Laurie Dalrymple

Daily Mail Sport understands there is concern among the club’s leading sponsors at the on-field struggles and that several leading ex-players now have nothing to do with their former employer, despite the expertise they could offer in a time of need.

‘No one has a relationship. It’s really bizarre,’ one said. ‘There’s a lot of Harlequins connections and rugby intellect there. I’m not saying that would fix everything on the field, but it would make the club a better-connected place. I really believe the club is in a mess.’

The facts facing Gilmore and his fellow Australian Robbie Deans, who is performance director, are that Harlequins have to improve and quickly. Another campaign of disappointment will surely not be tolerated by owners Duncan Saville and Charles Jillings. Saville joined the Harlequins board earlier this year to keep a closer eye on proceedings, and he can’t be happy at what he’s seen.

Sources have indicated there are too many ‘yes men’ at Harlequins. Decorated former Test guru Deans’ employment as performance director involves him spending ‘extended periods in the UK at critical points throughout the season’, though he also spends time abroad.

One gets the feeling that if he wasn’t already, Deans must be heading for the team’s Guildford training base as a matter of urgency given the way the first two games have gone. Things already look critical.

At Gloucester, Harlequins conceded a mammoth 21 penalties. It was one of a number of shameful statistics, after moments of promise against Bath. Last weekend, Gilmore’s men made just three entries into their opposition’s 22 and produced only four clean line breaks.

Perhaps most embarrassingly of all, given they are a team historically known for free-flowing attacking, and the number of tries being scored in PREM Rugby is as high as it’s ever been, Harlequins couldn’t even get on the board.

Care, who made a record 395 Harlequins appearances and now works for PREM broadcaster TNT Sports, said: ‘There have to be signs of improvement. There has to be a clearer playing style.

At Gloucester, Harlequins conceded a mammoth 21 penalties. It was one of a number of shameful statistics, after moments of promise against Bath

‘There have to be signs of improvement. There has to be a clearer playing style,' says Quins' record appearance-maker Danny Care

'They’ve got to get their best players on the pitch as much as they can because the turnover of injuries, with whatever was going on, isn’t good enough. I'd like them to give Marcus a platform to be able to show what he can do. Because if he gets that, then he can be the most dangerous player in the league.’

As a 10-team competition, the PREM is now played in short bursts around other competitions and international windows, meaning it can be difficult to re-establish momentum quickly, especially when you're rock bottom.

Another problem for them is that Newcastle, traditionally the league’s whipping boys, look much improved after another summer of investment from owners Red Bull.

‘I don’t know how they fix it or what they can hang their hat on,’ a source said. ‘Scoring zero points in a league where every team is finding it easy to score is not a good sign for a team whose USP is supposed to be their attacking game. There are better teams in the PREM than them at that now.’

Their base, in a well-heeled area just a stone’s throw from Twickenham, has meant Harlequins have always been able to charge high prices for tickets. While many are affordable, the top seats can cost more than £80.

For how much longer will loyal supporters be willing to spend such sums to watch a team that is badly underperforming?

The club’s decision to allow Ellie Kildunne to leave their women’s team was also unpopular with fans. England ace Kildunne is the most high-profile figure in the female game, but the World Cup winner has now joined Bristol Bears.

It has meant Harlequins have not only lost a hugely talented player, but one of rugby’s most marketable from either sex.

The club’s decision to allow Ellie Kildunne to leave their women’s team was also unpopular with fans - not only have Quins lost a hugely talented player, but one of rugby’s most marketable

As for Marcus Smith, Care fears he may look elsewhere soon if results don't improve

Smith, who has played more rugby for England at full-back than at No 10 in the past two years, is contracted at Harlequins until 2028. But his former half-back partner Care is concerned his club’s underperformance – alongside him being a bit-part player internationally – could cause him to look elsewhere.

Smith has previously been a target for big-spending French clubs and held talks with Paris-based Racing 92. ‘He's still got a couple of years, so I think that's great for the club,’ Care said of Smith.

‘But they're probably going to have to get better in the next couple of years to give him what he needs because I know how high his aspirations are. He wants to be winning games and winning trophies.’

Right now at Quins, that looks a long way off.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo 'will NOT return to Portugal while Jorge Jesus remains in charge' with superstar, 41, 'outraged' by new manager's stance after he walked out on national team
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo will reportedly refuse to return to the Portuguese national team while manager Jorge Jesus remains in charge.

Jesus extended an olive branch to Ronaldo on Sunday night when he insisted he would be welcome back in the next international break – despite his furious walkout midway through this round of fixtures.

Ronaldo was livid after being left on the bench for Portugal's win over Norway on September 27 – the first time he has been an unused substitute during his 18-year international career.

That led to him skipping three training sessions and abandoning the camp for Portugal's last two matches of the international break, fleeing to Spain via private jet.

But just when it looked as if the situation could be repaired, with the esteemed Jesus and multiple team-mates expressing their openness to Ronaldo's return, Portuguese journalist Rui Santos says the superstar will not come back while the manager remains in post.

'He reportedly vented that he will not return to the national team, at least while Jorge Jesus is in technical command,' Santos told CNN Portugal.

Cristiano Ronaldo has reportedly said he will not return to the Portuguese national team while Jorge Jesus is in charge

Jesus is a highly respected manager, having won 25 trophies, and he has won all four of his games with Portugal so far

'He is not satisfied in the slightest with the handling of this entire process. He was particularly outraged by the content of the statements made by Jorge Jesus, the head coach.

'He has stopped believing and stopped trusting in contradictions between the expressed desire to bring Cristiano Ronaldo back, so he can still participate in the Nations League, but at the same time saying and fully emphasizing that "there are no apologies from anyone, I am not here to ask for apologies, I am the one who makes the squad selection" - and therefore an exercise of authority.

'The narrative was one of inclusion, of including Cristiano Ronaldo, not of exclusion [but it hasn't worked].'

Manager Jesus's public comments have only ever been peaceful, but after the initial affront of being left to stew on the bench, Ronaldo has seen everything through a haze of red mist.

He did not even watch the most recent match of their Nations League campaign against Norway on Sunday because he was on his private jet with his family.

His stance puts Portugal in an awkward position. No doubt they want to appease their most legendary player, but equally, with the superstar aged 41, the view that he is a liability is becoming increasingly popular.

Jesus is a highly respected manager who has a better career win rate than Sir Alex Ferguson and has won 25 trophies. His start with Portugal has been perfect - four wins from four - after he was appointed on a four-year contract in July.

He was vindicated in leaving Ronaldo out of the first encounter against Norway as Portugal won 2-1. They then went and backed that up with further victories over Denmark and Norway again after Ronaldo had stormed off.

After leaving camp, Ronaldo said: 'I will tell the truth to all Portuguese people about the reasons that motivated my departure'

Bruno Fernandes (right) has held clear-the-air talks with Ronaldo after the latter stormed out of the Portugal camp

Portugal boss Jesus insists he will have Ronaldo back if the forward wants to return

Ronaldo risks a six-month ban from Portugal duty for his conduct after he pledged to tell 'the truth' about the scandal one day – but Jesus insisted he is welcome back for the next international break in November.

The gaffer initially insisted in a press conference there was 'no incident whatsoever' and 'nothing to make a fuss about', even understanding Ronaldo's frustrations at not being substituted on.

He then added after the most recent Norway clash: 'As far as I'm concerned, everything is open. It's up to Cris to decide his own life. In the next call-up, if Cris is playing and wants to be in the national team, why not?

'Resentment? Nothing, it was a misunderstanding. In my opinion, it's easy to resolve. When will I resolve it? I don't know. The game is over, and only afterwards will we know how things will turn out.

'It's not up to me. To reach an agreement with two people, both people need to talk and agree. That's not up to me.

'Just because it was him, and perhaps rightly so because he's a symbol, this whole problem of him coming on, warming up, not coming on. How many players warmed up today and didn't come on? Will there be a problem? No.

'With Cris it's different, he's a symbol. But is it a problem? For me it wasn't a problem. If Cris wants to and is playing for Al-Nassr, he'll be in the next squad. We talked before this squad and we can talk before the next one. It's Cris who will decide.'

Ronaldo's fiery withdrawal – months after a World Cup in which it was perceived that he held back Portugal – has been one of the dominant stories of the international break.

Georgina Rodriguez leapt the the defence of Ronaldo after his controversial walkout

Rodriguez and Ronaldo married in the summer after more than a decade together

He confirmed in a statement on Instagram that he had left the team's camp because of comments made by manager Jesus in a press conference.

Ronaldo said: 'After the national team coach's press conference, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp.

'In due time, I will tell all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to my departure from the national team, to which I have always dedicated myself.

'Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates.'

Sports.title: VOICE OF THE PADDOCK: Formula One's DNA is being stripped away by the woke brigade - abandon the charade and rip up these joke electric engines now, writes JONATHAN McEVOY
Sports.content:
VOICE OF THE PADDOCK: Formula One's DNA is being stripped away by the woke brigade - abandon the charade and rip up these joke electric engines now, writes JONATHAN McEVOY

Formula One is in its biggest bind of the modern era. The engines they have are a joke, as well as woke, half-electric to save the planet, if you will, in a series that flies all around the world with a carbon footprint bigger than Jupiter.

As Max Verstappen said, rightly, racing is reduced to Mario Kart, the computer game from Nintendo. The four-time world champion gave his verdict at the start of the season, realising that the DNA of the sport is being stripped away by the random deployment of power as the battery part of the engine charge comes and goes.

These engines provide overtaking moves, many of them, but none of significant merit. A charade. ‘I’ll pass you, and you’ll pass me when your power goes up.’ It is ostensibly good to watch but is not what Formula One should be about.

This was not a self-serving comment from Verstappen because he was not driving a Red Bull that is contesting the title. He was genuinely aggrieved by the erosion of the sport he loves down to his bones. He knew it was hocus-pocus.

It came to roost this past weekend in Malaysia, staging the Bahrain Grand Prix away from home owing to the conflict in the Middle East, when the race was delayed and delayed again for over an hour and a half because the engines could not run in the wet due to software issues.

Think about that. Software issues! What does that mean?

As the winner of the Bahrain Grand Prix Max Verstappen said about the new F1 engines, rightly, racing is reduced to Mario Kart, namely the computer game on Nintendo

The race was delayed and delayed again for over an hour and a half because the engines could not run in the wet due to software issues

These engines are unpredictable and need to be jettisoned way earlier than 2030, when V8s are due to be back. This reality confronts the FIA and the sport’s owners right now.

The fact is that, despite all the years of development of the combustion engine, which has had a role in revolutionising the world, the globe’s most advanced sport was restricted to stupefying non-movement in Malaysia. This at a point, incidentally, when engine manufacturers are pulling out of the electronic urge, Audi among them, officially abandoning their move to all-electric road cars. There is not a big enough market for it.

Hamilton, whose Ferrari stopped because of the software malfunction, said it was like a Lego race, a stunt concocted ahead of the British Grand Prix in July.

Mercedes’ George Russell said: ‘It didn’t feel very F1. I would have been disappointed if I was in the stands and watching that unfold.’

And Carlos Sainz – like Russell, a director of the Grand Prix Drivers’ Association – went further. The Spaniard contended: ‘F1 needs to have a hard look at themselves and see how we ended up in this situation.

‘It is clear the regulations are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the power units and for the manufacturers. Who decided five years ago that this was the direction to go?

‘We are doing the best with what we are given as a sport and as regulations. The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can, but clearly what was decided four or five years ago was wrong. We need to learn as a sport not to make those mistakes again.’

The FIA are conducting a full review. What is clear is that they need to rip up these engines now. It will take a year or so, perhaps. But they need to bang heads together and do it for 2028. Otherwise, it is a case of sticking plasters over the sore.

George Russell climbs out of his car after engine failure brings his race to a premature end

VOWLES RUES 'COST-CAP TRAP'

I was mixed about comments James Vowles, the Williams boss, made over the cost cap of fractionally over £160million this year.

His argument went: ‘What I didn’t realise when I moved from Mercedes to Williams is just how little facilities there are. When you make a cost cap, I’m not spending money on the car. I’m spending tens of millions on basic systems so you know where a part is in the factory. It’s not going on an upgrade. We’re caught in a cost-cap trap.’

By which he means the bigger and traditionally better financed teams already have an infrastructure to get the job done. They already have the essentials in place.

The cost cap was meant to level the playing field rather than, say, Ferrari spending gazillions of Marlboro money on this and that when the strugglers couldn’t. The cap has worked up to a point, and, to be honest, Williams would not be as financially secure as they are without it.

In fact, Dorilton Capital, a US-based private investment firm, would never have bought the team in 2020 without the cost cap due to be introduced and the security it promised to provide. Nor would Vowles, therefore, have landed the job he is doing.

Dorilton took over from the Williams family for some £150m in 2020 and the team is worth literally 10 times as much today. So, for them, it was not all bad, was it?

Perhaps a compromise – in a season that is poor for Williams under new regulations that offered them the chance of revival – is that they and other teams should be granted freedom to develop in certain areas outside the cap that, as Vowles protested, sets them in aspic.

Williams boss James Vowles (right) with Carlos Sainz in Kuala Lumpur. Vowles says his team are struggling to keep up with the leading team

McLAREN'S SECRET POTION REVEALED

On to a very serious topic. And without wishing to give away state secrets, I have been served the vital ingredient of McLaren’s recent success, and it has nothing to do with engineering prowess.

A colleague, Philip Duncan of the Press Association, felt a bit croaky-voiced and a kind hospitality lady brought out their magic potion, which we should have downed in one. They routinely serve it up in the garage to their boys as a lifter.

It is a ginger-based concoction with celery and apple added. It’s pungent. Though I am a jetlag-denier, I thirstily got it down my throat fast in the name of rehabilitation.

LEWIS MAY HAVE SAVED VASSEUR'S JOB

Lewis Hamilton drove brilliantly well to come from more than a minute down to finish third in Malaysia. It probably saved his boss Fred Vasseur’s job, at least for now.

It was a terrible strategy call to put Hamilton on slick tyres on a drying but wet circuit. At moments he was nine seconds off the pace – 2min 1sec a lap compared to Kimi Antonelli’s 1min 52sec. Hamilton drove superbly well to clamber up the field, albeit helped by conditions improving.

Vasseur is under pressure and last week Ferrari gave him the 'dreaded’ vote of confidence. What if Hamilton had not performed his escape act? The implications for Vasseur?

Lewis Hamilton's superb drive in Malaysia in his Ferrari has taken the heat off his boss Fred Vasseur

THE MASSES DESCEND ON SEPANG

Driving into the Sepang circuit has never been easy and some of those who had not been here before complained about disorganisation.

I don’t buy that. It’s simply a busy place of more than two million people and everyone seems to drive. Queues happen. And, in the early years of the Malaysian Grand Prix, masses of people abandoned their cars at the roadside and walked to the track.

To an extent they did so again on Sunday, so you had the dangerous spectacle of fans ambling along the side of four-lane highways back to their parked-up vehicles. It was like strolling on the hard shoulder of the M25.

There were also lawless motorbikes assailing you from every angle. Thankfully, my driver had eyes in the back of his head and we managed to get in and out for four days – sometimes two-hour journeys each way from Kuala Lumpur – without incurring a manslaughter charge.

Sports.title: The man staking his reputation - and £100m - on taking down Man City: Richard Masters has faced down mutiny, a pandemic and the Premier League owners club. Now insiders reveal how he'll fight the biggest scandal in British sport
Sports.content:
The man staking his reputation - and £100m - on taking down Man City: Richard Masters has faced down mutiny, a pandemic and the Premier League owners club. Now insiders reveal how he'll fight the biggest scandal in British sport

A couple of days after Manchester City were found guilty of cheating, the former chairman of a Premier League club attempted to describe the challenge of imposing law and order on British football.

He had a little think and then offered this soundbite to Daily Mail Sport: 'It can be a bit like managing a creche.'

That view was then relayed to an executive at one of the current 20 clubs comprising our top-flight. He made a slight update to the assessment: 'It's more like a difficult high school now - the kids have grown up and in some cases become delinquent.'

They were both joking around a serious point, but played to the common sentiment that few jobs in sport exist with the same complications as those faced by Richard Masters.

Since his appointment as CEO of the Premier League in December 2019, Masters has been confronted with a global pandemic, the Project Big Picture manoeuvrings from Manchester United and Liverpool, the mutinous intentions behind a Super League, an acceleration in foreign and state ownership and, of course, the era-defining trial of Manchester City.

To cite one of Masters' former colleagues and a close friend: 'Taking those areas as a whole, it's a f****** tough hand to be dealt.'

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters' reign will be defined by the eventual outcome to their legal case against Manchester City

Masters would strongly reject any notion of a crusade against Man City, highlighting that guilt was reached by an independent commission and that his job is to administer rules set by clubs

Daily Mail Sport has consulted a dozen sources who know Masters and have worked around him to better understand the highest-ranking individual on the side of the establishment.

Most are quick to agree on three details. One: Masters is nothing like his long-time predecessor, the charismatic Richard Scudamore, an arch-politician who found it easier to charm or coerce the room during a reign of constant financial growth. Two: The landscapes in which they worked have changed dramatically. Three: Masters would strongly reject any notion of a crusade against Manchester City, highlighting that guilt was reached by an independent commission and that his job, in the most reductionist terms, is to administer rules the clubs themselves had voted to play by.

But, on the latter, there is an observation worth making – the appetite to commit an estimated £100million in legal resources to the City battle has challenged the perennial accusation of judicial bias in favour of the big clubs. British football has never known a confrontation of such stakes.

Irrespective of whether Masters finds the personalisation of this fight inaccurate, his reign will be defined by its eventual outcome, as will a somewhat bigger issue – the integrity of the past two decades of the Premier League.

It is a far cry from Masters' arrival in the role, which occurred in highly unusual circumstances, because he was only fourth choice to replace Scudamore. A shambolic recruitment process that stretched 18 months had seen Susanna Dinnage named as successor, but she declined after her appointment had been announced and the current BBC director general Tim Davie also turned it down. Completing a chaotic hat-trick, David Pemsel was given the job but resigned before starting because of allegations about his private life. All of which opened a sliding door to Masters.

As a sales and marketing man, with long stints at the England and Wales Cricket Board, the EFL and the Premier League, his perception as an accidental candidate didn't help in the hornet's nest of football politics.

'Richard wouldn't have been human if there wasn't a little bit of imposter syndrome in the initial months in the job,' said one former colleague well acquainted with the machinations of a Premier League stakeholder meeting. Another source adds that there were individuals in those meetings, typically attended by two representatives per club and a further dozen Premier League staff, who felt Scudamore's replacement wasn't up to it.

Much of that derives from comparisons between very different men. One Premier League executive describes Scudamore as routinely making phone calls beyond midnight to corral the 20 clubs on big issues across his 20-year reign. 'A chief whip in another life', said the source.

Masters is viewed as being nothing like his predecessor Richard Scudamore, an arch-politician who found it easier to charm or coerce the room during a reign of constant financial growth

Masters is more corporate in style and less charismatic in nature, but his approach has slowly been viewed as a strength as football landscape has required a different kind of diplomacy

The depiction is of a CEO in Scudamore who never knowingly entered a vote without being reasonably sure of the outcome. 'Didactic' and 'controlling' were words used with some affection by a former staffer, with Scudamore's sharpest achievement rated as his ability to 'keep the peace' between 20 separate entities with conflicting agendas. By consensus, that was a more impressive feat than overseeing the consistent rise in television revenues.

Masters, an Aston Villa fan who turned 60 in June, is more corporate in style, more process-driven, far less charismatic in nature. For a time, that was interpreted as worse. But within Premier League circles it has slowly been viewed as a strength after a seven-year period in which the football landscape has required a different kind of diplomacy.

'There are still one or two in the room that are not convinced by him,' said a prominent source at a Premier League club.

There is no denying that Masters has had questionable moments – his reference to Everton and Nottingham Forest as 'small clubs' during their Profitability and Sustainability Rules skirmishes in 2024 was easy fodder for some of those who have detected two-tier justice in how the Premier League apply its rules.

A bigger matter was the takeover of Newcastle United by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. The Premier League claimed they have 'legally binding assurances' that the Saudi state would not control Newcastle, which has long struggled with the smell test for one fact above others – the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman is also the chair of the Public Investment Fund.

Some will see such decisions as flawed and acts of willing delusion; another would say that football's world has changed beyond recognition and there are not enough tiny violins to play notes of sympathy for those trying to control it. Masters' record within it is not without blemishes, especially in the balancing between financial regulation and the stifling of ambition. But there is an acknowledgement that he has overseen a uniquely challenging time, starting with Covid just months after taking office and extending to the City debacle.

'There was a perception that the Masters regime was worse than the Scudamore regime but that has softened quite a bit,' said an executive at a Premier League club.

'Scudamore had great abilities to do certain things. He was a master politician and a superb negotiator. He was a brilliant anticipator of problems and would get ahead of them. If Richard Masters could do anything better, it might be for him and Alison (Brittain, the Premier League chair) to get ahead of the problems quicker. They aren't as skilled politically, don't have the same nous, but he is very strong at working through a problem.

The takeover of Newcastle United by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund has been among the key challenges faced by Masters during his time as Premier League chief executive

'The stuff Masters has had to contend with is more extreme than his predecessors. He has done a very decent job of it in very, very choppy water. Covid was a huge thing to deal with – almost overnight, the revenue streams were being stopped and he was the man on a Zoom call having to answer 40 faces on a screen about when football could resume.'

A different source cites the threat of a Super League as the biggest crisis and City merely the messiest. 'It helps that he is a very calm guy,' said a club source. 'Whatever people think of how the Premier League works under him, he is a decent man with decent values and he is mostly applying the rules we as clubs have voted for.

'I have never seen him lose his temper in the meetings and there have been times when the criticism has been personal.

'He can be blamed for anything and everything. If there is a bad refereeing decision, he will get a call. If the economy in Singapore affects revenue, he will get blame. But again, he is very calm in the way he works through the role, very good at compartmentalising an issue, and I think he has done a solid job on balance.'

In a room of Premier League clubs, 'solid' and 'decent' can pass for a compliment.

Those meetings, of which there are around five per year, can be feisty. Some can spend hours arguing about the seemingly trivial. According to a source, one recent debate saw multiple changes to the draft of a rule about which side of the dugouts should be used for substitutes warming up mid-match.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the meetings around the Covid protocols or the Super League breakaway are understood to have been the most heated. Discussions around Manchester City have not reached those levels. Presumably, too much popcorn was being consumed in the creche to kick up a fuss.

Sports.title: Grinning Cristiano Ronaldo returns to Al-Nassr training after walking out of Portugal camp - as Piers Morgan brands boss the 'Ten Hag of international football' by trying to 'belittle' star
Sports.content:
Grinning Cristiano Ronaldo returns to Al-Nassr training after walking out of Portugal camp - as Piers Morgan brands boss the 'Ten Hag of international football' by trying to 'belittle' star

A smiling Cristiano Ronaldo has returned to Al-Nassr training after stunningly walking out on the Portugal squad during the international break following a rift with head coach Jorge Jesus.

Al-Nassr warmly welcomed back the star, whose walkout dominated headlines around the Portugal camp during the international break.

'The GOAT in the heart of Najd, at Al Nassr', the Saudi Arabian club shared on social media, as Ronaldo arrived at the club's training centre.

While Ronaldo's focus has turned back to his club, his international future remains unclear after his clash with Jesus.

The star, 41, left Portugal's camp after Jesus's press conference last Wednesday, as the head coach appeared to confirm the forward would not start against Denmark in the Nations League.

It came after Ronaldo had been left on the bench for the entirety of the 2-1 win over Norway last weekend.

Cristiano Ronaldo returned to training with Al-Nassr after walking out of the Portugal squad during the international break

Ronaldo left the camp following a dispute with Portugal's head coach Jorge Jesus

Broadcaster Piers Morgan has claimed the dispute between Ronaldo and Jesus centres around broken promises by the Portugal boss, who he branded as the '[Erik] Ten Hag of international football'.

Ronaldo had previously spoken to Morgan in an explosive interview back in 2022, which effectively ended his Man United career, as he stated he did not respect then Red Devils boss Ten Hag.

Morgan, speaking on Sports Uncensored, has claimed Jesus tried to 'belittle and embarrass Ronaldo' and went back on his word over the star's playing time.

'What this goes down to is nothing about money or fame or any of these things,' Morgan said.

'He was given absolute guarantees about how he would be used, it was one of the reasons he decided to continue his international career.

'The new guy Jorge Jesus, who knows him from Saudi Arabia, said to him with the Nations League, they agreed he would play the first two games and would be rested for the next two.

'The first game he was told “you get 90 minutes” and he gets yanked after 67 minutes so he’s a bit p***ed off and afterwards the coach apologised to him and that he would go out and explain this shouldn’t have happened.

'He goes out and does the opposite, he pulls a Ten Hag, where he goes out and tries to belittle and embarrass Ronaldo and put him back in his box and say “all the players are as important to me”, which also p***es off Ronaldo.

Piers Morgan has claimed Jesus broke promises made to Ronaldo, leading to the star walking out of the camp

Morgan compared Jesus to former Man United boss Erik ten Hag, stating he had tried to 'belittle and humilate' Ronaldo

'Then he goes to Ronaldo and says “I know we said you would be rested for the second two games, but I want you for 30 minutes against Norway”.

'He went “okay, if that is what you want, I’ll do it”. He sits there and gets warmed up for 25 minutes and never gets on the pitch. So again he is p***ed off at the lack of respect.

'For him it is a question of respect, being promised one thing then the opposite happening, being warmed up and not used. Eventually he went f*** you and got on a plane and left.

'Does it sit well with you guys that Ronaldo might not get a farewell game for Portugal because a coach has decided he wants to be the big dog and humiliate him.'

Jesus has insisted Ronaldo could return in the next international break in November, saying: 'As far as I'm concerned, everything is open.

'It's up to Cris to decide his own life. In the next call-up, if Cris is playing and wants to be in the national team, why not?

'Resentment? Nothing, it was a misunderstanding. In my opinion, it's easy to resolve. When will I resolve it? I don't know. The game is over, and only afterwards will we know how things will turn out.

'It's not up to me. To reach an agreement with two people, both people need to talk and agree. That's not up to me.

Ronaldo's Portugal manager and team-mates insist he is welcome back should he choose

Jesus has insisted the situation is a 'misunderstanding' and is easy to resolve

'Just because it was him, and perhaps rightly so because he's a symbol, this whole problem of him coming on, warming up, not coming on. How many players warmed up today and didn't come on? Will there be a problem? No.

'With Cris it's different, he's a symbol. But is it a problem? For me it wasn't a problem. If Cris wants to and is playing for Al-Nassr, he'll be in the next squad. We talked before this squad and we can talk before the next one. It's Cris who will decide.'

The feud started when Ronaldo was left on the bench for Portugal's win over Norway – the first time in 18 years he had missed the full 90 minutes for the national side barring injuries and suspensions.

Ronaldo said: 'After the national team coach's press conference, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I have decided to leave the national team training camp.

'In due time, I will tell all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to my departure from the national team, to which I have always dedicated myself.

'Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates.'

The tension seems to have boiled over following Jesus' press conference. The manager said: 'There was no incident whatsoever.

'Any player - and I was a player myself - when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don't get on, no-one is happy about that.

After leaving camp, Ronaldo said: 'I will tell the truth to all Portuguese people about the reasons that motivated my departure'

A sign has been placed outside the Estadio da Luz in Lisbon, backing Ronaldo over Jesus

'Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It's nothing to make a fuss about.

'It's not difficult for me to focus,' he added. 'You know what's difficult for me? It's not understanding what's going on inside. It's not knowing how to train my players. That's what's difficult for me. The rest... zero.

'What's important is what we have to do. The things that happen don't separate the group, they haven't separated us and they won't separate us.'

Despite Ronaldo's walkout and controversy over his departure from the camp, Jesus's side won all four of the Nations League matches during the international break.

Ronaldo's former Man United team-mate Rio Ferdinand has insisted Jesus needs to apologise to the star and claims the Portuguese Football Association have been 'panicking' after the rift.

‘The coach needs to come out and apologise,' Ferdinand said on Rio Presents.

‘Trust me, I think he has to come out and say “listen I have judged this situation wrong”.

‘I am telling you, something has gone on, I am sure something has happened when you look between the lines.

Rio Ferdinand has claimed Jesus should 'come out and apologise' to Ronaldo

‘The president has come out and they’ve done the “Cristiano is the best, he’s the greatest, he’s this and that and the other".

‘They are trying to settle the situation, they are panicking behind the scenes now.

'This situation doesn’t play out the way it has if there are good communication skills.

'I think there has been terrible communication skills.

'I said this during the World Cup with Roberto Martinez and I think the same with this manager now, you have to sit with Cristiano Ronaldo and tell him this is what I want to do. And if you don’t want to be a part of it, then just tell me, but this is how I want it to work.

'That conversation I don’t believe has been had, because I don’t think you would be here with Cristiano going mid camp walking out like that.'

The international break had remarkably begun with Jesus and Ronaldo sat side-by-side at a press conference, where the former had labelled the star as a 'symbol of Portugal'.

Ronaldo had revealed he had considered retiring from international football in the summer before deciding to continue, but would walk away if the national team told him he was no longer required.

'Whenever they say they don't want me in the national team, I will be the first one to go,' Ronaldo said.

'When I think I am not adding anything to the team, or that I create an atmosphere, I will be the first to go. I will take my suitcase and leave.

'The Portuguese count on me, that's why I'm still here, just look at the numbers, I'm sure you can make some calculations, I'm still doing well.

'The day they don't count on me, no problem, I will leave. I will always be the No 1 fan of this federation.'

Sports.title: 'Mischievous' Chris Sutton pokes fun at Match of the Day's 'dating' co-hosts Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates live on-air - as it's revealed BBC colleagues 'didn't KNOW' about romance
Sports.content:
'Mischievous' Chris Sutton pokes fun at Match of the Day's 'dating' co-hosts Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates live on-air - as it's revealed BBC colleagues 'didn't KNOW' about romance

BBC pundit Chris Sutton joked suggestively about his colleagues Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates on live radio, amid reports that the Match of the Day co-hosts are dating.

Cates, 51, and Chapman, 52, have been stars of the BBC show's three-person presenter panel alongside Gabby Logan since the start of last season following Gary Lineker's departure.

The pair have become public figures on our TV screens over recent years – but have grown close in private, with reports emerging on Sunday that the BBC stars have been dating.

A new report has claimed BBC colleagues were unaware of the romance.

Chapman also serves as the regular host of BBC Radio 5Live's Monday Night Club, which typically wraps up the weekend's football.

He was absent for the show on Monday night and Cates – an occasional stand-in host – also did not feature.

Match of the Day co-hosts Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates are reportedly dating each other

Cates and Chapman have been on the three-person presenter panel since Gary Lineker's exit

Chris Sutton questioned the absence of host Chapman on the Monday Night Club live on radio amid the reports. Pictured: Sutton and Chapman on the show in 2025

Chapman's absence prompted regular guest Sutton to poke fun at the expense of the duo at the start of the show, after being introduced by stand-in presenter Alistair Bruce-Ball.

'Chris Sutton has got a rather mischievous look on his face this evening, which worries me slightly,' Bruce-Ball said.

Sutton responded: 'I just wondered where our leader is this evening, where's Mark?' with Bruce-Ball replying: 'Mark Chapman… Not here this evening.'

'So then normally second in charge is Kelly Cates... where's Kelly Cates this evening?' Sutton questioned.

Bruce-Ball replied: 'I don't know Chris, otherwise engaged I think. If they are not listening to the show, whatever they are up to, it is available to listen by the podcast, if that is what they want to do.'

Cates was instead hosting the Legends of Football awards, which saw Thierry Henry and Karen Carney honoured on the night.

A source told the Sun that BBC Sport staff had been unaware that the presenters were dating.

‘The chatter in the BBC Sport department since their relationship was revealed has been off the charts,' the source said.

‘No one appears to have known they were dating.

Cates was hosting the Legends of Football awards, which honoured Thierry Henry and Karen Carney

‘When the news came out, people were talking about it and were flabbergasted as no one knew it was going on.

‘Chappers and Kelly have clearly been very professional and have been very discreet about their relationship.

‘Their romance has been the best-kept secret in sport.’

Chapman split with estate agent Clere Collier earlier this year, who accused him of starting the relationship with Cates while they were still together, an allegation he denies.

Chapman and Cates became the main co-presenters for Match of the Day alongside Gabby Logan last season after Gary Lineker left.

While their shifts presenting the show do not overlap, Chapman and Cates did appear on Celebrity Gogglebox on the same sofa together in July.

Chapman, a highly respected broadcaster paid between £335,000 and £340,000 a year by the BBC, was already heavily involved with the show as Match of the Day 2 presenter before his promotion.

He was married to his wife Sara, the mother of their three children, for 19 years until she died aged 44 in 2020 after a battle with cancer.

Clere Collier accused Chapman of starting the relationship with Cates while they were together, which he denies

It was revealed in 2024 that he had started dating again after entering a relationship with estate agent and socialite Collier.

They appeared to be in a good place, with Collier, who is based in Dubai, regularly making trips over to the UK to visit Chapman – and they were even pictured walking hand-in-hand through the streets of Altrincham together.

She shared several gushing social media tributes towards Chapman, including one that labelled him as her 'one love' and 'devilishly handsome' after he turned 51, before they split in April this year.

Meanwhile, Cates, daughter of Liverpool icon Sir Kenny Dalglish, was married to TV producer Tom Cates from 2007 until their divorce in 2021.

The pair have two children together and lived in Chiswick in south-west London.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May.
