Amid the destruction of Gaza’s schools and universities, Niveen Al-Gharabli has built a makeshift book stall from books salvaged from rubble and damaged homes. She restores and sells them at low price, or gives them away to students and those who cannot afford them.

World.title: How hunger is devastating Yemen’s children
World.content:
Al Jazeera travels to Yemen’s displacement camps to measure the toll of malnutrition on the country’s children.

“My daughter is dying. Save her,” Tahani’s father pleaded, after years of knocking on the doors of officials and aid organisations in the hope they would be able to save his eight-year-old daughter.

More than 2.2 million children under five in Yemen are acutely malnourished, over half a million of them severely, the United Nations says.

The war, which began about 12 years ago, has left more than 22 million people in need of humanitarian assistance and 18.3 million facing acute food shortages. Yet the country has received only a fifth of the $2.2bn it needs to help them this year.

Tahani’s case led Al Jazeera Arabic to investigate the stories of other children enduring the same suffering, and to ask: where do the billions in aid sent to Yemen go, and why does it not prevent children from reaching dire levels of hunger and malnutrition?

Al Jazeera visualises where malnutrition is severe in Yemen, how aid funding is distributed, and why experts say aid is treating the symptoms rather than the causes.

Severe malnutrition rising among children

The search for answers took Al Jazeera to displacement camps, nutrition centres and hospitals.

The family of Jiyad Mohammed Jalal, who has not turned two yet, resides in the al-Khadeesh camp in Abs district of Hajjah governorate. The war forced them out of Haradh district. Jiyad is severely malnourished. His weight has fallen to dangerous levels and he needs continuous treatment, so the hospital has become part of the family’s routine.

Children like Jiyad reach nutrition centres only after displacement and poverty have taken their toll. He is not an isolated case. According to ground reports obtained by Al Jazeera, more than 200 malnutrition cases have been documented in Abs over the past three years. In Dhale governorate, Al-Nasr Hospital received 269 acutely malnourished children between January and August 2026.

Almost a quarter of Yemen’s acutely malnourished children, 516,157, have the severe form of the condition.



Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population stated that between January and July 2026 there was an increase in cases of “severe” malnutrition among children under five compared with the same period in 2025.

According to the Health Ministry and data analysed by Al Jazeera Arabic, Taiz had 11,982 cases of severe malnutrition in children, followed by Aden (7,339) and Dhale (6,710).

These local figures do not, on their own, provide a national measure of the prevalence of malnutrition, but they reveal something else that is more important in fieldwork: that cases do not appear in a single centre, and that pressure on nutrition services is distributed across different parts of the country.

Taiz had 24,529 cases of moderate malnutrition, followed by Abyan (15,366) and Lahj (11,893).

Treating the symptoms, but returning to the same conditions

At clinics, treatment depends on severity. Children with severe malnutrition need a full medical assessment and those with complications may need to be admitted to hospital.

Stable cases can be treated and followed up as outpatients under the approved medical protocol.

Moderate cases are monitored at the clinic, where they receive therapeutic foods or nutritional supplements and have their weight and growth checked regularly.

In al-Sumayya camp in Marib, Dr Muajiba al-Mansouri runs a government nutrition clinic. Over the past year, she told Al Jazeera, it treated 33 children with severe acute malnutrition, 85 with moderate acute malnutrition and 84 mothers.

Lack of food or poor diet, illness, social conditions and feeding problems are all made worse by war, poverty and displacement, she said. The World Food Programme (WFP) supports treatment of moderate cases, while supplies for severe cases come through UNICEF and the governorate health office.

When al-Mansouri spoke to Al Jazeera, her clinic had recorded no deaths from malnutrition, thanks to timely treatment. In her clinic, four severely malnourished children regained their appetite and weight after their mothers learned therapeutic feeding. But a child saved in the clinic often returns to the same conditions that caused the problem.

Mothers are also facing the same risks. Some 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are estimated to suffer from malnutrition.

A mother feeding a child also needs food and care herself, but she lives in the same economic and health conditions as her family.

Expanding need and shrinking response

According to UN agencies, some 14.4 million people need water, sanitation and hygiene services, and only about 59.3 percent of health facilities are fully operational.



Funding has never matched declared need. According to Humanitarian Response Plan data, in 2022, $2.27bn of the required $4.27bn was funded. In 2024, the figure was about $1.51bn of the $2.71bn required. The 2026 plan seeks about $2.16bn but is only 20.6 percent funded. These figures cover all sectors, not just malnutrition.

The lack of full funding comes as Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, recorded a sharp rise in cases at the facilities it supports during the first half of 2026.

UNICEF said the shortfall in funding has forced programmes to prioritise life-saving treatment over prevention and has limited access to children in the areas most in need.

The Health Ministry said severe cases among children below five rose during January-July 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. The ministry said falling WFP funding roughly halved the programme’s reach, from 122 districts to 62, so a drop in some registered cases does not mean the situation is improving. It added that government support through the budget, therapeutic food and health workers is lacking.

Billions for the response yet malnutrition persists

As the investigation expanded, Al Jazeera contacted organisations about Tahani’s case. When they called her father back, they learned she had died. According to him, she died of hunger.

While Tahani was struggling, millions were being allocated to humanitarian projects. According to documents obtained by the investigation, a Norwegian Refugee Council project in Hajjah had a budget of about $1.1m and allocated roughly $353,000 to activities tied to its objectives. One beneficiary said he received cash assistance only once. A WFP project with Relief International, worth about $4.86m, included more than $2m for salaries and allowances and about $1.84m for storage.

Mousa Alaya, a specialist in humanitarian aid and war economies, argues that the question is not only how much money entered Yemen but what it changed. Aid, he says, operates within a network of interests and actors. It can save lives, but it cannot restore salaries, jobs or public services, or end the war economy.

World.title: Sahibzada Farhan named Pakistan’s T20 captain as Naseem Shah returns
World.content:
Salman Agha axed before T20 home series against Sri Lanka, but Shaheen Shah Afridi is retained as ODI captain.

Sahibzada Farhan has replaced Salman Ali Agha as Pakistan’s Twenty20 cricket captain, ushering in changes to the leadership and squad for the upcoming three-match home series against Sri Lanka.

Farhan led Pakistan to a silver-medal finish at the Asian Games, losing to India in the final on Sunday.

Batter Hasan Nawaz and fast bowler Naseem Shah were recalled to the T20 squad.

Nawaz had been out of favour since November, but in the Asian Games final he hit 96 and was out off the final ball as Pakistan lost by 19 runs.

Shah last played in the shortest format at the T20 World Cup in February. He was also added to the one-day international squad for the following tri-series with Sri Lanka and England.

Rising star Razaullah was rewarded for his impressive performance on his Test debut against England last month in Birmingham and was included in the T20 and ODI squads. He is yet to make his white-ball debut.

Fast bowler Shaheen Afridi was retained as ODI captain of a team that included Agha and Babar Azam.

But the selectors ignored Mohammad Rizwan because the wicketkeeper was under investigation by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Authority. Rizwan was one of the seven players who were summoned home after Pakistan lost the second Test to England at Lord’s in August.

Khawaja Nafay was the specialist wicketkeeper for the T20s while Ghazi Ghori, who made his Test debut in England, was the first-choice gloveman for the ODIs.

Rawalpindi will host the three Sri Lanka T20s from October 9-13. The tri-series begins on October 18.



Tait back as bowling coach

Former Australian fast bowler Shaun Tait was named as Pakistan’s bowling coach after his recent stint with the Bangladesh team. Under Tait, Bangladesh beat Pakistan 2-0 in the Test series this year.

Tait replaced Ashley Noffke, who has been contracted by the Netherlands.

Pakistan T20 squad: Sahibzada Farhan (captain), Abdul Samad, Abrar Ahmed, Arafat Minhas, Fakhar Zaman, Hasan Nawaz, Muhammad Imran Randhawa, Khawaja Nafay, Maaz Sadaqat, Naseem Shah, Razaullah, Saim Ayub, Mohammad Salman Mirza, Shadab Khan, Sufiyan Moqim.

Pakistan ODI squad: Shaheen Shah Afridi (captain), Abrar Ahmed, Salman Ali Agha, Arafat Minhas, Babar Azam, Faheem Ashraf, Fakhar Zaman, Ghazi Ghori, Haris Rauf, Hasan Nawaz, Naseem Shah, Razaullah, Saad Baig, Saim Ayub, Shadab Khan, Sufiyan Moqim.

World.title: Yemen war: What’s the latest on the battlefield?
World.content:
The internationally recognised government has retaken territories from the Houthis as fighting rages on the western coast.

Share Yemen war: What’s the latest on the battlefield? on social media

The Saudi-backed coalition in Yemen says it has seized several strategic positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from the Iran-aligned Houthis, as fighting intensifies along the country’s western coast.

The Houthis, meanwhile, claimed attacks targeting airports, oil infrastructure and military sites in Saudi Arabia.

The latest offensive by the Yemeni forces follows major Houthi gains in September, when the group swept over Yemen’s Red Sea coast, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, has said the government’s new operation – Dawn of Yemen – announced on Sunday, aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the group has controlled since 2014.

So, where does the fighting stand, and what could happen next?

What is the latest?

The heaviest fighting has been in southwestern Yemen, particularly along the Red Sea coast and around Taiz.

Government forces belonging to Yemen’s internationally-recognised government said they, together with the Popular Resistance Forces, had taken control of the al-Manzara, al-Ashari and Dhiban mountains in Haifan, south of Taiz.

Earlier, Yemeni government forces claimed they had captured Mocha, Dhubab, both in Taiz Governorate, as well as positions around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait during a rapid Saudi-backed counteroffensive.

Government forces, backed by heavy Saudi air strikes, reached the outskirts of Mocha on Monday as Houthi fighters retreated towards the highlands, four government sources told Reuters news agency.



Yemen’s Defence Ministry later said the city had fallen.

Without revealing any specifics, a Houthi military spokesman on Tuesday said the group remained in control of its battlefield gains and described reports from its opponents as “fabricated heroics”.

Al Jazeera has not independently verified the full extent of the government’s territorial gains.

Fernando Carvajal, a former UN Security Council adviser on Yemen, said the battle for the port city of Mocha will be key to the next phase of fighting.

“This will be a vital sign for us, if the Yemeni government forces, led by the Southern Giants and other southern forces, can hold this city. Because, at the moment, when you look at the battle plan, Mocha is surrounded by Houthis from all three sides, and you have the Red Sea,” he told Al Jazeera.

“So, we need to wait just a little bit more to see if indeed the government forces can hold this city and then use it as a staging point to take on the Houthis on other fronts.”

The fighting has also extended northwards along the Red Sea coast to Hodeidah, which has been under Houthis control since October 2014. The Houthis had captured the capital, Sanaa, weeks before.

The Saudi-led coalition said its naval forces struck Houthi “military targets” in the governorate, including weapons depots and facilities used to store explosive-laden boats and naval mines.

Al-Maliki said the operation had “thwarted a planned attack” on waterways in the southern Red Sea. The coalition also said its naval forces had carried out a military operation in Hodeidah.

Meanwhile, the Houthis said their forces carried out dozens of strikes on Tuesday targeting “enemy” reinforcements east of al-Jawf Governorate, resulting in an unspecified number of casualties.

The Houthis have simultaneously stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, according to Houthi-affiliated media. They targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, Abha airport and the Khamis Mushait military base with missiles and drones.

Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on those specific claims.

However, on Tuesday, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said the King Abdullah Bin ⁠⁠⁠⁠Abdulaziz International ⁠⁠⁠⁠Airport in Jazan and Najran International ‌‌‌‌Airport were targeted in two attacks on Monday evening, causing three minor injuries.



What is the humanitarian situation on the ground?

The escalation is worsening what was already one of the world’s gravest humanitarian crises.

The UN’s migration agency said on Monday that more than 184,000 people have been displaced since the war resumed.

According to the World Health Organization, the latest fighting has killed at least 959 people and wounded more than 4,200.

The fighting has also disrupted healthcare in the war-devastated country.

“Yemen’s latest escalation is pushing an already fragile health system towards breaking point,” warned Annette Heinzelmann, WHO’s emergency director for the eastern Mediterranean region.

What is the international reaction?

The escalation has drawn a response from Saudi Arabia’s regional allies, with Turkiye and Pakistan agreeing to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.

Signed in August, the pact is designed to strengthen collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against Saudi Arabia, Pakistan or Turkiye will be regarded as an attack on all three.

The United States, one of Saudi Arabia’s closest allies, is providing intelligence support to Riyadh, according to media reports.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday said Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government had “a right to defend themselves”.

“And obviously the Yemeni forces are going to try to retake territory that they were ousted from,” he told reporters.

World.title: Harmanpreet Kaur steps down as captain of India’s women’s cricket team
World.content:
The 37-year-old is the longest-serving cricket captain, among both men and women, to have captained in more than 150 T20I games.

Share ‘Done my duty’: Harmanpreet steps down as Indian women’s cricket captain on social media

India’s long-serving captain of the women’s cricket team, Harmanpreet Kaur, has stepped down from the role across all formats, bringing down the curtain on a successful stint as she led the South Asian team to their first ICC Women’s World Cup title at home in 2025.

Kaur announced her decision in a social media post on Tuesday, two weeks after leading India to a successful defence of their gold medal at the Asian Games.

“Today, I step down as captain of the Indian Women’s Cricket Team across all formats,” she wrote in an Instagram post.

“This is not an easy decision. It carries years of memories, emotions, sacrifices, and moments that will stay with me for the rest of my life.”

The 37-year-old was the Twenty20 captain for more than a decade after assuming the role in 2016, followed by ODI and Test captaincy in 2022.

Kaur, who made her T20I and ODI debuts for India in 2009, has had an illustrious career as skipper.

Indian media reports said Kaur’s decision came a day after she met Devajit Saikia, secretary of the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI), ⁠to discuss the future of the women’s team.

Opening batter Smriti Mandhana, who has been Kaur’s deputy since 2022, is the favourite to take over the captain’s role.

Under Kaur’s captaincy, India won their maiden Women’s Cricket World Cup title in November last year on home soil.

Most recently, she led India to title defence at the Asian Games, thrashing Sri Lanka, just after lifting the Women’s Asia Cup trophy earlier in September.



The top-order batter helped India reach the semifinals of the 2018 and 2023 Women’s T20 World Cups, as well as finish runners-up in the 2020 edition.

Kaur has captained India in five Tests, 51 ODIs and 155 T20Is, and is also the first cricketer — male or female — to captain her side in international cricket in more than 150 T20I games.

“I leave the captaincy today with a heart full of emotions, but also with peace … because I genuinely believe my team is in a good place,” she said in her Instagram post. “I feel I have done my duty.

“Captaincy may end today, but my love for Indian cricket never will.

“Now, I’m ready to play for the love of the game again. Captaincy ends. The journey continues.”

World.title: Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood attacker Nidal Hasan
World.content:
Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 at Fort Hood, to face execution under rare military order.

United States President Donald Trump has ordered the use of a firing squad in the execution of a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, the Pentagon spokesman has said.

Nidal Hasan, a US citizen of Palestinian descent, would be the first US soldier to be executed by the US military in more than 60 years.

Hasan will be killed by a firing squad under the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the approval of the president, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement on X on Monday.

The Army secretary will decide a time and place for the execution, he said.

“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.

Hasan was sentenced to death in August 2013 after a military jury found him guilty of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted murder for shooting a handgun in a medical facility at the Texas military base.

The attack killed 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman, and wounded 32 others.

Police arrested him at the scene, where he was shot and left partially paralysed.

The shooting took place weeks before Hasan was set to be deployed to Afghanistan.

He said during his court-martial that the shooting was an effort to stop the soldiers from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims, and made almost no effort to defend himself.

The Trump administration added death by firing squad as an appropriate method of execution in April, along with gas asphyxiation and electrocution.



Military executions are extremely rare in the US and can only be approved by the president under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. If the order is carried out, he will be the first member of the US military to be executed since 1961.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the 1961 execution was carried out by hanging. The apparent last known execution by a US military firing squad was one carried out “by musketry” in November 1945, the center reported.

World.title: Trump jokes about letting Iran bomb Los Angeles and San Diego
World.content:
NewsFeed Trump jokes about letting Iran bomb Los Angeles and San Diego

At a campaign rally in Nebraska, US President Donald Trump joked about letting Iran bomb Los Angeles and San Diego. Democratic leaders and lawmakers from California criticised the remarks, calling the president ‘deranged and dangerous’.

World.title: Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford
World.content:
President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base.

The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.

Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers.

US media reports suggested that the decision was made due to intelligence suggesting that Iran was plotting a drone attack. The BBC has not confirmed this and Trump has refused to be drawn on the question.

The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.

One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance.

Operation Spiderweb was an operation in June last year in which Ukraine smuggled drones into Russia. These were carried on lorries to locations near airbases by drivers who were unaware of their cargo, then launched and set upon their targets.

The source added: "Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously."

Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

World.title: Saudi Arabia urged to spare man sentenced to death over Facebook post
World.content:
"I plead for mercy for the wrongs committed by my son. Please forgive him and send him back to us."

Speaking through tears, Rasamanickam Yogalakshmi made a desperate plea for the life of her eldest son, Anojan Sivarasa. The 24-year-old migrant worker is facing the death penalty in Saudi Arabia after an appellate court found him guilty of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over a comment he made on Facebook.

The case has sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka, sparking widespread concern and civil society petitions across the country. Multiple political parties and government bodies have co-ordinated diplomatic efforts seeking clemency.

However, the family has had no updates on his condition since 28 September. The Sri Lankan government has instructed the family to refrain from making further statements while diplomatic efforts take place.

Saudi authorities have not published an official execution timeline, and it remains unclear when the sentence will be carried out. Saudi Arabia has a history of carrying out executions without warning families or foreign embassies, only informing relatives after the sentence has been carried out.

Anojan was prosecuted after a dispute on social media following an incident that took place during a Hindu pilgrimage in Sri Lanka. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online.

During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Anojan to post a response in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad.

Although Anojan promptly deleted his comment and posted an apology video, it was screenshot and brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July.

His personal devices were subsequently seized, and his social media accounts were deleted by Saudi officials.

"People in Saudi Arabia knew nothing about this matter. It was individuals in Sri Lanka who sent emails to the company where my brother worked. I do not even wish to mention who those people are," Anojan's brother, Hamsidan Sivarasa, told BBC Sinhala.

The company employing Anojan notified the authorities in Saudi Arabia who registered a case against him, according to Hamsidan.

Anojan was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of 3m Saudi riyals (about $0.8m; Â£0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. An appeal submitted on Anojan's behalf seeking to reduce his sentence was rejected, according to Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath.

The case took a drastic turn on 17 September after Saudi prosecutors filed an appeal for Anojan to be prosecuted under Sharia law instead of the country's cybercrime legislation. The appellate court granted the prosecution's request, increasing his sentence to the death penalty.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sri Lanka confirmed it is taking all available steps to assist Anojan.

His family met President Anura Kumara Dissanayake at the Presidential Secretariat on 21 September. The president assured them that the government would spare no effort to obtain a general pardon for him, instructing diplomatic channels to engage Saudi authorities.

The case has brought together cross-religious support. Senior Buddhist leaders, the Mahanayake Theros of the Ramanna Nikaya and the Amarapura Maha Nikaya, together with Hindu religious leaders, handed over a memorandum to the Presidential Secretariat calling for urgent state intervention.

In addition, a four-member Sri Lankan legal delegation is travelling to Saudi Arabia this week to meet Anojan's local defence lawyers.

"There are two law firms in Saudi Arabia handling Anojan's case. We are going there to meet the lawyers from these two firms, discuss the case and plan what can be done next," one of the team, Upul Kumarapperuma, President's Counsel, told BBC Sinhala.

World.title: Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway
World.content:
On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.

Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".

It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded.

The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory.

In addition to the strikes on Riyadh's international airport, the Houthis attacked an Aramco oil refinery, and Abha airport, as well as other sites, according to Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on Telegram.

According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east.

A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island.

They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.

The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced.

Additional reporting by Ottilie Mitchell

World.title: Kenya confirms its first Ebola death as outbreak spreads
World.content:
Kenya has confirmed its first case of Ebola - a Kenyan citizen who has been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo for the past seven years.

Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient, who fell ill a month ago, and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo, died days after arriving in Nairobi.

Duale said the patient boarded a flight on Saturday and underwent normal public screening at the main airport in Nairobi before he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city. Tests conducted confirmed positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus.

More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.
