World.title: LSDPC Takes Property Payments Digital, Launches 24/7 PayPortal
World.content:
Bennett Oghifo

The Lagos State Development and Property Corporation (LSDPC) has launched a digital payment platform, PayPortal, enabling customers to make payments online around the clock and receive instant transaction confirmation.

The initiative, according to the Corporation, is aimed at removing some of the traditional barriers associated with payment processes while improving accessibility, convenience and efficiency in its dealings with customers and stakeholders.

Speaking at the official launch of the platform, the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of LSDPC, Hon. Ayodeji Joseph, said the initiative marked another stage in the Corporation’s evolution as a public institution serving a rapidly changing Lagos.

Joseph said LSDPC, which has been part of Lagos’ development since 1972, could not remain tied to conventional processes as customer expectations and technology continued to change.

“Today is not simply about the introduction of a new payment platform. It is about evolution,” he said.

“It is about how an institution that has served Lagos for decades continues to adapt to the changing needs of the people it serves.”

According to him, modern customers increasingly expect public institutions to provide services that are accessible, convenient, responsive and available through digital channels.

He said PayPortal was developed to provide an additional channel through which LSDPC customers could access payment services without being limited to physical interactions and conventional payment processes.

Through the platform, customers can make payments 24 hours a day, seven days a week, while receiving instant confirmation of completed transactions.

Joseph stressed that the objective was not merely to introduce technology, but to use it to improve the overall customer experience.

“As a public institution, we have a responsibility to continually examine our processes, identify areas for improvement and adopt appropriate technologies that can make our services more accessible to the people we serve,” he said.

The LSDPC boss said the digital platform was part of the Corporation’s broader effort to modernise its operations and remain responsive to the realities of a rapidly evolving society.

He added that the launch should therefore be seen as part of a continuous transformation of the Corporation rather than simply the introduction of another payment channel.

“From 1972 to the digital age, we continue to evolve with Lagos. The city has grown, technology has transformed the way we live and work, and the way citizens engage with public institutions has changed. LSDPC must change with Lagos,” Joseph said.

He encouraged customers and stakeholders to embrace the platform and familiarise themselves with its operations.

To use the service, customers are required to visit www.payportal.lsdpc.gov.ng⁠�, create a username and password, enter the required details and proceed with their payments.

The Corporation said the platform offers secure access, 24-hour availability and instant confirmation, giving customers greater flexibility in managing their payment obligations.

Joseph also commended LSDPC management and staff, particularly the teams involved in developing and implementing the initiative, while thanking customers and stakeholders for their continued confidence in the Corporation.

He appealed to the media to help create awareness about the new platform and ensure that customers understand how to access and benefit from the service.

The launch represents a significant digital shift for LSDPC, which has played a central role in Lagos’ housing and property development landscape for more than five decades.

Joseph said the Corporation remained committed to building an institution that was “more accessible, more responsive and more convenient” for the people it serves.

He formally declared the LSDPC Digital Payment Platform launched, urging customers to visit the portal and take advantage of the new digital payment channel.

World.title: Pestra Tech Day 2026 Addresses Fire Safety, Intelligent Security
World.content:
Raheem Akingbolu

Fire and life safety in Nigeria’s built environment took centre stage at the fourth edition of Pestra Tech Day, where government officials, technology manufacturers and industry professionals gathered in Lagos to examine how stronger standards, deeper technical capacity and emerging technologies can make buildings safer, smarter and more resilient.

Hosted by Pestra Ltd in Lagos recently, the event was held under the theme “Closing the Fire Safety Gap in Nigeria’s Built Environment.” It brought together consultants, system integrators, contractors, end users and technology partners for a programme that combined policy discussion with technical presentations, product demonstrations and industry engagement.

Opening the discussions, Managing Director of Pestra Ltd, Mr. Paul Nwokolo, said Pestra Tech Day was conceived as more than a product showcase. He described it as a forum for examining technology in practical terms, bringing together the people who design, specify, regulate, deploy and use critical safety, security and communication systems.

“This is why Pestra Tech Day matters. Today gives us an opportunity to look beyond brochures and product specifications – to exchange ideas, challenge assumptions, learn from experts, experience emerging technologies and consider how global innovation can address local realities.”

Nwokolo’s remarks set the context for the day’s principal policy intervention: a keynote address by the Controller General of the Federal Fire Service, Mr. S.A. Olumode, on “Closing the Fire and Life Safety Gap in Nigeria’s Built Environment.”

Olumode placed fire detection and prevention at the heart of the discussion, emphasising the need to narrow the gap between modern building requirements and the systems, practices and professional capacity needed to protect lives and property. His address reinforced the wider purpose of this year’s Tech Day – to look beyond individual products and consider how safety systems are designed, specified, integrated, maintained and used throughout the life of a building.

From that policy focus, the programme moved into the technologies and operational practices shaping safer and more efficient facilities. Mr. Theo Everaers, Managing Director of Telecom – Pneumatic Tube Systems in the Netherlands, presented pneumatic tube technology and its role in improving internal logistics and operational workflows in modern healthcare environments.

The conversation then turned to intelligent security. Hanwha Vision’s Regional Manager for Africa, Mr. Abbassy Omar, examined the growing role of artificial intelligence in modern security operations, highlighting advances in intelligent video surveillance, video analytics, licence plate recognition, thermal imaging and related technologies designed to help organisations detect threats earlier, improve situational awareness and respond more effectively to security incidents.

That focus on AI-enabled security led naturally into the cyber risks surrounding increasingly connected buildings and edge systems.

Specialist Adoption Architect at Red Hat, Francis Anyaegbu, spoke on “Intelligent Security & the Quantum Challenge,” describing smart security cameras, digital access readers, edge telemetry nodes, video conferencing systems and other connected devices as an expanding front line of enterprise risk as artificial intelligence accelerates both cyberattacks and defensive capabilities.

In his presentation, Anyaegbu said data breaches now cost organisations an average of $5.0 million per incident, with exposure increasing by about $1,100 for every hour an adversary remains undetected. He also pointed to a 1,500 per cent surge in deepfakes, the spread of unmonitored “Shadow AI,” and the emerging threat that quantum computing poses to conventional encryption. He argued that organisations must move beyond traditional perimeter-based controls towards open, quantum-safe architectures built on digital trust, machine-speed defence and stronger visibility over automated AI agents and connected systems, highlighting post-quantum cryptography, digital sovereignty and tighter AI governance as foundations for long-term resilience.

Returning the discussion to fire and life safety, Senior Territory Manager at Honeywell Technologies, Mr. Ziad Hafez, highlighted developments across Honeywell’s life-safety portfolios, including advanced fire detection, intelligent alarm systems and connected life-safety solutions designed to support earlier warning, faster emergency response and more resilient buildings. He also underscored Honeywell’s collaboration with Pestra to strengthen access to its fire, life-safety and security technologies in Nigeria, providing consultants, system integrators and end users with a dependable local channel for genuine Honeywell products, backed by appropriate technical and after-sales support. The collaboration is intended to reduce the risks associated with counterfeit or improperly sourced equipment and give customers greater confidence that critical systems are built around authentic products supported through the manufacturer’s channel.

World.title: Cruxstone’s Destination Development, Nautica Beach Resort Hosts One Nation Festival
World.content:
Bennett Oghifo

One Nation Festival has made a strong debut at Nautica Beach Resort as Cruxstone advances its destination development vision.

Also, planning has begun for the 2027 edition, as Nautica strengthens its role in Lagos’ growing tourism, hospitality and leisure economy.

Planning for the 2027 edition of the One Nation Festival follows the successful inaugural celebration held at Nautica Beach Resort on Independence Day, October 1, 2026. The organisers said further information on the next edition would be released in the coming months, as the festival begins its journey towards becoming a recurring platform for celebrating Nigeria’s culture, creativity, tourism and shared identity.

The inaugural One Nation Festival, themed “Many Cultures. One People. One Celebration,” brought together culture, music, sport, food, hospitality, leisure and recreation in a day-long celebration at Nautica Beach Resort, reinforcing the growing role of destination-led experiences in Lagos’ tourism and creative economy.

More than an Independence Day event, the festival was conceived as a platform to celebrate Nigeria differently, bringing people together through experiences that reflect the country’s diversity, energy and cultural richness, while showcasing Lagos as a destination capable of hosting compelling lifestyle and tourism experiences.

For Cruxstone Group, the festival also represented a broader vision: creating destination developments that extend beyond physical infrastructure to become platforms for tourism, hospitality, community, culture and economic activity.

At the heart of that vision is the Nautica Ecosystem, conceived as an integrated destination bringing together complementary lifestyle, hospitality, leisure, recreation, entertainment and tourism experiences within one environment. According to Dr. Adetoro Bank-Omotoye, Chief Executive Officer, Cruxstone Group, Nautica reflects the Group’s ambition to rethink how developments are conceived and experienced.

“Our vision for Nautica has always gone beyond simply developing real estate. We are building an integrated destination ecosystem, a place that can create experiences, attract people, support businesses and contribute meaningfully to the tourism and hospitality economy of Lagos. We believe the future of development is not only about the buildings we create, but about the destinations, communities and experiences that grow around them.

“Nautica Beach Resort is already playing an important role in bringing that vision to life. It gives people a reason to experience the destination today while the wider Nautica vision continues to evolve. One Nation Festival is another expression of what is possible when culture, hospitality, leisure, entertainment and tourism come together within one destination.” Throughout the Independence Day celebration, guests experienced different expressions of Nigerian culture and contemporary leisure.

One of the festival’s major attractions was the Nautica Beach Resort x Socialiga Football Tournament, featuring eight teams, Cruxstone, Landmark, Page Finance, Triber, Medbury, Betking, Rise and 5Betking. Following a competitive series of matches, Landmark emerged winner of the tournament and received a ₦1 million cash prize.

Sport formed only one part of the experience.

At KiVu Beach Club, the beachside setting was transformed into a Palmwine Village, creating an atmosphere rooted in Nigerian culture and local flavours. Fresh palm wine, local dishes and traditional elements were combined with the resort’s contemporary waterfront environment, while cultural dancers and performers brought further colour and energy to the celebration.

Across Nautica Beach Resort, guests experienced music, food, fashion, recreation, culture and entertainment, creating an Independence Day celebration that went beyond the format of a conventional concert or beach event.

For Utibe Bassey, General Manager, Business Development & Strategy, Cruxstone Group, that distinction was central to the creation of One Nation Festival.

“The idea behind One Nation was to create a different way to celebrate Nigeria. Independence Day gives us an opportunity not only to reflect on who we are, but also to celebrate our culture, our creativity, our food, our music, our sports and the experiences that bring us together as a people.

“We also want One Nation Festival to contribute to a bigger conversation around Lagos as a tourism destination. Lagos already has an extraordinary cultural and creative energy, and our goal is to consistently create experiences that put the city at centre stage, attract visitors and give people more reasons to explore Lagos. We see One Nation growing into an important annual platform for that.”

The festival also demonstrated how destination developments can support a much wider visitor economy.

By bringing entertainment, sport, hospitality, food, cultural experiences and recreation into the same environment, destinations can create opportunities for hospitality operators, vendors, entertainers, creatives, event producers, lifestyle brands and other businesses whose activities are connected to tourism.

This philosophy sits at the centre of Cruxstone’s broader destination development strategy.

Rather than viewing development solely in terms of buildings, the Group is increasingly focused on creating places capable of generating activity, experiences and long-term value around them. Within the Nautica vision, Nautica Beach Resort is already providing a platform through which visitors can engage with the destination through leisure, hospitality, events, recreation and waterfront experiences.

According to Alex Okoh, Head, Marketing & Advertising, Cruxstone Group, building tourism requires more than infrastructure; it requires creating compelling reasons for people to visit, experience and return to a destination.

“Tourism grows when people have reasons to visit a place, spend time there, experience something memorable and want to come back. That is one of the important roles Nautica Beach Resort is beginning to play within the Lagos tourism landscape.

“We are creating experiences around the destination and showing that Lagos can continue to offer much more across leisure, culture, hospitality, recreation and entertainment. One Nation Festival plays a key role in that strategy because it gives us a signature platform through which we can celebrate Nigeria while also showcasing Lagos and Nautica to a wider audience. Our ambition is to keep building experiences that strengthen the city’s tourism appeal locally, across Africa and internationally.”

The growth of destination-led experiences also reflects the increasing connection between tourism, hospitality, entertainment and Nigeria’s creative economy.

For a city such as Lagos, this presents an opportunity to convert its cultural influence, music, food, fashion, entertainment and social energy into stronger tourism experiences capable of attracting both domestic and international visitors.

One Nation Festival provides a platform through which these different expressions can coexist.

From the Palmwine Village at KiVu and cultural performances to live music, food experiences and the Nautica Beach Resort x Socialiga Football Tournament, the inaugural festival brought different elements of Nigerian life together within one waterfront destination.

It was a celebration of Nigeria, but also a demonstration of what can happen when destination development is combined with culture, hospitality and experience.

As Cruxstone continues to develop the wider Nautica Ecosystem, Nautica Beach Resort is expected to remain an important experiential component of the vision, providing a place where the public can engage with the destination and where events, tourism, leisure and hospitality can continue to intersect.

With the first edition concluded, attention is already turning to what comes next.

Planning for One Nation Festival 2027 has officially commenced, with the organisers expected to begin releasing details, partnerships, programme information and other updates in the coming months.

The ambition is to build on the foundation established in 2026 and continue developing One Nation Festival as an annual celebration of Nigeria, one that brings its many cultures, people and experiences together while positioning Nautica Beach Resort and Lagos at the centre of a growing destination tourism story.

World.title: Alakija Building Collapse Deaths Expose Gaps, Experts Demand Tougher Enforcement in Lagos
World.content:
Bennett Oghifo

The loss of lives and property in the recent building collapse at Alakija in Amuwo-Odofin Local Government Area of Lagos State has renewed concerns about weaknesses in building regulation, professional supervision and emergency response, with built-environment experts calling for tougher enforcement, regular inspections and earlier action to prevent further tragedies.

The four-storey building collapsed on Old Ojo Road, near Alakija Bus Stop, off the Lagos-Badagry Expressway, Satellite Town, Lagos State, Nigeria. Eight persons died while 26 persons were rescued in the incident which occurred on Thursday, June 25, 2026.

The experts said the collapse highlighted the consequences of poor construction practices and weak oversight, stressing the need for competent professionals, quality materials and proper monitoring of buildings from construction through occupancy and maintenance.

These built-environment experts spoke at a conference organised by the Building Collapse Prevention Guild (BCPG), Amuwo-Odofin Cell, in Satellite Town, Lagos, with the theme, “Building a Resilient Lagos Through Synergy.”

The conference brought together the regulators, officials of the Lagos State Physical Planning Permit Authority, Lagos State Building Control Agency, Lagos State Materials Testing Laboratory, Lagos State Emergency Management Authority, the Nigeria Police and the Lagos State Neighbourhood Safety Corps.

This event served as a stakeholders’ meeting that enabled the regulators to interact with construction professionals, building artisans, developers, academics and the community representatives led by Mr Victor Okunola and Dr Michael Imitinito to discuss ways of improving building safety and urban resilience in Lagos.

The Coordinator of the BCPG Amuwo-Odofin Cell, Chubike Okafor, a builder, said the building collapse at Alakija, in this neighbourhood, was among the incidents that prompted the conference. According to him, the incident exposed weaknesses in emergency coordination and highlighted the need for better early-warning systems.

Okafor urged residents, property owners and community leaders to report structural cracks, flooding, settlement, tilting, spalling concrete, persistent water damage and other signs of building distress to qualified professionals or relevant authorities before they develop into emergencies.

The Chairman of the conference, Dr Austin Otuoke, an architect, said building safety could not be guaranteed by one profession or institution alone, particularly in a rapidly growing city facing increasing demand for housing and infrastructure.

He said professionals and regulatory agencies must ensure that buildings were properly planned, approved, constructed and maintained, with clear responsibility at every stage.

In his opening remark, the Chairman of Building Collapse Prevention Guild Lagos State Chapter, Pastor Joseph Akande, a town planner, stated that the BCPG has been adopting a grassroots approach to addressing the challenges of building collapse. Built-environment professionals residing or working in each of the local government areas of the state constituted themselves into a local BCPG Cell on a voluntary service to help promote construction of standard buildings and discourage unethical or unprofessional practices that could lead to building failures. Whistleblowing to the regulators on discovering a site of substandard building construction and defective or distressed structures, he further said, was part of the services the BCPG members have been rendering in order to protect the safety of the built environment.

The General Manager of the Lagos State Building Control Agency (LASBCA), Mrs Florence Gbaye, a builder, warned against the use of substandard materials and unqualified workers for critical construction activities.

Gbaye also criticised professionals who take on several projects but leave important responsibilities to unqualified persons. She urged developers and practitioners to involve regulatory authorities throughout the construction process.

She said LASBCA’s Certified Accreditors Programme, involving more than 150 private practitioners, was designed to improve regulatory efficiency and professional participation.

The Vice President, Africa, International Society for Soil Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering, Dr Sebastian Ozoamalu, a geotechnical engineer, said proper checks on soil and ground conditions before construction could help prevent structural failures.

He warned that neighbouring properties could have different ground conditions, making it unsafe to copy a foundation design simply because it had worked on another property.

Ozoamalu urged practitioners to work within their areas of competence and seek specialist advice where necessary.

Speaking on flooding and drainage, Ogonna Agwu, a surveyor, said accurate information about land levels and proper drainage planning were important to building safety, particularly in low-lying parts of Lagos.

He warned that errors in land surveys and poor connections between private and public drainage systems could increase the risk of flooding and damage to buildings.

He advocated better mapping and drainage planning, as well as measures to manage stormwater and erosion.

A retired Permanent Secretary in the Lagos State Ministry of Waterfront Infrastructure Development, Mrs Olayinka Patunola-Ajayi, an estate surveyor and valuer, said building safety should be viewed as part of the wider resilience of Lagos.

She said the city’s rapid population growth, low-lying terrain, coastal exposure and interconnected infrastructure meant that problems with housing, drainage, transportation and utilities could have wider consequences.

Patunola-Ajayi, who was once a director in the Lagos State Ministry of Housing, called for major projects to undergo broader risk assessments and for buildings and infrastructure to be managed throughout their useful lives. She also highlighted the potential of mapping and other digital technologies to improve planning and monitoring, while stressing that technology should support, not replace, professional responsibility.

A quantity surveyor, Tomi Ogundare, cautioned that cost, inflation should never be a reason for compromise in the standard of building construction. He called for the use of building collapse investigation outcomes to prevent recurrence of similar incidents by identifying and managing risks before failure.

According to BCPG records cited in his presentation, Nigeria recorded 817 building-collapse incidents between October 1971 and July 27, 2026, including 477 in Lagos.

Of the Lagos incidents, 325, representing 68.1 per cent, occurred while buildings were occupied, while 121, or 25.4 per cent, occurred during construction and 31, or 6.5 per cent, at the end-of-life stage.

Ogundare identified gaps in building records, investigations and early intervention as areas requiring urgent attention.

He recommended risk-based inspections, stronger controls on building alterations and changes of use, improved building records, updated fitness certification and a system for tracking distressed buildings until identified problems were resolved.

The Dean of the School of Environmental Studies, Yaba College of Technology, and Third Vice-President of the Nigerian Institute of Building, Dr Adesina Aladeloba, a builder, called for the training and recertification of artisans and craftsmen. He identified poor planning, inadequate financing, abandoned projects and weak project management as other challenges affecting the construction industry.

Aladeloba, who is also an estate surveyor and valuer, cautioned against the tendency of government prioritising revenue generation over the regulatory functions of its agencies.

The General Manager of the Lagos State Physical Planning Permit Authority, Kehinde Osinaike, represented by Mrs Busola Olatunji, a town planner, urged residents to adopt a “See Something, Say Something” approach by reporting unsafe buildings and unauthorised construction. She strongly warned against constructing buildings that did not pass through proper building approval process.

Other participants at the conference raised concerns about poor-quality construction materials, inadequate site investigations, poor workmanship and weak supervision. They warned against hiring professionals only to obtain building approval and then excluding them from the actual construction work. They said supervision was particularly important during foundation work, reinforcement, concrete work and other critical stages.

Some stakeholders at the event said building safety required more than regulations and approvals. They called for tougher enforcement, ethical professional practice, quality materials, competent supervision, regular inspections, effective maintenance and timely intervention.

Considering the importance of cement in mix ratio that could add durability to the elements of buildings, technical team of HBM Nigeria Plc (formerly Lafarge Africa Plc) made a demonstration at the interlude.

The Chairman, Association of Professional Bodies of Nigeria, Lagos State Chapter, Bldr Bashir Asimiyu, commended the approach of BCPG that usually brought various professionals together in finding a lasting solution to building collapse crisis. His predecessor, QS Ayuba Akere, who was the moderator of the conference, lent his voice behind this professional synergy as a pragmatic, result-oriented way of proving to the world the professionalism ingrained in the Nigerian system.

In his closing remark, the National President of BCPG, Tpl Sulaimon Yusuf, enjoined other state chapters of BCPG to replicate the grassroots stakeholders’ meeting in order to bring the advocacy close to prospective building owners, occupants, developers, building materials suppliers and constructors.

World.title: ISWAP Leader Responsible for Owo, Kogi, Niger Attacks Killed in Ondo
World.content:
Fidelis David in Akure

A senior leader of the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), Abdussamad Ohida, also known as Anwar, has been killed in a joint security operation in a forest in Owo, Ondo State, through intelligence that he was planning fresh attacks on civilians in some parts of southern Nigeria.

Ohida was reportedly killed alongside several other members of the terrorist group during an intelligence-driven operation involving the Nigerian Army, Department of State Services (DSS), and the Western Nigeria Security Network known as Amotekun.

Security sources said the operation was launched after intelligence indicated that the ISWAP commander was preparing to unleash attacks in some parts of southern Nigeria, particularly during the Yuletide season.

According to the sources, the intelligence was obtained partly from information gathered following the arrest of Abu Ikrimah, also known as Abu Uwais, identified as the former ISWAP Central Nigeria leader and Ohida’s superior. Ikrimah was arrested by the DSS in 2023.

Following Ikrimah’s arrest, Ohida allegedly assumed control of ISWAP operations across parts of the North-Central and southern regions, where he was said to have coordinated attacks and worked to expand the terrorist group’s operational network.

One of the sources said intelligence on the planned attacks was also corroborated by security partners in the United Kingdom, contributing to the decision to launch the operation against Ohida and his associates.

Ohida was allegedly linked to several attacks in Kogi, Niger and Ondo States, including the December 31, 2025, attack on the Ipele Divisional Police Station in Owo, where eight AK-47 rifles were reportedly stolen before the facility was destroyed with an explosive.

He was also accused of involvement in the July 28, 2022, attack on a military checkpoint along the Suleja-Zuba Road in Niger State, the July 11, 2022, assault on the Kuje Correctional Centre in Abuja, and the April 23, 2022, attack on the Ogaminana Police Station in Adavi Local Government Area of Kogi State, where five policemen were reportedly killed.

The source further attributed to Ohida the February 7, 2022, attack on the Okene Area Command and the December 24, 2020, assault on a naval checkpoint in Okene, Kogi State, which reportedly resulted in the deaths of two naval officers.

The latest operation, according to the source, represents a significant setback to ISWAP’s command structure and its efforts to establish a stronger foothold in central and southern Nigeria.

Ohida’s death came months after another senior Islamic State commander, Abu Bilal al-Minuki, was killed, further intensifying pressure on the terrorist group’s leadership and its efforts to expand its activities in Nigeria.

World.title: INEC, Editors and the Battle for Trust Ahead of 2027
World.content:
Iyobosa Uwugiaren, who attended the recent seminar organised by the Nigerian Guild of Editors and the Independent National Electoral Commission, examines the issues and concerns raised at the workshop.

With the 2027 general elections only 100 days away, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and the Nigerian Guild of Editors (NGE) have started confronting what many stakeholders in the democratic process described as one of the most difficult questions facing Nigeria’s democracy: how can public confidence in elections be restored and sustained in an age of misinformation, political tension and declining institutional trust?

That burning question dominated the strategic workshop for editors organised by the NGE in collaboration with INEC in Abuja recently.

The meeting was more than another pre-election engagement between the electoral umpire and the media. It was an acknowledgement by both institutions that the credibility of an election is shaped long before voters arrive at polling units on the election day.

For INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash O. Amupitan (SAN) the challenge is clear. Electoral integrity cannot be secured by the commission alone. It requires what he described as a partnership among electoral institutions, the media and civil society.

“The ultimate arbiter of electoral integrity is public trust,” the INEC chairman said. He argued that such trust cannot be constructed in isolation.

His message was significant. Nigeria has witnessed elections in which legal and technological reforms were introduced with the promise of improving transparency, only for operational difficulties, disputed results and poor communication to undermine public confidence.

The 2023 general election remains an important reference point. Technology, particularly the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) and the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV), were expected to improve the credibility of the process. But technical and operational difficulties, especially concerning result transmission and publication, became major sources of controversy. That experience hangs over preparations for 2027.

Therefore, Amupitan sought to reassure Nigerians that INEC is not merely preparing for another election but attempting to address weaknesses identified in previous exercises.

According to him, the commission has introduced improvements to BVAS, acquired 57,000 new devices, strengthened result-management systems and deployed measures aimed at improving cybersecurity.

There is also a renewed emphasis on online voter registration and printable voter cards. More than 10 million new voter registrations were recorded during the three phases of the Continuous Voter Registration exercise, according to the commission. INEC said that the national register now contains more than 103 million voters following the completion of its biometric verification and clean-up processes.

No doubt, the figures are impressive. But the real test is not the size of the register or the sophistication of the technology. The real test is whether Nigerians believe that the system will work when it matters most.

That is where the relationship between INEC and the media becomes critical.

The media remains one of the principal channels through which citizens understand elections. For millions of Nigerians, especially those who may not have direct access to electoral officials, newspapers, radio, television and digital platforms provide the information needed to understand registration, accreditation, voting procedures, results and electoral laws.

The editor therefore occupies an influential position. Amupitan described editors as “the final filter” in an increasingly chaotic information environment. He urged newsrooms to prioritise fact-checking and verification, warning that fake results, manipulated videos, deepfakes and unverified reports could inflame tensions and delegitimise an otherwise credible election.

There is little doubt that this threat is real. The information environment surrounding elections has changed dramatically. Political actors can communicate directly with voters without passing through traditional media gatekeepers. A short video, an altered photograph or a fabricated election result can travel across social media platforms within minutes.

By the time a newspaper or television station establishes the facts, millions of people may already have encountered the falsehood. But there is an important qualification to INEC’s call for closer media collaboration.

The media must collaborate with INEC without becoming its public relations arm.

This distinction is fundamental.

A credible election requires accurate reporting, but accurate reporting does not mean uncritical reporting. Journalists must verify information from INEC, but they must also scrutinise information provided by the commission.

The media’s responsibility is not simply to repeat what the electoral umpire says. It is to ask whether what the commission says can be independently verified.

That is why the opening statement by NGE President, Mr. Eze Anaba, was particularly important. Anaba acknowledged the responsibility of editors to uphold accuracy, fairness, balance and the public interest. But he equally emphasised that the media cannot perform its role effectively without credible, timely and accessible information from INEC. That represents an important two-way bargain. If INEC expects journalists to reject rumours, it must provide reliable information quickly enough to fill the information vacuum in which rumours thrive.

Silence from an electoral management body can be as damaging as misinformation from political actors.

When voters cannot obtain authoritative information about the location of polling units, technical problems, postponed processes or results, speculation inevitably fills the gap.

This is perhaps one of the most important lessons from previous elections: communication is not an accessory to election management. It is part of election management.

The same principle applies to technology.

INEC’s technological ambitions are welcome. BVAS can strengthen voter accreditation; electronic result management can improve transparency; online services can reduce barriers to voter registration; and cybersecurity systems can protect sensitive electoral data. But technology must not become a substitute for institutional accountability. A sophisticated machine can fail. A computer system can experience downtime. Data can be corrupted. Networks can collapse. Software can malfunction. Cybersecurity systems can be attacked.

Consequently, the question Nigerians should ask is not simply how much technology INEC is deploying but whether there are credible contingency arrangements when technology fails.

There must also be mechanisms through which journalists, political parties, civil society organisations and voters can independently establish what happened.

Transparency is strongest when it is verifiable by people outside the institution providing the information.

The same principle applies to INEC’s claim of zero tolerance for electoral offences. Vote-buying, political violence, intimidation and electoral manipulation have repeatedly threatened Nigerian elections. The chairman’s warning to political actors that attempts to buy votes or deploy violence will attract sanctions is therefore welcome.

But Nigerians have heard similar warnings before. What matters now is enforcement. The credibility of the 2027 elections will depend partly on whether electoral offences are investigated and prosecuted regardless of the identity, wealth or political influence of the person involved.

An election cannot be described as truly credible if powerful offenders believe that political connections will protect them from consequences.

INEC’s proposed collaboration with law-enforcement and financial institutions to monitor vote-buying and illegal campaign spending could be significant. But such cooperation must operate within the law and must not be selective.

The issue of violence is equally serious. The chairman’s warning that political competition must not become a “clash of weapons” comes at an important moment. The history of Nigerian elections shows that violence can discourage participation, displace voters and undermine confidence in the democratic process.

As the Executive Director of the International Press Centre, Lanre Arogundade, said, safety of journalists must be treated as an essential component of electoral integrity.

Reporters cannot provide independent coverage if they are intimidated, assaulted or prevented from reaching polling units and collation centres.

The proposed collaboration between INEC, security agencies and the media to protect accredited journalists is consequently necessary. But protection should never become a justification for restricting legitimate reporting. A journalist who witnesses misconduct must be able to report it—even when the allegation concerns an electoral official or security personnel.

This brings the discussion back to trust. Amupitan, Anaba, Arogundade, Dr Tony Onyima and other speakers at the workshop, identified trust as the foundation of credible elections. They are right. But trust cannot be created through official assurances alone.

It must be earned through consistent behaviour.

INEC must demonstrate that it can communicate bad news as effectively as good news. It must acknowledge mistakes when they occur and explain how they are being corrected.

The media, on its part, must accept that speed cannot replace accuracy and that political excitement cannot replace evidence.

Editors have an especially difficult responsibility. They must navigate between the pressure to publish first and the obligation to publish correctly.

In the era of social media, the temptation to chase breaking news can be enormous. Yet an erroneous election result published by a major media organisation can have consequences far beyond a correction published several hours later.

The NGE’s proposed stronger relationship with INEC should therefore be structured around verification rather than dependence. Regular briefings, dedicated communication channels, rapid fact-checking mechanisms and access to technical experts could help.

But the relationship must preserve the independence of the press.

Indeed, the media should be INEC’s partner in democracy, not its cheerleader. Civil society organisations also have an important role in this triangle. They can provide independent observation, document irregularities and bring the concerns of marginalised groups—including women and persons with disabilities—to the electoral process.

The success of the proposed partnership will ultimately depend on whether all three sides are willing to accept scrutiny. INEC must be prepared to be questioned.

The media must be prepared to be corrected. Civil society must be prepared to challenge both. That is what democratic accountability requires.

As the country approaches the 2027 elections, the Abuja workshop has opened an important conversation. But the real value of the workshop will be determined by what happens after the speeches. Will INEC’s promises of transparency translate into accessible information? Will new technology work reliably? Will journalists be protected?

Will vote-buying and political violence attract meaningful sanctions? Will errors be acknowledged rather than defended? And will the media maintain sufficient independence to scrutinise the electoral umpire even while working with it?

Those questions are more important than the rhetoric of partnership. Nigeria’s democracy does not need a media that is hostile to INEC, just as it does not need an electoral commission that is hostile to criticism. What the country needs is something more difficult: institutions that can cooperate without compromising their independence.

The 2027 election will therefore be a test not only of INEC’s capacity to conduct elections, but also of the country’s wider democratic ecosystem.

The ballot box is important, but so is the information environment surrounding it.

If voters receive accurate information, if electoral procedures are transparent, if technology is independently verifiable, if political offenders are held accountable and if journalists can report freely and safely, public confidence can grow.

But if information is withheld, technology fails without credible explanations, political actors act with impunity and the media becomes divided between propaganda and sensationalism, trust will remain fragile. The message from the INEC–NGE workshop is therefore both hopeful and cautionary.

Nigeria has the opportunity to make the 2027 elections a demonstration of institutional learning. But that opportunity will not be secured by speeches alone. It will be secured by evidence.

Ultimately, the most powerful partnership between INEC and the media should not be one in which both institutions agree on everything. It should be one in which they agree on the importance of democracy—and remain sufficiently independent to challenge one another when the public interest demands it. That may be the real battle for 2027: not merely winning votes, but winning the confidence of the people who cast them.

World.title: Tinubu Declares 3-day Mourning as 32 Die in Military Plane Crash
World.content:
• Orders probe, directs flags flown at half-mast nationwide

•Defence minister, senate c’ttee, others mourn

•Keyamo pledges ministry’s cooperation as service activates search, rescue

•NSIB, NCAA extend condolences

•Aiyedatiwa orders full support for rescue operations

Deji Elumoye, Chuks Okocha, Sunday Aborisade, Linus Aleke, Kasim Sumaina in Abuja and Fidelis David in Akure





President Bola Tinubu yesterday mourned the death of 32 passengers onboard the Nigerian Air Force (NAF) ATR-42 Jet that crashed near a naval base in Igbokoda area of Ondo State, instructing that a probe into the crash should be conducted, and ordering a three-day national mourning period for the deceased.

Also, the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Mr. Festus Keyamo, has announced his ministry’s total cooperation and assistance in the ongoing search and rescue efforts of the crashed Military aircraft in Ondo State.

This was as the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (NSIB), said it has commended the swift activation of search and rescue and the efforts of first responders at Igbokoda, urging the public to rely exclusively on official updates from the Nigerian Air Force on the rescue operation and on any investigation.

Besides, the Minister of Defence, Gen. Christopher Musa (rtd), has expressed deep sorrow over the tragic crash of the military aircraft with tail number NAF 931, involving the dedicated personnel of the Armed Forces.

At the same time, the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), stood ready to provide technical expertise and assistance as may be required to support the ongoing search and rescue operations.

Nevertheless, the Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, has directed the immediate mobilisation of state emergency and health agencies to support the ongoing search and rescue operation.

A military Jet yesterday crashed in Igbokoda, headquarters of Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State – killing 25 airmen and their families, seven crew members who were on board.

The incident, which occurred in the morning, reportedly crashed into a swampy terrain opposite the Naval Base in Igbokoda, throwing residents of the coastal community into panic.

Although the identity of personnel on board had yet to be officially confirmed, military gear was reportedly recovered from the crash site.

Chairman of Ilaje Local Government Area, Mr Maurice Oripelaye, who confirmed the incident in a telephone conversation with journalists, said the aircraft had been burnt to rubble.

Oripelaye said, “We have confirmed that a jet crashed in the area, but we cannot ascertain the number of people that were on board yet. Military gear was found at the scene, but the jet had burnt to rubble.”

However, the Ondo State Police Command through the Police Public Relations Officer, Jimoh Abayomi also confirmed the incident, urging members of the public, particularly residents of Igbokoda and adjoining communities, to remain calm and refrain from circulating unverified information, assuring that the public would be duly informed as soon as further credible information became available.

Meanwhile, Tinubu, in a release by his Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, disclosed that having been briefed by the Chief of Air Staff, directed the Nigerian Air Force to immediately commence a thorough investigation into the cause of the crash to prevent future occurrences.

The President, in a release issued by his Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga also directed that flags should be flown at half-mast nationwide as a mark of respect to the officers and ordered a three-day national mourning period.

“I commend the Nigerian Air Force for activating an immediate Search and Rescue operation following the accident. I pray for the repose of the souls of the gallant officers and for Almighty God to grant their families and the Nigerian Air Force the fortitude to bear the unfortunate loss.

“I assure the Nigerian Air Force of the continued support of our administration as they continue their vital role in securing our nation. I also commend the swift response of first responders and the Ondo State Government at the crash site”, Tinubu said.

The President expressed profound sadness over the crash of the aircraft which was on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos when the accident occurred.

Tinubu extended his deepest condolences to the family of the 25 passengers and seven crew members involved, the Chief of the Air Staff, Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke, and all officers, airmen and airwomen of the Nigerian Air Force.

“This is a painful moment for our Armed Forces and for the entire nation. Our Air Force personnel put their lives on the line every day to secure Nigeria. Their sacrifice will never be forgotten,” he stressed.

However, the Nigerian Air Force (NAF), while confirming the incident, said it had activated an immediate search-and-rescue operation.

In a statement by the Director of Public Relations and Information, NAF Headquarters, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, the Air Force said the aircraft involved was an ATR-42 which was on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos when the accident occurred.

The NAF said, “Search and Rescue operations, in coordination with relevant authorities and emergency response agencies, are currently ongoing,” adding that it remained committed to ensuring the success of the ongoing rescue efforts.

“The aircraft was on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos when the accident occurred. Search and rescue operations, in coordination with relevant authorities and emergency response agencies, are currently ongoing,” the NAF spokesperson said.

The NAF said it was committed to ensuring the success of the ongoing search and rescue efforts, adding that further details would be communicated in due course.

Keyamo Pledges Ministry’s Cooperation in Search, Rescue

The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Mr. Festus Keyamo has announced his ministry’s total cooperation and assistance in the ongoing search and rescue efforts of the crashed Military aircraft in Ondo State.

Keyamo, in a statement by his Special Adviser on Media, Tunde Moshood, said: “I regret to inform the general public that Air Traffic Controllers have informed me of the disappearance of a military aircraft with tail number NGR 931, enroute Lagos from Benin at 0913 hours earlier today. All efforts to reach the aircraft on radio proved abortive.

“Subsequently information however confirmed that the military aircraft has crashed close to the Naval Base in Igbokoda, Ondo State. The wreckage has been located and search and rescue operations are ongoing. Preliminary information suggests that there were 25 passengers and 7 crew members on board.”

According to Keyamo, “Whilst the control and regulation of military aircraft are completely outside the authority of the Ministry of Aviation, and Civil Aviation Authority, I have just spoken to the Chief of Air Staff, Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke. Further information on this unfortunate incident will be made available subsequently.

On its part, the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (NSIB) confirmed that Search and Rescue operations have been activated and were ongoing, in coordination with relevant authorities and emergency response agencies.

The Bureau, in a statement by its Director General, Capt. Alex Badeh Jr., extended its condolences to the Nigerian Air Force, and to the families and colleagues of all those on board.

“Our thoughts are with them, and with the Search and Rescue teams working at the site.The NSIB stands ready to assist the Nigerian Air Force, at its request, with whatever technical support may be required.

“That support can include the deployment of investigators and the use of the Bureau’s Flight Safety Laboratory for the recovery, readout and analysis of flight recorder data. As this occurrence involves a military aircraft, investigative responsibility rests with the Nigerian Air Force. The Bureau will provide assistance upon a formal request from the Air Force,” it said.

The NSIB said it has commended the swift activation of Search and Rescue and the efforts of first responders at Igbokoda, and urged the public to rely exclusively on official updates from the Nigerian Air Force on the rescue operation and on any investigation.

Badeh said further comment from the Bureau would be issued only as appropriate, and in consultation with the Nigerian Air Force.

Similarly, the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) said it received with deep concern the press release by the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development regarding the crash of a Nigeria Air Force NGR931 aircraft at Igbokoda, Ondo State, with approximately 32 persons on board.

A statement by its Director-General, Capt. Chris Najomo, noted that the Authority was deeply saddened by this development and extended its thoughts and prayers to the personnel of the Nigeria Air Force, the occupants of the aircraft, their families and all those affected by this distressing incident.

Najomo added that while military aviation operations were outside the regulatory oversight and operational mandate of the Authority, the NCAA remained committed to supporting the national response to this incident.

“Accordingly, the NCAA stands ready to provide such technical expertise and assistance as may be required to support the ongoing search and rescue operations.

“The NCAA is closely monitoring developments and will continue to cooperate with the relevant authorities and agencies in accordance with established national emergency response protocols.

“At this difficult time, the Authority stands in solidarity with the Nigeria Air Force and all those directly affected by this incident. We remain hopeful for a positive outcome and pray for the safety and successful rescue of all involved,” Najomo said.

Aiyedatiwa Orders Full Support for Rescue Operations

In the same vein, the Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, has directed the immediate mobilisation of state emergency and health agencies to support the ongoing search and rescue operation.

Reacting to the development, Aiyedatiwa expressed deep sadness over the incident, extending his condolences to the Chief of Air Staff, officers and personnel of the Nigerian Air Force, as well as the families of those aboard the aircraft.

The governor said the state stood in solidarity with the affected families at the difficult moment, noting that his thoughts and prayers were with them.

Aiyedatiwa, according to a statement by his Chief Press Secretary, Ebenezer Adeniyan, has been in contact with the leadership of the Nigerian Air Force, the Chairman of Ilaje Local Government Area, Hon. Maurice Oripelaye, and security agencies deployed to the scene.

To strengthen the emergency response, the governor directed the State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), Ministry of Health and relevant security agencies to immediately mobilise and provide full logistical and human support to the Nigerian Air Force and other agencies involved in the search and rescue operation.

He also ordered that the crash site and its immediate surroundings be cordoned off and adequately secured to ensure that rescue personnel could carry out their operations without hindrance.

The governor urged residents of Igbokoda and neighbouring communities to remain calm, cooperate with emergency responders and avoid spreading unverified information about the incident.

The statement added that the Ondo State Government would continue to monitor developments and provide further updates as more information becomes available from the Nigerian Air Force.

Aiyedatiwa, therefore, prayed for the safety of the officers involved in the operation and expressed hope for the success of the ongoing rescue efforts.

No Survivors, Bodies, Wreckage Found in Swamp, Eyewitnesses Say

One of the eyewitnesses, who visited the scene of the crash, has described a grim situation at the swampy crash site, saying human remains, aircraft parts and personal effects were scattered across the area.

The eyewitness, Oluboyo Olusola, said some bodies were also found inside the water, while the difficult terrain initially prevented residents from reaching the crash site until naval personnel assisted in gaining access to the area.

Olusola, who said the incident occurred at about 10am, explained that he did not witness the aircraft go down but was alerted by a deafening sound that sent residents rushing towards the scene.

“We heard a loud noise like thunder and rushed to the scene, only to discover that it was an aircraft crash. Initially, we thought it was a helicopter but later understood it was an aircraft,” he said.

According to him, the condition of the crash site and what was recovered there raised fears that there might be no survivor.

“It was difficult to access the terrain, but with the assistance of some naval officers, we were able to get there and saw the remains of the aircraft, as well as human remains, clothes, shoes and other personal effects.

“Some of the bodies were also inside the water. From what I saw, it appeared that there was no survivor,” Olusola added, stressing that the difficult terrain and waterlogged nature of the area posed a major challenge to those trying to reach the wreckage.

The Olu of Igbokoda, Oba Afolabi Odidiomo, who also spoke on the incident, said he was in court when the crash occurred and immediately directed some palace aides to proceed to the scene to ascertain what had happened.

The monarch said he initially feared the aircraft could have been a commercial passenger plane, which would have resulted in an even higher number of casualties.

“I was worried because it must not be a plane, because the number of casualties would be just too high,” he said.

Oba Odidiomo said if the crash had occurred within the town, such an occurrence could have resulted in a major tragedy.

“Our first thanks to Almighty God is that it did not happen inside the town otherwise, the casualties would have been too many,” he said, sympathising with the families of those involved.

Describing the crash site, the monarch said: “The aircraft crashed into the river and a swampy area. It was raining when the incident happened, and the place was waterlogged. The aircraft did not catch fire, but a substantial part of it has gone into the water.”

He said authorities were still working to establish the full circumstances surrounding the crash, adding that, based on information gathered so far, there appeared to be no survivor.

“We cannot describe the exact situation for now, but from my investigation and what we have gathered so far, there was no survivor,” he said.

PDP Faction Condoles With Victims

The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) last night said that it was deeply saddened by the crash of a Nigerian Air Force ATR-42 aircraft near a naval base in Ondo State, South-West Nigeria, yesterday.

In a statement by the National Publicity Secretary, Ini Ememobong, the party described the air crash as a sad event, lamenting there were no survivors among the 32 persons on board.

Reacting to the incident, the National Chairman of the Party, Kabiru Tanimu Turaki, SAN, said: “Our service personnel have given so much for the unity and survival of this country, and news of their deaths is deeply painful.

“On behalf of the PDP family, I extend our heartfelt condolences to the Nigerian Air Force and the families of the fallen. We pray that such tragedies do not recur.”

The party urged a thorough and transparent investigation into the cause of the crash and prayed for the repose of the souls of the departed.

Defence Minister Mourns, Prays for Families

The Minister of Defence, Gen. Musa (rtd), has expressed deep sorrow over the tragic crash of a military aircraft with tail number NAF 931, involving dedicated personnel of the Armed Forces.

In a statement he personally signed, Musa noted that the painful incident claimed the lives of brave officers and airmen who were engaged in a routine flight mission while serving the nation with courage, unwavering devotion and selfless patriotism.

The loss of these valiant patriots, he said, is an irreparable blow not only to the military high command and their comrades-in-arms, but also to the entire nation.

The minister said these fine officers and men exemplified the highest standards of military professionalism, loyalty and commitment to the defence of Nigeria.

“On behalf of the Ministry of Defence, I extend our heartfelt condolences to His Excellency, the President and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR; the leadership of the Armed Forces; and, most especially, the immediate families, loved ones and colleagues of our fallen heroes.

“We share in your immense grief and stand shoulder-to-shoulder with you during this tragic hour.Our hearts also go out to the families of the civilians on board the ill-fated aircraft. We share your grief.”

He, however, disclosed that a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding the unfortunate crash had been ordered to ascertain its cause and ensure that all necessary operational safety protocols are reinforced across military aviation units.

“We pray that the Almighty God grants the souls of the departed eternal repose and gives their families, the military community and all Nigerians the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss,” he prayed.

Yar’Adua: Fallen Personnel Answered Nation’s Call with Courage

Besides, the Chairman of the Senate Committee on Army, Senator Abdulaziz Yar’Adua, has expressed deep sorrow over the death of Nigerian military personnel in a helicopter crash in Ilaje, Ondo State, describing the incident as a “sad day” for the nation’s Armed Forces.

Yar’Adua, a retired military officer, condoled with the Nigerian Military, the Nigerian Air Force and the families of the personnel who lost their lives in the crash, saying the fallen officers and personnel paid the ultimate price in service to the country.

In a statement issued on Monday, the senator said the tragedy had plunged the entire military family into mourning, while assuring the Armed Forces of the Senate Committee on Army’s continued support for efforts aimed at improving the safety and welfare of troops.

Yar’Adua said, “As a retired military officer, I understand the pain and weight of this loss.

“These brave men and women answered the call to serve our nation with courage, dedication, and honour, and their sacrifice will never be forgotten.”

The Senate committee chairman also commiserated with the Chief of Defence Staff, the Chief of Air Staff and the entire Armed Forces of Nigeria over the tragic incident.

He said, “We commiserate with the Chief of Defence Staff, the Chief of Air Staff, and the entire Armed Forces of Nigeria at this difficult time.

“This is indeed a sad day for the entire military family and for the nation as a whole,” he stated.

Yar’Adua extended his condolences to the bereaved families, praying for divine strength for them to cope with what he described as an “irreparable loss.”

“Our thoughts and prayers are with the bereaved families. We pray that Almighty Allah grants the souls of the departed eternal rest and gives their families the strength to bear this irreparable loss,” he said.

The senator assured the military that the Senate Committee on Army would continue to support initiatives designed to honour personnel who lose their lives in the line of duty and strengthen the safety and welfare of serving troops.

“The Senate Committee on Army stands with the Nigerian Military and will continue to support all efforts to honour our fallen heroes and improve the safety and welfare of our troops,” Yar’Adua added.

World.title: Another week of water woes for Durban: Long list of areas warned of reduced supply
World.content:
A pump failure at Durban Heights Treatment Works is reducing bulk water supply to eThekwini. Image: canva

Residents across large parts of eThekwini have been warned to use water sparingly after a technical failure reduced the amount of water being supplied to the city.

The municipality said its bulk water supplier, uMngeni-uThukela Water (UWW), experienced a technical failure affecting pumps supplying the Durban Heights Treatment Works.

Repairs are under way and are expected to be completed by Thursday, 8 October. In the meantime, the failure has reduced incoming water flows to eThekwini by approximately 50 million litres per day.



The municipality warned that residents in affected areas could experience reduced water availability while it manages the lower supply.

The municipality said the reduced supply is expected to affect areas supplied through the Northern Aqueduct and Mount Moriah Reservoir, including Pinetown and surrounding areas.

The City said conserving water will help it manage available resources and, importantly, prevent reservoirs from becoming depleted while repairs are being completed.

Durban areas supplied by Mount Moriah Reservoir

Residents in the following areas could be affected:

Pinetown

Parts of New Germany

New Germany Industrial Area

Sarnia

Cowie’s Hill

Nazareth

Mosely Park

KwaDabeka

Clermont

Berkshire Downs

Northern Aqueduct areas

A much larger number of areas supplied through the Northern Aqueduct could also experience reduced water availability.

Phoenix 1: Mount Edgecombe Hospital, Mount Edgecombe Estate, Broadlands, Southgate, Stonebridge, Clayfield, Campbells Town and Greenbury.



Phoenix 2: Sunford, Hannaford, Phoenix Highway, Longcroft, Longbury, Plaza, Southbury, Eastbury, Grove End, Sastri Park, Caneside, Canehaven as well as Woodview.

Phoenix 3: Redfern, Phoenix Industrial Park, Fernham, Whetstone and Bridge City.

Phoenix 4: Westham, Trenance Manor, Gandhi Settlement, Lenham, Ferham, Brookdale, Whetstone, Bhambayi, Amaoti as well as Sunford.

Phoenix 5: Woodview, Cornubia, Ottawa, Palmview and Trenance Park.

Phoenix 6: Mount Moriah and Corobrick.

Montview: Mountview, Brindhaven, Southridge, Glenhaven, Parkgate and Rietriver.

Trenance 1 Reservoir: Dawncrest, Oaklands, Surya Heights, Sanna Township, Rietriver, Mountview, Parkgate as well as Trenance Old Phase.

Trenance 3: Amaoti, Trenance Park new and old phases, Redcliffe, Buffelsdraai and Groenburg Estate.

Aloes: Avoca Hills, Corovoca, Khabazela, Duffs Road and Quarry Heights.

Newlands 1: Castlehill, B5, Westridge, Riverdene, Newlands West, Earlsfield and Briardale.

Newlands 2: Hillgrove, Briardale, Newlands East and Fossa.

Newlands 3: Newlands East, V.N. Naik School, Riverhorse Valley as well as eThekwini Hospital.

Newlands 4: Riverdene, Westridge and Newlands West.

Umhlanga and Durban North

The affected supply network also extends into several northern Durban suburbs and parts of Umhlanga.

Umhlanga North: Umhlanga CBD.

Umhlanga South: Umhlanga CBD and La Lucia.

Umhlanga 2 Reservoir: Umhlanga, Umhlanga Ridge, Prestondale, Ilala Ridge, Hawaan Forest, Umhlanga Manors, Westridge as well as Blackburn Village.

Durban North reservoirs: Redhill, Durban North, Beachway, Athlone, Japanese Garden and Riverside.

Virginia Reservoir and Tower: Glen Anil, Glen Hills as well as Umhlanga.

Sunningdale Reservoir and Towers: Sunningdale, La Lucia, Glenshley, Glen Anil, Somerset, Umhlanga as well as La Lucia Ridge.

Ambleside Reservoir: La Lucia, La Lucia Mall and Glenashley.

Effingham Reservoir: Avoca, Effingham, Glen Hills, Glen Anil, North Coast Road, Redhill as well as Greenwood Park.

Tafuleni Reservoir and Tower: Amaoti and the Ngoqokazi area.

KwaMashu, Ntuzuma and surrounding areas

Several northern and north-western communities are also supplied by reservoirs affected by the reduced bulk water flows.

KwaMashu 1: KwaMashu sections K, J, L, M, N, F, G and H, and B5.

KwaMashu 2: KwaMashu sections A, B, C, D, E, F and G, and Siyanda.

Ntuzuma 3: Ntuzuma F, G and H, part of M Section KwaMashu, Inanda A, B and C, Bester as well as Mshayazafe.

Ntuzuma 4: Ntuzuma E and F, Soweto, Inanda Newtown A and Lindelani A Section.

Ntuzuma 7: Ntuzuma A, B, C, D and F, Richmond Farm and Lindelani areas.

Amaotana: Matikwe, Mzinyathi, Silwane, Mgangeni, Senzokuhle and Amatata.

The municipality said it is closely monitoring the situation and will continue providing updates as more information becomes available from uMngeni-uThukela Water.

Residents in the affected and surrounding areas are being urged to avoid unnecessary water use while repairs continue.

World.title: Feroz Khan uncle shot dead on the R21, and the timing has Mzansi talking
World.content:
Feroz Khan's uncle-in-law was shot dead on the R21 in Ekurhuleni on Monday night. Image: Pexels, for illustrative purposes.

Former Crime Intelligence deputy head Feroz Khan’s uncle-in-law has been named as the man shot dead on the R21 in Ekurhuleni on Monday night.

It started with a car breakdown.

A friend came to help. Then the shots rang out.



But it’s the timing that has South Africans talking.

The killing happened just hours before one of the country’s most controversial former police generals was due to testify.

The man has been identified in media reports as Preggy Padayachee.

He was the uncle-in-law of Khan, the dismissed deputy head of South African Police Service (SAPS) Crime Intelligence.

The shooting happened on Monday, 5 October, on the R21 near Griffiths Road, in the direction of OR Tambo International Airport.

Police have not officially confirmed his identity or his link to Khan.



WHAT HAPPENED ON THE R21

Gauteng police spokesperson Colonel Dimakatso Nevhuhulwi said a driver in a Fiat broke down and called a friend for help, according to TimesLIVE.

The friend arrived with two other people.

While they were attending to the car, shots were fired at them.

The driver tried to escape the gunfire but lost control, and the car crashed into a barrier.

He was declared dead at the scene.

One passenger was shot and taken to hospital, while a third person escaped unharmed.

Police have opened a case of murder and attempted murder.

The motive is unknown, and no arrests have been made.

According to SABC News, forensic teams combed the scene for much of the night.

The shooting is believed to have been a targeted hit.

Police say investigations are ongoing to establish what happened and to identify those responsible.

WHO IS FEROZ KHAN?

Khan is one of the most talked-about figures at the Madlanga Commission.

The inquiry was set up after Lieutenant-General Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged that organised crime groups had infiltrated government.

The commission has heard allegations linking Khan to procurement irregularities, suspected bribery, interference in sensitive police operations and the leaking of confidential information.

Khan has not been found guilty of any of these allegations.

He also faces a separate criminal case.

In May, Khan was arrested and released on R20,000 bail alongside Gauteng Hawks head Major-General Ebrahim Kadwa.

The charges relate to alleged illegal dealing in, and unlawful possession of, precious metals.

Then, on 28 June, Khan himself was shot in Houghton, days before he was due to testify. He survived.

WHO WAS PREGGY PADAYACHEE?

Padayachee became a familiar face after that June shooting.

He spoke publicly on behalf of the family.

Outside Milpark Hospital, he told EWN that the people responsible for shooting his nephew “must pay.”

He also responded publicly when Khan was arrested.

WHAT THEY’RE SAYING ABOUT THE FEROZ KHAN UNCLE SHOOTING

The timing has fuelled speculation.

Khan was finally due to testify behind closed doors at the commission on Tuesday, 6 October.

But police have not indicated that his appearance is linked to the shooting.

Whether it’s connected to the earlier attack on Khan has also not been established.

Online, the reaction was swift.

A breaking news post about the shooting by journalist Pule Letshwiti-Jones drew nearly 300,000 views within 10 hours.

Many South Africans questioned the timing, with some calling for Khan’s testimony to be made public.

Khan may return for further testimony when the commission resumes public hearings next month.

Police have not linked the killing to the Madlanga Commission, and the motive remains unknown.

Investigations are continuing.

World.title: How much does it cost to: Take a roadtrip from Joburg to Durban
World.content:
One of the most popular roadtrips in South Africa is the drive from Johannesburg to Durban and vice versa. How much does it cost to do the roughly six-hour drive in 2026?

HOW MUCH FUEL DO YOU NEED TO BUDGET FOR?

Due to the increase in fuel prices this year, the amount you would need to budget for your roadtrip would have jumped in comparison to previous years. In 2026, you can expect to pay roughly R2800 to R3800 for a return trip in a petrol car. This is dependant on your car and fuel efficiency.

The N3 route from central Johannesburg to Durban’s CBD is approximately 570km long and expected to take six hours. This makes a return trip about 1140km. Tolls are also necessary to budget for. After the March 2026 increase, a one-way trip along the N3 costs R347.50 for light vehicles. You will pass five toll gates: De Hoek, Wilge, Tugela, Mooi, and Mariannhill. That comes to about R695 for the return journey.



A toll-free alternative exists via the R103 and the old main road through Villiers, Warden, Harrismith and Van Reenen Pass. However, it is slower.

Fuel is the major cost. Inland 95 petrol was R26.92 a litre in September, but the Central Energy Fund projected an October increase that would take it to about R29.75, and other projections put it as high as R29.98 a litre when the adjustment takes effect on Wednesday 7 October.

For a return trip at that price, a fuel-efficient car using 6 litres per 100km would spend about R2050 on petrol, bringing the total with tolls to roughly R2750. An average car using 7 litres per 100km would spend about R2400 on fuel, or roughly R3100 in total. A thirstier car or small SUV using 9 litres per 100km would spend about R3080 on fuel, or roughly R3770 in total.

Diesel drivers shouldn’t expect relief either, as wholesale diesel was projected to rise by more than R2.60 a litre.

OTHER COSTS TO CONSIDER

While the other costs to consider are subject to the reason you’re visiting Durban (or Johannesburg), take a look at what else you could be spending on.

Accommodation: This varies widely depending on season and location

A couple of meal and coffee stops along the N3

Activities during your trip and more fuel to get around

There are some easy ways to save. Coastal petrol is cheaper than inland, so topping up once you reach KwaZulu-Natal can work in your favour. Keeping a steady speed helps too, since highway efficiency drops quickly above 110km/h. Splitting costs with passengers is the biggest saver of all.



So, you will need tp budget about R3000 to R3500 for fuel and tolls in a typical car, then add whatever you plan to spend on accommodation and spending money.
