World.title: Teen missing after swimming in Cape Vidal beach
World.content:
The National Sea Rescue Institute (NSRI) announced that a teenager went missing after he was caught in a rip current at Cape Vidal beach on Saturday (3 October) afternoon.

TEEN MISSING IN CAPE VIDAL

Melinda Snyman, NSRI St Lucia station commander, said that a teenager went missing after he was caught in a rip at Cape Vidal beach on Saturday 3 October. Cape Vidal Beach is situated in northern KwaZulu-Natal, north of St Lucia. The teen boy, 16, had been swimming with another boy, 14, when the incident occurred.

According to the NSRI Station, the 14-year-old was rescued by a bystander, who was on holiday from Benoni, who witnessed the incident.



“At 15h07, Saturday, 3 October, NSRI St Lucia duty crew were activated following reports of a drowning in progress at Cape Vidal Beach. Eyewitness reports indicated that 2 teenagers were in distress in the surf zone appearing to be caught in rip currents. NSRI rescue swimmers responded directly to the scene and our NSRI rescue vehicle, towing our JetRIB rescue craft, Rescue 40 Bravo, responded,” read the statement.

THE 14-YEAR-OLD BOY RESCUED SAFELY

On arrival on the scene the NSRI found that the 14-year-old boy had been rescued safely to the beach by “a female Good Samaritan, from Benoni, who had launched into the water to go to the aid of the 2 teenagers caught in rip currents.”

The NSRI rescue craft was launched from the beach and conducted extensive search efforts in and beyond the surf zone for a 16 year old boy who had gone missing in the surf zone. Despite extensive sea and shoreline search efforts there remains no signs of the missing teenager.

“NSRI medics attended to the 14 year old on the beach. He was treated on the scene for non-fatal drowning symptoms and handed into the care of SISILA EMS paramedics and transported to hospital by SISILA EMS ambulance in a stable condition. He is expected to make a full recovery.”

“The rescued teenager and the missing teenager, locals, from Mtubatuba, friends visiting the beach with family, had been swimming together when it appears they were caught in rip currents.”

Police have opened an investigation. Police Search and Rescue – WPDS (Water Policing and Diving Service), assisted by iSimangaliso Wetland Park rangers, are continuing in ongoing search efforts for the missing teenager.



This follows the news of a Grade 12 Affies learner passing away just a day after his 18th birthday.

World.title: 'What more is there to cut?' South Africans react to record fuel prices
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - There’s nothing more to cut.

Those are the sentiments of eNCA viewers after the government confirmed that fuel prices will reach record highs this week.

Petrol prices will rise above R30 a litre for the first time when the increases take effect on Wednesday.

For many South Africans, the latest increase comes after months of cutting back on household expenses.

Viewers say there is simply nothing left to cut, with some worried that rising fuel costs will make it even harder to afford basic necessities.

World.title: Duduzile Zuma, Nhlamulo Ndhlela challenge MK Party expulsion in court
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Expelled uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party members Duduzile Zuma-Sambudla and Nhlamulo Ndhlela are challenging their expulsion in the South Gauteng High Court.

The former MPs were expelled from the party in June after being accused of gross misconduct.

They have now approached the court, arguing that their expulsion was unfair and unlawful.

Ndhlela is also seeking to have his position as a Member of Parliament reinstated.

The pair allege that people close to MK Party leader Jacob Zuma influenced the decision to dismiss them.

In June, the MK Party said the duo’s social media activity and conduct at party events had caused confusion and fuelled divisions within the organisation.

“The national officials have resolved that Ms Zuma-Sambudla and Mr Nhlamulo Ndhlela have acted in a manner fundamentally inconsistent with the values, discipline, constitutional principles and organisational interests of the MK Party,” MK Party secretary-general Sibonelo Nomvalo said at the time.

World.title: Taxi industry feels the pinch as fuel prices jump
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The National Taxi Alliance is calling on the government to implement austerity measures to cut spending and cushion citizens from rising fuel prices.

The price of 93 unleaded petrol is set to increase by R3.12 a litre, while 95 petrol will rise by R3.33 from Wednesday.

This will be one of the biggest fuel price increases in recent years.

Diesel prices will also rise by between R2.84 and R3.24 a litre.

The increases come as the conflict between Iran and the United States continues to put pressure on global oil prices.

World.title: Feroz Khan expected to seek postponement at Madlanga Commission
World.content:
PRETORIA - Disgraced former Crime Intelligence boss Feroz Khan is expected to seek a postponement of his testimony before the Madlanga Commission following the fatal shooting of his uncle-in-law, Preggy Padayachee.

Padayachee was shot dead on Monday night.

Khan was due to begin his in-camera testimony before the commission on Tuesday.

Last month, the commission said it would lay criminal charges against Khan after he failed to appear at the inquiry despite being subpoenaed.

The commission also rejected his application for a postponement.

World.title: Reiger Park shooting accused back in court for bail judgment
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The men accused of killing two South African Police Service Anti-Gang Unit officers and two women in Reiger Park are back in court as they await judgment on their bail applications.

The two Anti-Gang Unit officers were part of a crime-prevention team patrolling the area when they were allegedly ambushed.

In the chaos that followed, two women, who were not involved in the confrontation, were caught in the crossfire and also lost their lives.

The accused have denied any involvement in the killings. They have presented alibis as part of their defence, maintaining that they were elsewhere when the shooting took place.

One of the main accused, Regan Collis, has also made a serious allegation about his alleged confession. Collis claims it was obtained under torture, challenging the circumstances under which the statement was made.

The court has also heard conflicting versions of CCTV evidence.

The State has relied on the footage as part of its case, while the defence has disputed aspects of what the CCTV shows and how it should be interpreted.

The State also alleges that the officers' service rifles were stolen during the attack.

World.title: You can finally opt out of pesky telemarketer calls. Here's how
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - South Africans could soon get relief from pesky telemarketing calls.

The Department of Trade, Industry and Competition and the National Consumer Commission have established an Opt-Out Registry to help consumers stop unwanted direct marketing calls and messages.

The NCC has published draft guidelines for the opt-out regulations, with the system set to be officially announced on Wednesday.

“We have started encouraging direct marketers to register,” says NCC spokesperson Pheto Ntaba.

The rollout will take place in phases. Direct marketers will first be required to register on the system before consumers are invited to create their own profiles.

The registry will allow consumers to indicate that they do not want to receive unsolicited direct marketing calls and messages.

Consumers are expected to be able to fully use the system by March. However, the registration website is already open.

World.title: Pirates eye record fifth MTN8 crown
World.content:
DURBAN - Defending champions Orlando Pirates will be out to retain their MTN8 crown when they face Mamelodi Sundowns in Saturday’s final at Moses Mabhida Stadium.

With silverware and bragging rights on the line, two of South African football’s biggest clubs are preparing for another high-stakes encounter.

Orlando Pirates have enjoyed considerable success in domestic competitions in recent years. But head coach Abdeslam Ouaddou believes that while past triumphs can offer a psychological boost, they will have little bearing on what happens on the pitch.

For Ouaddou, the final will come down to preparation, tactics and how each side responds to the occasion.

READ | Pirates victory closes gap behind Sundowns to one point

“Look, it’s a different game and a different era. You have to prepare for it with a lot of ambition and a lot of seriousness,” Ouaddou says.

“Some coaches can change their way to play; they may have a different strategy. These things can help mentally, but the reality will be the match and how you attack the match and how you prepare for it, especially how you study the opponent and how you can use the weaknesses of the opponent.”

The pressure of a final can often be as challenging as the opposition itself. But the Buccaneers insist they are determined to shut out the noise and concentrate on the job in front of them.

Pirates defender Thapelo Xoki says the team will treat Saturday’s showdown on its own merits rather than dwelling on previous finals.

READ MORE | Nkota returns to Pirates from Al-Ettifaq

“What is known to us is to always approach the final as it is and not look at past finals. The finals we have played in the past are all in the past for us.”

Pirates and Sundowns are no strangers to battles with major stakes attached. Both teams have also enjoyed strong form heading into the final, setting the scene for what Ouaddou expects to be a competitive and high-quality encounter.

“I think the two teams will come with a good mindset. I think we are in a good timing, either for them or for us. The two teams are doing well before the FIFA break. Hopefully, we will have a good game,” Ouaddou adds.

World.title: Asian stocks mixed despite tech-led Wall Street record
World.content:
HONG KONG - Asian stocks were mixed on Tuesday as a tech-led record on Wall Street was tempered by ongoing worries about a spike in government borrowing costs.

Oil held most of the losses seen in response to a G7 release of stockpiles, Saudi Arabia's price cut and a pick-up in Gulf exports to pre-war levels, though supply fears are keeping global benchmark Brent above $100 a barrel.

The US Nasdaq closed at a fresh peak thanks to rallies in tech giants including Nvidia, SpaceX and Meta, though observers pointed out that the market gains were increasingly concentrated on a few stocks.

Asia struggled to match the positive energy on Wall Street, where the Dow and S&P 500 also ended higher.

Tokyo, Hong Kong, Sydney, Jakarta and Wellington rose, but Seoul, Singapore, Taipei and Manila edged down. Shanghai was closed for a holiday.

The tepid performance comes amid long-running uncertainty among traders over the Middle East crisis, which has fanned energy costs and in turn pushed inflation higher -- putting pressure on central banks to hike interest rates.

This has pushed government bond yields up to levels not seen for decades.

Analysts have pointed out that the race to build out AI data centres, servers and chips has compounded that problem, with tech titans no longer able to rely on their vast piles of cash.

Oil prices inched up following Monday's drop of almost two percent, though Saudi Aramco's chief executive Amin Nasser, speaking after the G7 release, warned over global stockpiles.

Middle East oil exports, excluding Iran, surpassed their pre-war levels last week despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler.

World.title: Patient zero: Kenya confirms first ever Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health CS Aden Duale briefs on Kenya's first ever case of Ebola at Afya House, Nairobi. He is accompanied by other Ministry of Health, and WHO officials. [Jonah Onyango, Standard]

Kenya has today, October 6, 2026, confirmed its first case of Ebola.

The case was detected in a Kenyan citizen who travelled by road from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) to Kampala, Uganda, before flying to Nairobi aboard a Jambojet flight on Saturday last week.

The patient has since died after receiving treatment at Nairobi Hospital, The Standard can confirm.

According to Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, the patient underwent public health screening upon arrival at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), Nairobi, in line with health protocols.

The patient was picked up by a relative at JKIA and driven to Nairobi Hospital, where he was isolated before being transferred to the hospital’s East Wing Isolation Facility.

The confirmation comes months after public outcry over the government’s decision to allow the establishment of an Ebola quarantine facility in Laikipia County, funded by the United States government.

Activists and lobby groups protested the facility, arguing that it could expose Kenyans to the deadly virus. At least three protesters died during clashes with security officers in early June.

Kenya has over the last few months tightened its response to Ebola, with public health emergency centers activated at both levels of government, and screening intensified at all border points.

Health authorities in June said surveillance had been heightened following the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain in the DRC, which spread into neighbouring Uganda.

As at October 2026, the DRC has reported more than 8,000 confirmed Ebola cases and about 4,080 deaths since the outbreak began in May, according to the draft.

The World Health Organisation has described the outbreak as the worst ever.

World.title: How KNEC plans to stop cheating in 2026 exams
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) Chief Executive Officer Dr David Njengere. [File]

The Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) will use smart padlocks to secure all examination storage containers as more than 3.6 million candidates sit the 2026 national examinations and assessments.

KNEC Chief Executive Officer Dr David Njengere said the council would monitor the containers from its headquarters to prevent anyone from accessing examination papers before the scheduled times.

“Last year KNEC piloted the use of smart padlocks in 250 containers. This year all containers will be secured using the smart padlocks which will be monitored from the KNEC headquarters,” said Dr Njengere.

Under the system, officials will open containers at designated times. Officials will access Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA) and Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA) papers at 6 a.m., while centre managers will collect Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) papers at 7 a.m. and 12:30 p.m.

However, Dr Njengere identified mobile phones as the biggest challenge in preventing examination malpractice.

“Mobile phones remain our biggest challenge in administration of KCSE examination,” observed Dr Njengere.

He warned that the council would not allow candidates or examination officials to have mobile phones at examination centres during examination sessions.

“Any contravention of this rule will constitute a malpractice as per the KNEC Act and the Rules and Regulations,” noted Dr Njengere.

The council will deploy 342,005 contracted professionals to administer and manage the examinations and assessments. They include centre managers, supervisors, invigilators, security officers and drivers.

For KCSE, KNEC will deploy 10,765 centre managers, 12,274 supervisors, 57,432 invigilators and 21,388 security officers. Each examination centre will have at least two police officers.

Centre managers will collect KCSE papers twice a day, and KNEC will place morning and afternoon papers in marked cartons to reduce mix-ups and unauthorised access.

KNEC has personalised question papers with candidates’ details, and examiners will receive anonymised scripts with those details removed.

The 2026 examination and assessment season will involve 3,634,846 candidates, a 6.13 per cent increase from the 3,424,836 registered in 2025.

KCSE rehearsals will take place on Friday, October 16. Examinations for papers with low candidature will run from Monday, October 19 to Friday, October 30, while papers with large candidature will run from Monday, November 2 to Friday, November 20.

KPSEA and KJSEA assessments will run from Monday, October 26 to Friday, October 30.

KNEC Chairperson Prof. Julius Nyabundi said the council was preparing for possible disruption from El Nino rains.

“As we start off the 2026 field administration season, one of the risks we contend with are the attempts to cheat in assessments and examination,” said Prof. Nyabundi.

He urged candidates, parents and examination officials to protect the integrity of the examinations, warning that malpractice could undermine public confidence in the education system.

“Cheating in examinations undermines public confidence in the credibility, fairness and quality of the entire education system,” noted Prof. Nyabundi.

KNEC will operate a 24-hour call centre with toll-free numbers for candidates, officials and members of the public to report incidents and seek assistance during the examination period.

The 2026 cycle will continue the implementation of Competency-Based Education assessments, including School-Based Assessments in primary, junior and senior school.

Grade 10 learners are undertaking their first School-Based Assessment, which will contribute 15 marks towards the Kenya Certificate of Basic Education.

World.title: Mbadi hits out at Sifuna, says opposition lacks economic agenda
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

National Treasury CS John Mbadi after opening new classrooms and administration blocks constructed by the M-Pesa Foundation at Ligongo Primary School in Suba South Constituency. [James Omoro, Standard]

The National Treasury CS John Mbadi has hit out at Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, saying that criticising President William Ruto should not be an agenda for a presidential candidate.

Speaking when he opened new classrooms and administration blocks constructed by M-Pesa Foundation at Ligongo Primary School in Suba South Constituency, Mbadi said lack of economic agenda makes the opposition unsuitable to lead the country.

“I have heard of opposition leaders who want the presidency, but they do not have an agenda for the economic transformation of this country,” he said.

The CS claimed that none of the opposition leaders is suitable for the presidency.

“These opposition leaders cannot make any economic change in this country. They should not be elected,” he said.

He told Nyanza residents to shun the new wave of opposition led by Sifuna.

Mbadi claimed that opposition leaders lack political direction.

He said Sifuna had taken too long to unveil a political party that he will use to run for the presidency.

“Do not join the opposition bandwagon. We are just a few months away from the General Election, but Sifuna still doesn’t know a political party he will use to run for the presidency. They are still leaving in confusion,” Mbadi said.

He said Sifuna has not demonstrated how to improve this country’s economy.

“Former President Uhuru Kenyatta left the economy of this country in tatters. We have tried to improve it but we are not yet where we want it to be,” Mbadi said.

He urged Nyanza residents to support Ruto.

The CS said Ruto’s government had improved mega infrastructural projects across the country as part of economic transformation.

He cited the 74 km Mbita- Sindo- Sori road, Lake Victoria ring road and other infrastructure projects as some of the reasons residents should support Ruto.

“I urge you to support Ruto so that we can continue acquiring more development projects in this region,” Mbadi said.

World.title: Kericho Annex Prison under scrutiny over death of remand prisoner
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Brenda Chemutai, 19, who allegedly committed suicide inside the Kericho Annex Prison where she was awaiting trial for an offence of being in possession of bhang that was seized in a vehicle allegedly belonging to a senior police officer. [Courtesy]

Questions are mounting over security and accountability at Kericho Annex Prison following the death of a 19-year-old remand prisoner in a suspected case of suicide.

Her family is demanding answers about how she obtained a bedsheet and why they were not notified until nearly 10 hours after the incident.

Brenda Chemutai was reportedly found hanging from a double-decker bed at around 9 am when her fellow cellmates were having breakfast on Friday.

The cell had eight inmates, who had gone for breakfast, according to a police report.

However, her relatives state they were not informed until about 7 pm, after her body had already been taken from the prison and transferred to the Kericho County Hospital Mortuary.

The delay has raised serious concerns for the family, which calls for authorities to clarify what happened between the time Chemutai was discovered and when her next of kin were contacted.

Kericho East Directorate of Criminal Investigation (DCI) officer, Kennedy Apindi, said police have launched investigations following reports from prison officials that the incident was a suicide.

He mentioned that preliminary information indicated Chemutai allegedly used a bedsheet.

The family, however, insists that investigators determine when she was found, who discovered her, when the incident was reported to police, who authorised her body’s removal, and why her relatives were not notified immediately.

“We had spoken with Brenda. She was expected to be released around December, and by January we would all have been together at home,” said her sister, Phyllis Cherotich.

Cherotich added that the family had seen no signs indicating Chemutai intended to take her own life.

"Her death has shocked us deeply. She never mentioned any plans of this nature. We want to understand how this was possible given the level of security at the facility," she said.

The circumstances surrounding the alleged use of a bedsheet have also raised questions for the family.

Her uncle, Michael Rono, questioned how such an item came into Chemutai's possession while she was in a remand facility.

"I am deeply surprised. When one enters the prison, one is carefully searched. Where did the bedsheet come from? We ask the government to ensure justice is done," Rono said.

Chemutai had been in remand since 2024, with her relatives saying she was arrested while still a minor and had spent nearly two years awaiting the conclusion of her case.

She was being tried for the offence of possession of bhang in a vehicle allegedly belonging to a senior police officer.

Her death has consequently brought renewed scrutiny to not only what happened inside the prison but also the circumstances that led to her prolonged detention.

Youth activists from the Voice of Youth Organisation, led by Kelvin Kipchichir, have joined the family in demanding investigations into both the death and the case that resulted in Chemutai's detention.

Kipchichir claimed Chemutai was arrested alongside other suspects in a vehicle allegedly linked to an Officer Commanding Station serving in Kakamega.

According to the activists, police recovered 32 rolls of bhang from the vehicle, while some of the suspects allegedly fled, leaving Chemutai behind.

The claims have not been independently established.

Kipchichir questioned why Chemutai remained in custody for such a prolonged period and called for scrutiny of the circumstances surrounding the vehicle and its alleged connection to the police officer.

“We are concerned that an OCS in the National Police Service could allow a vehicle to be used by an individual with a known criminal record,” he said.

He called on the Ministry of Interior to establish who owned or controlled the vehicle and under what circumstances it was allegedly being used.

The activists said the vehicle was still at Kericho Police Station.

For the family, the tragedy has been compounded by personal loss. Chemutai's father died while she was in remand, while she leaves behind a young child.

Relatives said detectives had informed them that the person alleged to own the bhang had since been arrested and was being held in Kisumu.

But the immediate question for Chemutai's family is what happened during her final hours.

They want a clear account of the period between the reported discovery of her body at about 9 am and the notification of the family nearly 10 hours later.

They also want investigators to establish how the bedsheet allegedly used in the incident came into her possession and whether prison officers followed all required procedures after she was found.

The activists are calling for the inquiry to extend beyond the death of Chemutai to her arrest, the length of her detention and the handling of the case against her.

The family has demanded a transparent and independent investigation, saying it wants answers on how a teenager who entered the justice system while still a minor ended up dead in remand custody.

The family says it wants those questions answered before proceeding with burial arrangements.

World.title: Pregnant woman found dead by roadside in Kirinyaga with head, hip injuries
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The National Police Service (NPS) has launched investigations after the body of a pregnant woman was found by the roadside in the Itangi area of Mwea East Sub-County, Kirinyaga County.

The woman, identified as Catherine Njeru, was found early Friday morning along the Piai-Itangi Murram Road with visible injuries to her head and hip.

In a statement, NPS said the incident is being investigated as a suspected murder.

"The NPS condoles with the family, relatives, and friends of the deceased and commits to expeditious and conclusive investigations to ensure that any person or persons responsible for this barbaric crime are brought to justice," read the statement.

Police have urged residents of Itangi to remain calm and refrain from speculation as the investigation continues.

Anyone with information that could assist the investigation has been asked to report to the nearest police station or a law enforcement officer.

The matter is being investigated by Kirinyaga County Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) officers, local Sub-County police and Central Regional Police Command, led by the Regional Criminal Investigations Officer.

According to NPS, the Inspector General of the National Police Service has also been briefed on the incident and directed the Director of Criminal Investigations to expedite the probe and establish the facts surrounding the woman's death.

World.title: Ruto downplays rivalry over oil refinery in East Africa
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Former Nigeria President Olesugun Obasanjo, Ali Dangote, President William Ruto and Uganda President Yoweri Museveni during launch of the Lamu Refinery on September 30, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has played down suggestions of rivalry between Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania over competing refinery projects, saying East Africa’s growing demand for petroleum products can support several facilities across the region.

Speaking during a media interview at State House Mombasa, Ruto said Kenya had no objection to Uganda and Tanzania pursuing their own refinery projects, arguing that the different facilities could complement rather than compete with one another.

“There is no bad blood at all. There is no problem,” Ruto said.

His remarks came a day after he presided over the groundbreaking of the Lamu refinery project, which the government is positioning as a major component of a wider industrial complex on the Kenyan coast.

Ruto said he had discussed Uganda’s plans with President Yoweri Museveni and agreed that Kampala could proceed with a smaller refinery without threatening Kenya’s investment in Lamu.

He said Kenya would even be prepared to buy petroleum products from Uganda if they could reach the Kenyan market at competitive prices.

“If it is manufactured there in Uganda and the oil from that place is near Busia, and it can reach Busia at a lower price, we will buy oil from anywhere and bring it to Busia,” Ruto said.

The President argued that the size of the regional petroleum market meant there was room for more than one refinery.

“This one in Lamu cannot serve all of us; it will be necessary to expand,” he said, adding that East Africa had “enough opportunity” for multiple facilities.

Ruto also extended the same approach to Tanzania, saying Kenya could participate in a refinery project in Tanga if it is eventually developed.

“Even if the one in Tanga is built, we as Kenya will go and buy some shares there. There is no problem,” he said.

The comments point to a regional energy market in which petroleum products could move across borders depending on availability, transport costs and prices. Rather than treating refinery projects as competing national investments, Ruto said the facilities could strengthen economic cooperation within the East African Community.

The President said the Lamu refinery would also address some of the challenges Kenya faces from dependence on imported refined petroleum products.

“Lamu will give us an opportunity to have fuel without the fluctuations that we have now,” he said.

He linked the proposed refinery to the need to reduce Kenya’s exposure to international oil price shocks, disruptions caused by instability in oil-producing regions and costs associated with transporting petroleum products over long distances.

Ruto said local refining could reduce expenses related to insurance and transportation while providing Kenya with greater access to locally processed fuel.

However, he said the larger economic opportunity would extend beyond the refinery itself. The government plans to develop industries around the facility, including petrochemical, chemical and plastics manufacturing.

The refinery could also provide raw materials for industries producing fertiliser and bitumen, potentially reducing reliance on imports of some petroleum-based products.

The broader development is expected to create opportunities for employment, investment and trade while strengthening Lamu’s position as an industrial and logistics centre.

Ruto said Kenya’s policy would be guided by competitiveness, allowing businesses and consumers to obtain petroleum products from whichever regional facility can supply them efficiently and at favourable prices.

The President maintained that Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania therefore did not need to view their refinery plans through the lens of rivalry.

Instead, he said, multiple facilities could create a larger and more integrated petroleum market capable of serving the needs of East Africa.

World.title: Outrage as KDF officers detain human rights team along Malindi-Lamu highway
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Activists clashed with police at a Gamba roadblock after being stopped en route to Lamu. [Vocal Africa]

Six members of Muslims for Human Rights (MUHURI), including five staff and a board member, were detained by Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) officers along the Malindi-Lamu highway, prompting condemnation from human rights organisations.

The incident occurred on Monday as the team travelled from Lamu to Mombasa after a field mission. The officers reportedly intercepted them between Gamba and Minjila, detained them for about two hours, then released them.

The Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC) and MUHURI said the officers covered their faces and refused to identify themselves when the human rights team challenged them.

The five staff members were identified as Francis Auma, Abdulrahman Mwanga, Fredrick Okado, Lathan Yusuf and Mohamed Abdla, while the board member was identified as Khelef Khalifa.

In a joint statement, the two organisations said the officers' actions violated a High Court ruling by Justice Bahati Mwamuye requiring security personnel to wear clearly visible name tags or identifiable service numbers on their uniforms.

The ruling also prohibits security officers from wearing hoods, balaclavas or face masks to conceal their identities.

"We call on the KDF and other security agencies to comply with the court order. Officers who violate the directive should be held accountable and face legal consequences," the joint statement read in part.

The organisations also demanded immediate compliance with a recent court order lifting the dusk-to-dawn curfew that had been imposed for more than a decade along the Minjila-Lamu highway.

They argued that the curfew had created conditions for arbitrary stops, harassment and detention of travellers using the route, citing the detention of the MUHURI team as an example.

The organisations urged security agencies to respect court orders and protect the rights of travellers using the highway.

However, a senior Anti-Terror Police officer aware of the incident told The Standard that the officers from the Border Police Unit (BPU) manning such roadblocks and tactical borders conceal their faces to protect their identities.

"In high-risk areas prone to insurgent or terrorist retaliation, including Kanyoyo in Kitui heading to Garissa, Moyale and Lamu, anonymity is framed as a matter of personal and operational survival," she stated.

World.title: Kalonzo signals at working with Ruto if 2027 poll is free and fair
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka at St Michael and All Angels ACK Cathedral in Bondo, Siaya County on September 27, 2026. [Clinton Ambujo, Standard]

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka has signalled that the Opposition could accept the outcome of the 2027 General Election and consider working with President William Ruto if he wins through a free and fair contest.

Speaking at St Michael and All Angels ACK Cathedral in Bondo, Siaya County, Kalonzo said the political class must commit itself to democratic competition and be prepared to accept the verdict of voters.

“If you beat us, we will have to consider if you have behaved yourself, and if we beat you, we have to look at all these things,” he said.

The Wiper leader also called for stronger democratic institutions, warning against political confrontation that could deepen divisions in the country.

“We have a nation here. We have to make this country truly democratic. I do not think we have a shortcut,” he said.

Kalonzo used the church service to make a broader appeal for a united and effective Opposition, saying political leaders had a responsibility to work together in the national interest.

“Kenya needs a functional official opposition; one that is united and does not thrive on disunity. As leaders, we have a responsibility to work together and play our part in fixing this nation,” he said.

He said he had remained in the Opposition even when some political allies moved into government.

“I have stood in the opposition all these years. Even when others joined government, my brother Eugene Wamalwa and I remained steadfast, and we will continue to stand firm,” he said.

Kalonzo also turned his attention to Parliament, claiming that the National Assembly had been “captured” and challenging lawmakers in both Houses to exercise their constitutional responsibilities.

“The National Assembly has been captured. Let this message reach every leader in the National Assembly and the Senate: you have the power to change things, not just to complain later,” he said.

He urged legislators to defend the interests of the people who elected them and to put the country ahead of political considerations.

The former Vice President also defended retired President Uhuru Kenyatta against claims that he is financing the Opposition ahead of the 2027 contest.

Kalonzo argued that presidential campaigns have historically relied on networks of political allies and supporters rather than family resources alone.

“But here we are saying, please let Uhuru rest; he is a retired President. Stop saying he is our financier,” he said.

Kalonzo cited previous presidential campaigns involving Uhuru, former President Mwai Kibaki and Raila Odinga, arguing that major political campaigns require support from friends and associates.

“Even when Uhuru was running for President, or Kibaki and even Raila, no family has enough resources to support a presidential campaign. It is friends who support you,” he said.

He warned that Kenya was at a delicate political moment and urged leaders to avoid actions that could deepen instability.

“We should not allow the country to get to a worse situation than where it is. We are on the edge of a cliff; the country is at a crossroads,” he said.

World.title: Unprecedented student protests are rocking France. Here’s why they’re angry
World.content:
France is struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades. What started as a demonstration in support of striking teachers at a suburban high school to the north of Paris has snowballed into a national crisis.

Hundreds of schools have been forced to close and more than 5,000 people have been taken into police custody, most of them minors with no previous criminal records. Students, teachers and policemen have been injured. One student in the north-east city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade and another in Tours, the use of an eye.

The next big test for the government will come Tuesday when thousands of people are expected to join protest marches across the country.

Here’s what to know

What’s going on?

The original protest at Saint-Exupéry high school in a Parisian suburb on September 21 attracted little attention. Pupils had joined their teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff sent to the school, the strike ended, but by then the match had been lit. According to student leader Manès Nadel, it spread like wildfire.

“It’s an unprecedented number of schools that are now involved,” he said, adding that France’s Education Ministry had been “totally overwhelmed by the crisis.”

Police officers stand in front of protesters amid tear gas as demonstrators carry out blockading action near the Kerichen high school in Brest, western France, on October 2. Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty Images

Pupils at lycées in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances, and within days similar scenes were reported across the country, from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement. More than 100 high schools have been damaged since the start of the protest movement.

Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. One policeman was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in Alençon, a technique now prohibited by law.

The violence and the speed with which the protests have grown have taken many by surprise, but the grievances are long-standing — an overcrowded, ill-equipped and understaffed education system that many students feel is no longer fit for purpose. Videos have circulated for years showing classrooms with too few desks or chairs, or students finding their classes cancelled when an absent teacher is not replaced.

A fertility spike in France in 2010 has led to a rise in the number of high school students now attending schools that have seen years of real-terms funding cuts. Secondary schools now have fewer teachers than in 2008, despite an extra 250,000 students enrolled. In the public sector, 70% of classrooms have more than 30 pupils per class.

What is the government’s response?

Critics say the government’s response has been slow and tin-eared. Initially much of it was focused on the far-left LFI party and its presence at the barricades. The party, led by Jean-Luc Melanchon, who’s expected to do well in the country’s presidential election next spring, has repeatedly defended both the students’ right to protest and his party’s right to be there. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for a firm police response and the cost of the protest. Damage to schools in the greater Paris region alone is estimated at 7 million euros ($7.84 million).

There was an initial concession over the fees at technological high schools that had been planned for 2027 but this has now been removed from the government’s budget. “The government’s response has been irresponsible and it confirms exactly why the students are angry, because they are never heard,” said Manes. “They are responding only with repression.”

A teenager films with his mobile phone as police charge at demonstrators to disperse them on October 1 during the blockade of the Mounier secondary school in Grenoble, France. Benoit Pavan/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images

The protesters do now have the government’s full attention, especially after a spike in violence late last week, when the interior minister noted a shift from student protest to urban violence and some 2,000 people were taken into custody in a single day. On Friday, Edouard Geffray, the education minister, met with student leaders. No agreement was reached, however, and the student leaders called for a massive turnout on Tuesday immediately afterward.

The government’s response is being hampered by the poor state of the public finances. It is trying to pass a 2027 budget that narrows the deficit to around 5 percent of GDP, a feat that can only be achieved by painful belt-tightening. Last week France’s 10-year bond yield briefly topped 5 percent last week, its highest since 2002, as the protests compounded concerns about the country’s fiscal outlook.

The unrest has fired the starting gun on what promises to be a vicious race between the far right and far left for the presidency, with much of the center floundering in the polls. For the far left, the pupils are a natural constituency. For the government, they’re a source of disorder and of spending pressure at the worst possible moment.

Firefighters extinguish a fire at the entrance of the Leonard de Vinci secondary school following a blockading action by protesting students, in Paris on October 2, 2026. Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty Images

Historically, student protests have not gone well for French governments. The student protest of May 1968 turned into the largest strike in French history, in a country that knows a thing or two about strikes. One of its slogans was “be realistic, ask for the impossible.”

The difference now is that the students who’ve taken to the barricades once again don’t feel they are asking for much. In fact, they say they are demanding the bare minimum: an education system that allows them to learn.

World.title: Britain’s Green Party votes to class Zionism as a form of racism
World.content:
Reuters — Britain’s Green Party voted on Sunday to class Zionism as a form of racism, drawing criticism from British Jews and from the Israeli government which said it now viewed the party as “a body that gives legitimacy to terrorism.”

The party – which received six percent of the vote in national elections in 2024 – said it regarded Zionism as “an ethnonationalist political project” and repeated its call for Britain’s Labour government to end all arms trade with Israel.

“The motion also restates the Green Party’s backing for the right to self-determination and calls for the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine,” the party said in a statement.

The definition of Zionism – which inspired the foundation of the modern state of Israel in the 20th century – and what it implies for the rights of non-Jews in Israel and neighbouring territory, is contentious. Jewish groups sometimes define it as a right to Jewish self-determination.

The Green Party motion passed by a majority of 1,022 to 813 despite opposition from many senior figures. Party leader Zack Polanski, who is seeking election to Parliament on Thursday in former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s now-vacant London constituency, did not vote.

The result was condemned by British Jewish groups.

“The Green Party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party,” the Movement for Progressive Judaism said, adding that the support of some Jews for the motion did not mean it would not be used to discriminate against others.

Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar has decided to declare Polanski barred from entering Israel, the foreign ministry said in a post on X Sunday.

It said the Green Party motion “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination,” the ministry said.

Mothin Ali, deputy leader of the Green Party and a supporter of the motion, told Sky News on Saturday that the heavy Palestinian death toll in Israel’s conflict with Hamas – which followed the Palestinian militant group’s deadly 2023 attack on an Israeli music festival – was the key context for the vote.

“The motion defines Zionism quite clearly. It defines it as an ethnonationalist movement. It defines it as ethnic cleansing. It defines it as genocide,” Ali said.

Britain’s government views Israeli settlers’ actions in the West Bank as amounting to ethnic cleansing but has said courts must decide if other Israeli actions qualify as genocide.

Israel – which rejects claims of ethnic cleansing and genocide – called on Sunday for other British political parties to condemn the Green Party vote. “The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” it said.

Polanski and other senior Green Party figures said they would “continue to call out the heinous crimes of the Netanyahu government,” and that “there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.”

World.title: Trump may be in political trouble. But Trump-style global populism isn’t
World.content:
President Donald Trump might be in a political hole, but his brand of conservative populist nationalism is flourishing across the globe.

Rising star Flávio Bolsonaro’s shock win in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election Sunday bolstered Trump’s project of remaking the Western Hemisphere in his political image.

Populist right-wingers are also on the march in Europe, fueled by the same failures of foreign leaders to tackle the cost of living and deliver promised change that are haunting US Republicans as the midterm elections draw near.

The radical anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) is catapulting into a national force as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government flatlines. France’s far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election.

These parties aren’t Trump clones, and some predate his MAGA movement. But his rise to power and endurance inspire them. And the administration loudly supports its nationalist brethren threatening to topple the centrist European leaders the president meets at international summits.

Supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) arrive for an election campaign rally ahead of state elections on September 18, 2026, in Neubrandenburg, Germany. Sean Gallup/Getty Images

Many far-right parties share the populist ethos that powered Trump’s stunning 2016 and 2024 campaigns, embracing protectionist economics and emulating his hostility to elites, globalization and mass immigration.

It would be ironic if right-wing populists peak elsewhere just as Trump’s star fades. But he makes an unlikely lame duck, and may copy other second-term presidents who aggressively tried to imprint their legacies on the world before leaving power.

The strength of conservative populism has conjured an existential moment for leaders like Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and his new British counterpart Andy Burnham. Both are leading a fight-back by adopting rhetoric and programs designed to blunt the right and reinforce moderate, centrist government.

But Trump’s violent political shifts seem to be stirring a separate counter-reaction, especially in the United States, as the success of democratic socialists in some midterm primaries heralds a new wave of left-wing populism.

A stunning result in Brazil

Bolsonaro is the eldest son of Trump buddy and former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, who was imprisoned after being convicted of plotting a coup against Brazil’s current leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva after 2022 general elections.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro leaves the DF Star hospital in Brasilia, Brazil, on September 14, 2025, after undergoing a series of medical examinations while under house arrest. Sergio Lima/AFP/Getty Images/File

Lula has only three weeks before a runoff election to mount a comeback that would stop the most populous Latin American democracy from careening to the right.

Trump will loom large over the second round after Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, Tim Kaine and Peter Welch wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month to accuse the administration of using tariffs and economic sanctions to interfere in Brazilian democracy.

Trump, meanwhile, marked Brazil’s Sunday election by casting doubt on America’s democracy, noting that 125 million people voted and results came out the same day, unlike in some US states. “Voting in America is CORRUPT !!!” he posted.

Bolsonaro Jr.’s surprising ascent follows that of Abelardo De La Espriella, a right-wing insurgent who won Colombia’s presidential election earlier this year. Conservative governments friendly to the White House now rule in Costa Rica, after the election of populist Laura Fernández Delgado, and in El Salvador, Chile and Honduras.

In Argentina, President Javier Milei, the Trump acolyte who gifted a chainsaw to Elon Musk at a conservative conference, benefited from a $20 billion currency swap offer Trump made conditional on voters supporting his party in legislative elections.

Trump is also stamping his influence on the region by propping up the leftist authoritarian Venezuelan regime while concluding oil-exporting deals that critics have styled as 21st-century imperialist plunder.

A new populist tide in Europe

The populist tide may lift one of the right-wing nationalist movement’s most abiding figures in France next year after three previous failed presidential bids. Le Pen has in the past been thwarted by her country’s two-stage electoral system as voters coalesced around moderate rivals. But the collapse of establishment center-right and center-left parties means she may face left-wing populist Jean-Luc Mélenchon — whom she’s currently expected to beat — in a runoff.

Le Pen has remodeled her National Rally party, which evolved from the National Front of her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen. But she still advocates nationalist, anti-immigration, protectionist policies and antipathy to the EU. She’d be the most right-wing French president of the modern era and would shake the establishments in Paris and Brussels just as Trump did in Washington.

French far-right leader Marine Le Pen delivers her speech on September 13, 2026, in Henin-Beaumont, northern France. Jean-Francois Badias/AP

European centrists are even more alarmed by the AfD, since far-right parties court particular notoriety in Germany, which has spent 80 years processing the shame of Nazism.

The AfD is to the right of Le Pen and MAGA, and its critics accuse it of historical denialism, antisemitism and ethno-nationalism. But it’s now the second biggest single party in Germany’s federal legislature.

In 2025, Vice President JD Vance outraged Europeans by meeting the AfD leader Alice Weidel in Munich while warning that immigration was destroying Western civilization. Last month, Trump backed the AfD on social media after a landslide win in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, writing, “THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore!”

Trump has long projected leadership over global populism. He claimed in 2016, for instance, that he “called” Britain’s vote to leave the EU, which was a harbinger of his own populist surge to the presidency a few months later.

But he’s not had things all his own way. Far-right MAGA hero and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán fell from power this year despite Trump’s efforts to save him. And the president’s friendship with another conservative populist, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, soured over the Iran war and his claim that she “begged” him for a selfie.

A counter-populist movement is organizing

Carney reacted to Trump’s demands for Canada to become the 51st state by emerging as an informal leader of the Western democracies in a role vacated by Trump. In January, he warned that at “a time of rising populism and ethnic nationalism, Canada can show how diversity can be a strength, not a weakness.”

Burnham used his speech at the Labour Party annual conference last week to address the resentment arising from economic blight that feeds right-wing populism. He blamed the “British Right” dating back to Margaret Thatcher’s governments of the 1980s for pushing deregulation, de-industrialization and privatization.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers his keynote speech on Day 3 of the Labour Party Conference on September 29, 2026, in Liverpool, England. Christopher Furlong/Getty Images

But if Burnham fails, Trump’s populist pal and Reform leader Nigel Farage is waiting to pounce.

Burnham sounds a little like former President Joe Biden, who tried to drain the well of Trumpism in decaying post-industrial areas with vast infrastructure and social spending bills.

But Biden long underestimated the size of the task. He said back in 2012 that he expected the “fever” of radical conservatism to break and later forecast a GOP “epiphany” after Trump left office in 2020.

Trump-style populism may wax and wane, but its resilience suggests it’s now a permanent feature in global democracies, whatever the political fates have in store for its patron.

World.title: Egyptian TV host Ahmed Moussa issues harsh message against Israel
World.content:
Egyptian TV host Ahmed Moussa issued a stern message to Israel, warning that any recklessness or attempt to infringe upon Egypt’s territory could lead to a “lesson greater than 1973,” as he warned.

Speaking on his program “Ala Mas’ouleety” (On My Responsibility) on Monday, Moussa said that Egypt would not tolerate any violation of its territory or encroachment upon Sinai.

He stressed that the Egyptian state currently possesses the strength to safeguard its national security, despite surrounding pressures and challenges.

Commenting on remarks made by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich regarding Egypt and Sinai, Moussa said: “If the Zionist entity acts recklessly, it will spell its own end; the ambitions of tyrants shatter at Egypt’s doorstep.”

Smotrich on Monday warned: “There will be no Sinai if Egypt moves to attack Israel.”

“What would keep Egypt from attacking us? The realization that if they attack, there will be no Sinai—at the very least. No, that will not happen again.”

In response, Moussa stressed: “All 120 million Egyptians would die defending Egypt, and Israel would pay a heavy price if it took any step threatening Egyptian national security.”

He asserted that neither Smotrich, nor his country, nor any other nation on earth would be able to come anywhere near even a single inch of Sinai.

Remembering 1973

During the episode, Moussa recalled key moments from the October 1973 War—including the capture of Israeli soldiers by Egyptian forces—while discussing Egypt’s military capabilities and the message of deterrence that he believes remains relevant today.

Moussa assured that Egypt does not seek war, stating, “What happened then will never be repeated, for we are advocates of peace.”

At the same time, however, he stressed that peace does not mean abandoning the protection of Egyptian territory or national security.

Moussa’s statements follow warnings he had previously issued over the past few months against testing Egypt’s military capabilities.

In June, he warned Israel not to put Egypt to the test, emphasizing that the Egyptian Armed Forces are continuously enhancing their capabilities and are fully capable of safeguarding national security and the country’s borders.

Egypt and Israel are bound by a 1979 peace treaty that ended the state of war between the two nations and established security and military arrangements in Sinai and along the border areas.

Cairo officially affirms its commitment to peace while simultaneously emphasizing the protection of its sovereignty and national security.

World.title: Emirates suspends codeshare operations with Flydubai for Tel Aviv flights
World.content:
Emirates announced on Monday the suspension of its codeshare operations with Flydubai for flights to and from Tel Aviv, effective immediately and until further notice.

In an official update, the airline said that affected customers would receive the necessary support to complete their journeys, advising travelers to contact their travel agents or the Emirates contact center for the latest information regarding travel arrangements.

The decision follows Flydubai’s suspension of flights to and from Israel, prompted by an incident aboard flight FZ1073—traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv—on September 30.

The co-pilot attacked the captain inside the cockpit using an emergency axe before crew members and passengers managed to subdue him; the aircraft was forced to land at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.

The UAE Public Prosecutor described the incident as a “terrorist act.”

Reuters reported on Monday that investigations indicate the co-pilot—an Omani national—told UAE investigators he had planned the attack before joining Flydubai and had considered carrying out a similar attack during a previous flight to Tel Aviv.

UAE authorities have not yet announced formal charges against him.

Flydubai has announced the temporary suspension of its flights to Israel while investigations into the circumstances and causes of the incident continue.

World.title: US Embassy in Riyadh warns citizens against potential attacks
World.content:
The US Embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert regarding the current security situation in Saudi Arabia, warning of the potential for drone or missile attacks targeting the Saudi Arabia.

In a security alert issued on October 5, the embassy strongly urged all US citizens in Saudi Arabia to exercise caution and vigilance, and to follow the directives contained in national alerts issued by the Saudi Civil Defense.

It called on all US citizens to follow all official safety and security instructions and guidelines, given the current security situation and the possibility of aerial attacks on areas within the kingdom.

This alert is part of the precautionary measures taken by the US mission to monitor security developments and advise its citizens to exercise the utmost caution.

World.title: Hamza al-Eily to play Mostafa Mahmoud in upcoming series ‘Between Doubt and Certainty’
World.content:
The production team behind the series “Bayn al-Shakk wa al-Yaqin” (Between Doubt and Certainty) is preparing to shoot the opening scenes in Minya Governorate later this week, ahead of its scheduled broadcast during the Ramadan 2027 drama season.

The series stars actor Hamza al-Eily, who portrays the renowned scientist and thinker Dr. Mostafa Mahmoud.

The upcoming drama follows Dr Mahmoud‘s biographical, intellectual, and personal journey. It chronicles his transformative path between science and philosophy and the various stages in his life – culminating in his status as one of Egypt’s most distinguished thinkers and scientists.

“Between Doubt and Certainty” is directed by Kamla Abu-Zekry, with a dramatic treatment by Mohamed Hisham Obeya and production by Mohamed al-Saadi, while Maha Selim serves as executive producer.

The series also stars Ashraf Abdel-Baky, Mourad Makram, Hassan Malek, Mayan al-Sayed, Tara Abboud, and Yasmina el-Abed.

The production team is set to reveal further details about the series in the coming period, coinciding with the start of filming and final preparations for its broadcast during the Ramadan 2027 drama season.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Rains of varying intensity expected in Egypt on Tuesday
World.content:
The Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) forecasts rains of varying intensity on Tuesday across different areas of the country, while hot to slightly hot weather conditions will persist.

Satellite imagery indicates the movement of low and medium-level clouds toward parts of the Matrouh Governorate, accompanied by a chance of rain ranging from light to heavy—with possible thunder as the day progresses.

The rain is expected to spread to the rest of the northwestern coast and parts of the northern Lower Egypt governorates (Al-Alamein, Alexandria, Beheira, and Kafr al–Sheikh) as the night advances, continuing into the morning hours; these governorates will experience rapid and severe weather fluctuations.

Weather maps predict continued movement of cloud cover into parts of the Western Desert, northern Upper Egypt, Greater Cairo, the Gulf of Suez, the Canal Cities, the northeastern coast, and Sinai, potentially bringing a chance of light, scattered, and sporadic rainfall.

The weather will be autumnal and slightly hot during the day along the northern coasts; hot in Lower Egypt, Greater Cairo, and northern Upper Egypt; and very hot in southern Upper Egypt.

Conditions in the evening will be moderate initially, turning slightly cool towards the end of the night and in the early morning.

The EMA indicated that winds will be active across most regions—with speeds ranging between 30 and 40 km/h—helping to moderate the temperature at night.

Forecasts show a high of 29C for Greater Cairo, while the northwestern coasts will see 26C and the northeastern coasts 27C.

Temperatures will reach 30C in northern Upper Egypt and 36C in southern Upper Egypt.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Liberia: Amid Kemayah’s Fiery Defense, Lawyer Accuses AREPT of Witness Tampering; Task Force Denies Allegation, Wants Claim Tested in Court
World.content:
Monrovia – A troubling confrontation outside the courtroom has opened a new front in the criminal trial, with defense lawyer Gbawou Kowou accusing the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce AREPT of intimidating or improperly engaging defense witnesses after they testified.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The drama unfolded as former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah insisted on the witness stand that he “did not steal one grain” of the Saudi-donated rice.



AREPT has categorically denied the allegation, saying the witnesses were not summoned for questioning, were not interviewed, and were immediately asked to leave its premises after agency lawyers discovered that they had recently appeared in court as subpoenaed defense witnesses.

The dispute, coming as prosecutors prepare to present rebuttal witnesses in the Saudi rice case, has raised a question over the treatment of witnesses in an ongoing criminal proceeding, and whether witnesses who have already testified for the defense can be approached or brought to a prosecutorial agency without their lawyers being informed, and concern over where legitimate investigation ends and improper interference begins.

The answer, both sides now said, should come from the court.

AREPT, in a statement signed by its Public Relations Officer, Joseph F. Daniels, said the incident resulted from a misunderstanding rather than an attempt to interfere with testimony.

According to the task force, a potential witness who had previously provided a statement during the investigation was asked to appear at its office along with other persons familiar with the Saudi rice matter.

The agency said the potential witness arrived with two individuals whom he identified as persons knowledgeable about the matter.

AREPT said its lawyers did not initially know that the two individuals had recently appeared before Criminal Court “C” as defense witnesses.

“Upon recognizing them, AREPT lawyers immediately asked the two individuals to leave the premises,” the statement said.

The agency stressed that the witnesses “were not invited by AREPT, were not interviewed, and no statement was taken from them.”

AREPT therefore rejected the accusation that its lawyers threatened, intimidated or attempted to influence the witnesses.

The agency challenged the defense to take the allegation before the trial judge.

“If defense counsel has evidence of witness tampering or intimidation, that evidence should be presented to the court, where such allegations can be properly addressed,” AREPT said.

But Kowou is not backing away.

The defense lawyer has characterized the circumstances surrounding the witnesses’ presence at the AREPT compound as serious, particularly because the individuals had already testified on behalf of the accused.

Kowou said the witnesses included members of the Group of 77 and members of the community of persons living with disabilities who had appeared before Criminal Court “C” as defense witnesses.

According to the lawyer, the witnesses told him they had been pressured or threatened to report to AREPT following their appearance in court.

Kowou subsequently went to the taskforce’s headquarters in Paynesville, where he livestreamed the confrontation and demanded access to the compound.

“I’m live at AREPT. Witnesses who testified on our behalf yesterday were brought here and threatened,” Kowou said during the broadcast.

At another point, he accused officials of locking the facility’s gate.

“They have locked the gate. The witnesses are in there,” he said. “If the witnesses are not there, open the gate.”

The confrontation eventually drew the attention of Liberia National Police officers, with Kowou continuing to insist that the matter involved possible interference with witnesses in an ongoing criminal proceeding.

He was later allowed into the compound and subsequently taken to a police station following the confrontation.

Kowou later said AREPT officials characterized the incident as a misunderstanding.

But the defense lawyer maintained that the circumstances remained troubling.

Harassing Vulnerable Witnesses?

The controversy is particularly sensitive because of the identity of some of the witnesses at the center of the dispute.

Kowou said the witnesses were drawn from vulnerable and organized community groups and had appeared in court to give evidence for the accused.

For the defense, the central issue is not simply whether AREPT lawyers spoke to the witnesses.

It is whether any contact occurred in circumstances capable of influencing, intimidating or otherwise affecting witnesses who had already placed their testimony on the official record.

That distinction could become important as the matter moves before the trial court.

Under Liberia’s Penal Law, witness tampering is a serious offense where prohibited conduct is used with the purpose of influencing testimony or preventing or altering a person’s participation in an official proceeding.

Kowou did not speak further on the next course of action, but a defense lawyer who prefers anonymity told FrontPageAfrica that the defense team has already taken action against the alleged situation, in line with the laws of Liberia.

However, an accusation of witness tampering is not itself proof that tampering occurred.

AREPT’s position is that its lawyers did precisely the opposite of what Kowou alleged; once they realized that the individuals were defense witnesses, they asked them to leave.

The agency said no interview took place, no statement was taken, and no effort was made to influence their testimony.

The competing accounts now create a factual question that may have to be resolved through evidence.

A Trial Already Defined By Contested Evidence

The witness controversy comes against the backdrop of an increasingly combative Saudi rice trial, where the prosecution and defense have presented sharply different accounts of how a Saudi government-to-government donation was received, stored, transferred and ultimately distributed.

The case involves 13 former government officials accused of corruption-related offenses arising from the handling of the Saudi-donated rice.

The defense has consistently challenged the prosecution’s interpretation of the documentary record, the quantity of rice received, the role of the National Disaster Management Agency, the involvement of the General Services Agency and the authority exercised by officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

That battle intensified when Kemayah himself took the witness stand.

Kemayah: ‘I Did Not Steal One Grain’

Kemayah delivered a forceful and emotional defense of his role in securing and managing the humanitarian rice project.

His central message was blunt: “I did not steal one grain of rice.”

The former minister acknowledged that he personally negotiated with Saudi authorities to secure the donation.

But he rejected the prosecution’s characterization of his involvement as an abuse of authority.

Kemayah told the court, in substance, that his intervention was motivated by the need to secure food assistance for vulnerable Liberians.

He said the government could have routed the rice through institutions such as the Liberian National Red Cross Society or the World Food Programme but instead selected NDMA to handle the humanitarian component.

For Kemayah, that decision undermines any suggestion that he secretly seized control of the project.

“I negotiated this rice,” he emphasized, arguing that no one ordered him to seek the donation and that he took the initiative because Liberians needed assistance.

The Saudi Video

Kemayah also relied heavily on a video documentary showing what he described as the formal signing ceremony between the Government of Liberia and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

He presented the footage as evidence that the rice donation was the product of an official government-to-government arrangement.

According to his testimony, the documentary showed Liberian officials and Saudi representatives participating in the process surrounding the donation.

Kemayah said Saudi representatives were assured that the rice would reach vulnerable Liberians rather than government officials.

For the former minister, that assurance is important because it contradicts any theory that the project was created as a mechanism for personal enrichment.

“Where Is the Note of Exchange?”

Kemayah also seized on testimony from Acting Foreign Affairs Minister Etta Davies, who reportedly told the court that officials searching the Ministry of Foreign Affairs failed to locate the Note of Exchange connected to the Saudi donation.

The former minister questioned how the absence of a copy from Liberia’s current ministry records could invalidate the existence of the diplomatic transaction.

He argued that because Saudi Arabia remains a diplomatic partner of Liberia, missing government-to-government documentation could be sought through diplomatic channels.

The issue has now become another point of contention over the reliability and completeness of government records.

The 29,412-Bags Question

Perhaps one of the most key factual battles in Kemayah’s testimony centered on the quantity of rice.

Kemayah maintained that 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice were received from Saudi Arabia.

The defense has repeatedly challenged figures presented by the prosecution, arguing that the physical quantity of rice, its monetary value, and the logistics surrounding its transportation and storage must be reconciled with the documentary evidence.

Kemayah questioned figures he considered inconsistent with the actual shipment.

For the defense, the dispute over quantity is not merely mathematical.

It goes directly to the prosecution’s theory of what was allegedly diverted or unlawfully handled.

‘To Rescue the Rice’

Kemayah also rejected the allegation that he improperly interfered with NDMA’s statutory responsibilities.

He relied on testimony from former GSA Director-General Mary T. Broh and former NDMA Board Chairman Varney A. Sirleaf concerning the movement of rice from NDMA facilities to GSA warehouses.

Kemayah characterized the decision as an effort to protect the rice from deteriorating because of storage concerns.

He described his intervention as an attempt to “rescue the rice.”

He argued that the movement involved several government officials and institutions and was therefore not a unilateral decision taken secretly by him.

Kemayah further pointed to NDMA officials’ participation in meetings concerning the rice as evidence that the agency’s statutory responsibilities had not been taken over.

‘I Never Distributed A Grain’

The former minister was equally categorical in denying personal involvement in the distribution of the rice.

He told the court that he never recommended, authorized or personally distributed a single grain of the donated rice.

He challenged the prosecution to produce documentary evidence proving otherwise.

“If there is anything, I am prepared beyond this case to redeem my name,” he maintained.

‘Conspire With Who? Rice?’

Kemayah also attacked the conspiracy allegation.

With visible emotion, he questioned why he would conspire with others over humanitarian rice that he had personally worked to secure.

“Conspire with who? Rice? For what?” he asked rhetorically.

He maintained that the project involved multiple government institutions and officials and that the evidence should be viewed in the context of a government humanitarian operation rather than an individual scheme.

His Mother’s Death

The testimony also took a deeply personal turn when Kemayah recounted the circumstances surrounding his arrest and the subsequent death of his mother.

He said armed security personnel arrived at his residence to execute a search and arrest while his mother was staying with him.

According to Kemayah, his mother suffered from a pressure-related illness and was deeply distressed by the events surrounding his arrest.

She was later taken to a Catholic hospital but, he said, never fully recovered.

Kemayah carefully stopped short of directly accusing security personnel of causing her death.

Instead, he maintained that the emotional trauma surrounding his arrest contributed to the deterioration of her condition.

‘This Is Not My Area’

Kemayah ultimately returned to the central theme of his defense, that stealing was not his motive and that his involvement in the Saudi rice project was part of his responsibility as Foreign Minister to mobilize international support for Liberia.

He cited his administration’s efforts to pursue reforms at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, engage international partners, and improve services for ordinary Liberians.

He maintained that the Saudi rice project belonged within that record of public service.

“Stealing is not my area,” he declared.

But the prosecution continues to maintain that the defendants unlawfully handled and diverted a substantial portion of the Saudi donation.

The New Battle, Witnesses

Now, as the prosecution prepares to present rebuttal evidence, another battle has emerged, this time over the treatment of witnesses.

The defense said witnesses who had already testified were taken to or summoned to AREPT’s headquarters and subjected to pressure.

AREPT said that account is false.

The taskforce insists that the witnesses were not invited, questioned or interviewed and that its lawyers asked them to leave as soon as they recognized them as defense witnesses.

That leaves the court with a potentially consequential question of what actually happened inside and around the AREPT compound, and was any attempt made to influence witnesses who had already testified.

The answer could determine whether the episode remains a heated dispute outside the courtroom, or becomes a formal evidentiary and legal issue inside it.

For now, both sides are pointing toward the same place for resolution, the court.

And with Kemayah fighting to dismantle the prosecution’s case from the witness stand while his lawyer raised allegations of possible witness interference outside the courtroom, the Saudi rice trial has entered an increasingly volatile phase, one in which the credibility of witnesses, the integrity of government records and the conduct of the parties themselves may prove just as consequential as the rice at the center of the case.

The final determination remains with Criminal Court “C” and the jury after consideration of the evidence presented by both the prosecution and defense.
