World.title: Liberia: As Talk of a Truce with President Boakai Swirls, Ex-Lawmaker Kolubah Says He Regrets His Relationship with the Liberian Leader
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberian politics has no shortage of dramatic turnarounds, but few would have raised eyebrows like this one. Yekeh Kolubah, the outspoken former Montserrado County District 10 representative, was said to be preparing to sit down with President Joseph Boakai, the leader he backed in 2023 and later turned on.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The rumor ran for days. Then Kolubah went on air and, intentionally or not, poured cold water on it.



A Rumor with Official Fingerprints

The talk did not come from nowhere. It began with a Facebook post by Kolubah’s own media consultant, which said the former lawmaker was ready to reconcile with the President. The post blamed his frustration on what the office called the “disintegration and unseriousness” of the opposition.

His PRO, Samson Moseray, reportedly backed it up. A meeting with the President was being arranged, he said, and Kolubah had chosen to “mend fences and put Liberia first.”

Kolubah himself added fuel. He has repeatedly said he will return to Liberia on October 10 to address the media on the matter. For a politician known for theatrical announcements, that was enough to convince many that something big was coming.

Sunday Night on Spoon TV

On Sunday, the Spoon Show gave him the chance to settle the question. The host asked bluntly whether he was coming home to “beg the president for forgiveness.” Kolubah’s opening line was that he regrets his relationship with President Boakai. Peacemakers rarely start that way. Expressing regret over a past association is the language of someone closing a chapter, not reopening it. And as the conversation went on, there was little sign of the softening one would expect from a man about to extend a hand.

The Statement That Started It All

To understand why reconciliation looks so hard, one has to go back to April 17, 2026, when 49 lawmakers voted to expel Kolubah from the House of Representatives. The move followed uproar over remarks attributed to him about the Liberia–Guinea border dispute. It remains one of the most debated decisions of the 55th Legislature.

On Spoon TV, the host pressed him on the subject. Kolubah held his ground and maintained that the land Liberia occupies belongs to Guinea.

In other words, the position that cost him his seat is one he has just repeated in public. It is hard to picture a reconciliation that leaves that issue untouched. If Kolubah has not changed his view, and his words suggest he has not, then the cause of the breakup has not gone away. It has simply been restated.

An Oath That Raises the Stakes

The most dramatic piece of the puzzle is a pledge Kolubah is reported to have made. According to those accounts, he has said that the day he reconciles with President Boakai, it will be him who killed his mother.

Whatever one makes of the rhetoric, the vow changes the calculation. Most political disputes can be patched up with a communiqué, a handshake, or a quiet word from respected elders. A promise that invokes a mother’s memory is different. Breaking it would hand his opponents a weapon they could use for years. For a figure who has built his brand on defiance, it could cost more than any seat in the Legislature.

Weariness With Allies, not a Change of Heart

Since his expulsion, Kolubah has toured the country alongside the opposition and spoken harshly of the government. His camp’s recent message about the opposition’s disintegration points to growing disillusionment with that coalition.

That could explain why the reconciliation story gained traction. A politician who feels let down by his allies might start looking for a way out. But there is a difference between being fed up with friends and warming to a former benefactor turned adversary. So far, nothing Kolubah has said publicly suggests he has made that leap.

The Empty Chair in District 10

The saga also unfolds against a constitutional backdrop that critics say is being ignored. Article 37 of the 1986 Constitution says that when a legislative seat falls vacant through death, resignation, expulsion or otherwise, the presiding officer must notify the National Elections Commission within 30 days. The Commission must then hold a by-election within 90 days, unless general elections fall within that window.

Nearly 170 days have passed since the expulsion. Commentators say no replacement has been chosen and that the presiding officer, Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, has apparently not notified the Commission. For residents of District 10, that means months without a voice in the House. Some observers suspect the vacancy may be part of the political bargaining, a seat left open while the larger drama plays out.

There are reasons to take the reconciliation talk seriously. It came from Kolubah’s own office. It was framed around national interest. Kolubah has a history with the Unity Party, and the October 10 media address suggests an announcement of some kind is on the way.

But the case against is stronger. He opened his Spoon TV interview with regret over his relationship with the President. He has refused to retreat on the border claim. He has reportedly bound himself with a deeply personal vow. And every grievance that produced the split remains in place.

The most likely outcome, if anything happens at all, is something smaller than a true reconciliation: a conversation framed around peace and national unity, with neither side conceding much. A full return to the President’s camp would require Kolubah to unsay nearly everything he said on Sunday night.

On October 10, the country will find out which Kolubah steps off the plane: the peacemaker his office has described or the combatant who spoke on Spoon TV. For now, his own words are the best evidence available, and they point firmly toward no.

World.title: Liberia: A Government Assessment Shows Liberia Is 69 Percent Ready for Ebola. Frontline Health Workers Say the Missing 31 Percent Matters
World.content:
Dr. Sia Wata Camanor, National Public Health Institute of Liberia’s acting director general, spoke at the Ministry of Information press briefing this month, where she released the findings of the Institute’s Ebola preparedness assessment.

Summary:

• A nationwide Ebola preparedness assessment found Liberia 69 percent ready overall, while logistics scored only 47 percent, leaving major gaps in equipment, supplies, isolation facilities and training.

• Frontline health workers say those logistics gaps can mean the difference between safely isolating a suspected patient and exposing staff, other patients and communities.



• Health authorities say they are tightening procedures at major points of entry, but the next steps, funding and timetable for closing the gaps remain unclear.

By Augusta S. Lafalay, senior reporter with New Narratives

Liberia has stronger disease surveillance and laboratory systems than it did during the 2014 Ebola crisis, but the country is still only 69 percent prepared to respond to another outbreak, according to a nationwide Ebola preparedness assessment by the National Public Health Institute of Liberia. The weakest area was logistics, which scored just 47 percent.

At a September press conference to release the findings of the assessment, Dr. Sia Wata Camanor, acting Public Health Institute director general, said the country was in the “medium” preparedness range. “We don’t have the tools. We don’t have the materials,” she said. Though the risk remains low, she warned against complacency.

Health experts welcomed the government’s transparency, but they said that the number is more than a technical score. It points to shortages and weaknesses in the things health workers would need first if a suspected Ebola patient arrived at a clinic or hospital: personal protective equipment, functioning isolation space, transport, laboratory supplies, ambulances, trained staff, and a system able to move those resources quickly.

“When we say there is a lack of logistics, it can sound like we are simply talking about supplies. But for a health worker, it is much bigger than that,” said Lela Dolo, executive director of Help a Mother and Newborn in Liberia and a medical student training to become a doctor. “Do I have the personal protective equipment I need? Can a suspected patient be safely isolated and referred? Can a specimen be transported quickly? Is there an ambulance or vehicle available? Can the response team reach the community?”

The question is foremost in the minds of the country’s healthcare workers who bore the brunt of the disease in 2014. If an Ebola case reaches the country, gaps could put frontline workers at risk, slow the response and increase the chance that an infection spreads beyond a health facility and into communities.

The National Public Health Institute of Liberia’s assessment, conducted across all 15 counties, examined surveillance, points of entry, emergency operations centers, laboratories, isolation facilities, county health teams and rapid response structures. Health authorities have said surveillance officers and rapid response teams are operating nationwide, while laboratory testing and specimen transport have improved. But officials also identified the need to replenish protective equipment, maintain isolation facilities, run more simulation exercises and continue training newly deployed health workers.

For Liberia, the warning carries a painful history. During the 2014-2015 epidemic, 378 health care workers in Liberia had confirmed Ebola and 192 died, according to a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention review . Weak infection-prevention systems left health facilities vulnerable, with many lacking triage and isolation protocols, protective gear, or running water early in the crisis.

The toll weakened a health system that was already short of skilled workers. The infected health workers represented about 12 percent of Liberia’s confirmed Ebola cases, even though health workers made up only a small share of the population. Early in the epidemic, many facilities closed after transmission occurred among staff. Health workers who did not feel protected, walked away.

Dolo said the Liberian health system has learned from the last epidemic and has stronger surveillance and response systems. Her concern is whether those systems are backed by the practical resources needed when an emergency begins.

“You can train health workers to recognize Ebola and follow the right protocols, but knowledge alone cannot protect them,” she said. “They also need the tools and systems to safely do what they have been trained to do.”

Joseph Somwarbi, a pharmacologist and former head of the Legislature’s health committee, said logistics failures can quickly become safety failures. He said all parts of the chain must work together.

A shortage in one part of that chain can put frontline staff in a dangerous position. If protective gear is insufficient health workers may have to delay care or risk exposure. If laboratory agents or specimen transport are unavailable, confirmation can take longer. If supplies are concentrated in Monrovia, rural facilities can lose valuable time waiting for materials to arrive.

“Delay in procurement, delay in transportation means no access,” Somwarbi said. “No access means not available. Not available means you’re not prepared.”

Those weaknesses become especially serious in an Ebola outbreak, he said, because the first response begins before laboratory confirmation. A patient with symptoms and a relevant exposure history must be identified, separated from other patients, reported to surveillance teams, safely assessed and tested, while health workers use infection-prevention measures. Contacts may then need to be identified and monitored.

“When the system is not prepared, even 24 hours is too much of a time for disease to spread,” Somwarbi said.

The threat of Ebola remains constant. The latest outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (the country’s 17th outbreak) has reached 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths, according to the World Health Organization , making it the second largest outbreak after the 2014 outbreak in West Africa. Experts said cuts to international aid, especially by the United States, have dramatically reduced the capacity to contain the virus. That same outcome would likely play out in Liberia, which relied heavily on U.S. help to stamp out the 2014 outbreak, were the virus to reach the country.

Liberia has responded to the DRC’s outbreak by increasing screening and surveillance at airports, seaports and land crossings. Travelers are required to cooperate with screening and reporting procedures. Procedures, health experts said, are in place to make clear who screens travelers, what happens when someone meets a suspected-case definition, how referral and transport should work, and how information moves from border health staff to surveillance and response teams.

But the country has struggled with capacities at points of entry. A 2024 peer-reviewed evaluation of eight designated Liberian points of entry found gaps in areas including quarantine, communication, water, electricity, transport, and trained personnel.

Experts said the importance of clear procedures was underlined in May, when health authorities monitored 16 travelers arriving from countries of concern. None developed Ebola symptoms during the required 21-day follow-up, according to the Institute. But a WhatsApp voice message circulated claiming suspected Ebola patients had been taken to John F. Kennedy Medical Center, sparking fear and mistrust in the community.

Experts said the incident highlighted a basic communication challenge: officials needed to clearly communicate to the people what they were doing to increase trust. Dr. Camanor’s press conference and transparency about the assessment were a sign the government has learned from the May experience.

From here, Camanor said the assessment findings would be shared with the Ministry of Health, World Health Organization and other partners, and that the National Public Health Institute planned to take the findings to the Ministry of Finance, Cabinet and Legislature to seek support for closing the gaps.

In May, Dr. Louise Kpoto, the health minister, told lawmakers that the Ebola preparedness budget was $US4.2 million.

FrontPage Africa/New Narratives contacted Dr. Kpoto and National Public Health Institute leadership by telephone and email seeking answers on what the government will do next, whether any of the $US4.2 million has been approved or released, a timetable for addressing the gaps, and how progress will be measured. Neither responded by the publication deadline.

Somwarbi said a follow-up assessment would be one way to show whether new spending improves preparedness. That would allow the public and health workers to compare the current weaknesses with what has been fixed, rather than relying only on promises or budget figures.

For Dolo, the practical test is simpler. “If the first suspected Ebola patient walks into a health facility tomorrow, does the health worker who meets that patient have everything they need to recognize the risk, protect themselves, protect other patients and activate the response system immediately?” she asked. “If the answer is not yet a confident yes, then there is still work to do.”

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The funder had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: EFLA Accuses Boakai-Koung Administration of ‘Systemic Disregard’ for Liberians in Europe
World.content:
MONROVIA — The European Federation of Liberian Associations (EFLA) has accused the Boakai-Koung administration of systematically sidelining Liberians living in Europe from its flagship diaspora engagement initiatives, sharply criticizing the government’s annual diaspora conference as a platform that fails to represent the broader Liberian diaspora.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

In a statement issued on October 4, 2026, EFLA President Francis M. Mensah said the organization was taking exception to the manner in which the government has organized its annual diaspora conferences, arguing that the events have increasingly centered on Liberians in the United States while excluding communities in Europe.



The criticism comes as the Joseph Boakai-Koung administration has made diaspora engagement a major component of its domestic policy, holding two annual diaspora conferences in the United States since 2025.

EFLA, which describes itself as the umbrella organization for Liberian associations across Europe, said it expected the conference to bring together Liberians from across the world to discuss issues affecting the diaspora and Liberia.

Instead, the organization alleged that the conferences have become heavily U.S.-focused.

“The Annual Diaspora Conference, by its goals and objectives, should bring together all Liberians in the diaspora to assemble, network, and discuss issues affecting the wider Liberian Diaspora community, as well as the issues the government of Liberia faces,” EFLA said.

“Unfortunately, the past two diaspora conferences have been turned into a spectacle of prom and pageantry,” the organization alleged, claiming that senior government officials and their associates have traveled to Washington, D.C., at government expense.

EFLA said Europe was not represented at this year’s conference, arguing that such an omission undermines the stated objective of creating a global platform for Liberians abroad.

‘Systemic Neglect’

The European group said its concerns predate the current administration, noting that it has repeatedly attempted to engage successive Liberian governments over what it described as the “systemic neglect” of Liberians residing in Europe.

The concerns, according to EFLA, range from consular challenges in the Nordic countries to the limited participation of European-based Liberians in government-sponsored diaspora initiatives.

The organization also pointed to the financial contribution of Liberians in Europe through remittances and businesses in Liberia.

“So, we must not be taken for granted!” EFLA said.

The organization further accused conference organizers of being insufficiently intentional about involving Liberians from Europe, alleging that panel discussions and other side events are often structured to accommodate government allies, friends and family members.

“The sad truth is that the organizers have never been intentional about getting Liberians in the European Diaspora involved, but continue to pretend to include diaspora Liberians from Europe,” the statement said.

Government’s Diaspora Push

President Boakai’s diaspora initiative was launched from a commitment made in late 2024 to establish a structured global platform for Liberians living abroad.

The government has said the initiative is intended to move beyond the traditional focus on remittances and encourage the more than 500,000 Liberians living abroad to contribute to Liberia through entrepreneurship, investment, technology transfer and professional expertise.

The inaugural Liberia Annual Diaspora Conference was held in Washington, D.C., from September 26–28, 2025, under the theme “Building the Future Together.” The gathering brought together hundreds of delegates physically and more than 1,300 virtual participants, according to organizers.

The 2026 conference, held September 25–27 at the Hilton Alexandria Mark Center in Virginia, was organized under the theme “From Dialogue to Delivery: Diaspora Capital, Innovation, and the Next Liberia.”

The second conference sought to move discussions toward practical economic initiatives, including investment, agribusiness, innovation and youth empowerment.

EFLA, however, argues that the geographic concentration of the initiative contradicts its stated global character.

Europe Threatens Wider Pushback

EFLA said it would no longer participate in what it characterized as poorly organized diaspora activities conducted by government functionaries.

“Going forward, Liberians in Europe will not be involved in any haphazard activities organized by government functionaries,” the organization declared.

The group also warned that it could seek engagement with European institutions over what it described as the Liberian government’s failure to include Liberians residing in the European Union in its diaspora activities.

“Europe hosts some of Liberia’s development partners, and we, as Liberian taxpayers in Europe, can engage the European Union Parliament about the Liberian government’s flagrant disregard for including Liberians residing in the EU in diaspora activities it organizes,” EFLA said.

The group stressed that no segment of the Liberian diaspora should be treated as more important than another.

“No one group of diaspora Liberians is better than the others,” EFLA said, demanding that Liberians in Europe receive the same level of respect and opportunities afforded to their compatriots in the United States.

EFLA said it has been involved in advocacy and humanitarian initiatives benefiting both Liberians in Europe and communities in Liberia. It also cited its role, alongside partners including ALCOD, in advocacy that contributed to the passage of Liberia’s Dual Citizenship Act and its ongoing efforts to promote voting rights for Liberians abroad.

The organization said it remains committed to contributing to Liberia’s development but wants the government to recognize the European diaspora as an equal partner.

“In Union Strong, Success Is Assured!” the statement concluded.

World.title: Liberian Entrepreneur LeAnn Knowlden Honored in Zimbabwe, Tanzania and Ghana
World.content:
Founder of Top Agency, who started a school newspaper at 14, picks up three continental recognitions in 2026

MONROVIA – Liberian entrepreneur and media personality LeAnn Knowlden has earned recognition in three African countries this year, adding continental attention to a career that began with a student newspaper she launched as a teenager.

Knowlden, founder and CEO of Monrovia-based Top Agency, was named among Africa’s Top 100 Female Leaders 2026 by the SOWA Awards in Zimbabwe. In Tanzania, Iconic Africa named her Iconic Woman of the Year 2026 in the Business Leadership and Social Impact category. In Ghana, she was listed among the 100 Most Influential Africans in Infrastructure 2026.

The three honors cover different areas: women’s leadership, business and social impact, and infrastructure.



Early start in media

Knowlden’s interest in media dates to her school days. At about 14, she founded The Jaguar’s Journal, a student newspaper at her school in Liberia.

She has recalled that the paper’s success earned her a chance to meet then-Vice President Joseph Nyuma Boakai. She had hoped to meet the President that day, but met Boakai instead and sold him two copies of the paper.

Boakai, who served as Vice President from 2006 to 2018, was elected President in 2023.

Zimbabwe and ‘Africa by Africans’

Knowlden’s trip to Zimbabwe for the SOWA Awards also advanced Africa by Africans, a cultural storytelling project she leads. The visit produced her first hospitality partnership in Southern Africa, with Victoria Falls Safari Lodge.

The project promotes the idea that Africans should travel the continent, support African businesses and tell African stories themselves rather than relying on outside accounts.

Social impact in focus

The Tanzania recognition highlighted her social impact work. Knowlden helped promote a fundraising campaign for Tilnette Woods, a young Liberian woman who needed hip surgery. The campaign met its goal, and Woods has since had the surgery and is recovering, according to Knowlden’s office.

A broader view of infrastructure

On the Ghana recognition, Knowlden has described infrastructure as more than roads and buildings, extending to the systems, partnerships, platforms and businesses that open access to economic opportunity.

Through Top Agency, she has worked in communications, events, brand strategy, cultural programming and entrepreneurship. She also hosts television programming and runs Planet LeAnn, a cultural storytelling platform.

Knowlden describes her work across business, tourism, media and community building as parts of one goal: connecting people, brands and opportunities across Africa.

World.title: Liberia: Monrovia Celebrates as Temi Nkem Claims Victory in Big Brother Naija Season 11
World.content:
MONROVIA — Reality TV fans across Liberia joined the rest of the continent over the weekend to celebrate as Temi Nkem officially emerged as the winner of Big Brother Naija Season 11, tagged “Show Ya Sef.” Her triumph marks a historic moment in the reality franchise, making her the fifth female winner to take home the coveted crown.

The finale concluded an intense 10-week journey that captivated viewers throughout West Africa, including a massive following here in Liberia, where fans frequently gathered at local view centers and tuned in via DStv

to root for their favorite housemates.

After millions of votes were tallied across Africa, Temi Nkem secured the top spot by pulling 25.87% of the total votes. She narrowly edged out first runner-up Aikou, who garnered 23.68%, while Sheba finished as the second runner-up with 9.80%.



As the Season 11 champion, Temi Nkem walks away with a grand prize package featuring a brand-new SUV and 90 million Naira in cash.

The remaining 10 million Naira from the grand 100 million Naira cash pool was set aside for the season’s Most Influential Player of the Week (MIPOW) prize fund.

This season proved to be one of the most unpredictable and dramatic in BBNaija history. A total of 24 housemates competed through grueling Head of House games, weekly nominations, and game-changing twists like the “Gambit play” and revolving veto powers.

It also set a show record by recording two disqualifications and a voluntary exit—marking the first time all three events occurred in a single season.

Speaking on the successful run of the show, Atinuke Babatunde, Executive Head of Content and Channels, West Africa at MultiChoice, expressed gratitude to the loyal fanbase across the region.

“Season 11 has been another exciting chapter for Big Brother Naija,” Babatunde stated. “We saw 24 housemates bring their personalities, perspectives, and individual approaches to the game, and we are pleased to have shared their journey with our viewers.

We thank everyone who watched, voted, and joined the conversation throughout the season, as well as our sponsors and partners for their continued support.”

Big Brother Naija continues to solidify its position as Africa’s most-watched reality television platform. For Liberian youth and pop culture enthusiasts, the show remains a cultural touchstone and a vital launching pad for continental stars in media, fashion, music, and film.

World.title: Liberia: LMDC Pushes Tighter Regulation of Traditional Medicine, Warns Against ‘Cure-All’ Claims
World.content:
SANNIQUELLIE, Nimba County — The Liberia Medical and Dental Council (LMDC) is calling for stronger regulatory, research and monitoring frameworks to govern traditional medicine and ensure its safe integration into Liberia’s healthcare system.

The call was made by LMDC Registrar General Dr. Augustus Garlet Quiah on behalf of Council Chairperson Dr. Ayun K. Cassell III and members of the Council during the 24th African Traditional Medicine Day celebration in Sanniquellie, Nimba County.

Held under the theme, “Reflection on Research and Development Efforts of Traditional Medicine towards Achieving Universal Health Coverage in Liberia,” the event brought together traditional and conventional healthcare practitioners, government institutions, researchers, community stakeholders and health-related organizations.



Dr. Quiah said sustained investment in research, policy development, capacity building, monitoring and regulation is necessary to ensure that traditional medicine practices are safe, responsible and appropriately incorporated into Liberia’s broader healthcare system.

“There is a need for clear policy and regulatory frameworks that will guide and monitor traditional healthcare practices, including establishing appropriate treatment limits and ensuring that practitioners do not make blanket claims that their remedies can cure all diseases and medical conditions,” Dr. Quiah said.

He said effective regulation would also create opportunities for stronger collaboration among government institutions, academic and scientific researchers, conventional healthcare providers and traditional medicine practitioners.

“Through collaboration, research and effective regulation, Liberia can create a more inclusive and resilient healthcare system that responds to the needs of every citizen, while ensuring that public safety remains a priority,” he added.

Traditional Medicine’s Role

The LMDC Registrar General acknowledged the significant role traditional medicine continues to play in Liberia, particularly in rural and underserved communities where access to conventional healthcare services remains limited.

While stressing that conventional medicine remains an essential component of Liberia’s national health system, Dr. Quiah said the potential contribution of traditional medicine to achieving Universal Health Coverage should also be recognized.

However, he cautioned that efforts to promote traditional medicine must be accompanied by scientific research, evidence-based practices, professional capacity building, monitoring and appropriate regulation to protect patients and the wider public.

The celebration was organized by the Ministry of Health through its Division of Traditional, Complementary and Alternative Medicines.

Participants included representatives of the Liberia Intellectual Property Office (LIPO), Liberia Medicines and Health Products Regulatory Authority (LMHRA), West African Health Organization (WAHO), LMDC, Ministry of Local Government, Traditional Medicine Association of Nimba, Liberia Traditional Medicine Federation (LIMEF) and the Nimba County Health Team.

The Office of Nimba County Superintendent Kou Meapeh Gono also participated, with the Superintendent represented by her Special Assistant, Prince Yeah, who served as keynote speaker.

Medicinal Plants Garden Launched

As part of the celebration, organizers officially launched the Nimba Medicinal Plants Garden, an initiative intended to highlight the importance of medicinal plants and preserve traditional healthcare knowledge.

Traditional healthcare providers were also certificated in recognition of their contributions to healthcare delivery through traditional medicine.

Meanwhile, local authorities have pledged to strengthen monitoring of traditional medicine practitioners, particularly those who use radio stations and other public platforms to advertise remedies while claiming that their products can cure all diseases and medical conditions.

The LMDC said such claims require closer scrutiny as part of efforts to protect the public from unsafe practices and misleading medical information.

Registration, Licensing Urged

Traditional and complementary medicine practitioners were encouraged to formally pursue registration and licensing in line with Ministry of Health and World Health Organization guidelines.

According to the LMDC, practitioners should begin by expressing their interest through the Ministry of Local Government, followed by engagement with the County Health Team before proceeding to the Complementary Medicines Unit at the Ministry of Health.

Final licensing or certification is to be handled by the Liberia Medical and Dental Council.

The Council said it remains committed to working with the Government of Liberia, health professionals, healthcare institutions, development partners, communities and other stakeholders to strengthen health regulation and promote a safe, accountable and quality healthcare system for Liberians.

World.title: Liberia: Gandhi’s Legacy of Compassion Lives On as India Donates Medicines to Liberia’s Group of 77 Disabled Center
World.content:
MONROVIA — The Embassy of India in Liberia has marked the 157th birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi with a call for peace, nonviolence, dialogue and compassion, while strengthening its humanitarian engagement with Liberia through a donation of medicines to the Group of 77 Disabled Center.

By Patience M. Jones, [email protected]

The celebration, held Friday at the Indian Embassy in Mamba Point, brought together members of the Indian community, government officials, disability advocates, educators, students and other invited guests, including a delegation of Liberian legislators led by Hon. Ellen A. Attoh-Wreh, Chairperson of the Women Legislative Caucus of Liberia (WLCL).



A major highlight of the commemoration was the unveiling of a newly installed bust of Mahatma Gandhi on the lawn of the Embassy’s Chancery.

The Embassy said the bust is intended to serve as a lasting reminder of Gandhi’s philosophy and his call for humanity to choose peace over violence, love over hatred, dialogue over confrontation, compassion over indifference and service over self-interest.

Gandhi Jayanti, observed annually in India as the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, is also commemorated by the United Nations as the International Day of Non-Violence.

Speaking at the ceremony, Indian Ambassador to Liberia Manoj Bihari Verma welcomed the Liberian lawmakers and other guests, describing their participation as a reflection of the growing partnership between India and Liberia.

Ambassador Verma also recalled Gandhi’s famous Talisman, which urges decision-makers to consider how their actions affect the poorest and most vulnerable members of society.

He said Gandhi’s philosophy remains relevant beyond India, emphasizing that his message belongs to humanity as a whole.

For Liberia’s disability community, however, the commemoration carried a more direct humanitarian significance.

As part of the celebration, medicines were donated to the clinic of the Group of 77 Disabled Center by members of the Indian pharmaceutical and business community in Liberia.

The contributions came from Abeer Pharmaceuticals, Lucky Pharmaceuticals, Bunty Pharmaceuticals and other members of the Indian community.

The donation was formally received on behalf of the Group of 77 Disabled Center by Senior Administrator Raymond Kolubah Zarbay Sr. and Deputy Health Services Director Fatu Sirleaf.

Zarbay, speaking on behalf of Madam Synleseh Stephenie Dahn Koung-Second Lady of Liberia and Executive Director of the Group of 77 Disabled Center, expressed appreciation to the Embassy of India, Ambassador Verma and the Indian business community for their support.

He said the donation followed engagements between the Center and the Embassy in November 2025 and September 2026, during which the needs of persons with disabilities and possible areas of cooperation were discussed.

According to him, the medicines will strengthen the Center’s capacity to provide healthcare services to persons with disabilities and surrounding communities.

He also reaffirmed the Center’s commitment to ensuring accountability and responsible distribution of the donated medical supplies.

The medicine donation, the Center said, represents more than material assistance, describing it as a demonstration of solidarity and friendship between the Indian and Liberian peoples.

The humanitarian gesture came as the Embassy concluded Seva Pakhwada, a fortnight-long service campaign observed from September 17 to October 2 by India and Indian diplomatic missions abroad.

During the campaign, Embassy officials participated in a Swachhata Pledge, beach-cleaning activities and the planting of coconut saplings under the Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam initiative.

The Embassy said the campaign reflects the spirit of seva, or selfless service, which was central to Gandhi’s philosophy.

At the Gandhi Jayanti celebration, the connection between the philosophy of service and community action was further underscored through cultural performances by schoolchildren, including traditional dances and Gandhi’s favorite devotional songs, known as bhajans.

The program also featured reflections on Gandhi’s life and values and the singing of Vande Mataram.

Meanwhile, WLCL Chairperson Ellen A. Attoh-Wreh highlighted the continued relevance of Gandhi’s principles of peace, nonviolence, service, dialogue and reconciliation.

She said the values are particularly relevant to the work of legislators as they seek to promote inclusion, dialogue and peaceful resolution of differences.

The Liberian legislators’ participation also followed their recent South-South Peer Learning Mission to India from August 10–15, 2026, under an IBSA Fund-supported project titled “Women Legislators in Liberia: Promoting Voice, Leadership and Gender-Responsive Governance for Sustainable Development.”

The project is supported by the governments of India, Brazil and South Africa.

The Embassy of India also praised the Indian community in Liberia for its continued contribution to Liberia’s social and economic development and for helping strengthen the longstanding bonds between the two countries.

For the Group of 77 Disabled Center, the partnership signals an opportunity to deepen cooperation in healthcare, disability inclusion and community development.

The Center said it looks forward to strengthening its engagement with the Embassy of India and members of the Indian business community, particularly in addressing the healthcare and inclusion needs of persons with disabilities.

As Gandhi’s bust now stands at the Indian Embassy in Monrovia, the occasion served not only as a commemoration of his life, but also as a practical demonstration of one of the values associated with his legacy: service to humanity.

World.title: Simuuwe Says Hichilema Third-Term Clips Are Out Of Context, Backs Lifting Two-Term Limit
World.content:
Lawyer Mr Mark Simuuwe says video clips of President Hakainde Hichilema rejecting a third term are being shared out of context. He insists the President was speaking about the eligibility case of the late former President Edgar Lungu, not giving a final position on whether a leader may serve beyond two terms.

Mr Simuuwe supports changing the two-term rule. He said the Head of State had issued no statement on the matter, and that in any case the power to change the Constitution rests with Parliament, not the President.

The clips have spread widely on social media. They show Mr Hichilema on several occasions speaking against a third term, including remarks after the Lungu eligibility case about sticking to what the Constitution provides. Mr Simuuwe said the clips strip away the setting in which those words were spoken.

That setting, he explained, was the question of how long Mr Lungu would have stayed in office had he won in 2021. A term is understood to be five years, and he said Mr Lungu had already served about eight. Another victory would have kept him in power for 13 years, which Mr Simuuwe said would have created a constitutional crisis because the Constitution makes no room for a president to stay that long.

“We do not have such a provision in the Constitution,” he said.

It was against that prospect, the lawyer said, that Mr Hichilema and others took a stand against a third term at the time. In his view, those circulating the clips today have left that part out.

“So there was an argument and people have cut that part,” Mr Simuuwe said, referring to the position taken then against a third term.

Asked whether his own stand conflicts with the one the President has held since 2021, Mr Simuuwe said Mr Hichilema had not spoken on the question now before the public. More importantly, he said, the decision is not the President’s to make.

“President Hichilema has not issued any statement,” he said. “But at the same time we need to be very clear that the President does not make the Constitution in Zambia.”

That power, he said, lies with the legislature. He cited Article 62 of the Constitution, read together with Article 79, as the source of Parliament’s mandate to make and change laws.

“The Constitution or laws are made by Parliament, the legislature,” Mr Simuuwe said.

He was equally firm that the push for change is not coming from State House. It comes, he said, from people like himself and many others who believe that changing the two-term rule would settle a question Zambia has wrestled with for many years.

“It’s not about HH,” he said.

His central case is that a strict two-term limit can force the country to give up its strongest leader and settle for a weaker one. He said voters should be free to keep a leader they still want, rather than lose that person to a fixed limit.

“You flush out the best leader because of two terms. You end up with a very useless leader,” he said. “So if people still need that quality leader, they would still maintain that person.”

Mr Simuuwe said the principle behind his position was to write laws that serve the country long after those who propose them are gone, rather than rules built around any one individual.

“At the end of the day we need to make laws that will outlive all of us,” he said. “Laws that will help this country even when Mark is gone. That’s the principle.”

He added that Zambia would not be breaking new ground, pointing to other countries that have already changed their rules on presidential tenure.

“Our colleagues are changing, so it’s not harmful that we are moving in the direction of what other countries are doing,” he said.

The President has yet to speak on the matter. Mr Simuuwe says any change to presidential term limits would have to begin in Parliament.

World.title: Zambia Ready To Sign US$1.5 Billion US Health Deal After Specimen-Sharing Clause Is Dropped
World.content:
Zambia is set to sign a five-year, US$1.5 billion health agreement with the United States this week. Minister of Health Prof Roma Chilengi said negotiators removed a clause that would have required the country to send specimens from its disease surveillance system to America.

Prof Chilengi said the revised Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) now addressed the concerns Zambia had raised over health data, specimen sharing, intellectual property and benefit sharing.

“As we speak now we are completely aligned,” he said. “We are completely comfortable with the MOU that has been finalised now. We are hoping that it can be signed this week.”

Government suspended the signing earlier this year to allow further diplomatic and technical discussions on provisions it considered unsuitable for Zambia. Prof Chilengi said the original document was a standard framework drawn up for several beneficiary countries in the region, and some of its terms did not sit well with Lusaka.

The Minister was frank about how the first draft was received at home.

“The MOU itself was broadly unpopular because it had clauses that were uncomfortable to ourselves,” he said. “And so for our part as Zambia we engaged and we had many, many meetings to discuss technical details of the contents of the MOU and it was a back and forth activity.”

The talks did not run to schedule.

“Many deadlines didn’t work out because we couldn’t agree on a number of things, but as we went on we kept agreeing and agreeing,” Prof Chilengi said.

Zambia’s biggest gain came on specimens. The original agreement required the country to share certain specimens collected through its disease surveillance system with the United States. Prof Chilengi said Zambia had negotiated the removal of that requirement, which means no specimens will leave the country under the agreement.

Beyond specimens, Zambia asked for clarity on intellectual property and benefit sharing in cases where research using its specimens or other health resources leads to new medicines or vaccines. It also pushed for capacity building and skills exchange between Zambian and American scientists, so that the partnership benefits both countries.

Under the agreement, the United States will provide US$1.5 billion over five years, with the annual allocation falling each year. In turn, Zambia will raise its own spending on health so that the gains made with American support are sustained after the funding tapers off.

The Health Minister stressed that the hard bargaining had not changed the relationship.

“We need to be clear here that the US Government are our biggest supporter to the health sector and they are a very cherished partner to the health sector in this country,” he said.

The Zambian deal belongs to a new generation of bilateral pacts under Washington’s America First Global Health Strategy. The strategy replaced traditional grants from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) with five-year MoUs worth roughly US$11 billion to US$14 billion. Older aid often flowed through multilateral organisations. The new deals instead tie funding to specific national policy commitments.

Those commitments have met resistance across the continent. Some draft compacts required countries to share biological resources, virus samples and epidemiological data for up to 25 years, with no guarantee that they would receive the vaccines or medicines developed from them. Others barred national regulators from inspecting imported medical products. Several demanded high levels of domestic co-investment, and some sought alignment with wider geopolitical or mineral-access goals.

Zimbabwe halted talks on a US$350 million deal over concerns about control of its health data and eventually walked away. Washington then moved to phase out its core HIV and infectious disease funding there.

At home, the opposition wants to see the final text before any pen touches paper. Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) president Mr Antonio Mwanza said an earlier draft reportedly made the health agreement conditional on a separate Bilateral Compact. He said Zambians had objected to linking health assistance with negotiations over critical minerals.

“If that is the case, publish the final agreement before signing it,” Mr Mwanza said. “Zambians have the right to know every condition, obligation, performance requirement, financing arrangement, data provision and commitment attached to this money.”

“Let the public see the revised text and verify that for itself.”

The DPP leader said the deal raised a deeper question. He asked why a country with copper, cobalt, nickel, gold and emeralds still depends so heavily on outside financing for essential services. He cited estimates from the Financial Intelligence Centre of illicit financial flows of K9.93 billion in 2022, K51.25 billion in 2023 and K85 billion in 2024, a combined K146.18 billion, with tax evasion identified as the main underlying offence.

“We should welcome support without surrendering transparency, national interests or economic sovereignty. But Zambia must also build the capacity to finance its own development,” he said.

Mr Mwanza said Government should close tax loopholes, fight tax evasion and illicit financial flows, strengthen revenue collection and make sure Zambians receive a fair return from their natural resources.

Meanwhile, Ghana has taken the opposite road. President Mr John Dramani Mahama said his cabinet rejected a proposed US$109 million US health compact, calling its terms humiliating and a threat to national sovereignty.

“Ghana is a sovereign nation. And we have our processes, we’re a democratic country,” Mr Mahama said.

He said Ghana’s Health Ministry studied the compact and brought it to cabinet, which flagged several provisions. One required Ghana to hand over its pathogen profile, meaning a record of the diseases endemic in the country. Another demanded its medical records.

“I mean, who takes another country’s medical records?” the Ghanaian leader said.

The compact also required Ghana to put its own money into the programme. It would have denied the country’s Food and Drugs Administration any right to inspect medicines and medical products brought into Ghana.

“I mean, it was humiliating,” Mr Mahama said.

He said cabinet threw the compact out faster than any document he had seen. It then instructed the health minister to tell the US ambassador that Ghana did not need it.

“We’ll manage ourselves,” he said. “And we’re doing fine.”

World.title: Mundubile, Makebi Want Sedition Trial Moved To Lusaka, Say Solwezi Venue Blocks Their Witnesses
World.content:
Mundubile, Makebi Want Sedition Trial Moved To Lusaka, Say Solwezi Venue Blocks Their Witnesses

Tonse Alliance president Mr Brian Mundubile and his running mate Mr Makebi Zulu want their sedition case moved from Solwezi to Lusaka. They contend the State set the trial in North-Western Province to cut them off from their witnesses and undermine their right to a fair trial.

Principal Resident Magistrate Mambwe Mukonde has reserved ruling to October 13 on a preliminary issue raised by the defence. The defence has also asked for constitutional questions in the case to be referred to the High Court. The ruling will decide whether the Solwezi court has jurisdiction and whether plea can be taken.

The two leaders of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) face two counts of seditious practices contrary to Section 57, as read with Section 60, of the Penal Code, Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia. Neither has taken plea since the matter opened.

In their challenge, the pair say the choice of Solwezi places an unreasonable burden on them. They list hardship, procedural unfairness, financial strain and difficulty securing witnesses who are not based in the area.

They put their objection in direct terms.

“The choosing of the location of this (Solwezi) Court as the venue for the trial is merely intended to deprive us of easily accessing our witnesses, putting us at unnecessary financial hardship and denying us timely opportunity of adequately preparing our defence thereby impeding our right to a fair trial,” the two said.

Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu arrived at court under tight security. Police cordoned off and barricaded the court to keep supporters off the premises. A combined team of Zambia National Service, Prisons and police officers in riot gear stood guard, and armoured police vehicles blocked the roads leading to the court.

Outside the cordon, hundreds of Solwezi residents gathered and sang songs of solidarity for the pair. Former Mines Minister Mr Richard Musukwa, Mr Chanda Kabwe and other party officials were among those who came to follow the proceedings.

Inside, the defence jointly filed a notice of motion asking for a preliminary issue to be referred to the High Court, contending that the case raised constitutional questions. The State objected strongly. The defence then asked for an adjournment so it could respond properly to that objection, and the court granted it.

Lead counsel Mr Sakwiba Sikota said the court had directed the defence to file written submissions within three days. That meant there was no need for another appearance before the ruling.

“The court has given us that and stated that we should do so within three days, written submissions,” Mr Sikota said. “We don’t need to come back here.”

He said the ruling would settle two questions together: whether the Solwezi court can try the case at all, and whether it should be moved to Lusaka.

“That’s when the court will make its ruling on whether or not the court has got jurisdiction and whether or not this matter be referred to be heard in Lusaka,” he said.

The location of the alleged offence lies at the heart of the defence challenge. Defence lawyer Mr Bonaventure Mutale told the court that the alleged offences were committed in Lusaka, not Solwezi. He said hearing the matter in North-Western Province went against the Subordinate Courts Act and the Criminal Procedure Code.

On that point, the State offered no resistance. Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri told the court that the State did not dispute the contents of the warn-and-caution statements taken from the two. Those statements indicate that the alleged offence was committed in Lusaka.

Mr Phiri did oppose a defence application for the accused to give oral evidence based on those statements, telling the court the request was not supported by law. Magistrate Mukonde dismissed the application. She ruled that the issues raised orally had already been adequately covered in the documents before the court.

The prosecution maintained that the delay was not of its making. The State said it had lined up seven witnesses and had come to court expecting the two accused to take plea so that trial could begin.

It said it had also been ready at the previous sitting, with witnesses available both times.

“We just want to show that the State is ready to prosecute this case and deal with it in the most expeditious manner,” the prosecution said.

Access to the accused also came before the court. Defence lawyers complained that police restrictions were making it hard to reach their clients.

Mr Phiri assured them that better arrangements would be made. He said officers had a duty to secure the court premises, but security measures should not stop lawyers from reaching their clients or holding private consultations.

Magistrate Mukonde directed the State to ensure that lawyers had easy access to the court and could speak privately with the two accused. She said the arrangements should take into account the heightened public interest in the case and the need to keep the premises secure.

The charges arise from statements the pair made after the vote. In count one, the prosecution alleges that the accused called on the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) to release results and officially announce the winner of the August 13, 2026 general election. It says they claimed their own parallel vote tabulation pointed in a certain direction.

In count two, the State alleges that the accused announced Mr Mundubile would address the nation at a date and time still to be set.

The prosecution further alleges that the two acted together and published material through livestreams on their Facebook pages. In those livestreams, it says, they claimed their parallel vote tabulation showed NRPUP had won the presidential election and a majority of parliamentary seats.

The case now waits on the October 13 sitting. The court will decide whether the trial stays in Solwezi or goes to Lusaka, and plea and the start of trial could follow depending on the outcome. The State says its witnesses are ready.

World.title: Kasenengwa CDF projects progressing well
World.content:
The implementation of projects under the 2026 Constituency Development Fund (CDF) in Kasenengwa District, Eastern province is reported to be progressing well.

Kasenengwa Town Council Assistant Public Relations Officer Kamela Ntambo told the media in an interview that the council is currently implementing a number of projects from different components of CDF.

Ms Ntambo explained that under the community projects component, the local authority is constructing six 1 by 2 classroom blocks across six wards.

“These projects are from different components of CDF, and so under community projects we have six 1 by 2 CRBs in six different wards across the district”, she highlighted.

She revealed that the classroom blocks are being constructed at a total cost of 850, 000 Kwacha each.

Ms Ntambo explained that of these only one has been completed while others are still under construction, ranging between 80 and 90 percent completion levels.

She added that the local authority has installed solar lighting in five health facilities at a total cost of K400, 000, using the 2026 CDF allocation.

“Using the 2026 CDF we have installed solar lighting in five health facilities at a sum of 400, 000 which is currently at 100 percent completion”, she explained.

Ms Ntambo cited Kawawa, Chinunda, Mkowe, Kanzutu and Chiwoko as the health facilities that have had solar lighting installed using CDF this year.

She further explained that the local authority is also constructing a staff house at Zungula primary school in Chingazi ward at a cost of K650, 000 and that it is 80 percent complete.

World.title: Mkushi child rights committees trained on abuse cases
World.content:
Lifeline Childline Zambia in partnership with Strategic Youth Organization has trained Community Child Rights Committees in Mkushi District to strengthen their capacities to identify, handle and refer cases involving violence and abuse against children.

The training of Chibefwe and Kasokota Child Protection Committees is aimed at equipping community structures with knowledge and skills to protect children’s rights.

Speaking in an interview with the media, Lifeline/Childline Zambia Project Manager Don Miyanda said the programme is designed to ensure committee members are adequately equipped to handle child protection cases professionally while safeguarding the welfare of victims.

Mr Miyanda said it is important for committee members to understand how to respond to cases without exposing children to further victimisation.

“We want to build their capacity so that they can handle child protection cases in a more professional manner and with a human face so that they can refer them to the District Child Protection Committee,” he said.

He said the committees are also expected to remain vigilant and identify child protection cases within their communities.

Mr Miyanda stated that the trained committees should become change agents by taking an active role in promoting children’s rights and reporting cases of abuse.

Strategic Youth Organization (SYO) Executive Director Bright Mumba said the training will contribute towards reducing violence against children in the district.

Mr Mumba said stakeholders need to be proactive in identifying child protection cases instead of turning a blind eye to abuse occurring in their communities.

“We want stakeholders to be well trained so that they can be able to quickly identify cases that surround child protection. We want them to stop pretending that they are not seeing what is happening,” he said.

Meanwhile, Chibefwe Child Protection Committee Secretary Eunice Musukuma thanked the organizers for conducting the training, saying it has strengthened their understanding of their responsibilities in protecting children.

Ms Musukuma urged community members to become whistle-blowers by reporting suspected cases of child abuse to the relevant authorities.

“If they see that the rights of the child are being abused, they should report and as a committee we will do our level best to ensure that the rights of the child are protected,” she said.

She stressed that cases of sexual abuse should be reported regardless of the relationship between the victim and alleged perpetrator.

“Even cases like defilement, even if you are related to the perpetrator, you are supposed to report because if you don’t, you are ruining the child’s future,” she said.

World.title: Corruption hinders Zambia’s development agenda- AAC
World.content:
Alliance Against Corruption (AAC) Executive Director Noel Chisebe says corruption remains the greatest obstacle to Zambia’s national development agenda.

Speaking to the media in Kabwe in an interview, Dr Chisebe cautioned that Zambia’s aspiration for growth through the “Grow Zambia Agenda” will be unattainable unless far-reaching anti-corruption measures are implemented.

Dr Chisebe emphasised the urgent need for the government to provide real-time, adequate, and predictable funding to key oversight institutions among them the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) and the Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC).

He stressed that such funding should be ring-fenced for critical operations, including forensics, asset tracing, and the establishment of decentralized offices in all provinces and districts.

“We have noted with concern the funding status of oversight institutions. The Anti-Corruption Commission and the Drug Enforcement Commission, among others, need real-time funding,” Dr Chisebe said.

He further called for the restoration of funding for corruption prevention and public education initiatives, highlighting that these are more cost-effective than prosecution in combating graft.

“We need to treat the fight against corruption just like we treat economic infrastructure because every kwacha leaked from Constituency Development Fund (CDF), Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP), mining royalties, and health procurement undermines the Grow Zambia Agenda,” Dr Chisebe observed.

He noted that if the wealth generated by national programmes truly reaches the people, the Grow Zambia Agenda, President Hakainde Hichilema’s blueprint for development, has the potential to double Zambia’s economy and create the much-needed jobs.

Dr Chisebe also commended President Hichilema for his recent working visit to the United Arab Emirates (UAE), describing it as a strategic move aimed at transitioning Zambia from economic stabilisation to increased production, exports, and job creation.

He said the visit was the first major external engagement after the president’s inauguration and was focused on attracting investment, stimulating private sector growth, promoting value addition, fostering industrial development, and advancing the Grow Zambia Agenda.

World.title: Nyimba Teachers’ union calls for boy child retention programme
World.content:
Nyimba District Teachers’ Union Representative, Wilson Kombani has called on the Government to introduce a programme aimed at keeping boys in school, similar to the Keep Girls in School (KGS) programme.

‎

‎Mr Kombani said boys are also vulnerable to dropping out of school due to challenges such as drug abuse, charcoal burning among others.

‎

‎He was speaking in Nyimba District during the commemoration of World Teachers’ Day held under the theme, “Standing with Teachers: 60 Years of Protecting the Profession, advancing its Status and Shaping our Future.”

‎

‎Mr Kombani commended the Government for implementing the Keep Girls in School programme but said similar interventions should be extended to boys.

‎

‎He proposed the introduction of a Keep Boys in School (KBS) programme to address challenges affecting the boy child.

‎

‎ “Government is doing well with the Keep Girls in School programme, but what about the boy child? Boys are dropping out due to drug abuse, charcoal burning and early labour activities. We ask that KGS be complemented with a Keep Boys in School programme because the boy child is also vulnerable,” he said.

‎

‎Mr Kombani also called on the Government to expedite the confirmation of teachers who have served in acting positions for several years.

‎

‎He said teachers serving as Heads of Department, Deputy Head teachers and Head teachers should not remain in acting positions for extended periods without receiving acting allowances or confirmation letters.

‎

‎The Union Representative further appealed to the Government to facilitate the movement of teachers who are transferred by meeting their relocation-related costs.

‎

‎Mr Kombani called for the timely payment of settling-in allowances and leave travel benefits to deserving teachers.

‎

‎He also raised concern over teachers who have upgraded their academic qualifications but remain on the same salary scale for several years.

‎

‎”Long-serving teachers, some of whom have between 15 and 20 years of service, should be considered for promotion and advancement in their careers,” he said.

‎

‎He urged relevant authorities to ensure that teachers are promoted in line with their qualifications, experience and years of service.

World.title: Zambia open for Investment in Timber
World.content:
The government has underscored the need to unlock Zambia’s Forest Economy for sustainable growth through forestry investment in line with the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Minister of Green Economy and Environment, Gilbert Siame has noted that the forestry sector has potential to create millions of revenue, create jobs and contribute to Zambia’s growth agenda through forest plantation expansion.

Dr Siame highlighted that his ministry is ready to work with investors and is already identifying geographical areas along the strategic Lobito Corridor for wood-processing industries.

“We have a very good market and can export within the region. We can only win if we do it on a large scale,” he said.

He adds that the World Bank Group is ready to partner and collaborate with the ministry, saying that the government is also calling for investment along the TAZARA Corridor to support its expansion.

Speaking when a delegation from the Chinese Chamber of Commerce paid a courtesy call on him, Dr Siame highlighted that the ministry is targeting investment to expand forestry plantations by one million hectares.

Dr Siame noted that Zambia’s economy is growing and the demand for timber is increasing, emphasising that the country is well positioned to export timber in the region and beyond.

He described forestry as a viable sector for job creation, with opportunities across the entire value chain.

The Minister said he wants Zambia to become a leader in timber production and value addition, adding that a short documentation strategy will be established as a guide in line with the expansion project.

“Those in timber processing in China, willing to invest are fully welcome. By having more we will have accessible, affordable and quality goods, both local and for export,” Dr Siame said.

He added that the TAZARA Corridor is strategic to this goal and his ministry wants to establish aggregators and out grower schemes to drive economic growth, stressing the importance of involving traditional leaders along the sited areas.

The Ministry’s Permanent Secretary, Douty Chibamba adds that the forestry sector has potential in green economy particularly with the out grower schemes that will feed into the broader vision of the forest plantation.

Meanwhile, the Chinese Chamber of Commerce President Tie Li said the chamber is ready to work with the ministry in this regard.

Mr Tie noted that the forestry industry is relatively new to Chinese investors and proposed working through the Chinese Embassy and Chinese research institutes.

He added that aside from timber, fruit trees could also be planted to benefit local farmers.

He also proposed working with ZEMA to improve compliance policies in Zambia and encouraged more private-sector players to come on board to help make the forest expansion venture a reality.

The corridor’s favourable rainfall patterns are expected to support faster timber growth with potential sites for the plantation project already identified.

The government is also putting major infrastructure and technology in place to manage risks, including forest fires.
