An opposition party enthusiastic to vote is a major warning sign for the president's party, especially in a midterm year.

History is not on the side of the president's party in midterm elections

In 18 of the 20 midterms since World War II, the president's party has lost House seats. On average, it's 26 seats, and it's nine more than that when a president's approval rating is below 50%.

The last three midterm elections have seen fewer lost House seats, despite unpopular presidents, in large measure because the universe of competitive districts is smaller.

The president, himself, though, has acknowledged multiple times the political headwinds his party faces in midterms.

"Whether you have a great president or not, Republican or Democrat, they don't do well in midterms," Trump said Friday at a campaign rally in Alabama. "I don't know why. Nobody's explained it."

There are reasons, however.

First, turnout in midterms is historically about 30% lower than in presidential years. So, the voters most fired up to vote show up in outsized numbers.

Anger is a great motivator, and often the voters more aligned with the opposition party most want to register their frustration. And, as noted earlier, the intensity of opposition to Trump is at historic levels.

Sponsor Message

A CBS poll out Sunday found Democrats with the enthusiasm edge – 84% of Democrats and 82% of independents surveyed said they are "definitely" going to vote compared to 77% of Republicans.

What's more, a key indicator of which party does well in midterms is pointing in the Democrats' direction. Surveys, including the NPR/PBS News/Marist poll, ask a version of: "If November's election for Congress were held today, which party's candidate are you more likely to vote for in your district?"

In an average of the 2026 polls, Democrats have a nine-point advantage on this question, known as the congressional ballot test. Democrats tend to need a larger lead on the question historically than Republicans, given how districts have been drawn. But +9 is in the range of what Democrats need.

To put a finer point on it: in each of the past seven midterm elections, the party with the advantage on the congressional ballot has made gains.

Loading...

With independents and Latinos, two swing groups, souring on Trump during this second term, that's an added problem for Republicans in competitive districts.

Their jobs are made even tougher when Trump says things like "pretend" he's on the ballot and makes the election a "referendum" on him.

The White House's theory of the case is that Trump has had success turning conservatives out when he's on the ballot, and Republican candidates need them to show up in big numbers.

But whether that's enough is going to be tested. In swing districts and some key Senate races, candidates also usually need voters in the middle to win.

The bottom line is with less than a month to go until all the votes are in, the political compass is pointed in Democrats' direction. For multiple reasons, Democrats' gains might not be as big as similar numbers might indicate in past elections, but there is no doubt that, right now, they have the wind at their backs.

World.title: Wildfire smoke affects animals in unique ways. Scientists are trying to understand it
World.content:
Wildfire smoke affects animals in unique ways. Scientists are trying to understand it

toggle caption i Ari Daniel/NPR

Olivia Sanderfoot stands on a flower-freckled hillside in Amherst in Western Massachusetts. She listens for a moment — and a volley of birdsong flutters forth.

An Eastern Wood-Pewee. A goldfinch. A downy woodpecker.

"It's just magical," she says with an air of reverence. There are birds foraging among the flowers. Fluffy fledglings are darting about, learning the ways of the world.

"Every day that I get to start birding is a good day," she says. "If you want to get the widest range of species and hear the most songs, you want to be out here in the morning."

For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.

Sanderfoot, a global change ecologist at Cornell University, knows that for the birds that live here, not every morning is this idyllic. Over the summer, this area was suffused with toxic smoke from distant wildfires in Canada. It's an increasingly common problem, even in places untouched by flames. Fire season is starting earlier, lasting later, burning more land — and as a result, producing far more smoke.

Sponsor Message

"Smoke can blow hundreds to thousands of miles away from that burn site," Sanderfoot explains. "That means that the footprint of a smoke event greatly exceeds that of any fire. How do birds deal with that?"

This is the central question animating Sanderfoot's desire to form a new field of study called "smoke ecology." The goal, she says, is to understand how the smoke billowing off of wildfires may be disturbing wild places and creatures — and whether anything can be done to prevent possible harm.

Air today, gone tomorrow

Sanderfoot's curiosity about how birds cope with smoke emerged in 2018 when she was living in Seattle and wildfires blazed in Eastern Washington. "The air smelled acrid," she recalls. "The city was just blanketed in this sickly yellow, gray haze."

She was told it was a one-time event — yet the same thing happened two years later.

"I remember walking outside and my eyes were just burning," Sanderfoot says. "And I thought, 'What on earth are animals doing? Are they OK?'"

toggle caption i Aaron Gouveia/Mass Audubon

Very little was known apart from anecdotes — like the absence of birdsong or the arrival of droves of birds to a backyard, famished and parched.

"Smoke is a toxic soup of substances," she says. "It's not just about what [birds are] inhaling, which is inevitably bad for them. It's also about how the cues that they use to navigate their world are upended when it gets smoky outside."

To puzzle out what was going on, Sanderfoot realized that she needed to collaborate with researchers from a range of other disciplines, including conservation biology, statistics, ecophysiology, and atmospheric chemistry.

Sponsor Message

"Real-world problems don't map cleanly onto the same academic silos that have been set up for decades," says Tracey Holloway, an atmospheric chemist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, the lead of NASA's Health and Air Quality Applied Sciences Team, and a colleague of Sanderfoot's. "We need to be tackling new problems with new partnerships."

For instance, in order to understand what birds are inhaling, one has to know what's moving through the air in time and three-dimensional space. "It depends on which way the winds are blowing," says Holloway, "what chemical processes are happening in the air, and also patterns of rainfall and where the emissions are coming from." The science depends on air quality monitoring, satellite data, and evermore sophisticated computer modeling.

Birds are especially sensitive to smoke in large part because of how they breathe. A human being has soft lungs that allow inhalation and exhalation of air. By contrast, birds have rigid lungs surrounded by a collection of air sacs that act like bellows, pushing air continuously through the system.

"This allows birds to take up about twice as much oxygen with each breath that they inhale compared to us," says Sanderfoot. "This means that they're vulnerable to all the other things that are in the air, too."

Morgan Tingley, an ecologist at UCLA, is another member of the burgeoning smoke ecology cohort. "What we're trying to do is getting smoke to be recognized as a disturbance in and of itself distinct from fire that is worthy of our concentrated attention," he says.

For much of his career, Tingley has studied wildfires — events with a clear start and stop, and defined borders. But the smoke produced by those wildfires can present its own unique set of problems, as it can spread far from the original blaze.

"Smoke is extremely hard to predict and it's highly variable," he says. "It can be there one day, one hour, and gone the next. Which means that it's hard to actually disentangle what its impacts are because you can't really control it."

Sponsor Message

This means that it's not possible to anticipate where smoke will appear, or when. Scientists also prefer not to subject animals to smoke intentionally.

So when it comes to studying wildfire smoke and birds, the trick is to gather data everywhere. To do so, the researchers rely on legions of amateur birders and professional conservationists and ornithologists across the country who are already on the ground collecting data when smoke happens to blow in.

Big army, little birds

One such individual is Pam Sowizral, the bird project coordinator at Mass Audubon's Drumlin Farm Wildlife Sanctuary in Lincoln outside of Boston. On a sunny morning in late August, she walks up to a bluebird nest box and gently raps on the outside.

toggle caption i Ari Daniel/NPR

"Always give a little knock first," she advises quietly. "Let them know you're coming." When she lifts the side panel, she reveals two feathery puffballs huddled on a bed of pine needles. These baby bluebirds are the last of the season here.

Sowizral says that nearly every year for the last 20 years, three times a week in spring and summer, she and her volunteers check the bird boxes here and count the nests and the eggs and how many chicks fledge. They check when the weather's good, when it's bad (within reason) — and when the smoke rolls in.

"Those periods of time when the smoke was here, the air somehow felt a little different," she says. But "that didn't stop us from doing our usual monitoring of our boxes."

That's key. Nationally, counts like this one provide a portrait of bird activity and behavior before, during and after smoke events.

toggle caption i Ari Daniel/NPR

Sanderfoot of Cornell University says she's using these kinds of observations, alongside observations of breeding behavior, to help her understand how birds are coping with wildfire smoke in a variety of places.

Sponsor Message

She's revealed three distinct strategies, depending on the species and the individual birds. They either hunker down and stay put, fly away, or shift their behavior — by not vocalizing as much or venturing out less often, say.

"This could be an attempt to mitigate their exposure," says Sanderfoot. "It might also be how they are forced to respond if they feel unwell."

In addition, she and her colleagues have observed that repeated exposure to smoke appears to impair the body condition of a variety of birds, leading to lower weight overall.

"They all respond in different ways," she says. "And we need to figure out what those ways are and how effective they are in order to design effective conservation strategies for a rapidly changing world."

This is one of Sanderfoot's top priorities: determining what might constitute what she calls smoke refugia for birds — safer spots where they can hunker down until conditions improve. "I want to know where birds are going when it's smoky," she says, "what resources they're seeking out, and what we could provide to help them during a risky time" — like water and perhaps shelter or food.

"I would like to be able to give people something they can do to help," she says.

Sanderfoot's personal experience with wildfires didn't end in Seattle. "I almost feel like the smoke is following me," she says.

In early 2025, she and her family fled the fires in Los Angeles where they were living at the time. And this summer, she watched as a blanket of smoke descended upon parts of the U.S., including Ithaca where she lives now, blowing off the remote Canadian infernos. She says she doesn't think it's a coincidence.

"Let's put it this way," she says: "We can expect that the future will be smokier."

Sponsor Message

It's a fact that's true for birds and people, which means that what Sanderfoot and her colleagues learn about smoke ecology may reveal a clearer way forward — for us all.

"By learning more about birds," she says, "I think we might learn something about how we can take care of ourselves and each other."

World.title: 'We could all hear her breathing': Witnessing the failed execution of Christa Pike
World.content:
'We could all hear her breathing': Witnessing the failed execution of Christa Pike

toggle caption i George Walker IV/AP

Last week, I was one of the seven media witnesses who observed Tennessee fail to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike, the first woman to face the death penalty in the state in almost 200 years.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

From our previous reporting , each of us had an inkling that the lethal injection process might not go according to plan.

Pike's attorneys had asked the Tennessee Supreme Court to allow her to be hanged instead , citing concerns that a platelet disorder and small veins would make the actual injection not only painful but ineffective.

And Tennessee had already botched an execution attempt in May, when healthcare workers failed to establish complete IV access into Tony Carruthers, who was sentenced to death after being convicted for his involvement in the kidnapping and murders of three people in 1994.

Sponsor Message

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said after the failed execution of Carruthers, who has maintained he is innocent, the state wouldn't try again to kill him for at least a year. After Pike left the execution chamber in an ambulance on Sept. 30, Lee announced he would suspend lethal injections for the rest of the year.

The morning of Pike's scheduled execution, I and the other media witnesses arrived at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville by 8:30 a.m. and waited to be ushered into the prison with nothing but our driver's licenses in hand. The plan was to wait inside until Pike began her journey to the death chamber at 10 a.m.

But we didn't make it that far.

toggle caption i George Walker IV/AP

Before the Department of Correction's staffers began moving us away from the outdoor media tent and our belongings, the reporters' phones all went off. A federal circuit court had stayed the execution. This was my fifth stint as a media witness to an execution, and I'd never seen a stay issued. We didn't know what that would mean.

It turned out to mean waiting for nine hours at the prison, barred from leaving the grounds. We spent most of it in the boardroom where parole hearings take place.

Sponsor Message

Hours of waiting. Then, 'It's a go.'

Throughout the wait, the victim's family often came up in conversation. In 1995, Pike, then 18 years old, killed Colleen Slemmer, who was 19. Slemmer's family lives in Florida and traveled to Tennessee for the execution with money raised through crowdfunding. It's unclear where they waited while the last-minute legal wrangling played out.

Sometime around 6 p.m., the prison system's communications director, Dorinda Carter, told us: "It's a go."

toggle caption i George Walker IV/AP

Tennessee had asked the U.S. Supreme Court to lift the stay, and it did. Carter read the ruling aloud to us.

For unknown reasons, it took another hour or so for the security team to usher us into the witness bay, an all-white cinderblock room with black pleather chairs in two rows and a big window overlooking the death chamber. A loudspeaker pipes sound into the room from the chamber when the microphones are on.

A black curtain hangs in front of the window inside the death chamber. Department of Correction workers open it once IV lines are inserted into the condemned prisoner.

The curtain is there to obscure the workers who place the IVs, in order to shield their identities as required by state law. That process is enshrined in the "Lethal Injection Execution Protocol," which is the guidebook the Department of Correction writes for itself. There is no other regulation over executions in the state.

My employer, the Nashville public radio station WPLN, is a party in a lawsuit challenging the state's concealment of the IV insertion. When executions are botched, it's often due to something going wrong while IVs are placed — or with the subsequent step if IVs fail, placing a central line in a deeper vein through the chest, neck, or groin.

A lower court ruled in favor of WPLN and other media plaintiffs in January, but the state appealed the order, and it has been halted while higher courts consider the case.

Sponsor Message

The death chamber

The American Medical Association officially bars doctors from participating in executions, and many other health professionals also consider assisting an execution to be unethical.

Outside of prison staffers and the execution team, only the prisoner's spiritual adviser and attorney are allowed in the room with the prisoner while the IVs are inserted. So generally, attorneys' descriptions are the only account of the procedure.

Under normal circumstances, witnesses sit in the bay for 10 or 15 minutes with the curtain closed. That's how long it tends to take for the IV team to place a line and start running saline, to prepare for the 5 grams of the sedative pentobarbital that will be pumped in to kill the prisoner.

Once the lines are set, the execution team enters an adjacent, concealed room. The IV lines run through the wall into that hidden chamber, from which the drugs are administered.

But at Pike's execution, we sat in the bay for 45 minutes with the curtain closed and the microphone turned off.

Until Carruthers' failed execution, the Department of Correction kept the lights off in the witness bay during the wait. Witnesses at his execution said they sat in a dark room for an hour and a half as the execution team tried and failed to place an IV line. This time, the prison kept the lights on.

The clock we use to give a minute-by-minute account is in the death chamber, so we can't see it with the curtain closed. John North, a reporter with the television station WBIR in Knoxville, was the only witness wearing a watch. The rest of us asked him over and over what time it was.

After half an hour, it was clear the IV team must have been struggling.

We wondered whether Pike's execution would unfold similarly to Carruthers'. That time, the governor called and ordered the execution halted before the curtain ever opened.

Sponsor Message

But at 7:27 p.m., we heard the curtain being drawn away.

We saw Pike in profile, lying on the gurney, facing the window for the other bay, where the victim's family and prosecutors sit.

We saw Pike's spiritual adviser, Mikey Noechel , who wore a wine-red sash over his suit. Together, they sang and talked about Buddhist teachings.

Under the state's protocol, the spiritual adviser is allowed in the death chamber as the pentobarbital flow begins, though the attorneys are not.

There is no signal when the lethal drugs start flowing, but it's assumed to begin after the prisoner delivers her final words. It's typical for the spiritual adviser to offer prayers and other support, and for there to be a back-and-forth between the two.

Pike spoke.

"I just want to say that I'm going to leave this world the way I've spent most of my life, and that is with love," she said.

She said that she had love for those who hate her, and that she was at peace with her death.

Moments later, Pike told Noechel her arm was burning. She said it was in one specific spot and asked corrections staff in the room whether that was normal.

Pentobarbital is alkaline, so it burns like drain cleaner if it touches skin. If the IV is administered correctly, that is unlikely to happen.

But Pike and Noechel chatted for what seemed a shocking amount of time. Prisoners tend to show signs of being sedated a few minutes in. Pike didn't.

Something is wrong

The Tennessee Department of Correction uses an odd practice to announce the drugs have been fully administered. There's a small, hinged door built into the wall between the concealed drug management room and the death chamber, with a platform beneath it.

Once the drugs have completely flowed through the IV, the staff open the door and place a rock on the platform. That initiates a five-minute waiting period, after which the curtain closes again to obscure a doctor, who enters the death chamber, checks the prisoner's pulse, and certifies the death.

Sponsor Message

In each of the executions I've witnessed, the prisoners look unconscious long before the rock comes out, and in the minutes following they're presumed dead.

The rock came out at 7:41 p.m. At 7:44 p.m., Pike was still speaking quietly to Noechel.

My jaw dropped. It was clear to me then that something was very wrong.

Once the five minutes are up and the curtain closes to conceal the doctor, who confirms the time of death, the spiritual adviser moves into the witness bay and stays there until everyone leaves the facility.

But after Noechel entered the witness bay, staff came in and ordered him back into the death chamber. There was only one reason to do so: They were trying again.

The curtain re-opened.

The state's protocol dictates that, as a backup plan, prison staff can run a second round of pentobarbital. According to a statement from the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks execution attempts and their outcomes, Pike is "the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs."

Eventually, Pike stopped talking. She started snoring.

She continued to snore after the rock was put out the second time and the curtain closed again. We continued to hear her snore over the loudspeaker.

The state's protocol does not contemplate a second round of drugs failing to kill the prisoner, so there are essentially no rules for the situation the Department of Correction found itself in with Pike.

It's unclear what was happening behind the curtain. Her lawyers later said they weren't allowed in the death chamber.

The curtain closed at 8:16 p.m., and we listened to Pike's snoring for nearly 40 minutes.

Tensions rose between the media witnesses and Carter, the Department of Correction's communications director. I asked her: "Do they do a third round? Are you going to resuscitate her?" Carter didn't have an answer. Another witness, Steven Hale of the Nashville Banner, asked why the curtain was closed. The doctor wasn't certifying Pike's death. We could all hear her breathing.

Sponsor Message

At 8:53 p.m., the prison warden, Kenneth Nelsen, came over the loudspeaker and said, "Media witnesses, please exit the area."

'Intubated, on a ventilator'

We went out to the news conference, which the Department of Correction usually requires media witnesses to participate in. While one of us was speaking, several emergency vehicles arrived. We saw the caravan leave with its sirens on. That was our only insight into whether Pike was alive.

Pike's attorneys later confirmed she was hospitalized. As of Oct. 1 she remained in critical condition at an undisclosed Nashville hospital, according to her attorneys.

Her lawyers, in an emergency filing with the Davidson County Chancery Court on Oct. 2, alleged that the execution team apparently didn't "realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown" and that pentobarbital had "in whole or in part" entered her body instead of her veins.

Pike arrived at the hospital with both of her arms "swollen, burned, and blistered," they wrote. "She is intubated, on a ventilator, and remains unconscious."

Pike's future, as well as that of lethal injection in Tennessee, is uncertain.

Lee, the Republican governor who has paused executions for the rest of the year, leaves office in January. The front-runner in the Nov. 3 election to replace him, U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, has been a vocal supporter of the death penalty. After Pike's failed execution, the Republican candidate posted her solution to X.

"Bring back the electric chair and deliver justice for these victims swiftly," she wrote. "As your governor, I will do just that."

The electric chair was last used in the United States in Nashville when Tennessee executed Nicholas Sutton in 2020. He was one of five prisoners who chose the electric chair over lethal injection in the state from 2018 to 2020.

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with Nashville Public Radio and KFF Health News.

World.title: Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey's new Pentagon roles raise ethics worries
World.content:
Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey's new Pentagon roles raise ethics worries

toggle caption i Carolyn Kaster/Associated Press

A new Pentagon study focusing on the future of warfare is raising ethical concerns about its authors' potential conflicts of interest.

Last week, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced "Project Meridian: The Future of Warfare," a study of automated and AI-powered weaponry.

In addition to former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, the other two leaders of the project are SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey, the co-founder of defense technology firm Anduril. The study is expected to take 120 days.

Sponsor Message

"We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare," Hegseth's September 30 announcement said. "To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them."

The study's announcement came just days before an expected speech by President Trump at an Anduril facility in Baltimore on Tuesday.

toggle caption i Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images

Anduril Industries builds military drones that are used on land, sea and in the air and other related defense technologies. The company received its initial funding from tech billionaire and conservative political activist Peter Thiel.

SpaceX has secured over $8 billion in U.S. defense contracts in 2026 alone, according to government contract announcements. One of its flagship products is Starshield, a military-grade, low-Earth-orbit satellite network designed to provide secure communications for the government. The company's AI chatbot, Grok, is also being used by the Pentagon.

There is a concern that Musk and Luckey's study would be guided by their own financial interests, said Richard Painter, a professor of corporate law at the University of Minnesota and former chief White House ethics lawyer in the George W. Bush administration.

"They all want to sell stuff," Painter said. "So if we go into it understanding that [Musk], like all the other contractors, he wants to make a lot of money selling AI to the Defense Department. Whatever he proposes, but it's not like he's doing it as a neutral public service."

Sponsor Message

"It's a massive conflict of interest," said a former senior Defense Department official who requested anonymity out of fear of reprisal from the Trump administration. The official said that not only do both Luckey and Musk have billions of dollars in current defense contracts, but the study could also shape the types of munitions the U.S. buys in the future. For example, it could recommend more drones or space-based assets — which both Luckey and Musk build — and fewer tanks, which they don't build.

Hegseth said he has directed Emil Michael, the Defense Department's chief technology officer, to commission Project Meridian through the MITRE Corporation, a nonprofit company that manages federally-funded research across the country. Few details were released about the scope of the project in Hegseth's one-page memo.

"MITRE is responsible for the analysis and recommendations, and will evaluate all inputs with technical rigor while applying appropriate conflict-of-interest and information safeguards," said a spokesperson for the Department of Defense. "The Project Meridian effort will examine the technologies and operational concepts required to sustain U.S. military advantage across the full spectrum of future warfighting domains across a 10-20 year time horizon."

toggle caption i Finn Gomez/Getty Images

The Department of Defense did not disclose whether Musk and Luckey have been hired as special government employees — as Musk was when he led the Department of Government Efficiency cost-cutting effort — or as contractors. The nature of their employment on the project would dictate the rules they would need to follow, Painter said.

Executive branch employees are bound by federal criminal law that bans them from taking part in government decisions that affect their own money or the financial interests of their family and business. Contractors, however, are not subject to this law.

The Department of Defense did not respond to questions about the potential conflicts of interests of hiring Musk and Luckey to lead the Project Meridian study. SpaceXAI and Anduril did not respond to requests for comment about their CEOs' potential conflicts of interest.

Sponsor Message

While it is common for the federal government to assemble task forces with industry leaders, the findings and recommendations of the Project Meridian study will need to be scrutinized, said a senior official at the Government Accountability Office, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the press on issues they have not published reports on.

"There are safeguards that they're supposed to sign to keep them away from procurement activities and whatnot," the GAO official said. "That doesn't mean that we shouldn't be paying attention to what the project comes out with."

Additionally, the motivations for creating this task force are unclear, the official said.

"I don't know why we would need a new task force to talk about something since we've had many folks thinking about this issue for a while," the official said. "What would the point of this be?"

Another former Pentagon official who requested anonymity fearing retribution from the administration was less concerned. The official said there are always numerous efforts underway in the Pentagon and in the military services to ponder the future of war, and all those will likely feed into Project Meridian. The former official said it's one thing to be on such a panel and make recommendations, and for Congress to accept or reject them, and another for a panel member to write a requirement for a defense system and then bid on it.

The second Trump administration has employed different ethical standards than the administrations that preceded it, including holding stocks in companies that could stand to profit from contracts awarded by the government, Painter said.

"I do not know why they held on to defense stocks. In the Bush administration, we made everybody sell their defense stocks who went into the Defense Department," Painter said. "I never saw anywhere near as many financial conflicts of interest in any other administration. Even the first Trump administration wasn't as bad as this."

World.title: PQ in power, CAQ wiped off the map: Key takeaways from Quebec's election
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebec's electoral map has been completely redrawn, with the Parti Québécois securing enough seats to form a minority government.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon succeeded in growing his party from only three seats in 2022 to 59 on Monday.

But the PQ leader didn't get the majority he coveted, which will make it more difficult to follow through on his plans — including holding a referendum on Quebec independence.

Here is a closer look at where things stand and what to expect from the next government.

PQ dreams big

In his victory speech, St-Pierre Plamondon promised to work with other parties and be "direct and transparent" with Prime Minister Mark Carney, setting the stage for a tense relationship with Ottawa.

He also spoke in English, addressing his "English-speaking friends in Quebec."

"I just want to let you know very clearly that I'll be the premier of everyone in Quebec," he said, adding, "we share the same future."

WATCH | PQ leader addresses English speakers: Parti Québécois leader addresses English-speaking Quebecers in victory speech | Duration closed caption 0:33 Paul St-Pierre Plamondon took a moment to speak to anglophones in the province, saying that all Quebecers face the same challenges, and that he looks forward to solving problems together.

Near the end of his speech, St-Pierre Plamondon told supporters he still dreams of making Quebec a country, speaking of the "courageous struggle of francophones" to preserve their culture.

"We deserve it just as much as any other people who possess their own country and democracy," he said.

In practical terms, however, a referendum doesn't seem likely — at least in the near term.

The PQ would now need the backing of Québec Solidaire, the only other sovereigntist party in the National Assembly, to push forward with a referendum.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he would delay a referendum until 2029 or 2030, after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office, but minority governments in Quebec typically last less than two years.

CAQ wiped out

Just four years after winning a massive majority, the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) appears to be entirely wiped off the map.

The party failed to win a single seat.

Christine Fréchette, who took over as premier from François Legault, failed to win over voters frustrated after eight years of CAQ rule.

"I have Quebec tattooed on my heart," she said in her concession speech, noting she was the second woman to lead the province. "I gave everything I could."

There will be questions about the future viability of the party, which had little grassroots support and no longer has a single MNA.

It was co-founded by Legault as an alternative to the old debates between the Liberals and Parti Québécois over sovereignty — a dynamic that appears likely to play out once again at the National Assembly.

WATCH | Fréchette after a difficult night: CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette takes ownership of party’s fall in concession speech | Duration closed caption 0:48 At party headquarters in Trois-Rivières, Que., Fréchette thanked her National Assembly colleagues. She said the party’s fall was her responsibility alone, and that being premier was the greatest honour of her life.

Liberals in opposition

The Liberals are in a stronger-than-expected position after Monday, jumping from 19 seats to a projected 40.

Speaking to supporters, Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said Quebec voters elected a National Assembly without a majority, so the PQ will have an obligation to consider proposals coming from other parties.

He said the Liberals will be reviewing proposals put forward by the PQ and considering if they are in the province’s best interest.

“Preparing your referendum will find you facing a clear opponent in the Liberal Party,” Milliard said.

Switching to English, he said his party will collaborate on many issues, but “there is no way we will collaborate on a potential referendum.”

Conservative breakthrough

The Conservatives also had a good night, jumping from zero seats in 2022 to 19. The party could prove to be a partner to the PQ on some of its shared priorities.

Leader Éric Duhaime, who campaigned on tax and spending cuts, will now have a seat at the National Assembly.

“Tonight, hope has returned to Quebec,” Duhaime said. “We have just written a page in history.”

WATCH | Duhaime celebrates rise of Conservatives: Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime touts party as 'credible alternative' for anglophones | Duration closed caption 0:41 During a speech that celebrated the Conservatives’ rise, Duhaime made a direct appeal to English-speaking Quebecers, encouraging them to look past the Quebec Liberal Party to his own.

Time for electoral reform?

During the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon — alongside the Conservatives and Québec Solidaire — promised to finally overhaul the province's voting system. Monday’s results will only add urgency to that pledge.

For the first time in Quebec history, the PQ is projected to form the government with less than 30 per cent of the popular vote.

It is a historic anomaly that will immediately renew scrutiny of the province's first-past-the-post electoral system.

World.title: Boy recounts 1994 park attack on tape played at trial of alleged sex predator
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains graphic content and may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

As police drove him to Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children, the 10-year-old boy kept asking if they were nearly there.

"My stomach's turning," he told the two officers, as he lay in the back of the vehicle.

Thirty-two years after the child was tied to a tree and sexually assaulted, an audio recording of his September 1994 interview with police was played for the jury Monday at the trial of his alleged attacker .

Richard Neil has pleaded not guilty to 17 charges related to the incident, as well as two other similar past attacks on an eight-year-old boy and a 15-year-old girl. The list of allegations includes kidnapping, sexual assault causing bodily harm and administering a stupefying drug.

The three attacks in southern Ontario parks between 1992 and 1995 confounded investigators for three decades. Advances in DNA technology — including investigative genetic genealogy — finally helped police link the three crime scenes to Neil, a prosecutor told the jury Monday in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Brampton, Ont.

Richard Neil has pleaded not guilty to the 17 charges he’s facing, including kidnapping, sexual assault causing bodily harm and administering a stupefying drug. (Peel Regional Police)

Neil, now 67, was arrested in 2024.

The court heard the former postal worker doesn't dispute what happened to the three children, but insists he wasn't involved.

"He did a lot of rude things to me," the 10-year-old boy told Peel Regional Police about the unidentified attacker in 1994.

The victim, whose identity is covered by a publication ban, recounted saying hello to a stranger in Brampton's Norton Place Park after school that day. They struck up a conversation. The man claimed he had lost his wallet with $900 inside.

The boy said the pair walked around the park and chatted on a bench, until the man's mood suddenly soured, ostensibly accusing the boy of stealing his wallet.

"He tied my foot to the tree ... so I couldn't get away," the boy is heard telling police on the audio tape.

He described a series of lurid acts carried out by the man in a wooded area of the park, including urination, oral sex and anal penetration.

"It hurt," the boy told police.

After the attacker got away, the boy ran out of the woods, exiting near a branch of the Royal Canadian Legion adjacent to the park.

Witness David Kilpatrick, left, told a court in Brampton, Ont., how he spotted a young boy running shirtless out of the city's Norton Place Park on Sept. 29, 1994. Crown attorney Shazin Karim, centre, questions Kilpatrick at the trial of the accused attacker, Richard Neil, right, on Monday. (Pam Davies/CBC)

Witness recalls seeing boy run from park

David Kilpatrick, now a 71-year-old retiree, testified Monday about stopping at the Legion that evening to have a beer and play a round of pool.

Everything changed when he spotted the child wearing only his pants.

"I see this young boy coming out of the woods … shirt in hand, screaming, so I knew something was wrong," Kilpatrick told the court.

"You have to call my mom," he said the boy urged him. "I've been attacked."

Kilpatrick said the boy provided a basic description of the attacker: a white man with black hair, wearing a grey track suit.

He ran the boy into the Legion, told the bartender to call 911 and rushed into the woods himself to find the assailant, to no avail.

Kilpatrick fought back tears Monday as he spoke from the witness box. He said he promised the 10-year-old that day he would find his attacker.

"I was wound up like a clock," he told the court. "Still am, just talking about it now."

DNA tied 3 assaults to 1 man: Crown

That evening, the boy led investigators to the spot where he'd been attacked. DNA recovered from the Brampton park — as well as semen and men's underwear worn as a mask, each found separately at the scenes of two other assaults — proved crucial in linking the three incidents to one man, Crown attorney Shazin Karim told the jury.

In the first attack at Kitchener's Idlewood Park on Aug. 21, 1992, a boy said he'd been lured away from his sister and a friend by a man who promised to show him dozens of bicycles in a wooded area, Karim said.

Karim, centre, gives the Crown's opening address to the jury Monday in Brampton, Ont., at the trial of Neil, seen seated at far right in this court sketch. (Pam Davies/CBC)

She told the jury the assailant held a pocket knife and threatened to kill the eight-year-old "if he said a word."

On Aug. 31, 1995, at Oakville's Wildwood Park, a girl out walking her dog was approached by a man who threatened her with what appeared to be a loaded gun, Karim told the court in her opening statement. She said the 15-year-old cried as the man set up a video camera to record the assault.

World.title: U.S. Coast Guard identifies all 6 people aboard missing Canadian air ambulance
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. Coast Guard has named all six people, including four Canadians, who were aboard an Ontario-based air ambulance that went missing off the coast of Massachusetts on Saturday.

The four Canadian crew, employed by Ontario-based Latitude Air Ambulance, were Philip Gregory Childerhose, Thomas Henry Farquhar, Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir. The two Bermudian passengers are Marilyn Lavonne Bean and Sergio Wayne Lottimore.

"During this incredibly difficult time, our heartfelt condolences go out to the families and friends impacted by this tragic incident," Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, Commander of the U.S. Coast Guard Northeast District, said in a statement.

"We are grateful to the crews and partner agencies who quickly responded to this incident, and we will continue to support our Canadian partners as they conduct their investigation."

It was announced earlier Monday that the Transportation and Safety Board of Canada will be leading the investigation into the incident, something the Coast Guard statement confirmed.

WATCH | Transportation Safety Board to lead investigation into crash: TSB to investigate air ambulance crash after search called off | Duration 0:55 After an air ambulance crashed on its way from Bermuda to Boston, four Canadian crew members and two passengers are missing. The U.S. Coast Guard has suspended its search for them. Canada's Transportation Safety Board is now investigating the crash.

The air ambulance was flying to Boston from Bermuda when it went missing on Saturday.

Officials have said the two Bermudians were being airlifted to Boston when the plane lost contact with air-traffic control early Saturday.

Air traffic control audio shows the pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast.

The coast guard says debris from the plane was found 32 kilometres off Nantucket and suspended its search on Sunday after scouring roughly 7,000 kilometres of ocean.

"It is with profound sadness that we acknowledge the decision by the United States Coast Guard to conclude active search and rescue operations and transition to recovery efforts," Latitude Air Ambulance, the Hamilton-based company that operated the aircraft, said in a statement on Sunday.

"Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search and rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard … are presumed to have died."

World.title: Giant underwater Kelvin wave could 'pack a punch' for B.C. in mid-October
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A giant underwater wave of water connected to this year's El Niño weather pattern is moving up the west coast of the Americas, raising alarm bells among scientists about how climate change is magnifying the impacts of the naturally occurring phenomenon.

The so-called Kelvin wave is not unexpected. But like El Niño as a whole, it is happening on top of human-caused climate change that has already warmed the oceans and atmosphere.

A smaller wave already reached B.C. earlier this summer, and the next one is expected to arrive within one to two weeks, according to Bill Merryfield, a research scientist at Environment and Climate Change Canada.

"We actually did already see over 30 centimetres in some locations in June. And so the coming wave looks like it'll be a stronger one," Merryfield said.

What causes it?

The Kelvin wave is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon, just like El Niño itself. In normal years, winds blow from east to west along the equator in the Pacific Ocean, generally pushing water from South America toward Asia.

During El Niño years, however, those east-to-west winds weaken or can reverse direction, allowing water to move east instead.

"When these Kelvin waves reach the coast of South America, there's nowhere further east for this pile up of water to go. And so it splits and starts running up and down the coasts of the Americas" and eventually all the way up to Canada, Merryfield said.

Sea-level monitoring data collected at Tofino, on Vancouver Island's Pacific coast, shows the impact of the earlier Kelvin wave in June.

Rather than a giant tsunami-like wave, the Kelvin wave temporarily raises sea levels.

"You can think of it more like a very broad, hundreds of miles wide, but very shallow bulge in the height of the ocean surface, so by maybe a foot or so," University of California climate scientist Daniel Swain told CBS News last month .

What will it do to the West Coast?

Merryfield said the impacts are most pronounced during king tides, particularly high tides that happen when the gravitational pull of the sun and moon combine to produce higher-than-normal tides.

"So if you put that 30 centimetres of sea level rise on top of a king tide, and then maybe you add a winter storm to that, which causes a storm surge, that's when you really start to get into trouble," he said.

"This extra foot or so of sea level rise due to El Niño can pack a punch."

WATCH | El Niño's grim forecast: El Niño-fuelled heat could kill half a million people by February: study | Duration closed caption 1:51 The record global heat brought by this year's powerful El Niño could lead to nearly half a million more deaths worldwide by the end of February, according to a report that also highlights the impact of climate change on extreme heat.

Those surges could be intensified by another effect of El Niño, further raising sea levels along the B.C coast. El Niño can strengthen northward winds along the coast, pushing even more water toward shore.

These compounding effects — the Kelvin wave, stronger northward winds and winter storms, on top of climate change already raising sea levels and intensifying extreme weather — could worsen flooding and erosion along the coast. Strong El Niños in the past have caused widespread erosion on California's beaches.

Local authorities there are placing emergency sand on beaches and expect the Kelvin wave to raise water levels six to 12 inches, the Associated Press reports .

Exceptionally high king tides and powerful waves damaged protective sand and wooden berms in Long Beach, Calif. in June. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

The impacts of the Kelvin wave — and El Niño more broadly — could extend far beyond this season, Merryfield warned.

The oceans absorb much of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases, moderating global warming as humans continue to burn fossil fuels. During El Niños, however, some of that stored heat is released from the ocean into the atmosphere.

World.title: High-flying lawyer goes on trial for writing bad cheque allegedly to cover for collapsing firm
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Toronto lawyer who co-founded a law firm with his wife that collapsed spectacularly three years ago, after millions of dollars in client money was discovered missing from the firm's trust account, went on trial Monday on a fraud charge stemming from the police investigation into the case.

Nicholas Cartel, 62, faces one count of fraud over $5,000 based on allegations that he deliberately wrote a bad cheque for $300,000 in an attempt to cover up a shortfall in the trust account at Cartel & Bui LLP, the firm he ran with his wife.

The alleged fraud occurred in February 2023, when Cartel & Bui LLP was handling a property sale for a client. The law firm needed to pay out $2.22 million in proceeds to the client but didn't have sufficient funds in its trust account because Bui had been embezzling money from it for years, according to her own evidence in a separate civil case.

Bui is facing 32 criminal charges in a separate case stemming from the embezzlement.

The February 2023 incident foreshadowed a series of events in which more than 25 property owners and buyers in southern Ontario ran into problems closing on real estate deals because money was missing from the Cartel & Bui trust account.

One couple lost $2.16 million they had entrusted to the firm to buy a house in Toronto, while other clients — or home-purchase insurers — were out as much as $729,000.

Now-disbarred real estate lawyer Singa Bui leaves a Toronto courthouse in October 2024 after being sentenced to 30 days in provincial prison for civil contempt of court. The sentence was later reduced to 20 days. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

Cartel is not facing criminal charges in relation to those other cases, and has long maintained his innocence. He says he operated a separate legal practice at the firm focused on class actions and litigation, while the theft of client money occurred in the real estate side of the business run by his wife, Singa Bui.

With respect to the criminal charge alleging that he deliberately wrote a bad cheque, Cartel does not deny writing it but says his actions didn't amount to fraud.

He also maintains that prosecutors have improperly withheld evidence from him and misleadingly presented other evidence. At the outset of his trial Monday, he told the court he intends to bring an application under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to have his criminal charge stayed.

Bank employees testify

At the start of Monday's trial in provincial court in Toronto, prosecutor Dihim Emami called a witness from Royal Bank of Canada's investigations department to testify about records associated with the personal chequing account on which the $300,000 cheque was drawn.

The witness, Adkin Holder, a former Toronto police fraud-squad detective, testified that the account's opening documents showed it belonged to Cartel and that for months before the bad cheque was written, the account had a negative balance.

He said that because of that, a $300,000 cheque would have failed to cash, and the receiving bank could have been at risk of losing the money if it was unable to recover it from the person who wrote the cheque.

Prosecutors Megan Rauser, left, and Dihim Emami converse outside court at the end of the first day of Cartel's criminal trial. (Aloysius Wong/CBC)

Cartel later asked Holder whether it was possible the account was in fact a joint account at the time the bad cheque was written, which Holder agreed was possible.

Prosecutors then entered records showing that the account statements bore only Cartel's name, while statements for other joint accounts bore both his name and Bui's.

A second witness, from TD Bank, where the law firm had its trust account, began testifying Monday afternoon about transactions in that account and is expected to resume Tuesday.

Already jailed for contempt of court

Cartel has already spent 30 days in jail over the collapse of his firm, after a judge in separate civil lawsuits against him and his wife ruled in August 2024 that he had committed contempt of court by failing to produce records or answer questions about where the missing trust-account money went.

He filed an appeal of that ruling, but it was dismissed this past August because he failed to move it forward.

He is also on the hook for millions of dollars in default judgments against him obtained by former clients of his firm, though has said he will contest them.

His attempt to overturn one of those judgments , for $500,000, was rejected by the Ontario Court of Appeal in February.

Defendant dismissed his criminal lawyer

Cartel hired veteran criminal lawyer Richard Posner to defend him late last year, but split with Posner 4½ months later amid a dispute over his fees and trial strategy, according to records obtained by CBC from a separate case in which Cartel challenged Posner's billings.

Those records show Cartel wanted his lawyer to try to get his charge dismissed as an abuse of process — a rare remedy available when a defendant can show that the prosecution's conduct seriously compromised the accused's right to a fair trial.

"In my respectful view, there is no basis for advancing an abuse of process claim in this case," Posner emailed Cartel, according to documents from their fee dispute.

"If you want to bring this motion, you will need to discharge me and find another lawyer or represent yourself."

At another point, Cartel and Posner differed over whether they should agree at trial to certain of the prosecution's alleged facts.

"Why dispute or make the Crown prove things that are plain and obvious from the business records? In my view, it makes no sense to do so, but the choice is yours," Posner wrote to Cartel.

Ultimately, Posner wrote to Cartel in April of this year: "Based on the tenor and content of your email, along with your previous communications with the members of my office, it is my respectful view there has been a breakdown in our solicitor-client relationship. Accordingly, I will be requesting to be removed from the record on the next court date."

Cartel replied: "I was going to terminate your services Monday, in any event…. I have long ago lost any faith that you or your firm could represent my best interests."

Cartel told CBC News on Monday, on the sidelines of his trial, that he and Posner had settled their dispute out of court.

He is representing himself in his criminal trial. The judge, Rachel Grinburg, referred to that fact in court several times Monday, emphasizing that she wanted to ensure the proceedings were fair to him.

His law licence has been provisionally suspended since April 2024 by the Law Society of Ontario, which has levelled 20 disciplinary accusations against him, including 12 counts of misappropriation of client funds.

Bui was disbarred by the Law Society in December.

World.title: Whey up: Protein powder prices soar as global demand grows
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Jennifer Mason is trying to eat more protein and has supplemented her diet with whey protein powder over the past few years. But lately, soaring prices are giving her sticker shock. And as a new mom with rising expenses, she's rethinking her shopping list.

"I'm just cutting back. I'm trying to find protein in whole foods that I'm eating rather than actually getting products," she says.

To meet growing demand, food manufacturers and fast food companies are putting whey protein into everything from snacks to drinks. That's contributing to shortages of the ingredient and pushing prices to record highs. Now whey protein is also caught in the U.S.-Canada trade war, increasing costs that may end up being passed on to consumers.

Protein on the menu

From chips and Pop-Tarts to candy, protein-packed foods are popping up on grocery store shelves. Khloé Kardashian recently launched protein popcorn. Starbucks is offering protein cold foam, catching up with the whey protein shots on the menu at Booster Juice.

Khloé Kardashian's Protein Popcorn is made with 7 grams of protein per serving, using "Khloud Dust," a milk protein isolate blend coating the kernels. (Khloud)

Major brands are adding whey protein to their products to appeal to health-conscious consumers. Fitness influencers are pushing protein-maxxing, a trend of consuming dietary protein at every opportunity. And as more people take weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, some are also eating more protein to prevent muscle loss.

It's all eating into the global supply of whey protein concentrate, one of the most popular ingredients used in high-protein foods.

John Murray manages marketing for Daryl's Bars, a protein snack manufacturer in Tecumseh, Ont. He says as major companies secure large orders of whey, "that leaves the little guys like us scrambling to try and secure enough for our operations."

Canada imports most of its whey protein concentrate from the U.S., where prices have more than doubled over the past year and a half.

The U.S. Dairy Export Council says "domestic demand for high-protein whey has been insatiable" — so much so, that less whey is available for export.

That demand has also driven up prices. Whey protein concentrate, known as WPC80, rose 60 per cent in 2025. By June 2026, buyers were facing another 76 per cent increase.

Daryl's Bars marketing manager John Murray says the price of whey protein imported from the U.S. has gone 'through the roof.' (Daryl's Bars)

To keep up with rising costs, Murray says his company has been forced to raise prices on its protein snacks.

"We absorbed as much as we could, but over the last year it's just been impossible. It's been outstripping our margins completely," he said.

Most of the company's whey protein comes from Wisconsin, and Murray says there are few alternatives.

"If we could source 100 per cent of everything that we needed from inside Canada, we would opt for that."

Caught in the trade war

The trade war is further squeezing food manufacturers.

In retaliation for a fresh round of U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods, the federal government imposed 50 per cent tariffs on imports of American whey on Sept. 8, pushing prices even higher.

Canadian businesses can apply for relief through Ottawa's tariff-remission program, though they must demonstrate that the goods cannot reasonably be sourced domestically or from non-U.S. suppliers.

It will be difficult to boost supply quickly, said Mike von Massow, a food economist at the University of Guelph, because whey isn't produced on its own. It's a byproduct left over from making cheese. The liquid whey must be dried and turned into a powder, a complex process that requires special equipment.

"It's very expensive to dry something that is 95 per cent water and a little bit of protein," he said.

WATCH | How counter-tariffs on the U.S. could backfire on Canadian whey protein companies: How counter-tariffs on the U.S. could backfire on Canadian whey protein companies | Duration closed caption 2:28 As the trade war with the U.S. continues, it marks two weeks since Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs. As CBC’s Baneet Braich explains, the levies are especially having an impact on Canadian protein companies.

The U.S. produces a lot of cheese, which is why it's also a major producer of whey protein. But von Massow says Canada has limited processing capacity.

"We can't produce milk just for the whey. That's not economic. Even though the price is up, the rest of the milk would be a byproduct," he said.

The Dairy Processors Association of Canada says that with tariffs increasing the cost of U.S. imports, it expects Canadian companies to pivot toward New Zealand — though that comes with significant shipping costs.

Stretching their dollars

Von Massow predicts higher prices could be passed down through the supply chain.

"I think your protein drink is probably going to get more expensive and it's likely to stay more expensive for a while," he said.

Some protein users, such as Audrey Marcoux, say they will absorb the extra cost for now.

"Unfortunately, I'm still paying the more expensive price because it's part of my routine. I work out a lot," she said.

Nathan Bugiardini says that if prices go any higher, he'll consider cutting back.

"It's a little upsetting, frankly. I usually buy in bulk which helps the price a little bit."

Some consumers are turning to plant-based alternatives and unprocessed whole foods while whey protein prices remain high.

Nineteen-year-old Melania Antic says the steep costs have left her feeling stretched.

"It discourages me a lot, especially, like, to actually get motivation to go to the gym and take protein after."

World.title: ‘Crypto King’ Aiden Pleterski’s fraud trial begins in Toronto
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski's criminal trial will begin Tuesday morning in Toronto.

Pleterski, 27, pleaded not guilty to fraud of over $5,000 and money laundering ahead of jury selection in Ontario Superior Court on Monday.

He’s representing himself at trial.

A jury of seven men and seven women was selected Monday afternoon. Justice Shaun Nakatsuru decided on 14 people, given the trial is expected to last a month. However, only 12 jurors will deliberate at the end of the case.

Pleterski was arrested in May 2024, after a lengthy joint investigation by Durham Regional Police and the Ontario Securities Commission dubbed Project Swan. Police alleged Pleterski operated a multimillion-dollar fraud scheme with funds he received from investors between July 2020 and the end of July 2022.

CBC Toronto has reported extensively on Pleterski since the summer of 2022, when he was forced into bankruptcy by some of his investors trying to recover millions of dollars they gave him to invest in cryptocurrency and foreign exchange.

Crown prosecutors are expected to call more than a dozen witnesses over the course of the trial.

World.title: Foam Lake, Sask., mourns mom, 2 girls killed in crash with U.S. hunter
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A family friend of the woman and two girls killed in a recent crash near Foam Lake, Sask., about 150 kilometres northeast of Regina, says Amber Olson was a devoted mother to two enthusiastic daughters.

"Her daughters were every bit of her life," Cassandra Pendlebury said in a message to CBC.

Isla and Everly, aged five and eight, and 40-year-old Amber were killed when a truck trying to pass a semi collided with their SUV about nine kilometres west of Foam Lake.

"Amber had a beautiful heart and beautiful soul. She'd give the shirt off her back to anyone in need and anything possible to eat to someone hungry," Pendlebury said.

She said Halloween and Christmas were the family's favourite times of the year.

"If my kids weren't at her house, her kids were at mine," she said.

Shaun Didychuk, the girls' father, was also in the SUV and was taken to hospital by STARS air ambulance with serious injuries.

Pendlebury set up a GoFundMe campaign to help Shaun with medical bills and funeral costs.

"Our hearts are broken as we share the devastating loss of Shaun’s beloved spouse, Amber, and their two beautiful daughters, Everly and Isla, following a tragic accident," the page for the campaign says.

"No family should ever have to endure a loss like this, and no one should have to worry about financial burdens while grieving the people they love most."

The campaign was halfway to its goal of $7,000 as of Monday afternoon.

Amber Olson with one of her girls. (Submitted by Debbie Ford)

The driver of the truck, 40-year-old Kelly Knopf from Sumter, S.C., and a passenger were taken to hospital with injuries described as non-life threatening. Another passenger with serious injuries was airlifted by STARS, RCMP say.

Knopf was arrested after an investigation and charged with three counts each of dangerous operation of a vehicle causing death and dangerous operation of a vehicle causing bodily harm.

He is set to be transported to the Regina correctional centre Monday.

Knopf was scheduled to appear in Yorkton provincial court on the charges Monday, but was still in hospital. His lawyer, Brian Pfefferle, appeared via phone.

Yorkton provincial court, where Kelly Knopf was scheduled to appear on Monday. (Alexander Quon/CBC)

Pfefferle provided CBC with a statement on Knopf's behalf. It said there is no indication at this time that alcohol, drugs, or excessive speed were factors in the crash.

"We are still awaiting full particulars of the allegations."

Pfefferle said Knopf had travelled to Saskatchewan from South Carolina on a hunting trip, something he has done for several years.

"As a result, he has a connection to many in the area. He and his family are deeply grateful for the support and compassion they have received from the community as they navigate the many consequences of this tragedy which has impacted their community."

Pfefferle said he expects to address Knopf's release on Wednesday.
