World.title: Remains of 115 Polish WWII soldiers exhumed in Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of over 100 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending the city of Lviv – which is now in Ukraine but was then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of World War Two. The work continues recent moves towards reconciliation over the issue of exhuming victims of the war, which has long been a point of contention between the two countries. ℹ Komunikat o zakończeniu prac ekshumacyjnych na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie ⚠️ Zakończyły się prace ekshumacyjne na terenie dawnego cmentarza w miejscowości Hołosko Wielkie, znajdującej się obecnie w granicach administracyjnych Lwowa. Działania… pic.twitter.com/w9rSHuLeua — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) September 28, 2026 During the work on a 260-square-metre area at Holoskivske Cemetery in Lviv, which began in August, experts found 133 burials. They were identified as 115 soldiers from the Polish army and 18 from the German Wehrmacht. They died during the Battle of Lwów in September 1939, when Poland sought to defend the city from Nazi Germany, which had invaded from the west on 1 September, and the Soviet Union, which invaded from the east on 17 September. On 22 September, the Polish forces surrendered and the city came under Soviet control, as Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had decided when secretly agreeing to divide up Poland in the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact earlier that year. Efforts are now focused on identifying the remains. Experts have taken bone samples for DNA testing, which will be compared with samples from possible relatives. Another part of the puzzle will be the roughly 2,900 objects – including identification tags, bayonets, helmets and religious items – discovered at the site alongside the remains. “For us, the identification of the remains is the most important stage of the work, because it is important to return these people their names,” said Dominika Siemińska, a researcher from Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), in a statement published by Lviv city council. “Currently we have a list of 76 [potential] names,” she added. However, because “so many years have passed, it will be difficult to find their relatives”. Siemińska also expressed her gratitude to the authorities in Lviv “for providing us with protection, support and the opportunity to work peacefully”. She said that “cooperation with the Ukrainian side is going very well”. The final stage of the work will be the burial of the recovered remains of Polish soldiers at the Polish cemetery in the Ukrainian city of Mostyska. The date of the ceremony has not yet been announced. The German remains are being handed over to the Volksbund organisation, which specialises in searching for and reburying German soldiers, said the IPN. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 Last year, Ukraine also granted permission for the exhumation of Polish soldiers in Lviv. Researchers subsequently found the remains of 31 people, as well as possible remains of dozens more that were difficult to identify due to them having been reburied and the manner of their death in artillery fire. They were also reburied in Mostyska, at a ceremony attended by prominent officials from both Poland and Ukraine. Previously, from 2017 to 2024, Ukraine had banned searches for Polish victims of World War Two on its territory in response to the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist partisan formation that fought against the Soviets but also led the massacre of ethnic Poles. However, in a major diplomatic breakthrough last year, Ukraine allowed exhumations to resume, including both the Polish soldiers in Lviv as well as victims of the UPA-led massacres, tens of thousands of whom are believed to remain buried in unmarked mass graves. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Researchers have subsequently uncovered the remains of dozens of victims of the massacres, who have also been reburied in ceremonies attended by both Polish and Ukrainian officials. However, such steps towards reconciliation have been hindered this year by a dispute sparked by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision to name a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest state honour. Since then, both sides have moved to calm tensions, with Zelensky setting out a five-point plan to resolve the dispute, including issuing “a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. World.title: Polish coal mining giant JSW to shed 4,200 jobs – 21% of its workforce – this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state-owned mining firm Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa (JSW), which is the EU’s largest producer of coking coal and one of Poland’s biggest employers, has announced that it will cut over 4,000 jobs, 21% of its workforce, by the end of this year. The plans come as JSW seeks to turn around its finances after years of large losses, as well as a broader shift in Poland away from reliance on coal. Jastrzębska Spółka Węglowa do końca 2026 r. zwolni ponad 4,2 tys. osób. – Musimy kierować się interesem spółki – mówił na konferencji prasowej prezes JSW. Więcej: https://t.co/7Sxrhuuaja pic.twitter.com/evJoQal0c3 — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) October 1, 2026 On Wednesday, JSW’s management board announced that it expected the size of its workforce to decline by 4,248 by the end of this year, bringing it below 16,000, down from 20,135 at the end of March. “We anticipate that approximately 2,200 people will leave in the third quarter, and about 1,400 in the fourth quarter,” adding to those who have already left, said the firm’s CEO, Bogusław Oleksy, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Last year, Poland introduced a new law making it easier for coal companies to close mines and reduce their workforce. It provides for large severance payments and other measures intended to soften the blow for those who lose their jobs. News service Strefa Inwestorów says that, on this basis, more than 3,000 JSW employees have the option to take so-called mining or mineral-processing leave while just under 1,200 can opt for one-off severance payments. President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill that makes it easier to close down coal mines and provides severance pay of 170,000 zloty to miners. The measures are seen as a key part of Poland’s transition towards cleaner forms of energy https://t.co/vH6MU4nBsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 The workforce reduction is part of JSW’s recovery plan for 2026-2035, announced this week. Other key objectives include cutting costs and investment without decreasing production while increasing the share of coking coal in output. When asked how the workforce reduction would affect production, Oleksy said the company would optimise its operations to make more efficient use of employees and equipment. He noted that most of the losses would be administrative positions rather than staff directly involved in production. In February this year, the company reached an agreement with unions to reduce labour costs in order to help stabilise the company’s financial position. JSW employees almost unanimously supported the agreement, reported broadcaster TVN. The initial results of the cost-cutting measures are beginning to show. In the first half of 2026, the cost of extraction per tonne fell to 609 zloty (€139) from 778 zloty a year earlier. JSW’s long-term goal is to bring the cost down to around 560 zloty per tonne. The company is still posting heavy losses, though those have also fallen this year. JSW posted a net loss of just over 1.0 billion zloty in the first half of 2026, around half the 2.1 billion zloty figure from the same period a year earlier. For the full year 2025, the company recorded a loss of 6.3 billion zloty, which was down from a record figure of 7.3 billion zloty in 2024. Polish state-owned mining giant JSW, the EU's largest producer of coking coal, has reported a record annual loss of 7.3bn zloty. It attributed the results to falling coal prices, lower production volumes, and the impact of a one-off write-off https://t.co/vrSgRu630b — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 11, 2025 JSW’s announcement comes just as some officials and industry representatives are warning that the energy crisis caused by conflict in the Middle East could increase demand in Poland for coal, which is still used to generate around half of electricity and to heat almost a fifth of homes. Polish coal is among the most expensive in the world to extract, and the industry survives largely due to heavy public subsidies. In 2026, the state is expected to spend 5.5 billion zloty propping up the sector, after an outlay of 9 billion zloty last year. Successive governments have been seeking to move away from coal, which went from producing 87% of Poland’s electricity in 2015 to 52.2% in 2025. Meanwhile, between 2015 and 2024, the proportion of households using hard coal for heating fell from 40% to 17%, while those using natural gas doubled from 10% to 21%. However, the energy crisis prompted by US and Israeli attacks on Iran this year has resulted in natural gas prices soaring. As a result, Poland’s state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, said last month that the geopolitical situation meant coal’s role this year would be “larger than we anticipated”. “We are currently increasing output at coal companies and are aware of the energy sector’s demand for coal as a stabilising factor,” he said, quoted by news service Money.pl. World.title: Polish president backs down and approves government’s windfall tax on fuel companies
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has reversed course and signed into law a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits that he had previously blocked. The government had been pushing the president to approve the measures amid soaring fuel prices. In announcing his decision on Thursday, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition, insisted that he now expected the government to move to lower fuel prices for consumers. A few hours later, the government confirmed that it would do so, and on Friday morning it announced cuts in VAT and excise duty on fuels. Nie pozwolę rządowi dłużej odsuwać od siebie odpowiedzialności za tę trudną sytuację. Podpisałem ustawę dotyczącą nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych i zakończę proces ustawiania Polaków w roli politycznych zakładników. To rząd ponosi pełną odpowiedzialność za ceny paliw -… pic.twitter.com/7AX8v4a9Q0 — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) October 1, 2026 The windfall tax will levy a one-off charge of 60% of excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. It is expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€914 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset some of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by cutting VAT and excise duty and introducing a maximum daily price. Those measures were initially in place from March to June. However, in July, Nawrocki announced that he would not sign the windfall tax into law. He instead sent it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment. That process can take years, effectively killing off the bill. The president argued that the proposed measures “raised serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that the tax would be retroactive, applying to revenue earned from the beginning of March. Since then, he and the government have been locked in a dispute over the issue, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk arguing that measures to reduce fuel prices, which were briefly reintroduced in the last two weeks of August, can only be restored if Nawrocki signs the windfall tax. Nawrocki’s office, however, has argued that fuel companies would pass the costs of the tax onto consumers, therefore actually increasing prices. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In September, the government’s majority in parliament passed the windfall tax bill a second time. And Nawrocki has now backed down, announcing in a recorded speech on Thursday evening that he would sign the bill into law. However, he has still asked the TK to assess its constitutionality. Nawrocki declared that he was seeking to call the government’s bluff. He claimed that they were actually hoping the windfall tax would fail so that the treasury could continue obtaining normal tax revenue from high fuel prices, as well as dividends from state oil giant Orlen. By signing the bill, the president said he was “ending the process of holding Poles hostage”. He now expected the government to “immediately” reintroduce measures to bring down prices at petrol stations, as well as the cost of fuel for farmers. To nie ja wygrałem. Wygrali Polacy, którzy już w weekend zapłacą mniej za paliwa. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 1, 2026 In response, government spokesman Adam Szłapka told broadcaster TVN that they were ready to make the necessary decisions to reduced prices on Friday and that the measures could be in force already by the weekend. “It’s good that the president has stopped blocking this,” he said. On Friday morning, the government announced that it would reduce VAT on fuels from 23% to 8% and cut excise duty – both measures it also used earlier this year. The new policies will be in place until 31 December. Energy minister Miłosz Motyka told Polskie Radio that maximum daily prices would also be reintroduced. Earlier, on Thursday evening, finance minister Andrzej Domański announced on social media that he estimated fuel costs would be reduced by 1.2-1.3 zloty per litre once the subsidies were reintroduced. According to price monitoring service ePetrol, diesel prices are currently averaging around 9.14 zloty per litre while PB95 petrol is at 8.19 zloty. Those are both record highs. Ustawa o podatku od nadmiarowych zysków koncernów paliwowych właśnie wpłynęła do RCL. Jeszcze dziś będzie ogłoszona. Oznacza to, że już w weekend ceny na stacjach paliwowych będą niższe. Szacunkowo o około 1,2-1,3 zł na litrze. I po co były te gierki, Panie Prezydencie? — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 1, 2026 The dispute over financing fuel price cuts comes at a time of growing concern over Poland’s public finances, something Nawrocki referred to in his address on Thursday. Poland has been running one of the EU’s highest deficits, despite the government committing to bringing it down after being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time this year. Last month, Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3, pointing to a “deteriorating” fiscal situation and the “limited willingness or ability” of the authorities to take necessary action. The last time the country was at A3 level was in 2002. World.title: Leading Polish business owners invest in small nuclear reactor venture
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A group of prominent Polish businesspeople have announced that they are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by the country’s richest man, Michał Sołowow. Among them are Rafał Brzoska, founder of delivery giant InPost, and Mati Staniszewski, CEO of ElevenLabs, a leading artificial intelligence firm. The group is investing 500 million zloty (€114 million) in Sołowow’s Synthos Green Energy (SGE), which, together with 1.35 billion zloty from foreign investors, will secure the company’s financing for the next two years as it seeks to roll out BWRX-300 reactors in Poland, Central and Eastern Europe and the UK. As a European SMR development platform headquartered in Warsaw, Poland’s energy security is of special importance to us. We are proud to announce that today our founder, Michał Sołowow, unveiled a PLN 500 million investment by a group of leading Polish entrepreneurs in SGE’s… pic.twitter.com/J2SerVjIlG — SGE (@SGE_Nuclear) September 30, 2026 The investment, which was formally announced at a business conference in Warsaw on Wednesday, comes as Sołowow seeks to expand his nuclear project beyond SGE’s troubled partnership with Polish state energy giant Orlen, where disagreements have delayed plans to build SMRs in Poland. Alongside Brzoska and Staniszewski, the other new investors are Dariusz Gałęzewski, co-founder of drinks maker Oshee; Krzysztof Pawiński, CEO of food company Maspex; Michał Brański of media group Wirtualna Polska; and Michał Wypychewicz of ZPUE, the largest manufacturer of transformer stations in Europe. “They invested their own private funds because they understood the problem and then believed in the concept and the solution,” Sołowow told Business Insider Polska. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed on site, are seen by their proponents as a fast and cost-effective way of installing nuclear capacity. In July, SGE announced plans to build 14 BWRX-300 reactors with a combined capacity of 4.2 gigawatts (GW) across three sites in the UK, which it said would generate enough electricity to meet 11% of the country’s demand. The company also hopes to deploy up to 26 reactors across six locations in Poland. The BWRX-300 is a 300-megawatt water-cooled small modular reactor. Construction of the first ever unit began in Canada in 2025, with completion planned for 2029 and commercial operation expected in 2030. Synthos Green Energy, a firm owned by Polish billionaire Michał Sołowow, has announced plans to build 14 small modular nuclear reactors in the UK. It says that the £35 billion project could deliver enough power to meet 11% of the UK’s demand https://t.co/YTMIzYERuJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Brzoska said that developing SMR technology “is an investment in Poland’s future”, because without “reliable, predictable and competitively priced energy…it is difficult to talk seriously about further growth in industry, data centres, artificial intelligence, automation or modern logistics”. Staniszewski, whose company recently received an $11 million investment from Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) to establish an AI development centre in Poland, said lower electricity prices were important for the sector. SGE notes that demand for electricity is set to rise 40% in Poland over the next 14 years, according to grid operator PSE. Electricity prices have risen rapidly in recent years and are now the second most expensive in the European Union in relation to the cost of living. Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year. The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025 Poland remains the EU’s most coal-dependent country, with more than half of its electricity generated from coal. Over the past decade, however, the country has diversified its energy mix, with the share of renewable energy sources tripling to nearly 30% in 2025. Poland plans to reduce its reliance on coal further, including through the construction of its first nuclear power plant (of the traditional type, not an SMR). The 3.75-gigawatt project is scheduled to be commissioned in 2036. Sołowow has also been pursuing the deployment of SMRs in Poland through Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE), a joint venture between SGE and state energy giant Orlen, Poland’s largest company, to develop BWRX-300 reactors in Poland. OSGE is seeking a so-called contract for difference (CfD) framework, an agreement with a state that guarantees a fixed price for electricity and helps shield developers from market swings, covering 14 reactors at three sites. Polish state energy firm Orlen has announced an agreement to build the country’s first small modular nuclear reactor (SMR). It says Poland will be the first country in Europe to deploy an SMR developed by US-based firm GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy https://t.co/MPWXS3qZ1d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2025 The project, however, has been delayed by disagreements between the two shareholders. Sołowow told Business Insider Polska that they reached an agreement last month that would allow construction of two reactors to move forward, but said he regretted entering into the partnership with Orlen. “I find it deeply regrettable, because it is precisely due to Orlen’s unnecessary involvement that we are discussing this project in political terms, even though it is not a political project,” he said. Sołowow has argued that a private-sector model can shorten construction times and improve cost control compared with traditional state-led nuclear projects. At the same time, he has highlighted the importance of the state’s role in implementing the project, saying its success depends on coordination between private investors and state policy. This includes contracts for difference, administrative procedures and the preparedness of the nuclear regulator. World.title: Activists launch world’s first abortion pill delivery locker in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Activists in Poland have launched what they say is the world’s first delivery locker that provides women with abortion pills, access to which is normally tightly restricted. They have placed the device opposite parliament in Warsaw, a location intended to send a message to the politicians who have made Poland’s abortion laws among the strictest in the world. The locker (called an “abortomat” in Polish, combining the words aborcja, meaning abortion, and automat, meaning an automatic machine) has been launched by Women Help Women (WHW), a global organisation that provides “self-managed abortion”, and Abortion Dream Team (ADT), a Polish activist group. They emphasise that the installation “is completely real [and] not an artistic performance”. It consists of 22 numbered lockers and a numeric keypad. Women who have contacted WHM seeking an abortion are given a six-digit PIN code that opens one of the doors, inside which is a package containing the pills. Recipients can either take the pills at home or do so in a specially prepared space opened last year by ADT and where the locker is located. The activists emphasise that such delivery mechanisms for abortion pills are particularly important in Poland because of the country’s highly restrictive laws. Abortions are only allowed in two circumstances: if pregnancy is the result of a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. As a result, only 851 legal terminations took place in Poland last year. However, activist groups such as WHW, ADT and Women on Web (WOW) say that they help tens of thousands of women in Poland obtain abortions each year through other means, in particular by providing pills. But they face legal risks for doing so: assisting someone in obtaining an unlawful abortion is a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2023, ABW activist Justyna Wydrzyńska was convicted of that offence. Two years later, the sentence was annulled on a technicality and a new trial was ordered. Polish activist Justyna Wydrzyńska, who was convicted for providing abortion pills to a pregnant woman, has succeeded in having the conviction overturned on appeal. However, the case will now return to the lower court, where it will be heard again https://t.co/U3J5FmXdMw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 14, 2025 “The abortomat transforms a closely guarded, criminalised procedure into something as simple as picking up a package,” wrote ADT. “A door that opens when all others have slammed shut.” They say that the machine is intended for women who have an urgent medical need that means they cannot wait for the several days it takes to deliver pills by post, or who are in abusive, controlling relationships that make postal delivery unsafe. Wydrzyńska’s conviction came after the husband of a woman she helped obtain abortion pills found them and reported the case to the police. However, although assisting a woman in obtaining an unlawful abortion is an offence, the woman who had the abortion is not criminally liable. “The abortomat is not a human being, and the person collecting the pills, in accordance with the regulations, is not breaking the law,” said Wydrzyńska, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. WHW and ADT do not collect any personal information from women using the service. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that Poland violated the rights of a pregnant woman who had to travel abroad to obtain an abortion after her foetus was diagnosed with a birth defect https://t.co/TgckusMxmJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 13, 2025 Under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, the abortion law was tightened and was strictly enforced. In December 2023, a new, more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power, promising to liberalise the abortion law. However, it has so far failed to pass any such legislation. In 2024, a move to decriminalise abortion assistance up to the 12th week of pregnancy was rejected by parliament, after the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition joined the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Tusk subsequently admitted that it would be impossible during the current parliament to soften abortion laws. Instead, his government issued guidelines on when and how abortions can be carried out, with the aim of ensuring that doctors and prosecutors “take the women’s side” when making decisions on the issue. World.title: Roger Waters Brings New Pink Floyd Show to Prague in June 2027
World.content:
Roger Waters will bring a new Pink Floyd concert production to Prague next year, with LEGACY – A Pink Floyd Show scheduled for June 8, 2027, at O2 universum.

The new production has been created under Waters’ direction and will feature a ten-piece band led by his son, Harry Waters. The Prague show will focus on music from what is widely regarded as Pink Floyd’s most influential period, spanning 1971 to 1979.



The setlist will draw from four of the band’s best-known albums: The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

The music will be accompanied by a new visual production featuring high-resolution LED screens and imagery inspired by Pink Floyd’s original artwork and stage concepts.

Harry Waters will serve as the show’s musical director, performing on Hammond B3 organ and piano while also contributing vocals. He has a long history with the band’s music and spent more than 15 years performing alongside his father on major tours, including The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.

His connection to Pink Floyd goes back even further. As a child, Harry’s voice appeared on “Goodbye Blue Sky” from The Wall. He also saw the original The Wall concert production at a young age.

The band includes drummer Graham Broad, guitarist Edo Scordo, bassist and backing vocalist Dahniel Knight, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Ryan Saranich, keyboardist Matt Riddle, lead vocalist Clifton David Broadbridge and backing vocalists Eva Avila and Genevieve Little.

Roger Waters co-founded Pink Floyd in 1965 and became the band’s principal lyricist and conceptual leader following Syd Barrett’s departure. He played a central role in the creation of albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

Ticket prices start at 1,600 CZK

Live Nation Club and O2 presale starts October 8, 2026, at 10:00 AM

Tickets on sale via Ticketmaster and Ticketportal starting October 9, 2026, at 10:00 AM

World.title: GALLERY: Vltava Philharmonic Reveals Its Interiors for the First Time
World.content:
Prague’s planned Vltava Philharmonic has offered the first detailed look inside the building, releasing visualizations of its main foyer and the spaces serving its three principal concert halls.

The interior design will combine wood, glass and stone, with flowing shapes inspired by the Vltava River and the building’s distinctive sloping roof. The plans also emphasize open public spaces designed to connect the concert halls with the rest of the building.



The main foyer will be dominated by a large glass wall extending across several floors. Its curved geometry is intended to echo the movement of the Vltava and will separate the open foyer from other areas of the building.

Light-colored solid wood panels will cover the ceilings, following the contours of the roof above. Stone elements will be used in areas connecting the public foyer with the foyer of the main concert hall, including spaces designed for both seating and standing around bar counters.

´

The project has become significantly more expensive

The cost of the Vltava Philharmonic has increased sharply since the project was first estimated.

In 2021, the projected construction cost was CZK 6.1 billion. After the Danish architecture studio Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) won the international competition in 2022, the estimate rose to CZK 9.4 billion.

A more detailed architectural study completed in 2024 put the figure at CZK 11.65 billion. The latest estimate is CZK 11.98 billion for the building itself.

Once improvements to the surrounding area are included, the overall project is expected to cost almost CZK 17 billion.

Construction could begin in 2028

The city expects to obtain the permit in the first quarter of 2027. A general contractor would then be selected, with construction currently scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2028.

Trial operations are planned to begin in 2033.

The Vltava Philharmonic will occupy three underground and six above-ground floors. In addition to five concert halls, the complex will include facilities for the Czech Philharmonic and the Prague Symphony Orchestra (FOK), a music department operated by the Municipal Library of Prague, a creative hub, a restaurant and publicly accessible terraces.

The building is being designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, whose proposal was selected in the international architectural competition in 2022.

World.title: Up to 80 Startups to Pitch Investors at Prague’s Engaged Investments Conference
World.content:
The international Engaged Investments conference, taking place on October 21 and 22, 2026, is significantly expanding its scope this year.

The event, which brings hundreds of startup investors from all over Europe to Prague, is now fully opening its doors to tech founders and the broader innovation ecosystem.



Alongside the main program, the two-day event will feature two specialized industry tracks focusing on fintech and defense, pitches from up to 80 startups, and an extended accompanying program.

Real defense instead of geopolitical theories

The defense track is being organized in collaboration with the Invest in Bravery initiative, which is deeply involved in the Ukrainian ecosystem, alongside the European EUDIS Matchmaking program for defense and Cassini Matchmaking for space technologies.

A special guest will be Senior Lieutenant Mykyta Puz, Defense Industry Liaison Officer of the Azov Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine. He previously worked in business and AI product management before volunteering for the front lines in 2024.

He will shed light on what a modern army truly and urgently needs from the defense industry. Alongside him, speakers will include Erin Hallock, Managing Partner of the NATO Innovation Fund, a representative of the renowned Ukrainian fund Brave1, and others.

Fintech that solves business, not theory

The UnBundled Fintech track, which will run throughout the second day of the conference, is being prepared by The FinTechers in collaboration with Mastercard. The goal is to connect the traditional banking sector with technology companies and investors. The program will focus on stablecoins and tokenization, operational resilience of banks, liability for fraudulent payments, and the deployment of artificial intelligence in financial services.

In addition to new technologies, it will address what European companies need to grow into global players without relying on American capital and infrastructure.

Speakers will include Michal Vodrážka, Director of the Payment Systems Regulation Division at the Czech National Bank. In a debate with Jiří Raška, Chief Technology Officer of Partners Banka, he’ll raise the question of who takes the hit when a payment ends up in a fraudster’s hands. It’s a timely topic, with mandatory payee verification coming in 2027.

The block dedicated to stablecoins and new financial infrastructure will be opened by Dorothea Ysenburg, Vice President of Global Partnerships for Digital Assets and Blockchain at Mastercard. Maryna Muntian from J.P. Morgan will also present, discussing why Central European banks and investors still lack mutual trust when looking at the same deals.

A place where startups find real investors

Closing investments is one of the core components of the conference, which last year attracted investors from more than 20 countries. Up to 80 selected startups, ranging from early-stage to Series A, will have the opportunity to pitch their companies in three minutes to investors actively investing in their respective segments. This year will introduce new dedicated pitching blocks for startups in the fields of financial technology, defense, and space.

On October 22, the best fintech projects from the two-day “Coding the Future of Finance” hackathon—organized on October 19 and 20 by The FinTechers together with Deloitte, AWS, and other partners—will also be presented to investors.

World.title: Designblok 2026 to Take Over Six Prague Venues This Week
World.content:
The 28th edition of Designblok, Prague’s international design festival, will take place from October 6 to 11, 2026, across six locations in the city.

The professional program and conference begin on Tuesday, October 6, while the main festival opens to the public on Wednesday, October 7. This year’s theme is “Light,” with exhibitions and installations exploring both the practical and symbolic role of light in design.



The program will look at design as a tool for addressing social and economic challenges and examine its role in everyday life. Curated exhibitions, exhibitor installations, discussions on the Designblok Stage and the Designblok Talks conference will explore themes including knowledge, truth, hope and sustainability.

The Trade Fair Palace (Veletržní palác) will serve as the festival’s main venue. It will bring together hundreds of presentations by designers, brands, schools and emerging talents, alongside curated exhibitions, lectures and workshops. The venue will also host activities for children and adults.

At the Prague Castle Riding School, Designblok will present two curated exhibitions connecting contemporary design and craftsmanship with Czech cultural history.

The Museum of Decorative Arts in Prague will host one of the festival’s main exhibitions, as well as dozens of design presentations and a special project marking the 100th anniversary of the creation of the popular Czech puppet character Hurvínek.

The Industrial Palace will host much of the festival’s conference and social program, including Designblok Talks, a live edition of the Czech quiz show AZ-kvíz focused on design, and the Designblok Awards Gala. The venue is reopening following its recent reconstruction.

Saturday will also bring fashion shows featuring finalists from the international Diploma Selection competition, which highlights emerging designers from around the world.

Other Designblok venues include the Chapel of the Holy Cross in the Second Courtyard of Prague Castle and the UMPRUM Technology Centre on Mikulandská Street. The latter provides facilities for student projects and workshops.

World.title: Bollywood and Beyond: Prague Indian Film Festival Returns for Its 23rd Edition
World.content:
The Prague Indian Film Festival will return for its 23rd edition from October 8 to 10, bringing a selection of recent Indian films to Kino Světozor.

The festival will open with a historical drama and feature Bollywood, arthouse cinema, a Sundance-winning film and a vampire comedy.

The festival opens on Thursday, October 8, in the presence of the Ambassador of India with Main Vaapas Aaunga, directed by Imtiaz Ali.

Set against the Partition of British India in 1947, the film follows a young Sikh man and his Muslim girlfriend whose lives are transformed by the political upheaval of the period.



Friday’s program will offer two very different takes on contemporary Indian cinema. Bollywood fans can see Cocktail 2, a romantic comedy about a love triangle starring Shahid Kapoor, Kriti Sanon and Rashmika Mandanna. The film follows the successful 2012 movie Cocktail.

The festival will also screen Cactus Pears, an arthouse drama set in a remote village in Maharashtra. The story follows a man who returns home after his father’s death and, while observing traditional mourning rituals, reconnects with a childhood friend.

The film won the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival, where it drew attention for its portrayal of a relationship that goes beyond friendship.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Prague Indian Film Festival 🎥🇮🇳 (@pragueindianfilmfestival)

Saturday afternoon will once again be dedicated to popular Indian films from the 1990s and 2000s. This year’s selection is Rang De Basanti, the 2006 film starring Aamir Khan.

The film has also gained renewed attention in India in connection with recent student protests. Festival art director Radim Špaček said he followed the demonstrations online and saw Rang De Basanti become one of the films associated with the movement.

Saturday evening will take a turn toward horror with Thamma, which combines comedy, horror and vampire folklore. The film stars Ayushmann Khurrana and Rashmika Mandanna, who also appears in Cocktail 2. It is directed by Aditya Sarpotdar.

Dance will also be a major part of the festival program. The accompanying Indian Dance Festival will feature workshops and masterclasses with instructors from around the world, culminating in the Bollywood Fiesta dance gala at Prague’s Rokoko Theatre on Sunday, October 11.

The festival will also feature Indian food, cinema decorations by Sanu Babu and a Bollywood dance party on Saturday night. DJ Dance Sandeep will perform at Theatro Music Club at the Karlín Music Theatre.

World.title: Prague’s Oldest Nightclub Lávka is Closing After 36 years
World.content:
One of Prague’s best-known nightlife venues is closing after more than three decades beside the Charles Bridge.

Lávka, which opened in 1990 on the banks of the Vltava, held its final farewell party on September 30. The club will leave its historic premises by October 8 as the City of Prague prepares to renovate the building.



For 36 years, Lávka was more than a nightclub. Its programme included concerts, theater, exhibitions, fashion shows and other cultural events. Its visitors included former president Václav Havel, politician Karel Schwarzenberg and singer Karel Gott.

The venue also hosted Czech acts including Lucie and Lunetic, as well as international performers such as Supertramp and R.E.M.

The first version of the venue was modest. It began as a theater bar in the Bedřich Smetana Museum, replacing the building’s cloakroom. With little money available, co-founder Boris Gaydečka and his partners constructed the bar themselves using scaffolding and wooden boards found on the site.

Advertising on the newly launched Radio Evropa 2 helped attract customers, and the business soon outgrew its original space.

Over the years, Lávka became a regular stop for performers from very different parts of Prague’s cultural scene. Its stage hosted the avant-garde Opera Mozart, the Semafor theater and the Spejbl and Hurvínek Theatre.

During the catastrophic floods of 2002, water eventually reached the ceiling despite efforts to protect the premises.

The damage was extensive. Seating was destroyed, a piano borrowed from the museum was swept away and doors were torn from their hinges.

The building is now being cleared

The end of Lávka’s original premises is linked to a wider renovation of the historic building.

The former Old Town Waterworks building belongs to the City of Prague and has been associated with the Bedřich Smetana Museum since 1936. The museum will also leave the building as part of the planned renovation.

Lávka will continue operating a canteen and café in the neighboring building owned by the Czech Association of Scientific and Technical Societies.

World.title: Only 29 Percent of Czechs Have a Higher Education Degree, OECD Finds
World.content:
Only 29 percent of people aged 25 to 64 in Czechia have completed higher education, according to the latest data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.

The figures highlight a persistent difference in the country’s education profile compared with other developed economies. While university-level education remains less common in Czechia, upper secondary education is far more widespread.

Around two-thirds of Czech adults have completed upper secondary education, compared with an OECD average of 39 percent. Vocational secondary education remains particularly common, although its share is gradually declining, as younger generations attain higher levels of education.



The change is most visible when comparing age groups. Vocational secondary education is the highest level of education for around 70 percent of Czech residents aged 55 to 64. Among people aged 25 to 34, the figure has fallen to 52 percent.

Across the OECD, the proportion of younger adults completing higher education has continued to increase. Czechia, however, is also facing a less positive trend at the lower end of the education scale.

Among 25- to 34-year-olds, the share of people who have not completed upper secondary education increased from 6 percent in 2015 to 7 percent in 2025. The trend is moving in the opposite direction across the OECD as a whole, where the average fell to 12 percent last year.

Young Czechs have relatively low unemployment

Despite the country’s comparatively low share of university graduates, Czechia performs well on several employment indicators.

In 2025, just 7 percent of people aged 18 to 24 were neither in education nor employment. The OECD average was twice as high, at 14 percent.

The unemployment rate among recent graduates has also declined over the past decade. In Czechia, it fell from 3 percent in 2015 to 2 percent in 2025. The corresponding OECD average was 5 percent.

Education is reflected in Czech wages

The OECD data also show a clear relationship between educational attainment and earnings in Czechia.

People whose highest qualification is general secondary education, including graduates of gymnasiums, earn an average of 8 percent less than the national average wage.

The difference is larger for people with vocational secondary education, whose earnings are 16 percent below the national average. Those who have not completed secondary education earn 33 percent less on average.

Higher education is also associated with greater access to remote work. Around 31 percent of Czech employees with a university education work remotely at least occasionally. Among workers with secondary education, the proportion is approximately 10 percent.

Czech education spending remains below OECD average

The OECD report also points to differences in public investment.

In 2023, public expenditure on education from primary schools through universities amounted to 3.6 percent of GDP in Czechia. The average across OECD countries was 4 percent.

Czechia also spent less per student than the OECD average. Annual expenditure stood at $11,861 per student, compared with $13,601 across OECD countries.

The figures are included in the OECD’s latest assessment of education systems in member countries, covering education levels, employment outcomes, earnings and public spending.

World.title: Rising Number of Czech Families Struggle to Afford School Lunches
World.content:
A growing number of Czech parents are unable to cover the cost of school lunches for their children.

The non-profit initiative Lunches for Children (Obědy pro děti), run by Women for Women, cites divorce, job loss, or serious illness as the primary causes driving families to apply for help. Even state food subsidies are proving insufficient.



At the start of this school year, demand for support is especially steep. Between January and September, the program aided nearly 16,000 pupils through cooperation with more than 1,150 schools and cafeterias nationwide.

Participation rose by about 15 percent compared with the same period last year, with sharp increases in Prague and the Ústí nad Labem region. A typical lunch costs 30–50 crowns, but for older students, monthly totals can exceed 1,000 crowns.

Under Women for Women’s rules, schools help identify children in need. Class teachers, principals, and canteen managers evaluate applications based on factors such as low income, single-parent status, or sudden financial crisis. Schools apply on behalf of families; funding is granted under donation agreements and routed directly to the schools (not to parents).

The heaviest wave of applications arrives each September, when the new school year begins. In more strained regions, quota limits have already been reached. The Ministry of Education endorses the project as a model of effective public–nonprofit partnership.

Marta Hekl, the organization’s director, emphasizes that the school lunch is more than nourishment: “Children feel part of a community, gain confidence, and receive the energy they need for learning.” Nejedlá adds that even in Prague, the country’s wealthiest region, applications have risen by 20 percent, as living costs outpace wages.

Historically, need is greatest in regions burdened by high unemployment and social difficulties—especially Ústí nad Labem and Karlovy Vary.

Some corporate donors also back the program. For instance, ADM Olomouc offered a significant grant to the Lunches for Children project, helping nearly 100 children eat lunch with their peers all year.

World.title: Good news for buyers: Hungarian housing market is turning, Budapest prices fall for 2nd month
World.content:
Hungary’s housing market appears to be losing momentum, with nationwide house prices stagnating in September while prices in Budapest fell for the second consecutive month, according to the latest housing price index from ingatlan.com.

The slowdown marks a notable shift after a period of rapid price growth. Since mid-2015, it has happened only three times before that all eight Hungarian regions simultaneously recorded slower price growth or falling prices compared with the previous month.

Budapest prices fall again

Nationwide, house prices rose by 0.4% in August but remained unchanged in September. Annual price growth also slowed sharply, from 11.2% in August to 8.2% in September.

The change has been even more pronounced in Budapest. Prices fell by 0.7% in August and a further 0.2% in September. Despite the recent declines, homes in the capital were still 3.3% more expensive than a year earlier.

“The price surge of last year peaked in November 2025, when we measured annual price increases of 18.4% nationwide and 24.1% in Budapest,” said László Balogh, chief economic expert at ingatlan.com.

“By September this year, the pace of nationwide price growth had fallen to less than half of that level, while in Budapest it had dropped to roughly one-seventh.”

According to Balogh, the figures indicate that price growth is slowing, although prices remain high. The nationwide market is currently stagnating, while Budapest is already seeing a modest decline. Annual nationwide house price growth has not been this low since December 2024. In Budapest, the latest figure represents the weakest annual growth recorded since February 2024.

If you missed it: Hungarian house prices soar over 10% in a year – But then came a sharp quarterly drop

Some regions are already seeing falling prices

The slowdown is not limited to the capital. In September, prices fell by 0.6% month-on-month in Pest County and by 1.2% in the Northern Great Plain. In the Southern Great Plain, where prices had jumped by 2.2% in August, growth slowed to just 0.1% in September.

Meanwhile, prices rose by 1.5% in Central Transdanubia, 0.9% in Southern Transdanubia and 0.6% in Northern Hungary. Prices in Western Transdanubia remained unchanged.

Just a few months ago, annual price growth was at least 10% across all Hungarian regions. By September, however, only three regions remained above that threshold: Central Transdanubia, Southern Transdanubia and the Southern Great Plain.

Why is the housing market slowing down?

One factor behind the slowdown is the unusually high price base from last year. When Hungary’s Otthon Start home-buying programme launched in September 2025, nationwide house prices jumped by 2.8% in a single month. This September, they remained unchanged.

However, affordability also appears to be playing an increasingly important role. As homes have become more expensive, fewer potential buyers can afford to enter the market, according to Balogh. The changing balance between supply and demand is particularly telling. The supply of newly built homes has reached a five-year high, while demand has fallen significantly.

The Otthon Start programme initially gave demand a major boost, contributing to widespread price increases. Developers and sellers, however, were slower to respond by increasing supply. By the time more new homes reached the market, prices had risen so much that some potential buyers could no longer afford them.

Six Budapest districts are now cheaper than last year

The latest figures also reveal significant differences between Budapest districts. At the beginning of October, the median price per square metre for second-hand flats and houses in Budapest stood at HUF 1.41 million (EUR 3,860), around 2% higher than a year earlier.

However, prices were already lower than last year in six districts:

District IX: down 2.7%

down 2.7% District III: down 1.9%

down 1.9% District V: down 1.8%

down 1.8% District XII: down 1.7%

down 1.7% District XI: down 1.5%

down 1.5% District XIII: down 0.5%

At the other end of the scale, prices rose by 10–12% in Districts XXII, XVII, XXIII and XVIII. District V remained Budapest’s most expensive area, with a median price of HUF 1.99 million per square metre. District I followed at HUF 1.87 million, while District XII stood at HUF 1.75 million. District XXIII was the most affordable, with a median price of HUF 958,000 per square metre.

World.title: If you drive a car like this in Hungary, you have until 30 November to change its number plate
World.content:
More than 32,000 plug-in hybrid vehicles in Hungary still have green number plates that they are no longer entitled to use. Their owners have until 30 November to replace them, according to a statement from the Digital Government Agency (DMÜ) sent to MTI on Monday.

The DMÜ is urging owners and operators of the affected vehicles not to leave the process until the final weeks. The number plate change can be initiated at any government window (kormányablak) in Hungary.

Which cars are affected?

The DMÜ recalled that since 1 September 2024, only vehicles classified in environmental categories 5E (fully electric) and 5Z (zero-emission) have been eligible for light green number plates.

Cars in environmental categories 5N (plug-in hybrid electric vehicles with an increased range) and 5P (plug-in hybrid electric vehicles) that were previously issued green number plates can continue using them only until 30 November.

After that date, if the vehicle is stopped during a road inspection, the authorities will confiscate the number plate and registration document and initiate the vehicle’s withdrawal from traffic. This will remain in effect until a new number plate is issued, either through a re-registration or a change of vehicle type.

According to the DMÜ, there are currently 32,325 plug-in hybrid vehicles in Hungary that still have green number plates and are either in circulation or temporarily withdrawn from traffic.

Have you heard? Budapest Assembly ends free parking for electric cars

How much will the number plate change cost?

The operators of affected vehicles have two options. They can request a new-character number plate, which costs HUF 17,475 (EUR 48), including the issue of the new number plate and registration document. Alternatively, they can request a number plate with the same characters, for which the administrative fee is HUF 16,605 (EUR 45.2).

The key difference is that with a same-character number plate change, existing contractual arrangements linked to the previous registration number do not need to be amended because of the change. These include compulsory motor third-party liability insurance, comprehensive insurance (CASCO), and certain parking and access permits. However, the process requires two in-person visits.

What happens to motorway e-vignettes?

A valid motorway e-vignette can still be used after the number plate change. However, if the vehicle receives a new-character number plate, the e-vignette must be transferred to the new registration number through the toll-road customer service of Magyar Közút Nonprofit Zrt.

Drivers also do not have to pay the vehicle acquisition tax retrospectively because of the previous benefits associated with the green number plate. The DMÜ has published detailed information about the procedure and frequently asked questions on its website.

World.title: Hungarian footballer Milos Kerkez on the list of “Ukraine’s enemies”
World.content:
Hungarian international footballer Milos Kerkez has been added to a controversial website’s list of alleged “enemies of Ukraine” following a social media post by his father.

Kerkez caught up in controversy

The Liverpool left-back was reportedly added to the Mirotvorec (Peacemaker) database following Hungary’s 1–0 Nations League defeat to Ukraine last Friday. The match ended in a tense confrontation after Ukrainian substitute Oleksandr Nazarenko was sent off. Players from both sides became involved in a heated exchange, during which Kerkez clashed verbally with Ukrainian midfielder Viktor Tsyhankov. Both players were shown yellow cards.

After the match, Kerkez’s father, Sebastijan Kerkez, shared footage of the incident on Instagram, adding the song “Russian Paradise” by Russian rap group AK-47 to the video. The choice of music reportedly caused outrage among Ukrainian audiences. Mirotvorec subsequently listed both Kerkez and his father, accusing the footballer of supporting Russian aggression, writes HVG.hu.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

The Hungarian international rejects the accusation

The player has strongly distanced himself from the accusation, telling Hungarian media that he has never supported aggression. “I have never supported and do not support any aggression,” Kerkez said, adding that the incident on the pitch was simply about defending Hungary’s captain and his friend.

“I am not the type of person who accepts anything that could harm others”, Kerkez claimed. He also stressed that his father’s actions should not be attributed to him. “My father is not me. I cannot take responsibility for his actions,” the footballer said.

Website not linked to Ukrainian government

The Mirotvorec database is not an official Ukrainian government platform. According to Hungarian reports, the operators of the website remain unclear, and it has been viewed in diplomatic circles as a controversial and potentially problematic initiative. Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán also condemned the listing of Hungarian citizens and stressed that the website should not be confused with an official Ukrainian state channel.

World.title: Hungary’s ‘Indian summer’ is coming to an end – heavy rain and sharp cooling on the way
World.content:
Hungary’s current sunny and unusually warm autumn weather is about to change, with a frontal system bringing rain, showers and significantly cooler temperatures from Thursday.

Rain and thunderstorms could arrive from Thursday

According to Időkép, the high-pressure system currently keeping the weather dry and sunny is gradually weakening, while a trough is deepening over Western Europe. A wave of fronts is expected to reach Hungary from the west on Thursday and move away by Friday afternoon.

The system could bring rain and showers to many parts of the country, with thunderstorms also possible in some areas. The exact amount and distribution of rainfall remain uncertain, but some regions could receive more than 10 millimetres of rain.

In areas affected by heavier showers or thunderstorms, as much as 20–30 millimetres could fall locally.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Temperatures could drop by several degrees

The biggest change, however, will come after the front passes. Strengthening north-westerly winds will bring considerably colder air into the Carpathian Basin.

After days of temperatures hovering around 25°C, weekend highs are expected to fall to between 15 and 22°C, meaning temperatures may remain below 20°C in many parts of Hungary.

The cloudier and windier conditions could meanwhile keep nights milder, temporarily pushing an end to the near-freezing overnight temperatures seen recently. The large difference between daytime and nighttime temperatures is also expected to become less pronounced.

Have you seen this? Danube falls to historic low water levels in Budapest: just 1 centimetre

Wednesday could be the last chance for sunshine

Those hoping to make the most of the current calm and sunny autumn weather may want to do so soon. According to the forecast, Wednesday could be the last particularly good opportunity before the rain and cooler conditions arrive.

World.title: Hungary to stop blocking next stage of Ukraine’s EU accession talks, Financial Times reports
World.content:
Hungary will not block the launch of the next, technical stage of European Union accession talks with Ukraine, according to the Financial Times.

The London-based business daily reported on Monday, citing EU sources, that Prime Minister Péter Magyar has instructed Hungarian diplomats not to prevent the EU from sending letters to Ukraine and Moldova concerning the potential opening of the next two negotiating chapter clusters.

Hungary to allow technical talks to move forward

According to the Financial Times, the letters are expected to be discussed at working-group meetings this week. The two chapter clusters concern the EU’s single market and competitiveness policy areas.

However, the newspaper stressed that Hungary’s full political backing for opening negotiations on the new chapter clusters will depend on whether the Ukrainian parliament approves a bill on expanding education rights for national minorities at its 12 October session.

Ensuring the rights of Hungary’s ethnic Hungarian minority in Ukraine has long been a key issue for Budapest. The Financial Times reported that Hungarian officials have also been involved in shaping the bill and have provided feedback on the proposal.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Key vote could unlock formal process

According to EU officials who spoke to the British newspaper, approval of the legislation could make it possible to launch the formal political procedure leading towards the opening of the negotiations before the EU summit in Brussels, which is due to take place in ten days.

One EU official who told the Financial Times that they had been receiving updates on the talks with Budapest said that “Ukraine’s path towards accession is starting to take shape.”

World.title: Bringing people together over everyday bread: world-famous bakery opens on Andrássy Avenue
World.content:
Le Pain Quotidien has opened its first location in Hungary on Andrássy Avenue, at street level of the Foncière Palace. The arrival of the Belgian bakery-café chain in Budapest marks the brand’s entry into its 27th country and represents another milestone in its international expansion, through which Le Pain Quotidien now operates more than 200 locations worldwide.

With its Budapest opening, the city welcomes a concept that brings together a bakery, café and all-day dining experience under one roof. Le Pain Quotidien is not arriving as a traditional bakery or exclusively as a breakfast destination: from morning until evening, it offers food and drinks suited to different moments of the day, from a quick breakfast and a lunch break during the workday to an afternoon coffee or a relaxed evening get-together.

From Brussels to Budapest: an international brand born from a simple idea

The story of Le Pain Quotidien began in Brussels in 1990. Its founder, chef Alain Coumont, drew inspiration from childhood memories when he set out to create a loaf of bread that would remind him of the carefully made traditional bread prepared by his aunt. Unable to find anything similar in Belgium, he decided to make it himself. What began as a single shop has since grown into an international brand with more than 200 locations.

Here the bread becomes tartine

The foundation of Le Pain Quotidien’s bread is four simple ingredients: organic flour, water, sea salt and natural sourdough starter. The flour is stone-ground, and the bread is not only served on its own but also forms the basis of one of the brand’s best-known dishes: the tartine.

The tartine may still be a new concept for Hungarian guests, but it is a well-known way of eating in Belgium and France. Essentially an open-faced sandwich, it places fresh sourdough bread at the heart of the dish rather than treating it simply as a base for toppings. Seasonal and natural ingredients are then layered on top, ranging from vegetables and cheeses to meats and other fresh ingredients.

Le Pain Quotidien

The concept is simple yet highly versatile: the bread acts as a kind of canvas, providing a foundation for different flavours and textures. The Budapest menu features several variations, from avocado-based combinations to tartines topped with chicken and smoked mozzarella.

If you missed it: A taste of summer at Axis Café & Lounge: a lunch well Spent

A bakery for every time of the day

The Budapest Le Pain Quotidien operates as an all-day bakery-café and welcomes guests until 9 p.m. The concept is not built around a single dining occasion: a croissant and specialty coffee before the workday, lunch with colleagues, or an afternoon or evening pastry all have a place here.

The role of community

The idea of a communal space has been an important part of the Le Pain Quotidien brand since its beginnings. A defining feature of the first Brussels location was a communal table rescued from a flea market. It was long enough to accommodate many people, yet narrow enough to make it easy for guests to talk to one another. The communal table has since become a recurring element across Le Pain Quotidien locations.

Le Pain Quotidien Le Pain Quotidien Le Pain Quotidien

Over the past decades, Le Pain Quotidien has complemented its classic bakery-café format with a range of community and cultural programmes. One striking example is its international “morning rave” event series, which combines morning exercise, music and community: after a run or workout, participants continue their day with DJ sets, coffee and breakfast.

The concept illustrates how Le Pain Quotidien sees the role of a bakery-café: not simply as a place to stop for bread, coffee or breakfast, but as a space that can serve as a point of connection at different times of day and in different situations.

With the opening of the Budapest store, this concept -which has been in the works for more than three decades- has now found a new home on Andrássy Avenue.

World.title: Bulgarian souvenir shop sells mugs with your favourite dictators, such as Stalin, Kim Jong Un, Viktor Orbán and Péter Magyar
World.content:
A souvenir shop in Bulgaria has caught attention with an unusual collection of mugs featuring notorious historical figures and authoritarian leaders – including North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, and for some reason, former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán and current Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar.

The A-Team of corruption, on mugs

The peculiar selection was spotted by a Hungarian tourist in Borovets, a popular mountain resort in Bulgaria’s Rila Mountains, known for its ski slopes and hiking trails. Alongside the usual tourist fare, such as fridge magnets and postcards, the shop displays an extensive collection of mugs featuring recognisable faces. The unusual range has even been placed prominently in the shop window, seemingly inviting curious tourists to take a closer look.

Among the figures featured are Kim Jong Un, Vladimir Putin, Lenin, Joseph Stalin and former Romanian dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu. The collection also ventures beyond political leaders, with mugs depicting notorious Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar and US President Donald Trump, writes 24.hu.

Hungarian faces among the collection

The most puzzling part of the collection for Hungarian visitors may be the appearance of Hungarian political figures. Viktor Orbán features on one of the mugs, displayed alongside Trump. Interestingly, his name is apparently rendered, or rather misspelled as “Victor” on the product. The collection appears to have been updated to reflect Hungary’s current political landscape as well, with a mug featuring Péter Magyar also reportedly available.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

No connection to the country

Why the Bulgarian souvenir shop decided to include Hungarian politicians – and even Peppa Pig – among its World XI of bad guys of modern history remains unclear. There is no apparent Hungarian-themed connection to the resort, making their presence all the more unexpected. Maybe they just wanted their own share of the April elections, which was eyed by the world’s biggest media outlets as well.

But not every mug in the shop is political or controversial. Tourist favourites such as Peppa Pig and the crests of various football clubs are also reportedly available. For visitors looking for an ordinary Bulgarian souvenir, the shop therefore offers a rather unexpected alternative: a mug collection that ranges from cartoon characters to some of the most controversial figures of modern history.

World.title: Hungary’s September budget deficit improves, but nine-month gap remains high
World.content:
Hungary’s central budget deficit increased by HUF 92.8 billion in September, significantly less than the HUF 303.2 billion deterioration recorded in the same month last year, according to a preliminary report from the Ministry for National Economy.

Improved year-over-year, but the situation is still dire

Despite the improvement in September, the state budget remains under considerable pressure. The cumulative deficit for the first nine months of 2026 reached HUF 5,261.9 billion, equivalent to around 72% of the HUF 7,110 billion full-year deficit target included in the proposed budget amendment.

The September figure also needs to be viewed in context. While the monthly deficit was substantially lower than a year earlier, September has produced a surplus in several previous years. Moreover, the nine-month deficit remains well above the HUF 3,328.7 billion recorded during the same period last year. As Prime Minister Péter Magyar highilighted, the government saved a whopping HUF 1200 billion in their first four months with putting an end to “overpriced government spendings”.

Hungary’s government tightens the belt

One significant factor behind this year’s figure was the government’s pre-financing of HUF 2,186.9 billion in European Union funds in August under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). These funds are expected to appear on the revenue side later in the year. Excluding the impact of this EU pre-financing, the first-nine-month deficit would have been HUF 3,075 billion, around HUF 253.7 billion lower than a year earlier.

The ministry attributed the smaller September deficit partly to tighter spending. Expenditure by ministry-managed budgetary appropriations fell by 61% year-on-year in September. Spending on support for public utility services was also HUF 154 billion lower than a year earlier, although the ministry said this reflected differences in the timing of payments.

Interest expenditure has provided another positive development. During the first nine months, government interest costs were HUF 726 billion lower than in the corresponding period of 2025. At the same time, pension spending increased by 11%, while healthcare expenditure rose by 3.2%.

Revenue growth has been more modest. During the first nine months, revenues increased by 3.4%, compared with a 9% rise in expenditure. VAT revenue grew by 2.3%, household tax payments by 3.3%, and corporate tax receipts by around 1%.

Finance Minister says we should look at the whole picture

Finance Minister of Hungary, András Kármán stressed that individual monthly figures can be affected by one-off factors and should not be treated as a definitive measure of the budget’s performance. He nevertheless pointed to what he described as increasingly visible spending discipline and falling interest costs.

Hungary’s budget position remains difficult, even though September brought some improvement. With the annual deficit expected to remain exceptionally high, the government’s forthcoming 2027 budget will be closely watched for evidence of whether it can deliver a more substantial reduction in the deficit and strengthen confidence in its longer-term fiscal plans.
