World.title: Delhi court grants bail to 17 students, journalists arrested during CEC protest
World.content:
Delhi Police accused of misconduct with female journalist at Jantar Mantar..

Court sets bail conditions for accused

Police seek custody, defence cites right to protest

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A Delhi court on Monday night granted bail to 17 students and freelance journalists arrested during a protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, and directed jail authorities to ensure medical treatment for those who sustained injuries.In four separate orders passed between 9 pm and 9:25 pm, Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC) Animesh Kumar of Patiala House Court ordered the release of all 17 accused in connection with an FIR registered at Parliament Street police station.The court directed that the accused be released on furnishing a personal bond with one surety of the like amount. It also said they should be released immediately if their custody was not required in any other case.The court specifically directed the jail superintendent to ensure necessary medical treatment for accused who had sustained injuries, as advised by the medical officer.The accused have been directed not to directly or indirectly induce, threaten or influence anyone acquainted with the facts of the case or tamper with evidence. They have also been restrained from committing any offence while on bail.They must provide their correct permanent and residential addresses and active mobile numbers, keep the numbers operational and inform the court of any change in address.They are also required to appear before the concerned court on every date of hearing and cannot leave the country without prior permission.The court said the investigating agency would be free to seek cancellation of bail if any of the conditions were violated.The FIR was registered under Sections 223(a), 221, 132, 190, 191(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), along with Section 3 of the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act.Police alleged that the accused were part of an unlawful assembly, obstructed or blocked public space, manhandled police personnel and damaged public property.The investigating officer had sought 14 days of judicial custody, arguing that the accused could commit further offences or interfere with the investigation.The defence opposed the plea, arguing that the accused were young and that several were students exercising their democratic right to dissent and protest. Defence counsel also submitted that no individual role had been specified against the accused in the grounds of arrest.The defence pointed out that while police claimed around 50 people were protesting, only 17 had been arrested. It also argued that no CCTV footage of the alleged incident had been produced before the court.The defence further submitted that some of the accused had sustained injuries and their medical examinations had not been conducted immediately after the incident.The court observed that the allegations were serious and noted that a police official had allegedly sustained injuries. However, it said the right to protest peacefully could not be disputed, while assaulting police officials on duty was a serious concern.The court also noted that, except for the offence under Section 132 of the BNS, the offences invoked were bailable in nature. It further observed that the accused did not appear to be habitual offenders and had their entire careers ahead of them.Considering the facts and circumstances, the court ordered their release on bail subject to the specified conditions.The court directed that the accused be produced before the concerned court on October 6 and ordered that a copy of the bail order be supplied to the Deputy Commissioner of Police, New Delhi, for information and necessary compliance.

World.title: 'More skeletons are tumbling out': Congress trains guns at EC over new report on Bengal polls
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh on Tuesday accused the Election Commission of overseeing "mass manipulation and rigging" during the West Bengal assembly polls.

He further demanded accountability from Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as well as other two election commissioners along with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and home minister Amit Shah.

"More skeletons are tumbling out of the Election Omission of Indiaâs closet. Clearly the PM-HM strategy was to somehow capture and win the West Bengal Assembly elections at any cost. It was a text book case of mass manipulation and rigging which was overseen by the CEC.

The puppet has of course to go but the two puppeteers too have to be held accountable. They stand brutally exposed and now it is only a matter of time for them to meet their reckoning," Ramesh wrote in a post on X.

"Today, MPs of the INDIA janbandhan plus other Opposition MPs who have also been invited will be marching peacefully to the

to demand the CEC's resignation. Looks like the Parliament complex is already under an unprecedented security siege showing the extreme nervousness of the puppeteer pair," he added.





Jairam Ramesh's latest attack on EC

Ramesh's remarks followed a media report claiming that judges of more than a dozen tribunals appointed in West Bengal on the Supreme Court's directions to hear appeals related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), including those involving 27 lakh deleted electors, had flagged gaps in a digital portal created by the Election Commission's IT division.

The Congress has stepped up its criticism of the poll panel amid a wider dispute over the SIR exercise.

The opposition's latest attack also comes after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modification to Form 6, the application used by eligible voters to seek inclusion in electoral rolls.

A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said, "We will examine all the decisions. If any decision is not in accordance with the law, we will annul it. You know the power of the court."

The bench also said, "any modification to Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When records are produced, we would like to see who has modified it".

The Congress and other opposition parties have demanded Kumar's resignation, alleging that changes to Form 6 were made unilaterally during the SIR process. Rahul Gandhi on Monday said the CEC and others involved in what he called a "criminal assault on democracy" would be held accountable.

The Election Commission has rejected concerns arising from the reported differences, saying divergent views are part of institutional deliberations and that its orders have full legal sanction and follow established statutory procedures.

World.title: Bengal bypolls: AJUP chief Humayun Kabir detained in Murshidabad after casting vote
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Aam Janata Unnayan Party (AJUP) chief and MLA

was briefly detained by Rejinagar Police and taken away from his party office in Murshidabad on Tuesday following a heated argument with police.

The detention came after he cast his vote in the Rejinagar Assembly constituency by-election.

Voting began early Tuesday for by-elections to five Assembly seats across West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, along with a Lok Sabha seat in Assam.

In West Bengal, polling is being held in the Nandigram and Rejinagar Assembly constituencies. The Nandigram seat fell vacant after Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari won from two constituencies in the state Assembly elections earlier this year and chose to retain the other seat.

The Rejinagar seat fell vacant after Kabir, who had won from both Rejinagar and Nowda, resigned from one of the constituencies.

The Rejinagar contest includes BJP nominee Sakharav Sarkar, former Murshidabad district president; Mamata Banerjee-led TMC candidate Rabiul Alam Chowdhury; rival TMC candidate Safiuzzaman Sheikh; Congress nominee Mohammad Abdullahil Kafi; and CPI(M)'s Syed Asad Ali.

World.title: US nuke test detection experiment bid to assert its hegemony: Ex-nuclear chief
World.content:
MUMBAI: Former chief of Atomic Energy Commission of India, Anil Kakodkar, who played a key role in the Pokhran nuclear weapons tests, said the main aim of the US conducting what is called a non-proliferation experiment last week was to assert its global nuclear hegemony and prevent other nations from conducting atomic tests.

On Sept 30, the US conducted an experiment which will enable it to detect whether countries are carrying out low-yield nuclear explosions.

Kakodkar told TOI, âThe US is attempting to get more sensitivity in terms of nuclear tests detection. There is a generic understanding that nuclear tests will not be carried out. But what if a country executes a test camouflaged?â

Asked whether the motive of the test jeopardised nuclear sovereignty of countries, he said the main aim was to assert global US nuclear leadership and stop other countries from carrying out atomic weapons tests.

A recent study by Federation of American Scientists says that currently India has 190 nuclear warheads and has enough military plutonium for 140 to 225 nuclear warheads.

Anil Anand, considered the father of Indiaâs nuclear submarine programme, quoted US National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) and told TOI that in the experiment researchers gathered measurements using a broad suite of advanced sensors, including accelerometers, seismometers, chemical and radiotracer samplers.





He said, âTogether these measurements will improve scientistsâ understanding of the signatures produced by underground explosions and strengthen USâ ability to detect and characterise nuclear explosive events.

â

According to NNSA, it âconducted a subsurface, non-nuclear chemical high-explosive experimentâ at the Nevada National Security Site. An FB post by NNSA states, âIf foreign countries test in secret, we will know.

The goal? Keeping the US one step ahead.â It further said the experiment assumes significance in the context of China supposedly having conducted a nuclear test in June 2020 secretly.

âIt takes nuclear expertise to detect nuclear activities, and experiments like these ensure America remains unmatched in detection,â said Brandon Williams, NNSA administrator. âTrump Administration has made it clear that the US will lead from a position of strength. You cannot evade American innovation. With this experiment, we are sending a clear message that under this administration, America will never be outmatched.

World.title: India’s services sector growth touches three-month high in September on strong domestic demand: PMI
World.content:
India's services sector growth touched a three-month high in September, as new orders increased sharply, supported by strengthening domestic demand, a monthly report said on Tuesday (October 6, 2026).

The seasonally adjusted HSBC India Services PMI Business Activity Index rose to 55.2 in September, from 54.1 in August, signalling the strongest upturn since June.

The upturn in services sector activity, however, failed to lift the quarterly average above that seen in the previous period. "In fact, growth over the second fiscal quarter was the weakest since the three months to March 2022," the report said.

In Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) parlance, a print above 50 means expansion, while a score below 50 denotes contraction.

S&P Global compiles the HSBC India Services PMI from responses to questionnaires sent to a panel of around 400 service sector companies.

According to the survey, growth in India's services sector was driven by increased demand for digital solutions, food, insurance, loans, software, transportation, and tours and travel.

International demand for Indian services also improved, with panellists reporting gains from Germany, the UAE, the U.K. and the U.S.

"The PMI survey suggested that India's services sector continued to improve, supported by strengthening domestic demand. At the same time, export business continued to expand, although the pace of growth slowed," said Pranjul Bhandari, chief India economist at HSBC.

On the job front, improving order books and projects in the pipeline prompted service providers to recruit extra staff during September. However, the rate of employment was softer than in August.

Cost pressures, meanwhile, subsided at the end of the second fiscal quarter, with the rate of input price inflation retreating to its weakest since November 2025.

"Input-cost pressures on service providers eased to a 10-month low, reducing the need to raise selling prices. The outlook remained positive, with service providers reporting improved expectations for future activity for the second consecutive month," Ms. Bhandari added.

Going ahead, Indian services companies remained optimistic about the year ahead, supported by resilient demand and rising customer enquiries. Just under 16% of respondents expect output to increase over the coming 12 months, while the remainder anticipate no change from current levels.

The HSBC India Composite PMI Output Index rose to 55.9 in September, up from 54.3 in August, indicating the strongest upturn in private sector output since June.

Composite PMI indices are weighted averages of comparable manufacturing and services PMI indices. Weights reflect the relative size of the manufacturing and service sectors according to official GDP data.

As per the report, the reinstatement of job creation in the manufacturing industry and sustained growth at service providers resulted in greater employment at the composite level.

World.title: UCIL chief rejects link between uranium mining, health ailments in Jharkhand
World.content:
UCIL chief Kacham Anand Rao has dismissed allegations that radiation from uranium mines and mills in Jharkhand’s Singhbhum region is causing health problems such as skin diseases, cancer and congenital deformities, saying such ailments are largely linked to "backwardness" and local conditions.

Also Read: NHRC notice on leak from uranium mine

The Uranium Corporation of India Limited (UCIL) chairman-cum-managing director said the uranium ore mined in the state is of very low grade, with only 200-300 grams of uranium extracted per tonne of ore, and claimed it has little health impact.

"Whatever skin disease or cancer is being attributed to some people is not due to uranium mines. They are due to local conditions and backwardness of the area. At least 10 scientific studies have been conducted by different organisations, which have proved that there is no link between uranium operations and the diseases found in the area," Mr. Rao said during an interaction at Jadugora.

The UCIL operates seven uranium mines in Jharkhand – six underground mines at Bagjata, Jaduguda, Bhatin, Narwapahar, Turamdih and Mohuldih, and an open-pit mine at Banduhurang.

Local groups and social rights activists have for decades criticised uranium mining operations of the UCIL, alleging that radiation from the mines and mills is affecting surrounding areas and causing diseases such as cancer, tuberculosis and congenital deformities.

India's first uranium underground mine was started at Jadugora in East Singhbhum in 1964 and ore processing plant in 1968.

"Uranium ores mined here are of a very low grade. The radiation here is lower than radiation on sea beaches. After uranium is recovered at the mill, most of the processed material is left as tailings, which have very low radioactivity and less than the limit," the CMD claimed.

He said the UCIL has been conducting public awareness programmes among local people to dispel what he described as misconceptions about uranium mining.

"The best examples are the UCIL colonies, which are alongside existing uranium mine and mill operations. Nothing has happened there for the past several decades," Mr. Rao said.

He said they are going to conduct a fresh study on health impact, as the previous studies were conducted around 7-8 years ago.

"We will shortly conduct a fresh study so that local people are convinced that nothing harmful is being caused by the UCIL operations," he said.

The CMD, however, said finding a competent agency for such a study is a challenge, as very few organisations have expertise in the field.

Sai Prasad, 47, who is associated with uranium mining operations at Narwapahar for 18 years, claimed that he has not experienced any occupational disease.

"I have been working in the mine for the past 18 years. But neither my family nor I have experienced any radiation impact or occupational disease. I am a shift in-charge here. More than 700 people work here, and many of them have been working for more than two decades. They also did not experience such an impact while directly engaged with mining operations," Mr. Prasad told PTI.

An assistant superintendent (safety), Rupai Mahali, told PTI that he had been working at the Turamdih Mill for the past 20 years, amid direct exposure to uranium-related activities, but had not experienced any health impact.

A uranium mill crushes, grinds, and chemically treats the raw ore to extract uranium and concentrate it into a solid product called 'yellowcake'.

Dr. N.K. Setty, officer-in-charge of the health physics unit of the environmental survey laboratory under the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), said studies suggested that radiological conditions in the uranium mines were safe and that the radiation dose received by occupational workers was well below the annual limit of 20 millisieverts.

"The environmental impact of six decades of mining activities is insignificant," he said.

World.title: When Jeffrey Archer lay on the floor: The interview that turned into an argument
World.content:
There are a dozen ways an interviewee can react when you provoke him a little.

Lying sprawled across the floor is not one of them.

But that is what happened when I went to meet author Jeffrey Archer in 2013 as part of a regular workday while in a previous media organisation.

It was a sunny morning when I sauntered into Taj Coromandel in Chennai, to meet the popular bestselling British writer for Best Kept Secret, the third book in the Clifton Chronicles series. Growing up, Archer’s work occupied prime space on my bookshelf, jostling for space with the works of Sidney Sheldon, Michael Chrichton and John Grisham, and hence, meeting him was going to be extra special.

Nervous, I arrived well in time for the meeting. While waiting in the hotel lobby and scanning the day’s newspapers that had carried detailed reports about the ongoing India-Australia cricket match being played at Mohali, a thought struck me: Jeffrey Archer was an ardent cricket fan.

I remember reading somewhere about his passion for English county cricket, having played the game in some capacity in his growing-up years and his subsequent admiration for players from the subcontinent like Sachin Tendulkar and Rahul Dravid.

I was determined to use that context for my opening, ice-breaking line.

When my turn came and I was ushered into his room by an eager PR professional, I introduced myself and – looking at the television in his room that was playing the highlights of the previous day’s play – remarked how good India had been on the cricket field in recent times.

Archer looked me straight in the eye and got up. Without batting an eyelid, he lay on the floor and started to brush the carpet. “This,” he thundered at a hapless me, “This is how you wipe your cricket grounds.” Wielding an imaginary towel and mop, Archer continued the act till it reached my legs, even as I wondered in trepidation how this interview was going to pan out. “Rubbish,” he said, in a thick English accent, “Mops and buckets...rubbish.” Archer was referring to how Indian groundsmen sweep and sponge off rainwater from the playing arena, taking off from that first day of the rain-hit Test match at Mohali.

The Indian cricket fan in me turned annoyed, even a little angry. I gently reminded him that India had already won a couple of matches in that series, only for him to retort, in a booming voice: “But you lost against England at home – so don’t get me started on that!”

The room went quiet. The PR professional who had parked himself in a corner of the room froze.

I had just had an unnecessary argument with a globally-famous personality on a topic that had absolutely nothing to do with the book he had written.

I sat at the edge of the seat, my hands shivering. The photographer who had accompanied me had his finger on the shutter button but wasn’t clicking, lest the sound upset Archer.

All this while Archer was on the floor and looking up at me in anticipation.

Those few seconds inside the fancy suite at Taj Coromandel felt like eternity.

Archer realised that the tension in the room was building. He quickly rose, and patted my shoulder in reassurance. I let out a sigh of relief. Well, Indian cricket was in safe hands. More importantly, my conversation with the legendary author would turn out not so bad after all.

I let out a weak smile as Jeffrey Archer said: “Shall we begin the interview?”
