World.title: ‘The Ozu Diaries’: An engaging look at the man behind the myth
World.content:
The director of films once considered too domestic for foreign export, Yasujiro Ozu (1903-1963) now sits high in the world cinematic pantheon. From his signature low camera angles to the “pillow” shots that serve as postcard-like pauses between scenes, his technique has been obsessively analyzed but remains sui generis.

That, however, is not the main subject of the splendid Daniel Raim documentary “The Ozu Diaries.” Drawing from Ozu’s journals and essays as well as other archival materials, it focuses more on the man and artist than his aesthetics.

World.title: 7-Eleven exits India amid mounting competition
World.content:
All 7-Eleven convenience stores in India shut down in September, according to its Japanese parent company on Tuesday, as media reported the retail giant struggled to compete with local rivals.

7-Eleven is a global chain of convenience stores best known for quick grab-and-go snacks, beverages and household staples, often operating 24 hours.

“We confirm that our Master Franchisee, Reliance, which operates 7-Eleven stores in Mumbai and Pune, closed all 31 stores on September 30,” Seven & I Holdings, the owner of the world’s biggest convenience store chain, said in a statement.

After signing a licensing agreement with India-based Reliance Retail, the brand launched its first Indian outlet in Mumbai in October 2021, eventually expanding to a peak of around 60 locations, a Seven & I Holdings spokesman said.

Seven & I Holdings declined to comment on why the shops were closed, but the Nikkei and Yomiuri reported that the company had struggled against severe competition from local Indian retailers.

Seven & I Holdings has not given up on its business in India in the long term, it said.

“While our aspiration to serve customers in India remains, we look forward to exploring several options to advance our presence in the market over the long term,” Seven & I Holdings said.

Its rival Lawson reportedly said it plans to open its first shop in India in 2027 and to expand its business there to around 100 shops by 2030.

World.title: Road budget scandal could knock Takaichi’s ambitious agenda off course
World.content:
As parliament begins its autumn session, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi finds herself forced to deal with a sudden political scandal involving the agriculture minister, one that could further complicate the government’s efforts to pass its legislative agenda and raise questions about her judgment and leadership.

Agriculture minister Kazuo Yana, who was appointed to the post last month, is now the center of a controversy following reports he drastically cut the road budgets of municipalities in Tochigi Prefecture whose mayors did not support him in February’s Lower House election.

According to an audio recording from May revealed last Wednesday, Yana told a May meeting of his local Liberal Democratic Party branch office that the reductions were made after the mayors of Nakagawa and Nasukarasuyama failed to support him in the February election. It was confirmed Tuesday afternoon by the transport ministry that their road budgets were cut to about half compared with fiscal year 2025.

World.title: Suzuki undercuts BYD as competition grows in market for low-budget EV minicars
World.content:
Suzuki Motor has unveiled its first fully electric minicar, fueling competition in Japan’s most important vehicle segment.

Including government subsidies, the “e SKY” model will cost around ¥1.6 million ($10,120) when sales start in November, Suzuki said Tuesday. That’s cheaper than Nissan Motor’s top-selling Sakura EV and BYD’s first minicar, introduced by the Chinese company in July.

Minicars are affordable, ultracompact vehicles that account for more than a third of automobile sales in Japan.

The arrival of the e SKY adds to signs that the country is becoming a key battleground for electric versions of the tiny cars, with Nissan, Honda, Daihatsu and now Suzuki offering them. Together, the Japanese brands control about 80% of the market.

Suzuki targets around 1,000 monthly sales for the tiny EV, which has a battery range of 310 kilometers and a base price of ¥2.1 million. Government subsidies can bring its sticker down by around half a million yen. BYD said in July that its Racco minicar, which offers a minimum range of 210 kilometers, will cost less than ¥2 million including subsidies.

In Japan, where EV uptake is far lower than in the U.S., Europe or China, Suzuki is betting that its first electric minicar can help lower the barrier for customers to make the switch from gasoline vehicles.

“We asked ourselves what kind of product would convince minicar drivers to shift to an EV, and this is our answer,” the model’s chief engineer Tomoyuki Tsubata told reporters in Tokyo. “We’re hoping this will help them recognize that option.”

World.title: Western Pacific sees rare trio of storms
World.content:
Three storms are churning simultaneously across the western Pacific, an unusual October clustering that’s generating high waves around parts of Japan.

Typhoon Choi-wan, Typhoon Nolo and Tropical Storm Koguma were all active on Tuesday, marking the first time in five years that three systems have existed at the same time in the month of October, according to the Japan Weather Association (JWA).

The three storms are at different stages of development and are spread across a wide swath of the Pacific.

World.title: How to protect yourself against cybersecurity threats
World.content:
For as long as companies have been collecting users’ personal information, bad actors have endeavored to steal it.

Bolstered by the use of tactics like spoofing and tech such as deepfakes that allow fraudsters to obscure their true identities and AI agents that overwhelm security systems and speed up hacking operations, scammers have become extremely savvy at exploiting companies’ security vulnerabilities to access user data — including in Japan.

According to the Digital Agency, these scammers have targeted not only identifying information such as names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses, but in some cases are able to steal account login information and passwords, credit card numbers and drivers’ licenses.

At a Digital Agency news conference Tuesday, digital transformation minister Toshiharu Furukawa revealed three baseline measures citizens should take to protect themselves from undue cyberrisk.

First, users should set unique passwords for each service and avoid reusing passwords across accounts.

“If you use the same password across multiple services, there is a risk that if information is leaked from one service, your accounts on other services could also be accessed through unauthorized logins,” Furukawa said.

Furukawa also asked that users set up multifactor authentication, which could include approving a login via a smartphone prompt or inputting a one-time password. This measure helps users prevent unauthorized logins.

Finally, users should be cautious of suspicious emails and social media messages, as there has been a recent increase in phishing incidents in which scammers impersonate real companies or even government agencies.

A 2025 survey by the National Police Agency of companies, educational institutions, medical institutions, local governments, independent administrative agencies and special corporations found that 40.6% of respondents had been sent suspicious emails, including phishing emails, over the previous year — the most common type of cyberattack reported.

“Cyberattack techniques are becoming more sophisticated every single day. However, by thoroughly implementing basic security measures, many of these incidents can be prevented,” Furukawa said. “In short, please take responsibility for protecting your own information.”

World.title: South Korea’s Lee says AI appears to have been used in bank hacks
World.content:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that AI models are believed to have been used in some recent hacking incidents against banks and called for the country to develop cybersecurity methods suited to the AI era.

“In some hacking incidents, signs have emerged of AI being used, causing considerable public concern and anxiety,” Lee said during a cabinet meeting.

“Please establish the circumstances swiftly and clearly, and concentrate personnel and resources on minimizing the damage.”

South Korea’s police have launched a full-scale investigation into the hacking attacks against commercial banks that led to a breach of customers’ personal information, the Yonhap news agency reported on Tuesday.

Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and others had reported cyberattacks, the Financial Services Commission (FSC) said on Friday, while Yonhap reported that Hana Bank and Woori Bank also suffered breaches.

Authorities have not yet disclosed details on what kind of AI tools were used in the hacking incidents or the full scale of the breaches.

On Sunday, FSC Chairman Lee Eog-weon convened an emergency meeting with financial industry associations, regulators and executives from affected institutions, warning that the sector must respond with the highest level of vigilance.

Financial watchdog the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) and the Financial Security Institute shared data about 28 unique IP addresses and some country information linked to the recent hacking attempts with the financial sector, the FSS said on Tuesday.

In September, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorized access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.

An artificial intelligence research firm said last week that AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government website, casting the effort as a failed hacking attempt, while Canada said there were no indications its systems were compromised.

World.title: Remote-controlled traffic barriers to be installed at flood-prone underpasses
World.content:
The transport ministry on Tuesday released guidelines related to the installation of remote-controlled traffic barriers at underpasses that are at a high risk of flooding, to restrict access during heavy rain.

The move comes on the heels of a series of deaths at flooded underpasses, including during heavy rain in Chiba Prefecture in August.

“We will promptly take effective measures to prevent accidents in flooded underpasses, in collaboration with relevant organizations,” transport minister Tatsunori Ibayashi told a news conference.

Under the guidelines, compiled for road administrators including local governments, underpasses around the country will be categorized into four levels based on flooding risk, and administrators will determine the classification of each underpass.

The guidelines call for the installation of barriers at underpasses deemed to be at particularly high risk, especially those where flooding has led to casualties or property damage in the past. Traffic will be restricted in advance when weather alerts corresponding to Level 4 emergency warning are issued or when hourly rainfall has reached or is expected to reach a certain level.

The guidelines also stipulate that traffic restrictions and measures to prevent vehicle entry must be put in place when drainage facility abnormalities are detected.

World.title: Hong Kong remains world’s freest economy as Switzerland overtakes Singapore
World.content:
Hong Kong has retained its status as the world’s freest economy in the latest annual ranking by a top Canadian think tank, although its score has declined in recent years.

Switzerland overtook Singapore to claim second place, pushing the city state down to third in the rankings released on Tuesday by the Fraser Institute.

The 2026 Economic Freedom of the World report, compiled by the Vancouver-based public policy research organisation using data from 2024, ranked Hong Kong first among 165 jurisdictions.

Hong Kong lost the top spot for the first time in 2023, before reclaiming it in 2024 and retaining it in 2025.

World.title: China’s Transsion, Africa’s top phone maker, targets US$500 million Hong Kong listing
World.content:
Shenzhen Transsion Holdings, the maker of Africa’s bestselling phones, aims to kick off its Hong Kong share offering on Wednesday to raise up to US$500 million ahead of a targeted October 15 listing, according to people familiar with the matter.

The company, which already trades in Shanghai and has a market capitalisation of 62 billion yuan (US$9.24 billion), could offer up to 132 million offshore ordinary shares, according to approval documents from the China Securities Regulatory Commission for the planned listing.

The public offering will run from Wednesday to Monday, with trading expected to begin on October 15, while the fundraising target is half the amount the company reportedly sought last year, the sources said.

Founded in 2013, Transsion leads the African mobile phone market. Its three brands – Tecno, Infinix and iTel – sold more than 91 million handsets last year and captured 53 per cent of the regional market share, according to the company’s regulatory filings.

World.title: West Kowloon arts hub deficit widens to HK$998 million as operating costs rise
World.content:
The authority managing Hong Kong’s arts hub in West Kowloon recorded a wider deficit in the 2025-26 financial year but expects to generate more income next year by putting a residential development project out to tender.

The West Kowloon Cultural District Authority’s deficit ballooned to HK$998 million (U$127 million) in the year to March 30, from HK$769 million in the same period a year earlier. The increase was mainly due to higher operating costs as it prepared to open the new WestK Performing Arts Centre, which is due to open in autumn 2027.

Revenue jumped 19 per cent to HK$768 million in 2025-26, driven by growth in ticket sales, sponsorship, and sales of intellectual property and creative products, according to a document submitted to the Legislative Council on Tuesday.

“The deficit is still within control, below the HK$1 billion level,” the authority’s CEO Betty Fung Ching Suk-yee said. “We will have more revenue in the coming months such as from the upfront fees from the tender of the residential project.”

World.title: Mox, BOCHK, ZA Bank and Citibank apps land among Asia-Pacific’s 10 best, study says
World.content:
Banking apps from Mox Bank, Bank of China (Hong Kong) (BOCHK), ZA Bank and Citibank Hong Kong are among the top 10 in Asia-Pacific, according to a Sia Partners study exclusively previewed by the South China Morning Post.

Sia, an international consulting firm, assessed 145 banking apps in 20 markets in Europe, Asia and Australia using 100 criteria, including functionality, user experience and feedback, with each receiving a score from 0 to 100.

The app from digital lender Mox Bank – backed by Standard Chartered, in partnership with Trip.com, HKT and PCCW – ranked first in Hong Kong and fifth in Asia-Pacific with a score of 67, according to the annual Mobile Banking Benchmark study, to be released later this month.

BOCHK ranked second in Hong Kong and seventh in Asia-Pacific with a score of 65, ZA Bank ranked third in Hong Kong and eighth in Asia-Pacific with 64 and Citibank Hong Kong ranked fourth in Hong Kong and ninth in the region at 63.

World.title: Court hears ex-in-laws tried to turn children against Abby Choi over HK$72m flat
World.content:
Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung accused her former in-laws of turning her children against her after she tried to push through the sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the centre of a bitter dispute between the two families, a court has heard.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, on Tuesday said her daughter had become hostile towards her former parents-in-law, Kwong Kau and Jenny Li Sui-heung, in the months before the influencer’s death in February 2023.

Cheung wept in the witness box as she watched footage of her late daughter welcoming guests to the luxury flat, prompting the judge to temporarily halt the trial.

“My daughter was a really good daughter, a really filial daughter,” Cheung said tearfully. “She trusted and gave her heart to the wrong people. This family, this family really bit the hand that fed them.”

World.title: John Lee promises ‘high-quality’ experience for Apec finance meeting guests
World.content:
Hong Kong’s leader has pledged to provide guests attending this month’s Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting with a “high-quality” experience, as the city works closely with Beijing to assist delegations with the registration process.

About 500 guests, including finance ministers and senior officials from the 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21, which will be hosted by Hong Kong for the first time at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai.

Asked whether US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent would attend the summit, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday only that the Ministry of Finance in mainland China was handling attendee registration.

“The Hong Kong government will continue to maintain close communication and cooperation with the Ministry of Finance to assist the delegation in completing the registration procedures,” Lee said ahead of an Executive Council meeting.

World.title: John Lee urges public to tune in to Legco debate on city’s 5-year plan, policy address
World.content:
Hong Kong’s leader has urged residents to pay close attention to a coming three-day debate on the city’s inaugural five-year plan and latest policy address in the legislature.

The debate on the two policy documents is set to begin on Wednesday morning and continue until Friday, according to the Legislative Council ’s agenda.

“I look forward to tomorrow’s Legislative Council debate, during which government officials and lawmakers will conduct an in-depth discussion on the concept and details of the five-year plan,” Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday, adding that the sessions would be attended by government officials led by Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki.

“I encourage everyone to pay close attention, as this will help you better understand the importance and significance of the five-year plan, as well as how the policy address will implement the plan’s first-year initiatives.”

World.title: Hong Kong prepares reforms, accountability measures ahead of Tai Po fire report
World.content:
Hong Kong authorities have made “a series of preparations” to implement reforms and pursue accountability ahead of the final report of an inquiry panel on the Tai Po blaze later this month, the city’s leader has said, pledging to act “as soon as possible”.

The government has established a dedicated task force under the Public Service Commission, reportedly led by former deputy secretary for security Benjamin Mok Kwan-yu and former commissioner for sports George Tsoi Kin-pan, to investigate alleged official failings linked to the deadly fire at Wang Fuk Court.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday that the government would study and follow up on the recommendations of the judge-led independent committee investigating last November’s disaster, adding that details would be announced after he received the report.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.title: The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.content:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Your book explores how Transsion grew from the informal global phone market that emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when African and Arab traders began traveling to southern China to buy cheap knock-off — or shanzhai — handsets. What is the company’s connection to that era?

Lu Miao: Shanzhai phones were extremely common in the early 2000s. The Huaqiangbei electronics market in Shenzhen was a major hub, while Chungking Mansions in Hong Kong was an important gateway for knock-off phones going overseas.

The main buyers were small traders from Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Some scholars call them “suitcase entrepreneurs” because they would arrive with a few suitcases, buy phones, take them home, and distribute them to smaller towns.

By the time Transsion was founded in 2006, shanzhai phones had already swept through many African countries. On the one hand, they met the basic communication needs of many low-income users; on the other, they damaged the reputation of Chinese phones, which African consumers came to associate with cheapness and poor quality.

When I went to Ghana in 2019, I found that many of Transsion’s national distributors had started out-selling secondhand and shanzhai phones bought from traders in Chungking Mansions. After partnering with Transsion, they gradually became formal agents for a multinational company.

These local African distributors linked the shanzhai era to the Transsion era. The personal connections and distribution networks they had built up played a major role in helping Transsion establish itself.

There is also continuity in design. Features such as dual-SIM support and large batteries originated in the shanzhai phone ecosystem and were later adapted for African markets. Dual SIMs, for example, help users avoid costly cross-network calls in countries with patchy network coverage.

But Transsion also represented a break from that era. First, the phone business became more formalized and institutionalized. These distributors set up trading companies of their own, and their relationships with Transsion became governed by more formal contracts.

Second, Transsion did not want to make quick money and leave, as sellers had done in the shanzhai era; it wanted to build a brand and stay for the long term. That is why it invested heavily in its after-sales service network.

Shanzhai wasn’t simply about one manufacturer producing copycat phones. It was an ecosystem: factories, supply chains, designers, distributors ... Transsion grew out of that ecosystem, but also moved beyond the shanzhai model of the time.

Sixth Tone: Looking at the bigger picture, how has Africa’s digital communications sector evolved over time, and how has that affected Chinese companies like Transsion?

Lu: Take Ghana as an example. The country’s telecommunications companies were originally state-owned. But in the 1980s and 1990s, the country had to turn to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for loans to deal with ongoing economic and debt crises. One condition of these loans was structural adjustment, which meant privatizing the telecom sector.

After the reforms, one common outcome was a widening urban-rural gap. Commercial operators were reluctant to serve low-margin rural areas, where costs were high and consumer spending was low, so infrastructure such as base stations remained concentrated in cities.

The needs of rural and low-income communities were overlooked during the reforms, and after the state retreated, it did not step back in to meet those needs. That meant many people could only afford cheap Chinese shanzhai phones.

Transsion stepped into this market, offering affordable feature — or “dumb” — phones that were tailored to African users’ needs. It optimized its models for areas with sparse base-station coverage, making them better at picking up weak signals than many other phones. Electricity supply could also be unreliable in rural areas, so the long battery life of both shanzhai and Transsion phones was another important advantage.

Zhang Lin: Against this backdrop, you argue that we should understand global technology flows in terms of “technology translation” rather than “technology transfer.” What does this framework help us understand about how technology moves between countries?

Lu: I don’t really like the concept of “technology transfer” because it frames the process as one-way: advanced Western societies export technology to less-developed non-Western societies in order to help them develop. But the endpoint of development in this model is always Western modernity.

It also assumes that technology is neutral and fixed, as if transferring technology alone will solve social problems and generate economic growth. Yet many aid projects failed precisely because they transferred equipment without transferring the knowledge, skills, and institutional environment around it.

That is why I used the concept of “technology translation.” When a technology enters a new context, it is often reinterpreted, adjusted, and transformed. Examining the context and process of how technology is translated allows us to see how knowledge moves, and the politics embedded in the process.

Transsion did not simply take phones made in China and move them unchanged to Africa; its products were continually redesigned through their encounter with local markets. Chinese engineers and product managers, Ghanaian promoters, distributors, and repair workers all became “translators” in this process.

For example, Transsion’s dual- and multi-SIM functions were not simply extra hardware features; they responded to high communications costs, uneven network coverage, and users’ need to switch between operators. Cameras optimized for darker skin tones respond to the fact that imaging technologies have historically treated white skin as the default.

These features were not simply invented by an individual designer. They emerged through interactions among the company, users, distribution channels, and repair networks.

Zhang: You describe Transsion’s business strategy as “deep plowing” and contrast it with Silicon Valley’s “blitzscaling” model. How are they different?

Lu: “Blitzscaling” was a widely celebrated model in Silicon Valley from the mid-2010s onward. Popularized by (American internet entrepreneur) Reid Hoffman, it relies on large amounts of capital to expand rapidly, prioritizing speed over efficiency.

The idea is to capture the market first and then achieve winner-takes-all dominance. Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb are typical examples, as are Chinese companies such as ride-hailing firm Didi.

At its core, blitzscaling involves a deliberately inefficient use of capital. Companies sustain themselves through venture capital, and much of that money is wasted. It is a game only a small number of players can afford. Most fail; the few that survive can end up monopolizing the market.

“Deep plowing” is more commonly seen in the Global South. It is slower and depends much more on local knowledge and relationship networks. The term originally comes from agriculture, referring to a labor-intensive mode of production that requires long-term investment and continual care.

In business and technology, I use it to describe a market-driven, labor-intensive approach in which a company continuously interacts with local markets and adjusts its products and business strategies in response to feedback.

In many cases, this model is adopted out of necessity. Transsion chose to work deeply in rural markets overlooked by Western capital largely because it lacked large pools of capital and core technologies. It often had to create room for itself by understanding markets in much finer detail.

(Header image: An entrance to the Circle Market in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Courtesy of Lu Miao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.title: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.content:
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.

China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.

Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.

Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.

China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.

Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.

According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.

“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.

South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.

Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.

China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.title: When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.content:
SHANGHAI — “Great-grandma, your head seems to be a little loose,” Yu Mingrui jokes as he examines an ancestral portrait depicting nine members of a family across three generations.

The 28-year-old Shanghai restorer was commissioned to repair the Qing dynasty (1644–1911) portrait by a descendant of the family in Ningbo, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, which had been passed down through generations. Yu filmed the process and posted it on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

Amid the portrait’s cracks and damage, Yu found clean, deliberate cuts around one woman’s painted head, suggesting the section was once removed and replaced.

Yu commented that the painter might have added the faces after painting the bodies. But viewers offered their own explanations. Some hypothesized the painter had covered up a mistake and repainted the face. Others suggested that descendants of a male ancestor’s concubine had altered the portrait to replace his wife’s image.

The answer may never be known. But the mystery drew widespread attention online, with videos about the painting receiving more than 100 million views and likes across Chinese social media platforms.

On Chinese social media, independent restorers like Yu are demonstrating how damaged paintings, old books, and family records are taken apart, repaired, and preserved.

“A lot of people told me that they simply didn’t know that something damaged could actually be restored before watching my videos,” Yu told Sixth Tone.

The objects brought to independent restorers include ancestral portraits, genealogies, old books, and calligraphy passed down through families and kept in homes rather than institutions.

Often made from paper or silk, these objects are vulnerable to moisture, insects, light, and age. Even when damaged, they can retain names, images, and other details about the families that preserved them.

For restorers like Yu, the videos can also connect that work with owners who might otherwise have left such objects damaged at home. Those commissions provide restorers with work and, in some cases, allow families to recover information from records that had become too fragile or damaged to read.

Face value

When the Qing-era ancestral portrait arrived at Yu’s studio, its ink had faded, its paper had become brittle, and its edges were torn. A patchwork of old advertising flyers held it together, promoting everything from cakes to real estate.

At 3.4 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, the portrait barely fits into the worktable at the center of Yu’s roughly 40-square-meter studio in Shanghai’s rural Songjiang District.

Yu turned the makeshift repairs into another joke for his viewers. Families in China traditionally honor deceased relatives with food and other offerings. The flyers, Yu joked, had given the painted ancestors a modern assortment of their own.

“Whatever the ancestors are missing, they can just take it from behind the painting,” he said.

Repairing the portrait, however, was a more exacting process. Yu said the restoration is divided into four broad stages: washing away dust and stains, removing the backing paper and remnants of earlier repairs, patching tears and holes with paper matching the original, and retouching missing colors and lines.

Each stage depends on the painting’s condition. Even washing it requires the restorer to decide whether to use hot or cold water, whether mold and stains require chemical treatment, and how much the paper can withstand. Chemicals can remove stains quickly, but excessive treatment can damage the paper or alter the painting itself.

“The real difficulty lies in the uncertainty,” Yu said. “A restorer’s experience gives you certainty at the beginning, serving as a safety net to deal with the uncertainty that appears in the process.”

The portrait took around three months to restore. Before treatment, Yu said, face-detection software picked up only three of the nine painted faces. Afterward, when he photographed the restored portrait, the software marked all nine faces on screen. Yu charges around 10,000 yuan ($1,493) for a painting of this size and complexity.

Yu began posting restoration videos while studying Chinese antique restoration in college. After graduating in 2021, he opened his own studio. His videos often begin with an unusual detail, a question about an object’s history, or a joke designed to catch attention.

“History isn’t only made up of famous paintings or nationally protected cultural relics,” he said. “It is also made up of these seemingly insignificant objects. As I restore them, I’m also helping to pass that culture on.”

Genealogies, ancestral portraits, and other family documents offer a view of the past that differs from official histories and local gazetteers, Zhang Yi, a historian at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, told Sixth Tone. Genealogies, for example, can record more than 1,000 people, while larger volumes can include tens of thousands, sometimes with birth and death dates.

“These materials greatly enrich our understanding of the lives and personal histories of ordinary people in Chinese history,” Zhang said.

The videos have also helped Yu turn restoration into a livelihood. His online following attracts commercial sponsorships, which now account for roughly half his income, he said. Many clients bring him just one family object in need of repair, but together, those individual commissions have allowed him to build his own customer base.

Paper trail

Beijing restorer Lian Chengchun also works mainly for private owners, from collectors to families preserving books passed down through generations.

Her videos offer them a first lesson in how to handle and preserve those objects at home, and can prompt people to take a second look at old records before the stories they carry disappear.

“I see little distinction between collections held by organizations and individuals,” Lian said. “Whether a book is restored by a public institution, an independent restorer or a private collector, the goal is the same: to preserve it for future generations.”

Books kept in private hands can arrive in almost any condition. Some have been patched with tape, glue, calendars, or whatever paper was available, repairs that may hold them together temporarily but can cause further and sometimes irreversible damage.

“Others were stored in plastic bags, where trapped moisture can encourage mold and decay,” said Lian, 38, who’s spent 18 years restoring old books by hand.

Before starting such work, Lian studies a book’s age and history, along with its paper, printing style, and other materials, which can vary across periods.

“Only then can I decide how best to repair it,” she said.

Cai Yadong came across Lian’s videos just when members of his clan in Jiaozhu Village, in southern China’s Guangdong province, needed help repairing a badly damaged genealogy.

In 2023, two elderly clan members handed Cai a 111-page genealogy dating to 1920. The wider Huazhou Cai clan today numbers about 20,000 descendants across roughly 110 villages, but Jiaozhu’s own records had almost completely disappeared, leaving residents unsure how their branch fit into the family or even who its founding ancestor was.

“When I first saw it, it was barely recognizable,” Cai, secretary of the Huazhou Cai clan association, said. “The pages were mixed together. Some had been burned, and years of damage had left the book extremely fragile.”

After contacting Lian, Cai flew to Beijing to deliver it himself rather than risk shipping it. “It was simply too valuable to risk any accidents,” he said.

Restoring the genealogy took Lian nearly a year and a half. Because of the genealogy’s age and poor condition, the restoration required careful, piece-by-piece work, Lian said.

“We try to repair it in a way that preserves its original appearance, while retaining as much of the surviving text as possible,” she said.

Lian compared numerous samples before selecting restoration paper that matched the original pages in color and texture. She repaired torn fragments and holes one by one, reinforcing sections where the original characters remained legible.

“Saving each character felt like picking up the brush where the Cai ancestors had left off,” Lian said. “Each page I uncovered felt like a dialogue with people from hundreds of years ago.”

When the work was completed, the volume showed that more than 30 pages were devoted to Jiaozhu, detailing family members and major events.

One entry showed how Jiaozhu’s branch fit into the wider Huazhou Cai clan and identified its founding ancestor as Cai Wende. The restored volume also helped three other villages establish their own connections to the clan.

“If our generation does not do this, the family memory may be gone after another one or two generations,” Cai said. “Once it is lost, it will be very difficult to recover.”

Just weeks before the genealogy surfaced, Jiaozhu had held a ceremony to renovate an ancestral tomb. Villagers knew it as the tomb of their founding ancestor but no longer knew his identity. Once the book was restored, they added Cai Wende’s name to the tomb’s inscription.

Cai described the timing as uncanny. “Whenever we talk about it, we all get goosebumps,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Yu Mingrui at his studio in Shanghai, August 2026. Lü Xiao/Sixth Tone)

World.title: Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.content:
Beijing Wildlife Park has turned its fight against a surge of invasive caterpillars into a public contest, offering up to 10 park tickets to visitors who collect the heaviest haul each day. From Sept. 28 to 30, participants caught an estimated 120,000 larvae weighing a combined 18.5 kilograms.

The safari-style zoo on the capital’s southern outskirts announced the event with a call for “warriors” to battle a leaf-eating pest it dubbed the “forest food monster.” Initially scheduled for two days, the contest was extended through Oct. 7 after drawing strong interest and now runs throughout the weeklong National Day holiday.

Participants first register and receive a brief lesson on identifying the pest before staff hand out disposable gloves, food containers, and chopsticks. They search the park for larvae and submit their catches by 2:50 p.m., when staff weigh them and determine the day’s rankings. The captured caterpillars are destroyed rather than fed to the park’s animals.

Prizes are awarded each day based on the total weight collected. The first-place entry receives 10 park tickets, with five for second place and two for third. Everyone who participates receives a commemorative pin, while those finishing fourth through 10th also receive a themed headband.

Competition was stiff from the opening day. A visitor surnamed Liang collected about 4,000 caterpillars weighing 596.3 grams, filling six containers but finishing second. The winning entry came from a five-person team that brought in 1,069.5 grams, while third place went to a catch weighing 391.4 grams.

“The winners were a team of five and caught nearly twice as many as I did,” Liang, a pianist who has visited the park for a decade, told Beijing Daily. “I couldn’t keep up.”

Liang said there was no particular trick to catching the caterpillars, though she found more in less crowded parts of the park and in the shade beneath taller trees. “I brought my own plastic bottles and tweezers, which I found more convenient,” she said.

The winner on the second day, Zhang Hanfang, 18, collected 1.3 kilograms with a six-person team. A taxidermist who runs a studio specializing in insect, reptile, and bird specimens, he made the two-hour drive from neighboring Hebei province with a friend’s family the day after seeing the park’s announcement. The group shares an interest in natural science.

“There’s no secret,” Zhang told Sixth Tone. “Just keep your eyes on the trees and keep at it. It was intense and thrilling. The contest also satisfied our October itch to go bug hunting.”

A video about the contest posted on the lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, known in English as RedNote, received more than 31,000 likes and 1,400 comments. One commenter described the initiative as “crowdsourced debugging,” while a related hashtag on Weibo attracted nearly 3 million views.

In recent weeks, residents across Beijing have reported seeing fall webworm caterpillars — the larvae of an invasive moth native to North America — on sidewalks, balconies, and even people’s shoulders.

The city is experiencing the peak larval period of the pest’s third generation this year, with mature larvae descending from trees in search of sheltered places to pupate and survive the winter.

Yang Zhongqi, chief scientist at the Chinese Academy of Forestry, said the species is a major invasive pest that threatens more than 300 plant species, including forest and fruit trees, flowers, and crops.

“During severe infestations, the caterpillars can strip a tree of every leaf, damaging urban greenery and hindering the tree’s growth,” Yang said. “But they do not kill the tree.”

Beijing had released nearly 700 million parasitic wasps this year before beginning the release of another 400 million on Sept. 28. Harmless to people and pets, the wasps lay their eggs inside fall webworm pupae, preventing adult moths from emerging.

Yang Sihan, head of monitoring and forecasting at the Beijing Gardening and Greening Resources Protection Center, attributed this year’s surge to a cyclical pattern of severe outbreaks, warmer winters, and frequent summer rain that disrupted spraying.

At sites monitored over five consecutive years, the survival rate of overwintering pupae rose from 65.3% in 2023 to 84.2% this year, Yang Sihan said. Heavy rain also left fewer clear days for spraying and washed away pesticides after they were applied. A single female moth can lay 300 to 600 eggs and sometimes as many as 2,000.



Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A participant tries to catch a caterpillar at Beijing Wildlife Park, September 2026. From @北京野生动物园 on Xiaohongshu)

World.title: In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019091/In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.content:
China’s weeklong National Day holiday began Thursday, extending a travel period that started with the Mid-Autumn Festival less than a week earlier and fueling demand for long-distance trips at home and abroad.

The Mid-Autumn Festival, traditionally an occasion for family reunions, fell on Sept. 25 this year. National Day, which marks the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, followed on Oct. 1 and began a weeklong public holiday. With only three working days between them, people who took those days off could combine the two breaks into a 13-day holiday ending Oct. 7.

Chinese airlines are expected to carry 31.19 million passengers from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7, up 3.6% from the same period last year, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China. Bookings for domestic flights covering more than 2,000 kilometers rose about 14%, according to aviation data provider Umetrip.

International flight bookings for the period were up 22.5% year on year as of Sept. 24, the CAAC said. Flights to Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, and Laos increased by about 20%, while those to Britain, Germany, and Spain rose by about 15%.

Here are snapshots from the extended holiday period across China.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.title: Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.content:
Chinese Olympic diving champion Zhang Jiaqi has sparked debate after starring in a popular reality show and revealing years of criticism, little emotional support, and financial control from her mother.

The debate intensified Sunday after Zhang’s mother, Xiao Yingjie, read aloud a letter telling her daughter that, despite not having “performed very well,” she still chose to “trust” and “forgive” her. Xiao had written the letter ahead of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, where Zhang, then 17, went on to win gold in synchronized diving. Related hashtags later trended on microblogging platform Weibo, drawing tens of millions of views.

The 22-year-old from Beijing retired last year. She now studies sports training at Beijing Sport University and also works as a livestreamer. In late August, she joined the current season of “My Little One,” a reality show that follows female celebrities and their parents at home, inviting guests to provide commentary on family dynamics.

The show revealed that before Zhang retired, all of her earnings, including a prize of 810,000 yuan ($120,000) she had received as a teenager, and three bank cards were managed by her mother.

On “My Little One,” Xiao is seen repeatedly criticizing her daughter, complaining about everything from Zhang letting her cats onto the table to drinking ice water, eating snacks, and leaving the tag on her pajamas. On one occasion, she says to the show’s other guests, “Look how lazy she is.”

Xiao’s private communications to Zhang via the instant messaging platform WeChat — messages critiquing everything from her tone of voice to table manners, as well as forwarded educational videos — were also shown to viewers. Zhang largely responded with silence as they were presented. “It’s so suffocating (to watch),” one highly upvoted comment on the microblogging platform Weibo read.

The show also revealed that Xiao, despite having no other job commitments, rarely visited Zhang once she left home to attend training at age 6.

On the show, Zhang told Xiao that she often felt that her mother didn’t love her and that her parents were not what she “imagined.” She added that she “always hated” Xiao as a child and that she believed she had been raised not by her but by her diving team.

Popular social media comments labeled Xiao as “NPD,” short for narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis that has become an online shorthand in China for controlling, self-centered, or emotionally manipulative people.

One post with nearly 20,000 likes on Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, called Zhang a “survivor of criticism-based parenting,” praising her for expressing her dissatisfaction with her mother on the show and actively distancing herself from her mother’s control. Others questioned Zhang’s father for his apparent absence from the conflict.

Domestic psychologist Li Songwei, appearing as a guest on the show, described the conflict as “delayed adolescence” on Xiao’s part. In a Weibo post, Li later urged people not to vilify Xiao, saying she had since voluntarily signed up for courses on parent-child communication and apologized to her daughter for her mistakes.

“This is a typical mother who is blinded by anxiety,” Li wrote. “In fact, the reason young viewers see so many parental traits in Zhang Jiaqi’s mother that they find ‘annoying’ or even ‘infuriating’ is that they, too, are working through issues from their own adolescence. It is a path every family has to take.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Zhang Jiaqi (right) and her mother on the show “My Little One.” From Weibo)

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: Duterte didn’t declare P190M cash in bank in SALNs — prosecution
World.content:
The Vice President and her husband Mans Carpio allegedly maintain 30 active bank accounts across eight banks

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte and her spouse, Manases Carpio, had combined year-end bank balances totaling P190 million from 2022 to 2025 that were not declared in the Vice President’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs), the House prosecution panel said on Tuesday, October 6.

On Day 34 of Duterte’s impeachment trial, prosecutors presented six common offers of evidence for 13 bank witnesses, who were called to identify and authenticate the couple’s bank records.

Private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih said the bank records showed Duterte and Carpio maintained 30 active bank accounts across eight banks, with combined year-end balances of more than P59 million in 2022, over P71 million in 2023, over P22 million in 2024, and over P35 million in 2025.

“When taken together across the years 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025, the Vice President’s and her husband, Atty. Carpio’s bank accounts have a total ending balance of more than P190 million that are not declared in her SALNs,” Alih said in making the offer of testimony.

More to follow. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sara Duterte: So, who’s behind attacks against me? It’s Marcos.
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte, the country’s second-highest official, has a pattern of linking her misfortunes to former ally President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Now that she is facing allegations involving millions of pesos in deliveries by former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., Duterte points to no one but her 2022 presidential candidate.

“Sino ang nasa likod ng paninira sa akin? Administrasyon. Ang Palasyo, si BBM (Bongbong Marcos). Makikita ‘nyo naman ‘yong mga declarations, mga statements ng Office of the President eh. ‘Di ba? Andiyan pa ‘yong impeachment nila,” Duterte said during a press conference in Davao City on Tuesday, October 6.

(Who’s behind the smear campaign against me? The administration. The Palace, BBM. You will see in the declarations, statements of the Office of the President, right? They still have their impeachment.)

Gracioso, in his eight-page affidavit submitted to the National Bureau of Investigation, claimed that he delivered millions of pesos to the Vice President when she was Davao City mayor. This happened more than 10 times, alleged the dismissed cop.

He also claimed that the money came from Duterte ally, former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco, while former Davao City information officer Jefry Tupas allegedly received it on Duterte’s behalf.

“Kung makikita ‘nyo, ang ginagawa ng communications ng administrasyon, lahat no’ng bahid na katiwalian na dapat sagutin ni BBM ay pinapahid niya sa akin. So ang ginawa nila, ‘Oh, para ano, sabihin na siya din, gawa tayo ng [issue].’ Ang hindi nila alam, nagsisinungaling si Gracioso kaya nga nakikita ‘yong mga kasinungalingan doon sa archives,” Duterte added.

(As you can see, the administration’s communications team is throwing all the corruption allegations facing BBM at me. They thought, “Let’s drag her into it, let’s make an issue out of it.” What they do not know is that Gracioso is lying, as shown by the archives.)

Duterte devoted more than an hour of her press conference to denying Gracioso’s allegations. She said the former cop was motivated by his anger toward the Velascos and by money.

But for Malacañang, Duterte is responsible for her own predicament. Palace press officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the allegations facing the Vice President stemmed from her own actions.

“Kung may sumisira man kay Bise Presidente, siya ang may kagagawan no’n sa sarili niya. Sila ang nakinabang sa bawat sentimo na nakukuha nila o nadedeposito sa kanilang accounts ng mga banyaga at ‘di umanong drug lords,” Castro told Rappler in a message.

“Ang sarap at pagpapasasa ay nasa kanila kaya, huwag magturo sa iba kapag nagkakabulgaran na ng mga anomalya. Panindigan nila ang mga ginawa nila,” she added.

(If there is anything damaging the Vice President, it is her own actions. They are the ones who benefited from every centavo they received or deposited into their accounts from foreign entities and alleged drug lords. They benefited from it, so they should not blame others when they are exposed. They should stand by their actions.)

Again, it was no surprise that Duterte dragged Marcos’ name into the Gracioso allegations.

Just last month, on September 7, Duterte said in a video statement that the sufferings of many Filipinos, including the widespread floodings, hunger, and high commodity prices, were caused by no less than the administration she backed in 2022.

Duterte is facing a grave threats case before Quezon City Regional Trial Court due to her alleged assassination threat against Marcos and his family. She posted bail on September 5 and claimed she did not feel safe in the country.

Then two days later, on September 7, she accused the Marcos government of “child abuse” because law enforcers allegedly subjected even her children to continued “surveillance.” Duterte’s own father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, is facing trial at the International Criminal Court due to his drug war that killed thousands of citizens, including women and children.

Duterte is now in the middle of her impeachment trial. If convicted, she will be removed as vice president and barred from holding public office – and from seeking the presidential seat in 2028.

And if this comes to pass, will Marcos once again be named as the convenient culprit – her erstwhile ally and old friend who somehow remains responsible for her every new misfortune? – Rappler.com

World.title: Salubong sa Sandaan: Miriam College marks 100 years with day-to-midnight festivities
World.content:
The institution's centennial celebrations bridged generations, honoring its trailblazers and inspiring the bright potential of its students.

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Miriam College and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Miriam College (MC) ushered in its historic centennial year with Salubong sa Sandaan, a festive day-to-midnight event held on September 11 and extending into the early hours of September 12. The school community—comprising employees, students, and alumni—gathered at the Loyola Heights campus to mark this significant milestone and celebrate an institution whose century-long legacy is rooted in faith, education, service, and leadership.

A TRADITION. The Cultural Classical Dance Club of Miriam College High School led the traditional Karakol to open the Marian Procession, leading to the Centennial Mass.

The celebration opened with the entire community praying the Holy Rosary in honor of Mother Mary, after whom the school was named. Miriam is the Aramaic name of Mother Mary. This was followed by the Karakol, a traditional Marian procession, and the celebration of the Centennial Mass officiated by Bishop Honesto Ontioco, D.D., of the Diocese of Cubao.

ROOTED IN FAITH. Maryknoll Sisters in the Philippines and Miriam College’s past presidents Dr. Loreta N. Castro, Dr. Patricia B. Licuanan, and Amb. Laura Q. Del Rosario join the community during the celebratory mass.

The festivities continued throughout the evening with the screening of short films created by students and MC employees for the Miriam College Film Festival (MCFF). The program also featured the school’s homegrown talents from its three campuses—MC Loyola Heights, MC Nuvali, and MC Alviera.

TO THE BEAT. Sole2Soul and Company of One, two of the College’s homegrown dance groups, brought rhythm and energy to the festivities.

A much-anticipated moment was the MCFF awarding ceremony led by Miriam College President Dr. Maria Regina Lizares and Human Resources Director Dr. Noel Racho.

Celebrating a century of legacy

FIRST FILM FESTIVAL. The first Miriam College Film Festival (MCFF) themed Mga Kwento ng Isang Daan,features six original student and employee films inspired by the institution’s 100-year legacy.

The centennial celebration continued on September 12 as generations of Maryknoll and Miriam College alumni gathered at the Fairmont Hotel in Makati for the Centennial Night and the launch of the coffee table book, ‘The Legacy We Carry: 100 Years From Maryknoll to Miriam.’

REUNITED. Maryknoll and Miriam College alumni honor fellow alumna and newly-conferred National Artist for Design, Maria Beatriz “Patis” Pamintuan Tesoro (center), during the Centennial Night celebrations at Fairmont Hotel in Makati.

HONORING THEIR ROOTS. Miriam College President Dr. Gina Lizares and Sr. Marvelous Misolas, M.M. (2nd and 3rd from right) join the Maryknoll-Miriam alumni at the Fairmont Hotel for the launch of the centennial book, ‘The Legacy We Carry: 100 Years from Maryknoll to Miriam.‘

BLUE AND GOLD. Miriam College’s official colors flooded the night from the vibrant hosts to the dynamic crowd.

The evening brought together alumni from across generations for a night of bonding, dancing, and music. A highlight of the celebration was a fashion show honoring alumni and newly conferred National Artist for Design Maria Beatriz “Patis” Pamintuan Tesoro.

MC NUVALI REPRESENT! The campus’s Indayaw and Sikhayaw group wowed the community with their energetic moves.

From Maryknoll to Miriam, the institution’s influence on Philippine education—particularly women’s education—has become an enduring part of the nation’s history. From its beginnings in 1926 as a teacher-training school in Malabon–where it produced its first women graduates–the institution has gone on to nurture generations of students and distinguished alumni whose leadership and service have made a lasting impact across diverse fields, both in the Philippines and abroad. Today, Miriam College continues to expand its mission in education beyond the walls of its Loyola Heights campus with the opening of Miriam College Nuvali in 2014 and Miriam College Alviera in 2025.

OVERFLOWING TALENT. Miriam College’s centennial celebration was held in the campus’ outdoor field from the morning of September 11 until midnight of September 12 to welcome another exciting century for the institution.

RYTHM AND ENERGY. Faculty and students in the crowd cheered for their favorite group performances throughout the night.

Miriam College’s year-long centennial celebration is expected to continue until September 2027, with a lineup of activities that will bring together the school community and its stakeholders. Among these are the Christmas Bazaar, a concert by the Miriam College Music Center, the MC100 Fun Run, and the Academic Conference on Teaching and Learning.

Learn more about Miriam College’s upcoming activities through its Instagram and Facebook pages. – Rappler.com
