World.title: Negros Trade Fair 2026 doubles last year’s attendance at SMX Aura
World.content:
SM and ANP welcomed nearly 80,000 visitors to BÚTLAK, setting a new benchmark for the Negros Trade Fair in Manila.

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by SM Supermalls and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

BÚTLAK: The 40th Negros Trade Fair welcomed 79,512 visitors to SMX Convention Center Aura from September 22 to 27—double last year’s attendance and the highest foot traffic recorded in the fair’s Manila run. Organized by the Association of Negros Producers (ANP), in partnership with SM Supermalls through SM for MSMEs, and the Provincial Government of Negros Occidental, the six-day fair brought together 126 exhibitors across 177 booths. Visitors came to explore the food, fashion, crafts, home finds, and travel stories of the Negros Island Region—and left with more than a few bags in hand.

A TASTE OF NEGROS. From pantry staples and artisanal preserves to freshly made delicacies, visitors filled their bags with food finds that carried the flavors and stories of Negros beyond the fair.

BÚTLAK generated nearly P118 million in reported sales, based on submissions from 120 exhibitors, with six reports still being consolidated. Of this amount, P75 million came from spot sales, a 39% increase year on year and a strong indicator of direct consumer demand. Another P43 million came from business-to-business transactions involving institutional buyers, retailers, distributors, and other partners.

ONE BITE AT A TIME. From comforting bowls and smoky grilled favorites to sweet local treats, BÚTLAK gave visitors a delicious way to experience the region’s rich culinary heritage.

The strong sales were evident in the food section, where several exhibitors—including Cocina Javellana, Bacolod Chicken House, and Wawa Bing’s Kitchen—sold out as early as the second day. Many food booths had also run through their inventory by late afternoon.

Among the fair’s crowd favorites were Bacolod Chicken House’s inasal 21’s batchoy, Vaca Japonesa’s Wagyu Kansi and Wagyu Tapa N Rice; Wawa Bings Kitchen’s fresh lumpia; Cocina Javellana’s ube halaya; Felicia’s ensaymada and El Ideal’s freshly made hot piaya. Visitors also sought out Ading’s Gourmet Kitchen’s batuan fruit paste, blue crab paste, and smoked bangus; Ereñeta-Manaloto Chorizo de Bacolod; Nanette’s VCO, coco cider vinegar, and sinamak; and Filipino favorites from Imay’s Bar & Restaurant. The results point to a clear opportunity for future editions: helping exhibitors prepare more inventory and production capacity to meet growing demand.

A new generation refreshes Negros heritage

BÚTLAK’s strongest stories came from the meeting of legacy and new energy. Heritage brands continued to draw loyal customers, while younger founders and next-generation family members gave familiar products a fresh look, new flavors, and a stronger connection with today’s shoppers.

Bob’s, one of Bacolod’s most established food names, reintroduced itself through a retro-inspired Bob’s Sari-Sari Store concept, with members of the third generation helping man the booth. El Ideal, the heritage bakery founded in 1920, remained a crowd-drawer for its hot piaya while also attracting curiosity for its Guapple Pie. “We have been around for about 100 years because we never sacrificed quality,” said Maritess Sanchez of El Ideal. “The Negros Trade Fair has helped us expand our reach here in Manila.” The fair also made room for a newer generation of makers.

Upcycled by The Little Vintage Shop gave donated clothing a second life through circular fashion, while LAKAT featured locally made footwear incorporating pineapple-based textiles and other Philippine natural materials. NVC Foundation’s Artisans of Hope showcased handmade mosaic pieces that support Bacolod-based artisans, while Alter Trade Philippines connected shoppers to fair-trade products that support Negros sugarcane producers and rural livelihoods.

FOR MSMEs. ANP president Christina Gaston spotted at the Negros Trade Fair.

“For ANP, MSME development is about giving people the opportunity to discover what they can create, what they can become, and where their creativity can take them,” said ANP president Christina Gaston.

“Over 40 years, we have seen small businesses grow into enterprises and local products reach markets once thought beyond their reach.”

DISCOVERING THE DETAILS. Shoppers browsed handwoven textiles, handcrafted bags and contemporary apparel, connecting directly with the artistry and stories woven into every Negrense creation.

Young chefs put a modern twist on Negrense flavors

The celebration opened with Arima, the symbolic ringing of the bell that traditionally marks the start of the workday—and, for BÚTLAK, the festive opening of Negros in Manila. At the heart of the annual ritual is food: an invitation for guests to experience Negrense ingredients, heritage and hospitality at the table.

This year, Manila chefs brought contemporary flair to familiar flavors and ingredients sourced from participating exhibitors. Negrense chef Don Colmenares of destination restaurant Sauma served Kansi Croquetas with Negros beef, batuan mayo and langka purée, alongside an Atcharang Ukoy with dilis polvoron, sinamak mayo and malunggay pesto.

Chef Luis Locsin presented his signature Negrense-inspired pâté en croûte creations: a Pork and Native Chicken Mosaic Pâté en Croûte with native chicken, Victorias ham, dried fruits, almonds and Don Papa Rum; and a Pork and Duck Pâté en Croûte with Victorias bacon, oyster mushrooms, herbs and port wine. Chef Cara Davis of Halong created a Saravia Coconut Crab Lumpia, served with coconut chutney, atchara, fermented garlic, kiwot honey and Vietnamese green chili sauce.

Official caterer Epicura, the catering arm of Curio led by Pia Lago and chef Bettina Arguelles, completed the spread with KBL rillette on oat thins, seasonal seafood kinilaw with tultul salt, crab bibingka with calcag dust and bihod, corned beef kansi with kansi gravy, pancit luglug molo, and pork bellychon with batuan chimichurri.

New to this year’s Arima, private chef Bea Magalona reimagined familiar favorites through an Adobarquillo—barquillos filled with Ilonggo-style adobo cream—and Piaya Toast, made with langka piaya, kadyos hummus and pork. Together, the Arima menu showed how the flavors of Negros can remain rooted in heritage while finding fresh expression through a new generation of chefs and culinary collaborators.

A bigger marketplace for Negrense MSMEs

For SM Supermalls, BÚTLAK demonstrates how access to the right marketplace can help local businesses reach more customers and create new opportunities for growth.

SM Supermalls’ executive vice president for marketing Joaquin San Agustin.

“Every purchase does more than bring home a piece of Negros,” said Joaquin L. San Agustin, executive vice president for marketing at SM Supermalls, during the opening. “It supports a local business, celebrates Filipino creativity, and helps another entrepreneurial story move forward.”

CREATIVE COMMUNITY VISITS. Familiar faces from fashion, food, design and entertainment joined shoppers at BÚTLAK, exploring the people, products and stories that made the 40th Negros Trade Fair a standout Manila gathering.

Through SM for MSMEs, SM Supermalls works with partners such as ANP to help open doors for homegrown businesses—connecting them to shoppers, visibility, and bigger opportunities to grow. With nearly 80,000 visitors and nearly ₱118 million in reported sales, BÚTLAK’s milestone edition showed that when local products are given room to be discovered, the impact reaches far beyond the fair itself. It creates new possibilities for the people, families, and communities behind every product. BÚTLAK: The 40th Negros Trade Fair was organized by the Association of Negros Producers in partnership with SM Supermalls and the Provincial Government of Negros Occidental. — Rappler.com

World.title: Marcos in Singapore (again): A Forbes event… and an F1 Grand Prix
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his fifth State of the Nation Address at the House of Representatives on July 27, 2026.

Marcos has visited the city-state several times before — two of those times, he attended the Singapore Grand Prix

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is set to visit neighboring Singapore yet again from October 7 to 11, upon the invitation of Prime Minister and finance chief Lawrence Wong.

In a text briefing for the media, Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) spokesperson Analyn Ratonel framed the visit as an “initiative of the [Philippines] to deepen ties with Singapore, expand economic engagement, and promote cooperation in sectors that would benefit the country.”

Singapore is also set to take over chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) after Manila.

While in the city-state, Marcos is expected to engage in at least four major events:

Meeting with Wong

24th Forbes Global CEO Conference

A visit to the Singapore Nuclear Research and Safety Institute

The Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix

It’s the last event that sticks out. After all, Marcos has been criticized for attending the same event twice — in 2022, barely months into his term and again in 2023. His latest Singapore Grand Prix attendance happened days after a speaking engagement with the Milken Institute.

Marcos has visited Singapore several times before, including the 2022 and 2023 visits that included a Grand Prix attendance.

This is how Ratonel explained Marcos’ expected attendance at the Singapore Grand Prix: “The President has been personally invited by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong to the Singapore Formula 1 Grand Prix. The Singapore Grand Prix brings together government leaders, business executives, and investors from around the world. It would provide an opportunity for informal engagements to complement his meetings focused on attracting investment and strengthening the Philippines’ partnerships.”

Aside from Wong, there are no other planned meetings for Marcos in Singapore. “However, there may be opportunities for the President to engage with leaders and senior officials, not just from Singapore, but from other countries, as well as business executives, during the Singapore Grand Prix,” said Ratonel in the briefer for media.

Marcos will be joined by Finance Secretary Frederick Go, Trade Secretary Cristina Aldeguer-Roque, and acting Communications Secretary Dave Gomez. Ratonel did not say whether First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos would be part of the delegation, but she almost always joins the President in trips overseas.

The Philippine President is said to be fond of attending the Singapore Grand Prix — even amid turbulent times in Philippine domestic politics, it turns out.

His trip to Singapore coincides with the impeachment trial of erstwhile ally Vice President Sara Duterte which is at its arguably most controversial and contentious period — with the second-highest elected official of the land alleged of hiding her wealth and receiving money from the Chinese government through a business shared with her husband.

Marcos has distanced himself from these allegations, even as his alter-egos in the security and defense sector have called for further inquiries into allegations of financial ties between Duterte and Beijing.

Ratonel, in the prepared Q&A for media, echoed previous statements by the President in defending the quick Singapore sojourn.

“President Marcos has said that official foreign trips should be assessed based on their benefits to the country, not only on their cost. He has described these trips as investments that can help attract trade and investment, create jobs, strengthen security and diplomatic ties, and promote Philippine interests abroad,” she said. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Marcos Jr. did not say protecting VP Duterte from her case is ‘corruption’
World.content:
A viral Facebook graphic attributes a statement to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. about Vice President Sara Duterte’s legal troubles, but the official transcript of Marcos’ media briefing in India does not contain the remarks attributed to him

Claim: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he could not be blamed for Sara Duterte’s legal troubles, that he could not protect her from her case, and that if a president did so, “corruption” would be the result.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A viral Facebook graphic posted by Senior Rak Joe, a Facebook page with around 15,000 followers, attributes a statement to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

It claims that Marcos made the statement on September 13, 2026, amid his remarks about Vice President Sara Duterte. It had garnered around 102,000 views as of October 5, 2026.

The graphic says, “Yung pinanggalingan ng kaso niya galing mismo sa bibig niya, kilos at galaw niya, di niya ako pwedeng sisihin kung ano man ang mga nararanasan niyang pagsubok… Ano gusto niya gawin ko, protektahan ko siya sa kaso? Di naman pwede ’yun. Kung gagawin ng isang Presidente ’yan, corruption pa rin ang kalalabasan niyan…”

(The case against her stemmed from her own words, actions, and conduct. She cannot blame me for whatever challenges she is going through. What does she want me to do, protect her from the case? That’s not possible. If a president were to do that, it would still amount to corruption.)

On September 13, the President was in New Delhi, India, for the Philippines’ participation in the 18th BRICS Summit. He also held a Kapihan with the Media at the Taj Mahal Hotel.

The facts: On September 13, during a Kapihan with the Media, Marcos was asked about his thoughts on the issues surrounding the Vice President. In that press conference, the President did not say the quoted statement in the Facebook post.

The official transcript of his Kapihan remarks contains no statement saying that Duterte’s case came “from her own mouth,” that he could not be blamed for her situation, that he was being asked to protect her from the case, or that doing so would constitute “corruption.”

What Marcos Jr. actually said was, “You know, I hear about them, but I don’t really even have a response. If she feels very angry, I suppose, with what’s happening to her.”

“And I am the target of that anger, or the main target of that anger. What can I do? You cannot force anyone to love you,” he added.

The phrase “wala siya sa tamang pag-iisip” (she’s not in her right mind) also does not appear in his Kapihan remarks.

A similar remark, however, was made by Presidential Communications Office Undersecretary and Palace Press Officer Claire Castro during a September 11 press briefing in New Delhi.

While responding to Duterte’s statements, Castro asked, “Nasa tama ba siyang huwisyo? Nasa tama ba siyang pag-iisip?” (Is she in her right mind? Is she thinking clearly?)

Castro was referring to Duterte’s state of mind after the Vice President made statements against Marcos Jr. She also referred to “sleepless nights and anxiety” as possible factors affecting Duterte’s statements. – Ahyenne Neleah Estacio/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

Ahyenne Neleah Estacio is a graduating Bachelor of Arts in Communication student and campus journalist at Holy Angel University. The current senior editor and former editor-in-chief of The Angelite, she is an Aries Rufo Fellow for 2026.

World.title: Astana School Named Finalist for 2027 Zayed Sustainability Prize
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana’s General Education School No. 101 has been named one of three finalists representing Europe and Central Asia in the Global High Schools category of the 2027 Zayed Sustainability Prize, organizers announced.

The school was selected for an artificial intelligence-based system that monitors air quality in classrooms, allowing schools to detect changes in indoor conditions and respond before they affect the learning environment. The project is designed to help create safer and healthier conditions for students and teachers.

“General Education School No.101, Astana, a public school in Kazakhstan with 3,800 students, aims to develop an AI-supported indoor air quality system using LEGO Spike Prime and Raspberry Pi sensors to monitor classroom conditions and predict periods of poor air quality,” reads the official website of the prize.

The school is competing against Agrupamento de Escolas Gândara Mar of Portugal and Keban Multi-Program Anatolian High School of Türkiye. Overall, 18 schools from six regions were selected as finalists in the Global High Schools category.

The UAE-based award received a record 10,233 submissions from 177 countries in the 2027 cycle, up 32% from the previous year. Finalists were selected across six categories: health, food, energy, water, climate action and global high schools.

Other finalists include U.S.-based Elythea, which uses artificial intelligence to identify pregnancy complications using first-trimester data, and Japan’s TOWING, which uses biochar technology to improve soil health.

Each organizational finalist will receive $100,000, while school finalists will receive $25,000. Winners in the organizational categories will receive $1 million, while winning schools will receive $150,000.

The winners will be announced on Jan. 12, 2027 at the Awards Ceremony during Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week.

“The most powerful solutions are those rooted in real-world needs,” said Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, UAE Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and Director General of the Prize.

The Zayed Sustainability Prize says projects supported through the award have reached more than 411 million people worldwide.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Partners Target Falling Caspian Sea Levels With New Monitoring Project
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and international partners are stepping up efforts to address falling Caspian Sea levels, biodiversity loss and pollution, as Aktau hosted a high-level dialogue on Oct. 5 that also launched a Japan-funded monitoring and water management project.

The Caspian Sea has been shrinking for decades, raising concerns over biodiversity, coastal communities, infrastructure and economic activity across the five littoral states. Kazakhstan, which has the sea’s longest coastline, has increasingly sought regional and international cooperation as scientists warn that climate change and declining river inflows could accelerate the retreat.

Organized by the United Nations Development Programme in Kazakhstan with the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources and the Mangystau Region akimat (administration), the dialogue brought together government institutions, diplomats, international organizations, scientists, civil society and the private sector.

The participants discussed changes in the Caspian Sea’s water balance, geological risks, pollution, marine litter, biodiversity conservation and the circular economy, the UNDP reported.

Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Alibek Kuantyrov emphasized the need for coordinated action to address the Caspian Sea’s environmental challenges.

“For Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea is a vital part of the country’s environmental, social and economic development, a source of livelihoods for coastal communities, and a space connecting five states. That is why Kazakhstan has consistently advocated moving from discussions of individual environmental challenges towards systemic and coordinated action,” said Kuantyrov.

Japan-funded project to strengthen Caspian Sea monitoring

The Japan-funded project will support joint research involving experts from Caspian countries and establish a regional scientific coordination platform for exchanging data and expertise. It will also strengthen Kazakhstan’s capacity to monitor the Northern Caspian Sea, including through upgraded monitoring and laboratory equipment and professional training.

The project will help improve monitoring of sea level, river discharge, water temperature and salinity, and evaporation. The data, combined with meteorological, bathymetric and satellite observations, will support improved models and projections of Caspian Sea level changes and related risks.

Japanese Ambassador to Kazakhstan Yasumasa Iijima highlighted Japan’s expertise in water resources management, disaster risk reduction and environmental protection.

“The project will focus on two main areas: establishing a platform to strengthen cooperation among the Caspian littoral states, and advancing scientific monitoring, transboundary data exchange, dialogue and joint action. Japan has extensive experience and expertise in water resources management, disaster risk reduction and environmental protection,” he said.

The event was the first held under the Friends of the Caspian initiative, which aims to bring together Caspian states, international organizations, financial institutions, donors, scientists and civil society around the shared goal of preserving the Caspian Sea.

The initiative is expected to be presented to international partners on the sidelines of the UN Climate Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, in November.

World.title: Kazakhstan Accelerates Digital Transformation as Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Link Nears Launch
World.content:
ASTANA – Officials discussed implementing Kazakhstan’s Digital Qazaqstan Strategy at a government meeting on Oct. 6, outlining plans to expand AI-powered public services, develop large-scale computing infrastructure, and accelerate digital transformation across the economy.

The strategy, approved through 2029, covers digital government, data infrastructure, cybersecurity, telecommunications, IT, advanced manufacturing and emerging technologies, the Prime Minister’s press service reported.

$10 billion data center project

A Data Center Valley is being developed in Ekibastuz with a planned capacity of at least 1 gigawatt. Construction of the first facilities has begun.

The government plans to commission 186 megawatts (MW) in 2027 and a further 109 megawatts (MW) in the second quarter of 2028.

Kazakhstan has signed a $10 billion package of agreements with Firebird AI, and more than 20 international technology companies and investors have expressed interest in the project.

AI-powered public services

The national QazTech platform is becoming the foundation of Kazakhstan’s digital public services. Migration of 92% of systems planned for this year has been completed.

Through eGov GPT, 51 services are currently available, with the number expected to reach 150 by the end of this year. AI has processed more than 3.2 million appeals through e-Otinish.

The government plans to increase the share of public services using AI to 40% by 2028 and halve service delivery times by 2029.

Expanding the digital economy

More than 4,000 5G base stations have been deployed in over 20 cities. The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic project has reached 390 kilometers of cable between Sumgait (Azerbaijan) and Aktau, with the launch scheduled for October.

Kazakhstan’s IT service exports exceeded $1.1 billion in 2025. The target is to increase IT exports to at least $2 billion by 2029 and develop at least three unicorn companies.

AI in energy and industry

The energy sector has a portfolio of 45 AI projects, with a projected annual economic effect of around 23 billion tenge (US$50.4 million). The initiatives target a 25% reduction in accidents and a 90% reduction in energy-resource losses.

At KAZ Minerals, digital twins have increased copper recovery by 2% and factory productivity by 7%. In the automotive industry, AI has reduced defects by 39%.

Kazakhstan is also developing industrial robotics, autonomous transport and satellite technologies. Commercial drone delivery is planned for 2027, while commercial air-taxi operations are targeted for 2028.

Digital construction

BIM (Building Information Modeling), a digital method for designing, constructing and managing buildings and infrastructure, became mandatory in August for a range of technically complex facilities. Its application is expected to reach 100% of new technically complex projects by 2028.

AI is already being used to review construction documentation, with 864 projects processed through automated checks.

The government aims to complete the Digital Qazaqstan Strategy measures by 2029 and move key sectors towards data-driven management and greater use of artificial intelligence.

World.title: Where Kazakhstan’s Oil Goes: Key Export Markets and Volumes
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan exported a record 76.3 million tonnes of crude oil in 2025, up 7.4% from the previous year and 20% from 2015, according to data from the Bureau of National Statistics. Italy remained the country’s largest buyer, while the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) continued to carry the bulk of Kazakhstan’s crude exports.

Kazakhstan’s physical oil exports have generally increased over the past decade, rising from 63.6 million tonnes in 2015. The increase has been particularly pronounced in recent years. Kazakhstan exported 65.2 million tonnes in 2022, 71 million tonnes in 2024 and 76.3 million tonnes in 2025.

The growth coincided with record oil production. Kazakhstan produced 99.6 million tonnes of oil in 2025, with increased output at the Tengiz field among the factors contributing to the result. The country’s oil production target for 2026 is 96 million tonnes, down from 98 million tonnes after disruptions affecting the CPC.

In monetary terms, oil exports increased from $26.8 billion in 2015 to $40 billion in 2025, a 49.3% increase. The highest figure came in 2022, when oil exports were valued at $46.9 billion.

However, export volumes and value do not always move in the same direction. In 2025, Kazakhstan exported 7.4% more oil than in 2024, while export value fell 6.8%. The average calculated value per exported tonne fell from $604 to $524.

This illustrates the impact of global oil prices on export earnings: higher physical volumes do not necessarily translate into higher export revenue.

The $40 billion in oil exports represents the value of crude sold abroad rather than direct state revenue. Oil revenues are distributed among the companies and participants involved in production, transportation and investment, while the state receives revenues through taxes, special payments from subsoil users and its participation in oil and gas assets.

Italy remains the largest buyer

Italy was the largest destination for Kazakh oil in 2025, receiving 28.9 million tonnes worth $15.2 billion. The country accounted for 37.8% of Kazakhstan’s oil exports by volume and 38.1% by value. The Netherlands ranked second with 10.6 million tonnes worth $5.6 billion, followed by France with 5.6 million tonnes worth $3 billion, Romania with 5.3 million tonnes worth $2.6 billion and Greece with 4.3 million tonnes worth $2.3 billion. Together, the five largest markets accounted for more than 70% of Kazakhstan’s oil exports in both physical and monetary terms.

Other significant destinations included China, which received 3.8 million tonnes worth $2 billion; Türkiye, 2.9 million tonnes worth $1.5 billion; Germany, 2 million tonnes worth $1 billion; Singapore, 1.8 million tonnes worth $763.2 million; and South Korea, 1.5 million tonnes worth $807 million.

CPC remains key export route

The geography of Kazakhstan’s oil exports is closely linked to the country’s transportation infrastructure. The CPC remains the main export route. In 2025, it transported 64.8 million tonnes of Kazakh oil. Kazakhstan also continued exports through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan route at approximately 1.2 million tonnes per year. Azerbaijan has indicated that it is ready to increase its capacity to receive Kazakh oil to 2.2 million tonnes annually.

Diversifying export routes remains important for Kazakhstan as the country seeks to maintain reliable access to international markets.

Oil exports decline in first half of 2026

The export picture changed in the first half of 2026. From January through June, Kazakhstan exported 33 million tonnes of oil, down 6.7% from 35.4 million tonnes during the same period in 2025. Export value fell by a smaller margin, from $19.5 billion to $18.8 billion, or 3.6%. As a result, the average calculated value of an exported tonne increased from nearly $550 to $568.

Oil also accounted for a smaller share of Kazakhstan’s overall export revenue. Its share fell from 52.9% in January-June 2025 to 46.5% in the same period of 2026. At the same time, total exports increased from $36.8 billion to $40.3 billion, indicating a larger contribution from other commodity groups.

Italy remained Kazakhstan’s largest oil market during the first half of 2026, receiving 11.8 million tonnes worth $6.8 billion. The Netherlands followed with 4.4 million tonnes worth $2.5 billion, France with 3.2 million tonnes worth $1.9 billion, Türkiye with 2.1 million tonnes worth $1.3 billion and Greece with 1.9 million tonnes worth $1 billion.

Together, these five markets accounted for 70.9% of exports by volume and 71.8% by value. Other major destinations included Singapore (1.5 million tonnes), Romania (1.4 million tonnes), Spain and China (1.2 million tonnes each), and Germany (1 million tonnes).

Production and OPEC+ commitments

The decline in exports during the first half of 2026 coincided with lower oil production. Kazakhstan produced 45.7 million tonnes of oil during January-June.

At the same time, Tengizchevroil announced in July that it had reached design capacity following the expansion of the Tengiz field, with daily production reaching approximately 120,000 tonnes. The company expects to produce up to 40 million tonnes of oil in 2026.

Production and export levels are also influenced by Kazakhstan’s commitments under OPEC+. At a Sept. 6 meeting, participating countries, including Kazakhstan, agreed to maintain the production levels set for September in October. They also reaffirmed their commitment to complying with existing agreements. The next meeting is scheduled for Oct. 4.

For Kazakhstan, the significance of oil exports ultimately extends beyond the volume of crude sold abroad. Export revenues contribute to public finances through taxation and the National Fund, while oil companies also invest in infrastructure and social projects in producing regions.

As the country seeks to develop processing, petrochemicals and other higher-value industries, the longer-term challenge is to convert its natural-resource revenues into infrastructure, productive assets and human capital that can continue contributing to economic development beyond the period of strong dependence on oil.

World.title: Kazakhstan-Germany Relations Through Lens of Global Instability
World.content:
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s official visit to Germany in September took place in Berlin and Munich and, judging by its formal results, became one of the most productive in the history of bilateral relations. The parties signed more than 30 commercial documents worth approximately $2 billion and adopted a roadmap for industrial, technological and raw materials cooperation for 2026-2028. However, the main news from the visit was what was said about the war in Ukraine.

When it comes to settling the war in Ukraine, Europe and Russia speak different languages. Berlin proceeds from the premise that Russia will not win this war and that support for Ukraine will eventually push Moscow toward serious negotiations. Moscow and much of Eurasia proceed from the opposite premise. Russia cannot be defeated militarily, and therefore continuing the war only multiplies the losses of all sides. Few direct channels remain through which these two narratives could meet. The dialogue between Kazakhstan and Germany has become one of them. Since 2023, Tokayev has discussed the war with German chancellors three times, and each of these conversations has shown where the positions diverge and where room for convergence remains.

2023: Support for the sanctions regime

Since the start of the full-scale war in 2022, high-level contacts between Astana and Berlin have gone through three stages. The first was Tokayev’s official visit to Berlin in September 2023, when Olaf Scholz was chancellor. At the time, the Ukrainian issue was addressed mainly through the lens of sanctions. Following the talks, Tokayev stated that Kazakhstan would comply with the sanctions regime and that the German side should have no concerns about circumvention. Scholz, in turn, expressed hope that Kazakhstan would help ensure Germany’s energy security.

This logic defined the pragmatic foundation of the relationship. Germany gained a reliable supplier of oil and raw materials, while Kazakhstan received a political signal that its multi-vector policy was understood in Berlin. That same year, Kazakh oil began flowing to the Schwedt refinery through the Russian pipeline system.

2024: Russia cannot be defeated militarily

The second stage is linked to Scholz’s visit to Astana in September 2024. It was there that Tokayev made the statement that still shapes how his position is perceived in Europe. He told the chancellor that Russia is militarily invincible and that further escalation would lead to irreparable consequences for all of humanity. Tokayev also endorsed the Chinese-Brazilian peace plan, called the abandonment of the Istanbul agreements a missed opportunity, and proposed halting hostilities first and discussing territorial issues later.

Berlin’s reaction was restrained. Scholz disagreed with his Kazakh counterpart’s assessment and reiterated that Germany supports Kyiv. The joint press conference was cancelled, and the chancellor addressed journalists alone. A month later, at the Astana Think Tank Forum, Tokayev repeated the thesis, citing Russia’s military potential and history, and described the alternative to negotiations as a road to the abyss.

Notably, the economic agenda did not suffer from this disagreement. Germany effectively accepted a model in which political assessments of the war and business cooperation develop in parallel.

2026: A quick end to the war is unrealistic

The third stage came with the current visit. Tokayev’s counterpart was Friedrich Merz, whose position on Ukraine is tougher than his predecessor’s. At the joint press conference on Sept. 29, Merz stated that Russia will not win this war and that Germany supports Ukraine without any reduction. He also identified air defence as Ukraine’s weakest point ahead of the coming winter.

Tokayev presented his position in a new form. He acknowledged that a quick end to the war is unrealistic under current conditions and proposed freezing hostilities in order to then move on to diplomacy. At the same time, he explicitly referred to the need to preserve every country’s territorial integrity and to respect the Ukrainian people, their culture and language. A similar position was included in the joint declaration of Tokayev and Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

The second part of his answer drew a stronger response. Tokayev called Vladimir Putin an outstanding statesman and the most acceptable political figure for Central Asia, Europe and the world, and once again described Russia and Ukraine as good friends of Kazakhstan.

Comparing the two statements reveals one consistent line and one notable change. What has remained consistent is the sequence of steps Astana proposes. A ceasefire comes first, a political settlement second. Tokayev voiced this formula to Scholz in 2024 and repeated it to Merz in 2026, and in July 2026 in Omsk he proposed to Putin freezing the conflict on the basis of the Istanbul agreements. What has changed is the nature of the argument. In 2024, Tokayev spoke about the military balance and effectively offered a forecast of the war’s outcome. In 2026, he speaks about a procedure for exiting it and emphasises territorial integrity, a principle Berlin shares. The formula of Russian invincibility has disappeared from his public remarks in Berlin, although its logic persists in the thesis that a quick peace is unrealistic.

The format of the dialogue has changed as well. In 2024, the disagreement coincided with the cancellation of the planned joint press appearance, reportedly at the initiative of the Kazakh side. In 2026, the leaders held a joint briefing, each set out his position, and this did not prevent the signing of agreements. For relations between a middle power and the EU’s leading economy, this is a sign of maturity. The two sides have learned to record their differences without damaging the shared agenda.

Kazakhstan Affected by a War It Has Nothing to Do With

Tokayev’s position cannot be understood without taking geography into account. In summer 2026, the vulnerability of Kazakh exports became tangible. From 1 May, transit of Kazakh oil to Germany through Russia via the Druzhba pipeline was suspended, even though 2.1 million tonnes were shipped along this route to the Schwedt refinery in 2025 and around 3 million tonnes were planned for 2026. Overall, Kazakhstan supplied Germany with more than 10 million tonnes of oil in 2025. Most of these volumes still pass through Russian territory and ports.

This is why Astana simultaneously complies with sanctions, avoids public confrontation with Moscow and promotes the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR). According to Tokayev, freight volumes on the TITR grew by 22% in the first 8 months of 2026. For Germany, the route means access to Central Asian raw materials bypassing Russia. For Kazakhstan, it means reduced dependence on a single transit partner.

The raw materials component of the visit underlines the same logic. Kazakhstan accounts for about 13% of EU oil imports and 20% of natural uranium supplies, and critical minerals became a central topic of the talks. Trade between the two countries reached 4.5 billion in 2025.

Tokayev’s Berlin formula

Moscow responded to the Berlin statements in its own way. Dmitry Peskov noted that Putin regularly briefs Tokayev on the course of military operations. This is a reminder that Astana’s mediating rhetoric has its limits. Kazakhstan is unlikely to become a negotiating venue in the near future, but it may retain its role as a channel through which European capitals hear Eurasia’s cautious position.

For Germany, Kazakhstan remains a partner that does not share its assessment of the war but fulfills its sanctions obligations and increases raw material supplies. For Kazakhstan, Germany remains its main European partner, ready to accept its multi-vector policy as a given. The invitation to Merz to visit Kazakhstan in 2027, on the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations, will be the next test of this model. If a ceasefire is in place in Ukraine by then, Tokayev’s Berlin formula will acquire a practical dimension. If not, relations between the two countries will continue to rest on oil, metals and logistics, and the conversation about the war will remain a ritual, if unavoidable, part of every meeting.

Visit results and adaptation to new realities

The practical results of the visit show that differences over the war do not slow down the economic agenda. Ahead of the talks, the parties prepared 37 bilateral projects worth EUR 1.8 billion in industry, raw materials processing, energy and logistics. The joint declaration set out a course toward joint production and processing of critical raw materials within Kazakhstan and affirmed the strategic importance of the Trans-Caspian corridor. Recalling that the country produces 21 of 34 types of critical raw materials, Tokayev offered Berlin a joint value chain from geological exploration to component manufacturing and recycling, as well as a shared investment and financial platform. Among the concrete agreements, Linde and Qarmet signed a deal to build an air separation unit in Temirtau, and the Kazakh side agreed to export to Germany railway wheels manufactured on German equipment. At the same time, the US$2 billion figure so far reflects signed documents, and the real test will be financing, construction and the launch of enterprises.

The visit shows how two states at opposite ends of Eurasia are building relations amid a protracted war. Germany and Kazakhstan continue to seek a path to settlement in Eastern Europe while differing in their assessment of its conditions, and in parallel they are reshaping their economic ties to fit the new reality. Berlin needs reliable raw material supplies that bypass Russia and resilient supply chains after the 2022 energy crisis. Astana needs technology, investment and routes that reduce dependence on a single transit neighbour, and the halt of supplies via Druzhba made this need evident. In this model, diplomacy around the war and business cooperation work as two parts of one adaptation strategy. The deeper the mutual economic interest, the more resilient the channel through which Berlin and Astana can discuss the war without putting the partnership itself at risk.

The author is Eldaniz Gusseinov, a co-founder and head of research at Nightingale Int.
