World.title: Tokayev Orders Defense Reforms After Inspection Finds Systemic Failures
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev ordered reforms in Kazakhstan’s Armed Forces after a commission investigating a military incident in the Mangystau Region revealed serious shortcomings in planning, oversight and personal safety, reported the presidential press service on Oct. 5.

Tokayev held a meeting with members of the commission on Oct. 5, where its chair Aida Balayeva, who also serves as a deputy chair of the Security Council, presented the results of the work carried out across the main areas of the inspection.

The meeting noted that the events in the Mangystau Region exposed systemic problems within the Armed Forces. Preliminary findings indicate serious shortcomings in the planning of military activities and inadequate oversight by the previous leadership. The investigation into the circumstances of the tragedy identified deficiencies in the preparation and planning of exercises, risk assessment, organization of troop deployment and ensuring the safety of military personnel.

A pre-trial investigation into alleged criminal negligence by commanders is ongoing. Five officials have been arrested, while a final legal assessment of their actions will be made upon completion of the investigation.

Thirteen criminal cases launched

Law enforcement authorities opened 13 criminal cases during the first stage of the inspection over suspected embezzlement of state property and other alleged violations involving the Ministry of Defense and military units.

The inspection also uncovered lapses in military discipline and preventive work, including reported violence against service members that prompted criminal investigations.

Tokayev stressed that initial personnel decisions have been made and that all officials found responsible for the deaths of military personnel must face legal accountability. He stressed that the incident remains under his personal control.

Defense reforms to focus on modernizing the army

Tokayev instructed the commission and the Defense Ministry to draft proposals to address the shortcomings identified by the inspection. He said the findings should also be taken into account in preparing a broader reform plan for the Armed Forces.

Particular emphasis was placed on building a new-model army capable of effectively responding to modern challenges and threats, including stronger military discipline, improved safety standards and better conditions for service members.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Population Tops 20.6 Million as Astana Passes 1.7 Million
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s population reached 20.62 million as of Sept. 1, while Astana surpassed 1.7 million residents, according to the Bureau of National Statistics.

The capital’s population increased by 9,780 people in August alone and has grown by 61,209 people since the start of the year. Kazakhstan’s total population stood at 20,618,796 people as of Sept. 1, up from 20,499,822 at the beginning of 2026.

Almaty remains the country’s most populous city, with 2,387,896 residents. The population of the city increased by more than 8,000 people in August.

The Turkistan Region ranks second among the country’s most populous regions, with 2,142,709 residents. Unlike Almaty, however, its population declined by more than 2,000 people over the month.

Several other regions and cities also have populations exceeding one million. The Almaty Region had 1,615,631 residents as of Sept. 1, while Shymkent recorded 1,316,888. The Zhambyl Region had 1,210,084 residents and the Karagandy Region 1,130,123.

The country’s least populated region is the Ulytau Region, with 217,274 residents. The North Kazakhstan Region had 510,756 people, while the Abai Region recorded 590,702.

World.title: Tokayev Says Teachers Matter More Than Ever in AI Era
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said teachers are more important than ever as artificial intelligence and digital technologies reshape education, urging Kazakhstan to strengthen human capital and adapting its schools to a rapidly changing world.

“A teacher is a key figure in every person’s life. I believe everyone would agree with this. Deep respect for educators is an important sign that determines the maturity of a civilized society,” Tokayev said at an Oct. 5 ceremony in Akorda marking Teachers’ Day in the country.

“Today, in an era of rapid development of advanced technologies and enormous information flows, the role of the teacher has become more important than ever. This is an undeniable fact,” Tokayev added.

Expanding access to quality education

More than four million schoolchildren make up nearly one-fifth of Kazakhstan’s population, Tokayev said. He stressed that children should have the opportunity to grow up in a safe, developed society.

According to him, the quality of human capital is what determines the strength of an advanced and civilized state. The country’s position in the world and its economic potential, he added, depend directly on the level of education and science.

“I always emphasize in my speeches: both villages and cities should have modern schools that provide children with equal access to quality education,” he said.

Over the past seven years, 1,342 schools have been built in Kazakhstan, providing more than one million student places.

AI to become part of school education

Tokayev said Kazakhstan is implementing a program to introduce AI-based lessons in secondary schools.

“The government should pay particular attention to this extremely important area of work,” he said, stressing that the introduction of new technologies should be carried out systematically.

He said AI could help reduce the administrative burden on teachers and allow them to devote more time to students.

“When used properly, new technologies will significantly facilitate teachers’ work and become a reliable tool that eliminates routine tasks. Teachers should have more time for mentoring and direct work with students,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev said he makes strengthening partnerships with leading universities a priority during his foreign visits. At least 30 branches of foreign universities now operate in the country, including Cardiff University, Coventry University, and universities from the United States, South Korea, Italy, Russia, China and France.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s corruption whistleblowers: protection on paper and in practice
World.content:
Azerbaijan drafts anti-corruption bill

Azerbaijan has drafted a separate bill aimed at encouraging and protecting people who report corruption. The bill was submitted to the Milli Majlis on 5 October and is due to be discussed by a parliamentary committee on 6 October.

The initiative comes amid continuing complaints that police officers demand money from citizens, while journalists investigating corruption are sentenced to lengthy prison terms. Existing legislation already provides protections for people who report corruption. The key question, therefore, is from whom – and how – the state intends to protect citizens after they report such cases.

Protection provided by law

Article 11-2 of the Law on Combating Corruption prohibits disclosing the identity of a person who reports corruption without their consent, as well as threatening them or their relatives. It also prohibits dismissing an employee because they have filed a complaint, transferring them to another position, making unlawful deductions from their salary or obstructing their career progression.

If an employee provides evidence that retaliatory measures have been taken against them, the burden of disproving the allegation falls on the employer. The law also prohibits assigning a complaint for review to the person against whom it was made or to anyone with an interest in the outcome of the investigation.

Information registered through an internal reporting procedure must be examined within 20 working days, after which the person who submitted it must be informed of the outcome. If a complaint concerns the head of an organisation, the person may approach a higher-ranking official or a specialised anti-corruption body. The obligation to investigate reports and inform complainants of the outcome therefore existed before the new bill was introduced.

However, a 2025 report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) points to significant gaps in the implementation of these safeguards. Azerbaijan has no specialised body, unit or official dedicated exclusively to protecting people who report corruption. The authorities were also unable to provide examples of the provision placing the burden on employers to disprove evidence of retaliation being applied in 2023-2024.

The report also notes that public disclosure through the media and social networks is not recognised as a protected channel for reporting corruption. This gap is particularly significant for people who report wrongdoing to journalists rather than to state bodies.

Alleged $300 bribe demand and claim of violence

On 28 August, Gündəlik Naxçıvan reported that a young driver had been detained. According to the outlet, police officers said the driver was under the influence of alcohol. He denied this and said he was willing to undergo a medical examination at a hospital.

Instead of being given a medical examination, he was allegedly asked to pay 500 manats (about $300):

“They told me: either you pay the money now, or they will take both you and the car away.”

According to the outlet, after the driver refused to pay, additional traffic police officers arrived at the scene. Five or six officers allegedly used force against him. Witnesses said the driver suffered a broken arm and ribs as a result.

The complaint therefore concerns not only an alleged demand for a bribe, but also claims that force was used instead of allowing the driver to undergo a medical examination and challenge the allegation against him.

Threats of drug possession and other criminal charges

On 10 September, Gündəlik Naxçıvan published another complaint from residents of Ordubad. People who had returned from Russia said they were taken from their homes and brought to a police station, where they were tested for drugs in a toilet without a doctor present.

One complainant, who asked to remain anonymous, said his test was negative but that he was nevertheless asked to pay 10,000 manats (about $5,882). He said that after being threatened with arrest and torture, he paid 5,000 manats (about $2,941).

Similar allegations have been made in the past. In a Toplum TV report published on 17 December 2025, Shiraz Guliyev, who had returned from Turkey, said he was asked to pay 300 manats (about $176.50) near the Sadarak customs checkpoint on the grounds that he had allegedly dropped a cigarette butt. Guliyev said he told officers that he did not smoke, but was threatened with arrest on charges of resisting police if he refused to pay.

In June 2025, blogger Mehman Huseynov alleged that officers from Baku’s Khatai district police station No 37 beat five teenagers and released them after receiving money from their parents.

Lawyer Khalid Bagirov told Meydan TV that the problem was not the absence of mechanisms for holding officers accountable, but that those mechanisms were not being effectively applied.

What do the official figures show?

The Main Anti-Corruption Directorate under the Prosecutor General’s Office said it reviewed 5,655 complaints in the first half of 2026. A total of 54 criminal cases involving 102 people were sent to court. Of the calls received through the “161” hotline, 4,062 were registered as reports of corruption-related offences.

The figures show that investigations are being carried out. However, the number of cases sent to court does not indicate how effectively people who report corruption are subsequently protected from pressure or retaliation.

This distinction is particularly important in cases involving complaints against the police. A person who complains about an officer with the power to detain them, take them to a police station and formally record offences is seeking more than the return of money. They also need guarantees that those powers will not be used against them in retaliation. Receiving a complaint and protecting the complainant are two separate tasks.

According to an OECD report assessing the situation in 2023-2024, Azerbaijan has made no significant overall progress in combating corruption since 2022. The system for declaring the assets and interests of public officials was not operational, while gaps also remained in declaration forms and procedures for their electronic submission and verification.

In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, Azerbaijan scored 30 out of 100 and ranked 130th out of 182 countries. Despite an eight-point increase compared with the previous year, the score remains low in terms of perceived levels of public-sector corruption.

Arrests of journalists investigating corruption

The authorities’ pledge to protect those who report corruption also contrasts with the situation surrounding the Abzas Media case. On 20 June 2025, seven defendants in the case were sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven years and six months to nine years. They included journalists Ulvi Hasanli, Sevinj Vagifgizi and Hafiz Babali, who had investigated corruption.

The defendants rejected the charges against them. Reporters Without Borders described the sentences as the result of a politically motivated trial aimed at silencing those who expose corruption and injustice.

Against this backdrop, several questions arise: Is a person who reports an alleged demand for a bribe protected from retaliation? Is the alleged offence independently investigated, and are the findings made public? And can a journalist who exposes corruption continue their work without facing the threat of imprisonment?

World.title: Opinion from Yerevan: Baku steps up pressure on Armenia with new tools
World.content:
Opinion on Baku’s tougher rhetoric

Statements by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev should be seen as a “public expression of dissatisfaction with Nikol Pashinyan’s government”, according to political analyst Suren Surenyants.

Speaking at the eighth congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party, Aliyev said, among other things, that the blame should not be placed solely on Armenia’s former leadership.

“It is true that Armenia’s former leaders are war criminals and must be punished, but it was Armenia’s current government that made territorial claims against us and insulted the dignity of the Azerbaijani people with inappropriate and uncivilised statements. We must never forget this,” the president stressed.

Political analyst Suren Surenyants analysed what prompted the recent statements by Aliyev and his aide Hikmet Hajiyev, as well as Azerbaijan’s tougher rhetoric more broadly.

“Baku is effectively signalling that it is dissatisfied with the way Pashinyan is fulfilling his commitments and, if necessary, could use his previous positions and statements as an additional means of exerting pressure,” he said.

‘We would like to make peace not only with the Armenian government, but with the Armenian people’

Against the backdrop of Aliyev’s tough statements, the head of the foreign policy department of the Azerbaijani presidential administration also addressed the peace agenda with Armenia. Speaking at the CAMCA Regional Forum in Baku, he said Azerbaijan intended to build a long-term architecture for peace:

“That is why we always say that we want to make this peace not only with the Armenian government and the country’s prime minister. We want to make peace with the Armenian people. And that is why we continue to expect changes to Armenia’s Constitution. Of course, this is an internal matter, and we fully refrain from interfering in this process.

“We are waiting for just one final step – amendments to Armenia’s Constitution concerning territorial claims against Azerbaijan. After that, I think the final peace agreement will become a reality.”

Baku is demanding amendments to Armenia’s Constitution as a precondition for signing a peace treaty. Azerbaijan argues that the document contains territorial claims. The Constitution itself contains no wording that could give rise to such concerns. However, it refers to the Declaration of Independence, which mentions the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. A draft of Armenia’s new Constitution is currently under discussion. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that it should not contain a reference to the Declaration of Independence. At the same time, he insists that constitutional change is something Armenia itself needs.

Expert commentary

Political analyst Suren Surenyants notes that Armenia is building its entire policy around the peace agenda with Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan, far from softening its rhetoric, has been toughening it in recent months:

“One possible explanation is that Azerbaijan is seeking to consolidate as quickly as possible the political gains resulting from the military advantage it achieved through the war, recognising that the current balance of power will not last forever.”

In his view, this interpretation is also supported by statements from the Azerbaijani president’s aide. In particular, he points to Hikmet Hajiyev’s remarks that a peace treaty will only be signed after Armenia changes its Constitution, despite peace having already been established:

“This is not a contradiction, but a division of labour. One formulation is intended for an international audience, while the other is addressed to Yerevan, reminding it of the need to fulfil its commitments.”

Surenyants also considers the statement about seeking peace not only with the Armenian government but also with the Armenian people noteworthy.

According to him, this means Azerbaijan wants changes in Armenia to acquire “legitimacy enshrined through a referendum and to be made as irreversible as possible”.

The political analyst suggests Baku is in a hurry because the regional balance of power could change, primarily due to the growing Iranian factor:

“If Iran is able to capitalise on its regional influence, a shift in the balance of power in the South Caucasus could limit Baku’s ability to exert pressure on Armenia.”

Surenyants notes that:

Tehran has repeatedly said that any violation of Armenia’s territorial integrity, changes to international borders or alteration of the geopolitical status quo in the region constitute “red lines” for Iran;

Iran is particularly sensitive to the development of transport links through Armenia, viewing them through the prism of its own security and regional influence.

Surenyants argues that the demand for changes to Armenia’s Constitution is taking on additional significance and cannot be seen simply as a “mechanical precondition” for signing a peace treaty.

“Azerbaijan is seeking to achieve its desired outcome within Armenia at both the legal and political levels. And that outcome will not be limited to removing the reference to the Declaration of Independence,” he argues.

The analyst notes that discussions have intensified again in Baku, in particular about the return of Azerbaijanis to “Western Azerbaijan”, by which they mean virtually the entire territory of Armenia. He believes these developments will not end with changes to Armenia’s Constitution and is convinced that Azerbaijan will then present Armenia with a new list of demands:

“Does all this mean that Azerbaijan is preparing for a new military escalation? At present, there is not enough publicly available evidence to draw such a definitive conclusion.”

The political analyst believes Baku has not yet obtained everything it wants from Armenia and is therefore stepping up political pressure. In his assessment, this is driven by concerns that it may become more difficult to secure all its demands in the future:

“And Baku is rushing to get everything it wants while there is a government in Yerevan that regards Baku’s demand for constitutional amendments as part of its own agenda, and before regional developments close the ‘window of opportunity’ for exerting unilateral pressure on Armenia.”

World.title: Russian court fines Abkhaz journalist Nizfa Arshba for violating foreign agent law
World.content:
A court in Vladikavkaz, North Ossetia, Russia, has fined Abkhaz journalist Nizfa Arshba for violating Russia’s foreign agent law. However, no one notified her about the fine. Authorities allegedly sent the notice to an address in Russia where she has never lived.

The court imposed a 30,000 rouble fine [about $353] on 31 August 2026. It ruled that Arshba had “posted material on the social network Facebook without indicating that the material was produced or distributed by a foreign agent, or that it concerned the activities of a foreign agent.”

Nizfa Arshba

Arshba learned about the fine by chance after coming across the information online. The journalist said no one had officially notified her about it.

Opposition journalist Nizfa Arshba, who runs the Telegram channel Aiashara, was added to Russia’s foreign agent register by the Russian Justice Ministry in March 2025, shortly after Abkhazia’s presidential election.

Unlike another Abkhaz journalist, Izida Chania, who also appears on the sanctions list and holds dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, Arshba has only one citizenship — Abkhaz. She has never lived in Russia and has no ties to the country at all.

Under the procedure, Russian citizens, including those listed in the foreign agent register, receive notifications about fines through their personal accounts on the Gosuslugi public services portal. But Nizfa Arshba is neither a Russian citizen nor a resident, so she is not registered on the portal and could not have received notification of the Vladikavkaz court’s decision.

The court’s decision also says that Arshba did not attend the hearing and did not explain why she was absent. At the same time, the court claims that it notified Arshba of the time and place where officials drew up the administrative offence report, as well as the time and place of the hearing. It says authorities sent the notice to her last known place of residence in Russia.

“I would like to know how and by whom my place of residence in Vladikavkaz was assigned to me, given that I have never lived in Russia, never held Russian citizenship and never assumed any obligation to comply with the laws of any foreign state,” Nizfa Arshba wrote on her Telegram channel.

The journalist says she does not intend to pay the fine.

Nizfa Arshba has actively opposed draft laws and Russian-Abkhaz agreements that she believes run counter to Abkhazia’s interests. One example is the controversial bill that would have allowed Russian citizens to build, sell and buy apartments in Abkhazia.

Because of similar positions, two Abkhaz politicians, Kan Kvarчия and Leuan Mikaa, lost their Russian citizenship, while three journalists, including Nizfa Arshba, were added to the foreign agent register.

For Abkhazia’s residents, this label also makes it extremely difficult to travel abroad. Russia remains the most accessible foreign destination for them, and they also have to travel through Russia to reach the wider world. But those labelled foreign agents fear travelling to Russia.

If Arshba violates the foreign agent law again, she could face criminal charges. The local authorities in Abkhazia do not pose any threat to her.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nizfa Arshba fined by Russian court

World.title: All four German political foundations halt work in Georgia; ALDE calls for EU sanctions
World.content:
German foundations close in Georgia

German Ambassador to Georgia Barbara Voss said all four German political foundations that had operated in the country for many years have been forced to close because of restrictions introduced by new legislation, including the Law on Grants.

According to the ambassador, worsening relations between Georgia and Germany have put years of cooperation at risk, including ties in education.

Against this backdrop, the European Liberal, Democrat and Reform Party (ALDE) sent a letter to EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas, calling on the European Union to respond with concrete action.

On 30 September, the Konrad Adenauer Foundation closed its office in Tbilisi. The Georgian office of the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which had worked in the country for 20 years, followed. The Heinrich Böll Foundation and Friedrich Ebert Foundation have also closed their offices.

What the German ambassador said

Barbara Voss, who replaced Peter Fischer as Germany’s ambassador to Georgia in August 2026, said that years of cooperation between the two countries had been seriously damaged.

“All four of our political foundations, which have supported Georgia and its people for decades on their path towards European integration, have been forced to suspend their work following a decision by the Georgian government. Two of the four foundations were forced to close their offices just two days ago,” the ambassador said.

Voss also highlighted Ilia State University, which has long-standing academic ties with Germany and is, according to the ambassador, one of Georgia’s most internationally recognised universities.

She said the university is now at risk of closure.

“These developments are also worsening relations between Georgia and the EU. In the coming years, I personally, as ambassador, will work to preserve what can still be preserved,” Voss said.

The diplomat said Germany would continue to meet its commitments in certain areas, including support for civil society, environmental protection and conservation of natural resources.

The German ambassador also spoke about security cooperation between the two countries. She stressed that Berlin and Tbilisi share common interests and face common challenges in this area.

“Russia is trying to destabilise Europe and divide people through disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression,” Voss said.

She said the Georgian population was well aware of the consequences of Russian military aggression. The ambassador noted that 20% of Georgia’s territory is occupied by Russia and said Moscow’s goal was not to maintain a balance of power but to establish dominance.

According to Voss, Germany continues to support Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as its right to determine its own security policy.

“In this context, we will support cooperation with the Georgian Defence Forces within the NATO framework to further strengthen their defence capabilities against potential aggression and contribute to the security of the South Caucasus and Europe,” the German ambassador said.

“Enough! The Georgian Dream regime is silencing independent voices”

“Enough is enough! The Georgian Dream regime is squeezing out independent voices and pushing Georgia further away from Europe.

After more than 20 years in the country, Friedrich-Naumann-Stiftung für die Freiheit has been forced to close its Tbilisi office because it could no longer operate independently.

ALDE Party President Svenja Hahn and European Liberal Forum President Jan-Christoph Oetjen are calling on the EU to act.

Targeted sanctions against those responsible for repression and the systematic undermining of democracy. No more looking the other way. Our joint letter to Kaja Kallas and Marta Kos,” ALDE said in a social media post.

The letter says the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom was forced to close its Tbilisi office, which had operated in the country for more than two decades, after the Georgian authorities rejected its application for foreign funding.

“The Georgian authorities made it clear that the foundation’s activities would only be permitted if they were aligned with their priorities. Under these conditions, FNF concluded that it could no longer carry out its mission as an independent political foundation,” the letter says.

The letter describes this as “another clear example of the growing restrictions on independent civil society and the wider repression of protesters, opposition figures, journalists and independent voices.”

“These developments show how far the Georgian Dream government is moving away from the standards expected of an EU candidate country and send a worrying signal to all those with European aspirations.

What is happening in Georgia matters not only to its citizens, but also to the credibility of the EU’s enlargement policy and its commitment to democracy and fundamental rights,” the letter says.

The authors again called on the EU to “respond with targeted sanctions against those responsible for the repression and systematic undermining of democracy and fundamental freedoms in Georgia”.

“The EU must ensure that those defending democracy and fundamental freedoms are not left without support,” ALDE said.

“We are not concerned about unfair sanctions” – ruling party representative

“We are not particularly concerned about their [the EU’s] incompetent and completely unfounded sanctions packages, introduced year after year or month after month,” parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtchkhalia said in response to ALDE’s call.

“We should not be surprised by such statements from ALDE or the EU’s political establishment. For years, our country has been subjected to direct and unfair attacks from them.

No package of sanctions can force us to abandon the course chosen at the request of our society. That course is peaceful development, progress and prosperity for every citizen and, above all, the peaceful reunification of our country,” Kirtchkhalia said.

News in Georgia

World.title: Now ruling party leader indefinitely: Ilham Aliyev makes new tough foreign policy statements
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev rejects criticism from Turkey

At the eighth congress of the Yeni Azerbaijan Party, held in Baku on 2 October, the party abolished the five-year term limit for its chairperson. The leader – currently Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev – will now remain in the post indefinitely.

In his speech, Aliyev placed particular emphasis on claims that Azerbaijan achieved its military victories in the Second Karabakh War and the subsequent operation entirely on its own.

The president said no outside assistance had been provided to Azerbaijan and that all weapons had been purchased through regular channels.

The remarks came amid criticism in Turkish media after Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the UN General Assembly hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech on 24 September, unlike delegations from many countries that walked out in protest over Israel’s military operation in Gaza.

The ruling party leader can now remain in office indefinitely

According to the state-run APA news agency, the party’s congress removed a provision from its statutes that limited the chairman’s term to five years.

Nizami Safarov, who presented the amendment, justified the removal of the limit by pointing to the victories achieved under Aliyev’s leadership. He called Aliyev the “leader of Azerbaijan’s unprecedented victories” and said he considered the decision in line with the country’s political and legal realities.

According to Safarov, Aliyev’s indefinite leadership “will lead the party to new successes and greater victories”.

The change removes the requirement to re-elect the chairman after a set period. However, this does not mean that elections for party chairman will never be held again or that Aliyev will not take part in future party congresses.

The change concerns the party leadership and does not affect the procedure for electing the country’s president.

Politically, the change means there is no longer a mechanism for the party chairman’s mandate to be periodically renewed.

Role of Turkey in the Second Karabakh War: Aliyev denies any outside help for Azerbaijan

“We are shaping our foreign policy, and we must continue to do so in a way that prevents anyone from interfering in our affairs. We do not need anyone’s help or anyone’s protection.

When we needed help, no one helped us. When we had one million refugees, no one reached out to us. Everything we received, we bought with our own money. This includes all the weapons we acquired, paying world market prices down to the last bullet.

I am telling you this with full responsibility, as supreme commander-in-chief and as the person who oversaw all these processes. You know how much Azerbaijan strengthened its military capabilities since 2003: we developed our own production and bought weapons abroad.

Not once were we given a discount of even one manat or one dollar. In fact, sometimes weapons were sold to us at several times the world market price. We had to turn a blind eye to this. So this is a very serious issue.” […]

“Our advantage is that, unlike some countries, we do not need to create myths. In some countries, certain leaders try to take credit for past achievements or exaggerate their own role by distorting history. We do not need that,” Aliyev said.

In another notable part of his speech, Aliyev accused some leaders of trying to take credit for past achievements and “exaggerate their own role”.

Although he did not say whom he meant, social media users and experts have suggested that he was referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

From a political perspective, the remarks appear to downplay any role played by Turkey or other external actors in Azerbaijan’s military success during the Second Karabakh War.

Aliyev’s remarks have a specific historical context when viewed against Turkey-Azerbaijan relations.

On 28 July 2024, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, speaking in Rize about Israel, said: “Just as we entered Karabakh, just as we entered Libya, we can do the same to them.”

The Karabakh victory was therefore used in political speeches as an example of Turkey’s regional power even before the current debate over Azerbaijan’s position at the UN.

The earlier position of Aliyev himself is also important.

On 19 February 2024, speaking in Ankara, he said Turkey had stood by Azerbaijan throughout the war, and that Erdoğan’s initial statements had deterred other powers from intervening. In the same speech, Aliyev spoke about joint military exercises and the adoption of the Turkish army model in Azerbaijan.

Turkey’s support during the war could later have become a political and moral basis for expecting solidarity from Baku on other issues, including Israel. Ankara has not officially made such demands so far.

From this perspective, Aliyev’s remarks can be seen not so much as a denial of Turkey’s support, but as a rejection of the idea that such support creates political obligations: being allies does not mean that Baku has to coordinate all its foreign policy decisions with Ankara.

Why did Azerbaijan’s position during Netanyahu’s UN speech spark debate?

On 24 September, when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the UN General Assembly, several delegations, including Turkey’s, walked out. Turkish newspaper Sözcü and other media outlets specifically pointed out that the Azerbaijani representative remained in the hall.

Musavat.com reported that the man seen in photographs was Maksad Huseynov, first secretary at Azerbaijan’s permanent mission to the UN. Official materials from the mission also list Huseynov as first secretary.

The debate was further fuelled by the fact that, in the same speech, Netanyahu called Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan a “tyrant”.

For Turkish audiences, the issue was therefore about both Azerbaijan’s position on the war in Gaza and the presence of an Azerbaijani diplomat during a speech that included criticism of the Turkish president.

Turkish media reported that Azerbaijan’s position caused “great disappointment”.

However, these reports should not be considered an official protest by the Turkish government against Azerbaijan.

Baku-Tehran: Aliyev accuses Azerbaijani-language media of ‘provocations’

Many analysts believe that part of Ilham Aliyev’s speech about attempts to exert ideological influence through Azerbaijani-language media abroad was aimed at Iran.

Aliyev accused media outlets operating “in our neighbourhood” of provoking Azerbaijan.

“Why is an Azerbaijani-language media outlet created in another country? To help us? No, it is created to provoke us. To mislead our people. To poison the minds of young people. That is why.

If you see an Azerbaijani-language media outlet appearing somewhere, know that this is its purpose.

You don’t have to look far for examples. In our neighbourhood, provocations against us are being carried out day and night in the Azerbaijani language,” Aliyev said.

Such disagreements coexist with economic cooperation between Baku and Tehran.

Analysts therefore say this strong rhetoric should not automatically be seen as a sign of a diplomatic break.

The possible message behind these statements is that economic cooperation does not mean accepting ideological or political interference.

Aliyev also criticised Azerbaijani-language platforms in Western countries:

“Take Western countries. Azerbaijani-language media outlets have also been created there. Why? To undermine unity in the country, bring Azerbaijan under their control, force us to abandon our path of independence and then control us,” the president said.

Much of his speech was likely also aimed at a domestic audience. Aliyev called on members of the ruling party to step up their ideological work.

News in Azerbaijan

World.title: Two German foundations shut down in Georgia amid government restrictions
World.content:
German foundations, including the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, have ended their activities in Georgia after more than 20 years of work in the country.

Both organisations say the conditions set by the Georgian government under new legislation, known as the “Grants Law”, have made it impossible for them to implement projects and continue their activities.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said foreign political parties and foundations affiliated with them should not pursue political goals in Georgia.

What the foundations say

The Tbilisi offices of both foundations closed on 30 September 2026. In statements published on 2 October, the organisations said the Georgian government’s decision to reject their grant applications had limited their ability to continue working in the country.

The Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which has operated in Georgia since 2002, said it had applied under the new law on foreign funding and grants so it could continue funding projects and working with local partners. However, the foundation said the authorities required every component of its programme to align with state priorities and required it to obtain the necessary permits for all activities.

“It was not easy for us to take this step, but it was inevitable. The actions of the Georgian government make it impossible for the foundation to continue its activities in the country,” the organisation said.

According to the foundation, the authorities rejected its application on 28 July 2026. The organisation said that under the circumstances, it no longer saw a way to continue working in line with its values and principles.

The Friedrich Naumann Foundation worked in Georgia to support liberal ideas, an open society, the country’s European future and dialogue between societies. The organisation said it would continue to support Georgian citizens who are fighting for a free and democratic system in the country.

The Konrad Adenauer Foundation also said that the closure of its office in Tbilisi was not a voluntary decision but resulted from the political and legal conditions created by the Georgian government.

“The closure of our office in Tbilisi is a direct consequence of the political and legal framework established by the Georgian government, under which the foundation can no longer fulfil its core mission as a political foundation on the ground,” the organisation said.

According to the foundation, the government rejected its project funding applications on 28 July. The organisation said it had made active efforts, including with the involvement of the German federal government, to preserve the possibility of continuing its work, but those efforts failed.

The foundation said project approval appeared possible only if the projects no longer reflected the foundation’s political nature and mission. It also stressed that maintaining a physical presence in Georgia without the ability to carry out its core activities was not an acceptable option.

The Konrad Adenauer Foundation has operated in Georgia since 2003. Its work has focused on promoting democracy and the rule of law, developing parliamentarianism, strengthening German-Georgian relations and supporting Georgia’s European integration. The organisation has also supported young researchers and students through scholarships and educational programmes.

The foundation said it would retain its legal entity status in Georgia so that it could return to the country if the political situation changes.

Both organisations said they would maintain ties with Georgia and their local partners, and attributed the suspension of their activities solely to the restrictions introduced under the new legislation.

Shalva Papuashvili’s comment

In response to the Konrad Adenauer Foundation’s statement, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said foreign political parties and organisations affiliated with them should not pursue political missions in Georgia.

“In their statement, they [the foundations] say that they have a political mission and that, since they can no longer carry it out, they see no reason to remain in the country. This is somewhat surprising.

As we know, political foundations are affiliated with political parties. The Adenauer Foundation, for example, is affiliated with the Christian Democratic Union. Let me remind you that the Christian Democratic Union is part of the EPP and, therefore, is a partner party of the United National Movement. Yet it says it wants to carry out a political mission in Georgia. In my view, foreign political parties and their foundations have no political mission to carry out in Georgia,” Papuashvili said.

He said the government had explained to the Adenauer Foundation that, to approve its grant projects, it needed to exclude projects of a political nature. Activities in academic, educational and other fields could receive approval, he said.

“However, judging by their statement, they apparently have no interest in academic, educational or other similar activities. As their own statement makes clear, they were interested in carrying out a political mission, and they are leaving because they can no longer do so. The decision is theirs,” the parliament speaker said.

Papuashvili, who is now criticising the German foundation, himself worked for German organisations for many years. From 2003 to 2007, he served as a senior legal expert at the German Technical Cooperation Society (GTZ). From 2007 to 2020, he headed the organisation’s office in Georgia.

Comment

Historian and Ilia State University professor Beka Kobakhidze commented on the closure of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation’s office in Georgia. He noted that for many years the foundation had provided scholarships to top students and created a wide range of opportunities for them.

Beka Kobakhidze: “I constantly see posts from my students thanking the Konrad Adenauer Foundation.

Do you know how Georgian master’s students live? They have to work all day to pay for housing, food and transport. Then they have to make it to a lecture at 7 p.m., attend until 9 p.m., return home by 10 p.m., eat and study. In these circumstances, quality education often remains disconnected from real-life conditions. We launched the master’s programme in the history of modern Georgia in 2020, and from day one, the foundation provided scholarships to the top students in our programme. This financial support helped them with their studies and helped us maintain a high standard of education.

The Adenauer Foundation is a right-leaning organisation, but they never once said, ‘Let’s give scholarships to students with right-wing views and not to those on the left.’ Many left-wing students received these scholarships. They never told us what or how to teach. They placed their full trust in us and gave us complete academic freedom, while we awarded scholarships based on meritocratic principles. At the end of each semester, we reviewed academic performance, and the top two or three students received scholarships.

It is impossible to count how many international conferences our students attended thanks to funding from the foundation. These opportunities deepened their knowledge, and that knowledge led to numerous achievements: Tsinandali Awards, numerous awards from the FaRiG Foundation, books by our graduates that became bestsellers at book fairs, participation in international research projects, admission to doctoral programmes, and jobs as university lecturers. And the list could go on indefinitely. The Adenauer Foundation laid the foundation for all of this.

I am immensely grateful to the foundation’s staff, who have now become close friends of mine, and whom I met through our joint work.

As of 1 October 2026, the foundation has ceased its activities in Georgia. Do you know the background? The Adenauer Foundation was expelled from Russia in 2022.”

What does the so-called “Grants Law” provide?

A package of laws adopted on 4 March 2026 significantly expanded the definition of a “grant”. It now covers both financial and non-financial support if such support could be used to influence domestic or foreign policy, including activities linked to the interests of a foreign state or political force.

The law also strengthens the State Audit Office’s oversight of grants. When a foreign legal entity provides funding to a branch operating in Georgia without government approval, the authorities can impose sanctions, including a fine equal to twice the value of the grant.

Violations of grant legislation can also lead to criminal liability. The penalties include fines, community service or imprisonment for up to six years.

The amendments also affect the political process. People who work primarily for organisations funded by foreign sources cannot join political parties for eight years. Moreover, restrictions imposed on political parties also apply to structures that are not formally parties but effectively engage in political activity.

The legislative package also tightens administrative liability for private companies that engage in public political activities.

One of the most controversial aspects of the amendments involves new provisions added to the Criminal Code that expand the definition of “extremism”. Under the new article, public calls for actions directed against the constitutional order — including calls to disobey the authorities or establish alternative structures — may constitute criminal offences.

In addition, authorities classify crimes committed on the grounds of refusing to recognise constitutional state bodies as offences committed under aggravating circumstances. This increases the sentence by at least one year.

Experts say such wording allows for broad interpretation and increases the risk that the law could be used against dissent and critical activity.

Two German foundations shut down in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijani soldier enters Armenia, fires at local residents
World.content:
Azerbaijani soldier shot an Armenian resident

On 1 October, an Azerbaijani soldier entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. He shot a 39-year-old local woman in the leg with an assault rifle. The incident happened in front of her three children, two of whom also suffered injuries.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has opened a criminal case against Nasim Musayev.

The Armenian National Security Service issued a brief statement only after people began discussing the incident on social media. It emerged that Azerbaijan’s State Security Service had informed its Armenian counterparts on 29 September that a serviceman had left his unit under unknown circumstances.

“Authorities could not rule out the possibility that he had illegally crossed into Armenia. The competent authorities of Armenia and Azerbaijan then launched search operations,” the statement said.

According to Azerbaijani law enforcement authorities, Nasim Musayev went missing on 26 September.

It remains unclear when he entered Armenian territory. Authorities found and detained him only after he committed the crime.

Armenian analysts point to previous similar cases in which Azerbaijanis who illegally crossed the border and committed crimes went back to Azerbaijan. They expect authorities to punish the Azerbaijani serviceman to the full extent of the law this time as well. If Armenian authorities decide to return him to Azerbaijan, they suggest taking into account the fact that 19 Armenian prisoners remain in Baku’s jails.

The incident has sparked outrage in Armenian society and prompted widespread discussion on social media. Against the backdrop of repeated statements by the authorities that peace has arrived, users commented on the incident with the short phrase: “Long live peace.”

Witness accounts

“My brother and sister came home from their classes and saw that the window was broken. They called our mother. She and our father came by car. My mother had a knife in her hand. She always kept it with her in case something like this happened, so she could protect herself. My mother went inside and stabbed him with the knife. The man then fired a shot and ran away,” the injured woman’s son told a local media outlet.

Meanwhile, her sister said the Azerbaijani man took the children hostage, while their mother, who tried to protect them, lost three fingers on her left hand.

In an interview with Radio Azatutyun (Freedom), she said her sister’s two children were talking to their parents on the phone as they walked home from school. They then saw that the lock on their front door had been broken. When they entered the house, they saw an Azerbaijani soldier in the living room. They tried to call their mother for help, but the Azerbaijani man took their phone away.

According to the injured woman’s sister, the Azerbaijani man was pointing his weapon at the children when their mother entered the house. She tried to cover the barrel with her hand. Musayev then fired, causing her to lose fingers on her left hand.

The sister also said the injured woman had to defend herself. While the soldier tried to reload his rifle, she stabbed him several times. However, the soldier struck her and knocked her unconscious. Her 15-year-old son then fought with the Azerbaijani man and suffered a broken arm.

The health of the mother and children

The woman suffered gunshot wounds to her thigh and arm. She first received medical treatment at a medical centre in Sisian and then went to a clinic in Yerevan.

According to reports, her life is not in danger and her condition remains stable. However, she needs surgery.

The woman’s 15-year-old and 12-year-old sons also suffered injuries.

“The child born in 2014 has soft-tissue bruising, while the child born in 2011 has a fracture of the right wrist.”

Doctors put a cast on the boy with the fracture. The other boy needed psychological support.

Information from Yerevan and Baku

There is little official information about the incident.

The Armenian National Security Service initially issued a statement:

“At 14:15 on 1 October, the 112 emergency centre of the Interior Ministry received a report that an Armenian citizen had suffered a gunshot wound to the leg in the settlement of Shaki in Syunik Province. Operational teams from various police units went to the scene. They took urgent measures to establish all the circumstances of the incident. They established that an Azerbaijani serviceman had committed the crime and detained him.”

Armenian authorities reportedly passed details of the incident to the Azerbaijani side.

Baku provided information about the serviceman who crossed the border only after the incident in Shaki.

According to Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office, Nasim Musayev went missing from his military unit in Lachin on 26 September. Authorities opened a criminal case over his disappearance. The investigation confirmed suspicions that Musayev had left the military unit voluntarily.

“As a result of the measures taken, authorities established that Nasimi Musayev was in Armenia and that the relevant authorities of that country had detained him,” Azerbaijani law enforcement authorities said.

They also stressed that they were working with their Armenian counterparts to establish the details of the incident.

Criminal cases opened

Armenia’s Prosecutor General’s Office announced yesterday that it had opened a criminal case under charges of “causing serious bodily harm with the use of a weapon”, “illegal possession of a firearm” and “violation of the inviolability of a home”.

The omission of the illegal border crossing from the statement sparked outrage in Armenia.

Today, the authorities said they had added charges of illegally crossing the border and smuggling a firearm.

Analysts’ views

Political analyst Suren Surenyants highlighted the fact that the Armenian side received information about a possible border violation at least two days before the incident:

“It is worrying that, despite the warning and the announced search, authorities found Musayev in Shaki only after he used a firearm against an Armenian citizen. The search operations did not prevent him from potentially crossing the border illegally, entering Shaki or opening fire.”

According to Surenyants, the authorities need to clarify the following:

how the Azerbaijani serviceman crossed the state border and travelled from Lachin to Shaki,

where he entered Armenian territory, how he bypassed border controls and security systems,

why authorities failed to find him either within two days of the warning or roughly five days after he disappeared,

what legal procedures await the Azerbaijani serviceman?

“Authorities have already opened a criminal case. The next question is whether they will bring the case to its legal conclusion, meaning conduct a full investigation into the circumstances of the illegal border crossing and the use of a weapon against an Armenian citizen, or whether political agreements will determine the case,” he stressed.

The political analyst also expects answers to the following questions:

if Armenia considers handing Musayev over to Azerbaijan, will it raise the issue of returning Armenian prisoners held in Baku?

what legal and political conditions could determine such a decision?

Surenyants noted that, more broadly, the incident exposed the lack of effective border control in Armenia.

Azerbaijan expert Tatevik Hayrapetyan suggested viewing the events in Shaki in the context of previous cases. She recalled:

in 2019, Armenian authorities, with the support of the International Committee of the Red Cross, returned Elvin Ibrahimov to Azerbaijan after he illegally crossed Armenia’s state border. They described the decision as a “humanitarian step”.

in 2023, Azerbaijan also received Huseyn Akhundov, who killed 56-year-old Hayrapet Meliksetyan in Armenia and received a 20-year prison sentence.

Tatevik Hayrapetyan stressed that Armenia should rule out a similar approach in this case:

“An attack on the life and safety of an Armenian citizen cannot lead to the return of the perpetrator to Azerbaijan under ‘humanitarian’ pretexts. The authorities must investigate this case to the full extent of the law. If they establish his guilt, the perpetrator must serve the sentence prescribed by law.”

Comments on social media

“The incident involving the Azerbaijani soldier has once again shown the situation at the border. It is a good thing he came alone. He could have come with an entire army, and we would have greeted them with a large ‘Welcome to Armenia’ banner.”

“It turns out that an armed man can cross the state border unhindered, move around for several days, reach a settlement and harm a civilian. This, in turn, means that once again, the citizen has been left alone to fight for his own safety.”

“Peace means that, in ‘peacetime’, an Azerbaijani soldier cannot show up at your home and harm you in front of your children. By 29 September, authorities already knew that an Azerbaijani soldier had left his military unit, and the Armenian side had received information about it. Where was state control once authorities learned that the soldier had left his unit? What measures did they take to prevent him from entering Armenian territory? Where was the government that promised ‘peace’ during the recent election campaign?”

Azerbaijani soldier shot an Armenian resident

World.title: Prisoner in Georgia accuses guards of sexual abuse. Penitentiary Service denies allegations
World.content:
Prison violence in Georgia

Prisoner Giorgi Davitadze said staff at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi subjected him to sexual abuse. He says the incident took place on 21 December 2025, when staff moved him to a de-escalation cell. According to Davitadze, ten people attacked him there.

The Special Penitentiary Service denied the allegations. It said its video of the incident shows no signs of violence.

What happened?

TV channel Pirveli published an audio recording of testimony Davitadze gave at the Court of Appeals. According to the prisoner, the alleged abuse took place within view of surveillance cameras. However, he says the staff positioned themselves in a way that prevented the cameras from fully capturing their actions.

“They took me to a de-escalation cell and raped me with their fingers and hands. […] Ten men raped me; a guard was also present, and the whole thing is visible on camera,” Davitadze said during the hearing.

The prisoner claims that staff subjected him to pressure after he demanded a forensic medical examination. He told the court that he had tried to take his own life because he could no longer bear staying near the same staff members he accuses of abuse.

Davitadze also said staff verbally abused him in the de-escalation cell. “I tell the man, ‘I was raped.’ And the representative of the Public Defender’s Office simply lowers his head,” he said. He questioned why the verbal abuse he described to the court could not be heard on the camera recordings.

Davitadze told the judges that he would go on hunger strike unless the guards involved in the incident faced prosecution. The judges asked representatives of the service whether an investigation had begun. The prosecutor confirmed that an investigation into the incident was under way.

What does the Penitentiary Service say?

According to the Special Penitentiary Service, video footage shows that Davitadze refused to undergo a mandatory search while staff were moving him to a de-escalation cell and insulted prison staff. The service says staff later conducted a forced search using a handheld metal detector as part of their official duties.

“No violence was used against Davitadze — let alone any sexual abuse,” the Penitentiary Service said.

The service explained that it had previously refrained from publishing the footage because authorities were investigating the incident. It did not want anyone to interpret the release as an attempt to put pressure on the investigation. The service said it decided to publish the footage because of the strong public reaction and what it described as deliberate attempts by the prisoner’s family to discredit the institution.

The Penitentiary Service also said it had archived continuous video footage of Davitadze’s movements around the facility from 3 March 2026 to the present. According to the service, it can provide these recordings to all interested parties in accordance with the law.

What does Davitadze’s family say?

Irma Davitadze, Giorgi’s mother, is calling for not only the guards involved in the incident but also Shota Trapaidze, head of Prison No. 6, to face prosecution. She said the family would continue its fight until those responsible for the abuse receive punishment. In particular, she mentioned prison employee Giorgi Kvaratskhelia, whom she alleges has links to the use of violence against prisoners.

According to Irma Davitadze, the family has also collected information about possible violations that occurred at the facility in the past. The Penitentiary Service rejects these allegations, saying investigators and a representative of the Public Defender’s Office have already examined the video footage and found no signs of a crime.

Giorgi Davitadze is the son of Avtandil Davitadze, a former member of the Tbilisi City Council. Avtandil Davitadze joined the city council in 2014 on the Georgian Dream coalition list and served in the Georgian Dream–National Forum faction.

Prison violence in Georgia

World.title: Oman eyes trade corridor through its ports with Kazakhstan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. Oman is looking to expand trade cooperation with Kazakhstan through a corridor running via Omani ports, Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said said following expanded-format talks with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in Astana, according to the presidential press service.

Thanking Tokayev for the hospitality and the talks, the Sultan noted the steady development of comprehensive cooperation between the two countries.

"Oman attaches great importance to cooperation with Kazakhstan. We welcome the momentum that bilateral cooperation has gained in recent years. Exchanges of high-level visits and the work of the Joint Intergovernmental Commission have created a solid foundation that will allow us to reach a more ambitious level of cooperation," Sultan Haitham said.

According to the Sultan, Oman sees significant opportunities for growth, investment and cooperation with Kazakhstan across several sectors, including energy and mining, agriculture and food security, transport and logistics, financial services, tourism, and technology and artificial intelligence.

"We welcome the implementation of projects bringing together our sovereign investment institutions, the private sector and specialized government structures. Transport connectivity is another area of significant importance. Kazakhstan occupies a strategic position along the main global trade corridors connecting Asia and Europe, while Oman provides direct maritime access to key markets in the Persian Gulf, the Indian Ocean, Asia and Africa. Leveraging these complementary advantages opens up significant opportunities for growth and represents great value for both countries. We therefore look forward to developing cooperation in transport and logistics, including the development of a trade corridor through Omani ports, as well as strengthening air connectivity between our countries," the Sultan said.

He invited Tokayev to visit Oman at a time convenient for him.

During the expanded-format talks, Tokayev welcomed the Sultan to Kazakhstan, noting it was his first visit to Central Asia as head of state.

"We view Oman as a time-tested and reliable partner of Kazakhstan in the Arab world. Next year we will proudly mark a significant milestone — the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and Oman," Tokayev said, pointing to a recent visit to Astana by a high-level Omani delegation led by Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs Sayyid Theyazin bin Haitham Al Said as evidence of deepening synergy between the two countries.

Tokayev said the two sides would sign a significant package of bilateral agreements covering energy, transport and logistics, agriculture, information technology and digitalization, healthcare and other areas, along with a joint statement outlining priority areas of partnership.

The Kazakh leader also highlighted progress on a number of joint projects, including development of the Dunga oil field, Solidcore Resources' operations in the Pavlodar and North Kazakhstan regions, a joint investment fund with the Oman Investment Authority, and the development of hotel and resort infrastructure.

World.title: Germany ready to support Azerbaijan’s green energy export projects – official (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. Germany is ready to support Azerbaijan's green energy export projects, Deputy Director General at the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWi), Gerlind Heckmann, told Trend in an exclusive interview on Tuesday on the sidelines of the German-Azerbaijani Strategic Partnership and Connectivity Conference in Baku.

According to him, Germany sees great potential for the further development of bilateral economic relations with Azerbaijan, particularly cooperation in the energy sector, in the coming years.

He said that it is essential for the business community to develop concrete, structured, and economically viable projects to further expand economic ties.

"As the German government, we are pleased to support German companies operating in or exporting to Azerbaijan on a long-term basis, including by providing long-term export credits. We also collaborate with multilateral development banks to structure projects and financing packages aimed at funding specific initiatives and supporting businesses in both countries," Heckmann pointed out.

According to the official, the renewable energy sector holds great potential for Azerbaijan.

"Azerbaijan possesses significant potential for exploration and implementation in the renewable energy sector. Once concrete projects take shape in this area, the German government stands ready to support their realization," he explained.

Heckmann also spoke about Azerbaijan's plans to export green energy to Europe. He noted that the phased establishment of a "green corridor" is one of the key issues in this regard.

"If specific projects are identified, we can support them concretely and thereby contribute to their realization. I believe this is a process that takes time. It will not happen overnight, and we need to be somewhat patient. It is necessary to systematically examine and develop the entire structure of the 'Green Corridor'," Heckmann underscored.

The deputy minister stated that he considers the current period favorable for the development of German-Azerbaijani economic relations.

"Now is a good time to establish connections with businesses in both countries. I am optimistic. Positive developments are currently being observed in bilateral relations, and the political statements made this year have created a positive atmosphere," he noted.

Heckmann said that the sustainability of political relations and the long-term nature of the results achieved depend on economic substance.

"The sustainability of these relations naturally depends on economic substance. That is precisely what we need. For instance, the goal of the newly established German-Azerbaijani Business Council is to structure the economic dialogue more systematically. A bilateral political working group has been active for years, but now we want to focus more on economic substance on both sides," he mentioned.

According to him, the opportunities for cooperation between the two countries are quite extensive.

"There are broad opportunities for cooperation in infrastructure, transport, energy, agriculture, and other sectors. Germany's experience could be significant in all these areas. The German economy could seek to participate in the comprehensive and transformative processes underway in Azerbaijan," Heckmann added.

He also stressed that the peace process in the region would have a positive impact on economic development.

"Peace contributes to positive economic development in the region. For decades, conflict shaped the region's political and economic realities. Now, however, this landscape is beginning to change, and that is a very positive development," Heckmann said.

The official noted that ensuring lasting peace in the region is in the interest not only of the regional countries but also of Europe and Germany.

"This will enable the creation of new transport links, the exploration and development of new markets, and allow investors to make long-term plans. I believe this is precisely what we all need," Heckmann emphasized
