World.title: KazMunayGas digital twin targets 2.9m tons of extra oil by 2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. The scaling up of KazMunayGas' Digital Twin project is expected to generate 2.9 million tons of additional oil production by 2030, Chairman of the Management Board of KazMunayGas JSC Askhat Khassenov said at a government meeting.

This was announced by the press service of the Kazakh government.

“The scaling up of the Digital Twin will cover the top 12 fields, which account for about 90% of production. The expected effect from the implementation of the project by 2030 will amount to 2.9 million tons of additional production,” Khassenov said.

The first digital twin project using artificial intelligence has been implemented at the East Moldabek field, which has oil reserves of about 14.8 million tons, while the share of reserves developed for production stood at 36.7%.

According to Khassenov, a digital reservoir model using AI algorithms calculated more than 600 development scenarios in six days, compared with more than a month previously.

The modeling helped optimize drilling. Instead of the six vertical wells initially planned, the system determined that two horizontal wells should be drilled.

The optimization generated an economic effect of 640 million tenge ($1.41 million) and increased oil production by 45%, Khassenov said.

“Previously, such decisions were made based on a limited set of scenarios selected analytically in different systems. With the use of the Digital Twin, we see the potential to obtain additional oil production of 161,000 tons at this field, which is equivalent to about 16 billion tenge ($35.17 million),” Khassenov said.

A digital well for online drilling monitoring and digital production using intelligent control stations has also been introduced at the field.

These solutions reduce production losses by up to 5% and labor costs by up to 15%, according to Khassenov.

The exchange rate used by Trend is $1 = 454.98 tenge.

World.title: Azerbaijan plans 11 new power facilities in Zira by end-2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. Eleven new power generation facilities are planned to be built in the service area of the Electricity Supply and Distribution Authority in Zira by the end of 2026.

This was reflected in a report by Azerishig OJSC.

According to the report, five of the centers have already been fully installed and are ready for grid connection. The work aims to ensure a reliable, high-quality electricity supply for subscribers and to reduce energy losses.

As part of the reconstruction efforts, a new 250 kVA packaged transformer substation has been installed in the Khashakhuna Gardens residential area of Gala settlement. Work in the area includes laying 6 kV underground cable lines and 0.4 kV self-supporting insulated conductors, as well as replacing utility poles.

The electrical grid is also being reconstructed in several residential areas of Turkan settlement, where transformer substations of various capacities are being installed, and electricity meters are being replaced.

The project also covers the Pirallahi and Dubandi settlements. In Pirallahi, new SMS-enabled meters have been installed, and modern power supply facilities have been established.

World.title: Germany may back Azerbaijan projects with export credit financing
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. Germany may provide support in securing financing through export credits for long-term investment projects that Azerbaijan plans to implement in the areas of infrastructure, energy, and economic diversification, the Deputy Director General of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE), Gerlind Heckmann, said, Trend's correspondent reports.

She made the statement at the German-Azerbaijani Connectivity Conference in Baku on Tuesday

According to her, Germany has implemented reforms aimed at adapting its export credit support system to the realities of modern global value chains, strengthening the competitiveness of German companies and exporters, and increasing the attractiveness of German export credit guarantees for international buyers and financing partners.

“International supply chains are becoming increasingly complex and integrated. At the same time, competition among exporting countries has intensified significantly. Therefore, the modernization package is designed to ensure that German export financing remains a competitive and relevant tool for both exporters and borrowers,” she said.

Gerlind Heckmann noted that two key measures are particularly important within the reform package. One of them is the “Flex & Cover” mechanism.

“Traditionally, eligibility for German export credit guarantees has been closely tied to the share of German components in individual export contracts. However, this approach does not always reflect how companies operating on a global scale function today. Under ‘Flex & Cover,’ we consider a company’s economic activity in Germany in a broader sense. Factors such as employment, investment, and value added are taken into account,” Heckmann emphasized.

According to her, this approach allows German exporters to organize their international supply chains more flexibly while still benefiting from state support for export credits.

“At the same time, domestic buyers also benefit, as the complexity of managing purchases from multiple sources is significantly reduced,” she added.

Another important mechanism, according to the ministry representative, is “Shopping Line Cover.” She explained that this tool allows buyers and lending banks to create a financial structure that can then be used to make purchases from multiple German suppliers.

“For borrowers, this makes procurement more flexible and efficient, especially in the case of large-scale investment programs that require technology, equipment, and services from several German companies rather than from a single exporter,” Heckmann said.

She noted that the main advantage of government support for export credits for international buyers lies not only in the guarantee itself, but also in the long-term financing opportunities it creates.

“Today, many borrowers have access to various sources of financing. However, the more challenging task is securing long-term financing with repayment terms that match the economic life of the investment. This is precisely where financing backed by export credit guarantees can create significant added value,” she emphasized.

According to Heckmann, the financing term in the German export credit system can be up to 15 years, and in some sectors, up to 22 years. These opportunities are combined with attractive financing terms and a predictable repayment schedule.

“For capital-intensive investments, such as renewable energy, infrastructure, transportation, and industrial development, this can be a decisive advantage over market-based financing sources, which offer significantly shorter terms and repayment periods,” Heckmann said.

Citing Türkiye as an example, she noted that German financing, backed by export credits, had facilitated the implementation of major investment projects in that country, where long-term funding is a key requirement.

“The combination of German technology with competitive financing terms and payment terms suited to the long-term economic characteristics of infrastructure projects has proven very attractive to borrowers and project sponsors. Today, we can say that Türkiye is one of the most important markets in our export credit guarantee portfolio,” she said.

Heckmann emphasized that Azerbaijan also has similar potential.

“Azerbaijan has ambitious plans in areas such as infrastructure, energy, and economic diversification. Although financing can be obtained from various sources, financing backed by export credit guarantees can serve as a valuable additional tool, offering longer terms, greater financial security, and a financing structure suitable for long-term investment projects,” the German official said.

According to her, the reforms implemented are increasing the flexibility and competitiveness of German exporters, as well as expanding borrowers’ access to German technology and expertise.

“The modernization package is not just about technical changes. The goal is to provide German exporters and their international partners with access to financing structures that are in line with the realities of today’s global economy and to help them turn ambitious investment ideas into concrete, promising, and economically sustainable projects,” Heckmann added.

World.title: Commerzbank explores long-term financing for Azerbaijan’s renewables (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 6. Commerzbank AG, one of Germany's largest and leading banks, is exploring opportunities for the long-term financing of renewable energy projects in Azerbaijan, particularly in the wind and solar energy sectors, a representative of Commerzbank AG, Oliver Roth, told Trend in an exclusive interview on Tuesday on the sidelines of the German-Azerbaijani Strategic Partnership and Connectivity Conference in Baku.

He noted that Commerzbank is a long-standing partner in Azerbaijan and participates in financing, backed by export credit agencies (ECAs), investment projects that source equipment and supplies from abroad, primarily from developed economies such as Europe, the U.S., and Asia.

"We have been partners in Azerbaijan for a long time. We previously maintained an office here, though we currently manage our operations in Azerbaijan through our Tashkent office in Uzbekistan. There is significant potential for cooperation. In particular, there are a number of renewable energy projects requiring long-term financing, and this is one of the opportunities we can offer," Roth mentioned.

The Commerzbank representative emphasized their interest in financing projects within Azerbaijan's renewable energy sector.

"We don’t have a specific project at the moment, but we are actively looking for projects, particularly in the wind energy sector. We can provide financing in this area. One of the key offerings we can provide is very long-term financing. This period can even extend up to 20–22 years. This is the type of financing required for renewable energy projects," he said.

Roth highly appreciated Azerbaijan's renewable energy potential.

"The potential is immense. If we look at Azerbaijan's current energy mix, we see that approximately 90% of energy production relies on fossil fuels. At the same time, the country possesses significant solar and wind energy potential. This potential needs to be harnessed, a process that requires long-term financing," the bank representative stressed.

He added that the bank is exploring opportunities to finance specific wind and solar energy projects in Azerbaijan.

"We are currently seeking projects in the wind and solar energy sectors. Simultaneously, we are holding extensive discussions with local Azerbaijani banks to identify areas for cooperation, as they have a better understanding of their clients and their needs within the local market," Roth pointed out.

World.title: One Nation AI-generated video sparks cafe owner row with Lee Hanson
World.content:
A Tasmanian cafe and Pauline Hanson's daughter have become embroiled in a row over an AI-generated video depicting people ditching their social and political allegiances and revealing themselves as One Nation supporters.

Richmond Reading Room, a cafe business north of Hobart, posted to its social media pages expressing offence at the video, and making an unnamed reference to regular cafe-goer, One Nation candidate and Pauline Hanson's daughter, Lee Hanson.

"Seen the latest One Nation ad and felt absolutely disgusted like I do? Then you'll likely feel the same way when you see the orange ute outside our coffee shop," the post said.

"Unfortunately, our coffee is so good that even One Nation members spend their money here — owned and run by a gay, indigenous-descended, trans-inclusive, pro-multicultural, anti-flag, pro-choice, anti-generative AI, Greens voter.

" Any money spent by a member of one nation will be donated directly to Tasmanian Greens. "

An image from the AI-generated One Nation video, depicting a man in a field with an exploding wind turbine behind him. (Facebook: Pauline Hanson's Please Explain)

Titled "It's ok to come out … as a One Nation voter", the video begins with a family sitting around the dinner table over "vegan mung beans", with the son declaring he is "conservative".

The video goes on to depict a man of African appearance wielding a machete, a man of Middle Eastern appearance wearing what appears to be an explosives vest, and protesters outside a parliament building.

The video also deals with issues including bias by the ABC, bail laws, gender identity, mass migration, power prices, and money allocated to Indigenous Australians on the basis of "identity".

Lee Hanson says if the cafe owners "had an issue with me coming into their business, why not simply talk to me? I am a person. I am a local". (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

Lee Hanson, who lives in the area, responded on her social media, saying the cafe's post came as a "complete shock" and that she was "genuinely hurt".

"If the owners had an issue with me coming into their business, why not simply talk to me? I am a person. I am a local. I am a customer who has supported your business for years," she wrote.

"You do not have to agree with my politics. I would never expect you to. But surely we have reached a pretty sad place when someone's political beliefs determine whether their presence or their custom is considered acceptable.

"The irony of preaching inclusion while publicly singling out customers because of their political association is difficult to ignore.

" At least I now know where I stand. "

Lee Hanson said she would continue supporting local Tasmanian businesses, "just not businesses that publicly make people feel unwelcome because they happen to hold different political views, despite claiming to be for inclusivity".

The cafe has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Breaking: Jannik Sinner to miss rest of tennis season with knee injury
World.content:
World number one Jannik Sinner will not compete again in 2026 after opting to continue his recovery ‌from a knee injury that has kept him out of action ‌since his ⁠triumphant Wimbledon campaign in July.

"Me, together with the doctors, have decided that I need a course of treatment for my knee, which means that the 2026 season is officially over," Sinner said in a video message on Instagram.

" I also need to think about my long-term career so I will do everything possible to get back 100 per cent. "

Sinner has not played since beating Alexander Zverev in the All England Club final on July 12, with the 25-year-old missing the North American hardcourt swing, the US Open as well as the ongoing slate of tournaments in Asia.

He will now miss the European indoor hardcourt swing as well as the season-ending ATP Finals in Turin, where he won the title in the last two years.

Sinner's team said in a statement that he would follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee.

"The decision has been made to have the treatment now to give Jannik the necessary time to recover before beginning preparations for 2027."

Sinner's absence could open the door for Zverev to finish the year at the top of the world rankings.

The German world number two has cut the gap to Sinner after winning the French Open and US Open titles.

Sinner, the 2024 and 2025 Australian Open winner, will be hoping to reclaim his crown in January.

World.title: Australia's 'quite striking' move towards US defies trend
World.content:
As a key ally of the United States, Britain had hoped to avoid the scenario that played out last week at RAF Fairford.

For months its leaders tried to support the US without being drawn directly into its war with Iran.

Then an alleged plot emerged near the British air base used by US bombers conducting missions in the Middle East.

Six men were arrested on suspicion of terror and explosives offences — but all, including a British-Iranian national, have since been released on bail.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham publicly tied Iran to the incident — saying there were "strong indications" Iran had played a role.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi denied the allegation.

Mystery has continued to ensue as a British counter-terrorism operation plays out but overnight US President Donald Trump gave the clearest indication yet that the US believs that Iran was involved, after quietly ordering the nation's entire bomber fleet to be moved out of the UK.

"We actually know the people who made the threat," Mr Trump said.

US President Donald Trump remarked on the issue around the alleged plan. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

US vice-president JD Vance added to the narrative: "We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are … trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engage in acts of terrorism against the United States and against a lot of other people as well," he said.

Elisabeth Braw is a senior fellow at the international affairs think tank The Atlantic Council, specialising in 'grey zone' conflict — the murky space where states can threaten or disrupt rivals without firing a shot.

"The fact that a terrorist attack was suspected of having been planned against the UK was really alarming and troubling," Ms Braw told 7.30.

Ms Braw said the scenario is part of the reason why Britain was "hesitant" to allow the US military to use their bases.

The US removed a number of aircraft. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

"The government felt that having the US use UK military bases for its operations in the war would indirectly draw Britain into the war," she said.

"There is a risk of terrorist incidents around military installations."

Allies 'more vulnerable'

That risk is something Australian analysts are acutely aware of.

Gulf nations like Saudi Arabia, Oman and the United Arab Emirates have already experienced attacks because of their alliances with the US.

Emma Shortis is director of progressive think tank, the International and Security Affairs Program at the Australia Institute, and says those allies are already concerned.

Dr Emma Shortis is the director of The Australia Institute's International and Security Affairs Program. (ABC News)

"That is leading to what I think is a pretty dramatic reconsideration on the part of those allies and also a potentially pretty dramatic geopolitical realignment in the Middle East itself," she said.

Australia has increased its partnership with the US, not just through the AUKUS agreement but through an announcement last month to increase America's presence at military bases in Australia.

Ms Shortis says Australia doing the opposite even as other traditional US allies like Canada — which is in a trade war with the US — reconsider their alliance, is a questionable decision.

"It's quite striking that the Australian government doesn't seem to be doing that," she told 7.30.

" The Iran War has made it clear that the presence of US in other countries doesn't make them safer ... in the case of Iran it's made traditional allies more vulnerable. "

However, Ms Braw said the presence of US forces could bring security to the nations they were in.

"The first thing to remember is that having the Americans, the US armed forces around in our countries is a good thing." she told 7.30.

"They bring security, they're there to help and they do help ... [it] brings a larger measure of security to our countries, whether it be the UK, Germany, or Australia or South Korea."

The Department of Defence told 7.30 it was remaining vigilant in the face of any potential threat.

"Defence employs robust, layered security measures to protect its personnel, establishments and capabilities," a Defence spokesperson said.

Into a 'power war'?

New research by the Nautilus Institute found the US military and defence corporations now have access to around 70 per cent of Australia's defence facilities, reflecting what researchers describe as an unprecedented level of military integration.

Professor Richard Tanter, who led the research, is concerned by the depth of the arrangement.

"This is not a matter of US penetration of a small number of Australian bases, but a pattern of saturation of the Australian defence eco-system by US access and influence," Professor Tanter said.

"That raises questions about Australian strategic autonomy."

However

Those concerns are shared by Albert Palazzo, who is former Director of War Studies for the Australian Army.

Albert Palazzo is concerned about Australia having more US military in Australia. (ABC News)

"Our political class is well aware that the world is changing," Mr Palazzo told 7.30.

"There are forces out there that are redesigning the power balance ... when things change you're forced to do something different.

"But we are not preparing [the] ADF to participate in conflicts ... instead we're preparing it to be a subset of the US military and we're allowing them in our country to project power against China.

"It's short-sighted.

" We're inviting ourselves into the great power war and we're the proverbial mouse between two elephants, and when those elephants fight — it's never good for the mouse. "

World.title: Zach Merrett staying 'open-minded' after high-profile AFL move to Hawks
World.content:
Boom AFL recruit Zach Merrett is open-minded over what role he will play at Hawthorn under coach Sam Mitchell.

More than a year after the bombshell revelation that the Hawks were trying to lure Merrett from Essendon, a deal was finally struck for the former Bombers captain when the trade period opened on Monday.

Essendon will receive the number 15 and 25 picks in this year's national draft, as well as Hawthorn's 2028 second-round selection.

The bitter rivals were unable to reach a deal for Merrett in trade talks a year ago.

Merrett would obviously boost Hawthorn's midfield, but he noted on Tuesday in a club interview that he could also play in defence or across half-forward.

"It is funny that Gia and I are back together," he said of former Essendon assistant coach Daniel Giansiracusa, who is now at the Hawks.

"We worked for three years on trying to be the most flexible player in the competition, being able to play a number of different roles.

"I have no preconceived ideas with Sam. We're going to be pretty open-minded, to what that could look like.

Loading Instagram content

"There are already so many incredible players out there for the Hawks, so wherever I fit in, I will make sure I make that work — whether that's back, forward, mid, or wing, or whatever it looks like."

Merrett has toured Hawthorn's Dingley headquarters and met with captain Jai Newcombe.

"It's been a bit overwhelming, the last 24 hours," Merrett said.

"To see the whole facility and to get so many incredible messages, I feel extremely welcomed, and so is my family."

Last Thursday Merrett became the third player to win Essendon's best and fairest award seven times, alongside Dick Reynolds and Bill Hutchison.

"It was a really hard decision, it was probably something I weighed up for six to nine months," Merrett said of the move.

"It felt like Hawthorn was going to be the best place for me and my family, moving forward, to keep achieving, to achieve out of footy.

"I also have so much respect and love for Essendon as well, so it is a unique feeling, a little bit.

"But I'm keen to move forward, get stuck into work."

Hawthorn, whose season ended with an epic preliminary final loss to premiers Brisbane, are also expected to recruit key forward Ben King from Gold Coast.

World.title: Top OpenAI boss on hack apology tour 'can't explain' Australian AI distrust
World.content:
A top OpenAI executive who flew to Australia to mop up after the company's Medicare statistics hack said he could not explain why Australians are among the world's most distrustful of AI.

Chief strategy officer Jason Kwon made the comments to the ABC as he left a parliamentary inquiry into AI, in his first public appearance since the prime minister revealed the hack late last month.

Mr Kwon pledged to rebuild trust after the hack, while the company's handling of its disclosure drew criticism from the federal government.

Jason Kwon flew to Australia for the hearing. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

After touting Australia's adoption rate of OpenAI's ChatGPT, Mr Kwon did not have an answer for why some polls show that a majority of the nation does not trust the technology, a higher proportion than in most other countries.

"I can't explain the current sentiment; all we can do is continue to get better," he said.

OpenAI says it made changes to prevent future hacks

Mr Kwon said OpenAI now alerts staff when its models use the internet in ways they should not during training.

But he acknowledged OpenAI should have told the Australian government about the Medicare hack sooner, rather than waiting to establish more facts.

He said the company identified the NSW Parks and Wildlife breach last week and reported it to the state government much sooner.

Jason Kwon told the hearing the company has made changes to prevent future breaches. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

Mr Kwon also added that chief executive Sam Altman had not known about it when he met Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles on September 1, despite company staff having first found out about the hack several weeks prior.

While in Australia, Mr Kwon will interview several people for OpenAI's promised "taskforce" to help guide its own response to the hack, a spokesperson told the ABC this afternoon.

Anthropic would have told Australia if it had done the hack

Representatives of rival AI company Anthropic told the committee that it would have made a similar disclosure if it had discovered its technology had hacked another company.

The company also backed a proposal floated by the federal government's Office of AI that would require AI developers to report serious safety incidents, saying its current reporting commitments were largely voluntary.

Anthropic representatives also said it was finalising a deal to let Australia's AI Safety Institute independently test its models.

The Joint Select Committee hearing on artificial intelligence was held in Sydney today. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

Its international envoy, former US ambassador to Australia Jeff Bleich, told the committee that the company wants to train its AI in Australia.

But he said Australia's current copyright regime was an obstacle that needed to change, regardless of any licensing deals it might sign.

"You can't license the entire internet," he said.

Anthropic has not publicly disclosed signing any licensing deals in Australia.

Creatives and rights holders reject claims status quo isn't working

Groups representing musicians, writers and voice actors rejected calls to loosen copyright laws to attract AI investment, accusing the companies of taking their work without permission.

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd warned that such a deal would threaten Australia's music industry.

All eyes on OpenAI at inquiry It had been pencilled in for a centrestage performance, tapping into a bit of Silicon Valley star power, but it's a bruised OpenAI that's set to limp into the Australian political spotlight today.

"Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," she told the committee.

The groups argued that AI companies could already seek permission and pay to use creative work under existing copyright law.

They also said members were not just after payment but also control over whether AI companies would train on their work.

"The idea that payment is the only thing we're haggling about is a step in the wrong direction," Australian Writers' Guild executive director Claire Pullen said.

Big tech's old guard warns against drastic regulation

Later in the day, both Google and Microsoft appeared before the committee urging a less catastrophic approach to regulating the technology.

Microsoft said Australia should build on its existing laws, including privacy and anti-discrimination protections, updating them where needed and adopting AI standards that work across borders.

Google also called for common industry standards and rules that work across borders, warning against duplication while saying AI was too important not to regulate.

The committee is set to have another hearing in Sydney tomorrow.

World.title: Alan Jones kiss left 17yo feeling 'violated', court told
World.content:
A trial has heard Alan Jones grinned after he allegedly kissed and stuck his tongue into the mouth of a 17-year-old schoolboy, who the veteran broadcaster had first started talking to four years earlier.

The man, known as Complainant A, is the fifth and final male complainant to give evidence in Mr Jones's NSW Local Court trial.

The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching, relating to alleged incidents between 2003 and 2020.

Complainant A said he first contacted Mr Jones when he was 13 by letter, telling the broadcaster about his family's financial and personal struggles, and asking for help.

The court heard the pair exchanged emails and text messages for several years, with Mr Jones arranging assistance including more than $90,000 in support for his family.

The complainant told the trial after several invitations from Mr Jones, he finally agreed to stay at the radio host's Fitzroy Falls farm in the Southern Highlands when he had just turned 17.

He said on his second day at the property, an older male couple came over and the four shared dinner together before they all watched a movie in the living room.

The man said after the two guests left, he and Mr Jones were in the hallway near their bedrooms when he went to say goodnight.

"I said goodnight to Mr Jones and leant in to hug him to thank him for what was a lovely weekend and express my gratitude for the weekend and what he had done," Complainant A said.

"Mr Jones kissed me and he put his tongue inside of my mouth and then I froze. I didn't do anything."

Mr Jones denies the allegations against him. (ABC News: Simon Amery)

The then-schoolboy said the kiss continued until Mr Jones placed his hand on his buttocks, and at that point the 17-year-old "recoiled" and stepped backwards.

"I just said, 'that's enough Alan' and looked up at him and said goodnight," the complainant said.

Complainant A said Mr Jones did not reply and "had a grin on his face", which he said made him feel "very uncomfortable".

The man told the court he then turned around and went into the ensuite of his bedroom.

"I went in there [the bathroom] with a loofah, I just soaked it and scrubbed my mouth as much as I could," he said.

" I felt violated and I felt gross. "

Concern over financial troubles

He told the court he also felt "terrified" that if he made a scene after the incident that Mr Jones would withdraw the financial support for him and his mother.

"I was worried… about how I needed to be grateful… and being defiant is not being grateful and making a scene is not being grateful," he said.

The complainant said the next morning he saw Mr Jones who had the "same smirk" and that he "wanted to be as far from there as possible".

The court heard the boy later said goodbye to Mr Jones before his butler drove the schoolboy home.

He said he did not tell his mother about what happened until several days later when she noticed that he was not sleeping at night.

Complainant A said he then wrote his mother a letter saying that "something happened at Fitzroy Falls and that "someone did something they shouldn't have" but did not go into explicit detail.

"To other people, it's probably not that bad and I should just get over it," he said.

" While I was physically able to stop it from happening, it showed me the power of money. "

The court heard the boy went to police with his allegation a year after the incident.

Emails read at trial

After the boy's letter to Mr Jones four years earlier, the pair began to correspond by email and text message, with the schoolboy explaining in more detail that his father had left the home and was paying "intermittent" child support, and that the house he and his mother were living in was unfinished after the builder walked off the job.

"You sound a special sort of young man," Mr Jones responded, and asked the then-teenager for some more information.

The court was read emails which suggested over the course of about 12 months, from Complainant A's first letter to Mr Jones, the veteran broadcaster met with some bank contacts to assist in having the family's house remortgaged and $600,000 wiped from their debt.

"Just between you and me I wrote the proposal that [the lawyer] put to the Commonwealth Bank," Mr Jones told Complainant A in an email.

" That's between you and me… don't worry your mother. "

Mr Jones's emails referred to the teenager's "remarkable diligence" at understanding his mother's financial troubles and wanting to help her.

"You're the most brilliant 13 year old/14 year old I think I've ever met," Mr Jones once wrote to Complainant A.

Complainant A told the court after the house was remortgaged, Mr Jones paid some developer friends of his to finish work on the house.

After not hearing from Complainant A for several months, the court heard Mr Jones emailed the schoolboy and said that it was "very expensive work" that Mr Jones had paid for, and that he was "happy to foot the bill" but "would appreciate an update".

Complainant A emailed back to apologise and said he was trying not to bother the radio host, and that neither he nor his mother took any of the help for granted.

Multiple in-person meetings

Complainant A said he first met Mr Jones in person with his mother present, then was invited to meet with Mr Jones alone on at least three other occasions, including at his Circular Quay apartment and at a pub.

Mr Jones emailed Complainant A after the pub lunch, asking for more information about how he could assist in finishing the build on the house.

"You looked wonderful and fresh and bright, I can't believe you're 14 years of age," the email said.

About three years after Complainant A had first written to Mr Jones, the court heard Mr Jones began to raise concerns with the boy about the cost of the home building project, which the court heard had reached more than $86,000.

"This whole cost thing is getting out of hand… at some point I have to say no more," Mr Jones wrote.

"There can't be an endless dripping tape effect here," Mr Jones wrote in another email.

Complainant A responded that he and his mother were happy to make repayments to the broadcaster, but Mr Jones did not agree to that.

World.title: What to know about pneumonic plague after conflicting reports of a death in Russia
World.content:
Thoughts of the plague might conjure up images of masked doctors during the European Middle Ages.

But the deadly disease is back in the spotlight this week after news of the death of a 28-year-old "anti-plague" research laboratory worker in Siberia spread around the globe.

Local media in Irkutsk, Russia, reported a woman employed at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East died last week.

Russian authorities have quarantined part of a hospital and are monitoring her contacts, according to AP.

But state media outlet TASS reported that Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, confirmed that tests found no pathogens linked to her work and denied any incident at the laboratory.

Uncertainty about what happened at the lab raises questions about how the disease spreads and how to manage it.

Here's what we know.

What kind of plague infections are there?

There are three main clinical forms of plague infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which lives in rodents and the fleas that feed on them.

The three types are: pneumonic, bubonic and septicaemic.

Pneumonic plague, or lung-based plague, is the most virulent form.

Incubation can be as short as 24 hours, and it is transmitted via respiratory particles.

If not treated, it can be fatal.

The bubonic form is the most common and is caused by the bite of an infected flea, which causes the bacteria to travel through the lymphatic system to the nearest lymph node, where they replicate.

At advanced stages, the inflamed lymph nodes can turn into a sore filled with pus called a bubo.

Septicaemic plague occurs when the bacteria enter the bloodstream directly or as a complication of bubonic or pneumonic plague.

Symptoms of this form of plague are fatigue, fever, and internal bleeding.

What is the Siberian anti-plague institute?

The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East conducts research on plague control. It is located at the southern tip of Lake Baikal and was founded by the order of the Council of Labour and Defense of the USSR on June 5, 1934, according to its website.

A state TV station in Irkutsk reported on Monday, local time, that a lab worker, whom it named Darya Shipilova, died last week in a hospital in Shelekhov, a town just outside Irkutsk in Eastern Siberia.

An infectious diseases hospital in the town of Shelekhov, near Irkutsk, on Monday. (Reuters: Stringer)

Shelekhov district Mayor Maxim Modin said on Friday the hospital was no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory halted routine testing.

Anna Popova, head of Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk and met with Governor Igor Kobzev and other officials on Friday.

Kobzev said everyone who came into contact with the woman is under medical supervision.

He didn't identify the infection and called it a suspected case of "a particularly dangerous infection".

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday he doesn't think there is cause for alarm, but the United States is watching the case closely.

What is the black death?

The most famous outbreak of the bubonic plague was "The Black Death", a pandemic in Europe that lasted from 1346 to 1353.

The Black Death lasted several years and led to the emergence of plague doctors wearing bizarre bird-like masks. (Wikimedia Commons: Public Domain)

While historians still debate the Black Death's origin in Europe, it is thought to have arrived on ships carrying rats and fleas, and is estimated to have killed more than 50 million people, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

While the Black Death pandemic is named after the bubonic plague, the pneumonic plague, which had a higher mortality rate, was also believed to have contributed to the pandemic, according to the WHO.

Where is the plague still present?

Between 2019 and 2025, the WHO reported 3,847 suspected cases of plague and 423 deaths from 10 countries.

Australia has not recorded a human case since the 1920s.

The US has not recorded a case of person-to-person infection since 1924, according to its Centers for Disease Control.

WHO said the plague is found in animal populations on all continents except Oceania.

Can humans survive the plague today?

Today, bubonic plague is easily treated with antibiotics, while standard precautions can help prevent infection.

However, the pneumonic plague has a 100 per cent fatality rate if left untreated.

If patients are diagnosed early, antibiotics and supportive therapy are effective.

If not, the disease can progress rapidly and can be fatal within 18 to 24 hours of infection.

Preventive measures include informing people when animal-detected plague is present in their environment and advising them to take precautions against flea bites and to not handle animal carcasses.

WHO does not recommend vaccination, except for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to the risk of contamination.

How is plague detected?

Confirmation of plague requires lab testing.

The best practice is to identify Yersinia pestis from a sample of pus from a bubo, blood or sputum.

A specific Yersinia pestis antigen can be detected by different techniques.

One of them is a laboratory-validated rapid dipstick test now widely used in Africa and South America with the support of WHO.

World.title: Police investigate alleged assault of child by gymnastics coach
World.content:
A gymnastics coach has been stood down after an alleged physical assault of a child at a gymnasium in Brisbane.

Queensland police said they were investigating an allegation of assault at Splitz Gym in Sumner Park.

After receiving information alleging a "serious child safeguarding breach by a coach", gym officials escalated the matter to Gymnastics Australia and the Queensland Police Service (QPS).

A spokesperson from QPS confirmed that an investigation was ongoing "following reports of an alleged assault" on a child, but no arrests or charges had been made.

"Officers from the Inala Child Protection and Investigation Unit (CPIU) received a report of an assault at a business address on Jijaws Street on 5 October," the spokesperson said.

Gymnastics Australia and Gymnastics Queensland confirmed an investigation of a "serious child safeguarding allegation involving a coach" at a club was ongoing.

"As soon as the club became aware of the allegation, they correctly followed strict mandatory reporting requirements and the matter was quickly escalated," a spokesperson from Gymnastics Australia said.

The coach has been suspended pending an investigation. (ABC News)

In an email sent to parents of children who attended the gym, Gymnastics Australia said the full facts of the incident were under review, and at this stage it was an allegation.

"It is a serious allegation, and the issue has the full attention of Gymnastics Australia, Gymnastics Queensland and Splitz Gym," the email said.

Splitz Gym has suspended the coach allegedly involved immediately, pending the investigation, the email added.

It also made clear that Gymnastics Australia had placed "a provisional suspension on coaching" at any other affiliated clubs until the allegations could be fully investigated.

The spokesperson from Gymnastics Australia said it had "zero tolerance for any behaviour that places members or children at risk".

"Gymnastics Australia and Gymnastics Queensland remain firmly committed to ensuring gymnastics is a safe, inclusive, and supportive environment for all participants, and we are focused on supporting the local community through this challenging period."

Sport Integrity Australia was contacted; however, they advised they could not comment. Splitz Gym has also been contacted.

World.title: Fire, cyclones, extreme heat: Albanese’s hellish summer forecast
World.content:
PoliticsFederalClimate policy Fire, cyclones, extreme heat: Albanese’s hellish summer forecast Nick O'Malley Updated October 6, 2026 — 8:12pm ,first published 6:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nadi: Australia faces a dangerous summer of fire and cyclones spurred by the combination of climate change and a monster El Nino, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has declared at the opening session of climate talks in Fiji. Albanese told Pacific leaders Australia expected a summer of floods, cyclones and extreme heat “because the science told us that if we didn’t act to address global emissions, this is precisely what would occur, and tragically, that is playing out, which is why we cannot afford to let 1.5 degrees just slip from our grasp”. ”In Tuvalu, as in the rest of the Pacific, climate change is not a problem for the future,” he said after a visit to the tiny island nation threatened by rising seas. “It is here right now, and we know that sea levels here in the Western Pacific are rising up more than twice the global average, we know also that the forecast of Super El Nino may test us all.” At the meeting in Tuvalu, Pacific leaders declared the world must stop making false promises and end its addiction to fossil fuels, points apparently directed at Australia, which continues to expand fossil exports while vowing to amplify the Pacific’s climate concerns at upcoming climate talks. The comments were made on Tuesday afternoon as Albanese and Climate Minister Chris Bowen sat down with delegations in Tuvalu, alongside former prime minister Julia Gillard, to participate in a sautalaga – a traditional way of holding a frank and respectful discussion to find common ground.



Australia’s sales of fossil fuels were in focus during frank conversations on the island nation of Tuvalu. Getty Images Bowen, who with host nation Turkey will serve as co-chair of the UN’s annual climate talks next month, has shifted his emphasis from the importance of a fossil fuel phase-out, which was a key to COP talks in Dubai in 2023, to the need to ramp up renewables and electrification. “The science is settled, and the legal structures the world has built together are clear on our obligations,” said Fiji Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka during the leaders’ meeting in Tuvalu on Tuesday. Photo: Matt Golding “We must bring forward ambition, decarbonisation commitments and implement the transition away from fossil fuels. That is not radical. It is in line with our agreement, our obligation and the scientific reality.”



Tuvalu’s climate minister Maina Talia said neither his nation nor the world could afford to have the upcoming meeting become another “talking shop”. “We must urgently face our fossil fuels. A rapid transition to renewable energy is essential. Yet, far too long, we have been trapped in circles of empty promises, excess paperwork and bureaucratic delays.” Asked during a press conference in Fiji on Monday how Australia, as a coal-mining nation, could keep its commitment to the Pacific and its role in the COP31 talks, Bowen said the Pacific region was “unified, not uniform” on climate issues. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Pacific leaders in Tuvalu. AAP “We are unified in our objectives, but of course Pacific countries will express their views in slightly different ways from time to time. My position remains publicly and privately, the way to transition away from fossil fuels is to build more renewable energy, to replace the need for fossil fuels.”



He said that as a fossil fuel-exporting nation, “we can bring something different to the table, which is the need for countries to work together on the transition, both on demand as well as supply”. Gillard, who introduced a carbon tax as prime minister despite pledging during the 2010 election not to do so, accompanied Albanese on the leaders’ visit to Tuvalu. They arrived on Tuesday in a rain shower to witness first-hand the impact of climate change on one of the world’s smallest, most remote and lowest-lying nations, a chain of islands which stands just 1.5 metres above sea level in an area where oceans are rising faster than average. “Our planet is telling us something,” said Tuvalu’s Prime Minister Feleti Teo. “We are pushing its life support systems beyond safe limits. Our ocean is also telling us the same thing.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with former Australian leader Julia Gillard in Tuvalu on Tuesday. AAPIMAGE



At a keynote speech at the opening of the talks in Fiji on Monday, Gillard said countries should explicitly protect pregnant women and newborns in their climate-adaptation plans and ensure health workers have guidelines and training to respond to heat. Gillard is the chair of Wellcome, a London-based health research foundation. “This isn’t a future thing,” Gillard said in an interview with Bloomberg on Monday, pointing to a new five-country survey of maternity health workers. “They are already seeing women, children who have been impacted by extreme heat, and they haven’t been given the tools and help that they need to deal with these new challenges.” Pacific leaders insisted not only must fossil fuel use be reduced, and an effort made to reduce overshoot on the goal for 1.5 degrees of warming, but efficient and effective finance for small island states which did little to cause the crisis but bear the worst of the costs must be at the centre of negotiations. Under Paris Treaty rules, countries are responsible for the fossils fuels they use onshore rather than those they export, but as the climate crisis intensifies, and as Australia has taken on a larger role in climate talks, the Albanese government’s position is coming under increasing criticism.



Labor has made advancing the climate concerns of the Pacific key to its own goal of remaining the region’s “security partner of choice” as China seeks to increase its influence. As part of this strategy, it launched a bid to co-host this year’s COP talks with the Pacific in Australia. When it was forced aside by Turkey, Bowen secured the role of president of negotiations at the talks, as well as the ongoing Pre-COP meeting in Fiji. with Bloomberg Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Why this Brisbane band kept their misspelt name
World.content:
Welcome to CityChats, where Brisbane Times meets our city’s most interesting characters on our most iconic form of transport. This week, Mid Drift band members Sarah Engstrom, George Swan and Daniel Larsen tell us about turning female rage into fun, floaty, washy tunes, realising they’d spelt midriff wrong, and their dream venues to play. We meet three of the five band members at North Quay ferry terminal, fresh from their 9-5 jobs. We’ve been fretting about how we’re going to fit six people into frame at peak hour on the ferry, but Rowan Bowyer can’t get a park in the CBD, and John Reid also can’t make it. The CityCat is indeed busier than usual at 5pm, but not so busy that every seat is taken. Shout out to the woman who got up and moved, leaving a row open, after spotting our concerned scouting. Brisbane indie-rock band Mid Drift members Rowan Bowyer, Sarah Engstrom, George Swan, Daniel Larsen and John Reid. Mid Drift How did you guys meet?



George: Just through the music scene in Brisbane. It’s so small and tight. Everyone sort of knows everyone. You cross paths eventually. All of these guys were in a different band, apart from me. And I sort of knew you guys through the grapevine, but hadn’t really met yet. And I just messaged Sarah and I was like, “I need someone to play guitar for. I’m bored. I’m scared and lonely out here”. Oh, so you had a band before? Sarah: Yeah. There was four of us in a band before and we kind of split up. And then it just so happened we needed a really good guitarist, and George is a very good guitarist, and it just worked out perfectly.



How did you come up with your band name? Sarah: After one of the gigs we played, with that band that broke up, there was this girl, this woman, that came up to me in the crowd, and she said to me, “oh, you wear those little tops all the time, and you have your belly hanging out, and blah, blah, blah”. Anyway, then it just kind of stuck with me that I actually do wear like little tops all the time. Then we went through like a billion band names and landed on Mid Drift. Which, apparently, is the actual word for your belly being out after a shirt is ... Daniel: Midriff. But by the time you have a band name that’s not taken, you’re just so stoked that there’s one name left. You don’t change it. I actually did go back through your Instagram posts trying to see how many midriffs there were. I was like, “Is this a play on midriff?” I’m glad I was right.



Sarah: I’ve grown out of it a little bit. Daniel: You have more variety now. Sarah: I do. I thought it seems like it’s more boy midriff now. Sarah: Yeah, it is. The boys have been rocking it. They’ve been chopping their shirts. It’s our like pre-show ritual now. All the boys will chop their shirts together.



Related Article City life Pub Choir queen on why singing is ‘the closest to magic we can get’ George: Every time we get a new shirt, we’ll be like, “Who’s got the scissors?” What is the coolest venue you’ve ever played? George: The beach in Adelaide was incredible. I’ll be longing for that forever. Sarah: Yeah, we played at Glenelg Beach in Adelaide. I think our whole band will say that’s the most amazing. It was right on the beach, the biggest blue sky you’ve ever seen. The crowd was all in the sand. It was really cool.



George: Forum’s cool. Sarah: Forum in Melbourne. Do you have a dream venue you’d want to play at? George: Mine’s Riverstage. Definitely Riverstage for Brisbane. That’s a bucket-list goal. Like ‘we’ve done it, we’re here’. Daniel: I think probably Riverstage as well.



Sarah: What’s that Red Rocks place? Daniel: Oh yeah, Red Rocks in the US. Yeah, that’s beautiful. Weirdly, the Triffid was probably a venue for me that I had [on my list]. You’re in the green room and there are posters of gigs I attended up decorating it. That’s cool. That was my Brisbane venue. That was the one that I wanted to headline. What’s the best concert that you’ve seen in Brisbane?



Daniel: Karnivool. They did an anniversary tour for Themata. There’s a bunch of songs there that they have never played, or they’ve played live a handful of times. And to be in the room with like 700 people that, ‘oh, they’re playing this song that’s special’, and everyone kind of knows that. That was a really, really cool show. That is no surprise to these guys at all. George: Not even a little bit. Mine would probably be Yussef Dayes at the Princess Theatre. That was awesome. Beautiful venue. Doesn’t matter where you’re standing, it just sounds unreal. That was cool. What about you, bro? Sarah: I’m going to say Full Flower Moon Band at the Princess, which was just ... I love her as a frontwoman. She’s so cool, and her performance is amazing. Speaking of amazing frontwomen, I was going to ask you about your lyrics and how you decide what to write about. One of your songs in particular, for me, it’s very full of female rage.



Sarah: Washed. That one is female rage. I feel like I write these songs and I make them very honest. And I don’t like making up scenarios, which is unfortunate for me because everything that I write about is mostly true. But the good thing is, I write these angry, sad girl songs and I bring them to the boys, and they make them fun and floaty and washy. That’s what the boys are really good at doing; they’re good at turning my terrible sad hardship emotions into something that sounds cool. I love the difference between the sound and the lyrics. I think the first time I heard it on social media, I thought, “this is just perfect beach music”, and then I listened to the lyrics and was like, “oh, she’s been through it”. Sarah: I’m so glad. Thank you. Are there any particular artists you guys draw inspiration from? George: I think we all pull inspiration from so many different people. Definitely in Australia, it would be Ocean Alley and probably Spacey Jane as well.



Sarah: Tom Misch. George: Definitely Tom Misch for me. Dan: Parcels, that would be one. Peach Fur were a nice local band that we saw and played with a lot before Mid Drift was around. Loading It’s a very Aussie sound. It’s a beach sound, which is funny because we’re on a river like an hour from the beach. What do you think it is that inspires that kind of sound in Australia?



Sarah: What I always say – and the boys have heard me say this a million times – is that feeling where you’re driving back from the beach, you’re like a little bit sunburnt, the windows are down, you got an hour back from the Gold Coast to Brisbane, and it’s just that feeling. And I feel like the reason we connect with so much of the indie rock kind of music is because it ties in so nicely with saltwater and sun, and nice, flowy, kind of free days, is my take on it. You basically just described the playlist that I have you guys in: driving back from the beach with the windows down. Sarah: I love that. That makes me so happy. Daniel: We can see playlists on Spotify. It’s always just beachy days and driving in a convertible with wind in your hair. George: Emojis of the sun and waves.



You’re consistent. Sarah: I love when they’re a bit rogue, though. It’s like, “I just broke up with my boyfriend”, and it’s like so many songs, and I’m like ... oop. George: There are some good ones. I always forget people can see that. Sarah: I also forget. I should look into the playlists again.



Mine are sometimes very honest, so I should stop doing that. Sarah: No, don’t, don’t stop. We like it. We say goodbye to the band at Felons, staying on until Teneriffe. It normally takes Neesha 20 minutes to get into work from the ’riffe. We get there in 45. Dominique concedes maybe this is why people aren’t commuting on the ferry every day. She maintains the view outweighs the lack of convenience. She’ll probably move to Teneriffe soon and eat her words. World.title: Revealed: The Sydney schools where most families earn $500,000-plus
World.content:
Parents at four Sydney private schools now have a median annual household income exceeding half a million dollars. Four schools – Wenona, Queenwood, SCEGGS and Mosman Church of England Preparatory School – were the first to join the $500,000 club last year after parents’ median family pay packets crossed that income threshold, tax office records show. Wenona, Queenwood, SCEGGS and Mosman Church of England Preparatory School have joined the $500,000 club. Michael Howard At Cranbrook, the median parent income for that school jumped by $83,000 in two years, or 9 per cent annually, to $485,000, outpacing recent fee increases. Year 12 fees now stand at $52,000. Across 14 schools, median parent income jumped by $50,000 or more between 2023 and 2025, including at Shore, Monte Sant’ Angelo and St Catherine’s.



Other schools where parent income surged included St Vincent’s, St Ignatius and Stella Maris colleges. While some high-fee schools have total incomes of half a million dollars, some others are much lower. At King’s, the median is $260,000 and at Pymble Ladies’ College, it is $235,000, while it is $265,000 at Trinity. The government started collecting data on parent salaries using tax office data under its Direct Measure of Income method to distribute funding in 2022. It ranks schools based on parents’ income to determine how much government funding flows to each school. Independent Schools Australia chief executive Graham Catt said the education funding model was based on the principle of needs-based support for every student.



“It is more accurate to think of funding for students, not institutions. Governments spend, on average, about $26,140 per student in government schools and $13,550 per student in independent schools,” he said. “Students at the highest capacity-to-contribute independent schools attract considerably less again, and the parent-income data you are examining is already built into the funding.” The data was obtained in the federal parliament by Greens senator Penny Allman-Payne, who said private schools were heaping above-inflation fee hikes on parents while also receiving taxpayer funding. “It doesn’t pass the pub test that the richest schools in the state, attended by kids of the wealthiest families, plunder billions every year from the public purse while every single public school in NSW remains underfunded,” she said.



“The private school lobby claims they’re relieving pressure on the public school system but that’s a false economy. Related Article Exclusive

Education Almost 1000 NSW teachers were asked if screens helped students learn. Only 53 per cent said yes “Public schools are so underfunded that out-of-pocket costs are soaring and teachers are dipping into their own pockets to pay for classroom supplies. Meanwhile, private schools heap above-inflation fee increases on parents. “Our funding model is failing our kids. Australia has one of the most segregated and privatised school systems in the OECD. Instead of giving every kid the chance to thrive, we’re entrenching privilege and worsening inequality.” Education Minister Jason Clare said recent funding agreements would result in $20 billion flowing into public schools in coming decade under the needs-based Gonski funding model.



“It fixes the funding of our public schools,” he said. “We’re the first government to ever do this. This is the Gonski model. It’s based on need. “Schools with parents on higher incomes get less funding, and vice versa. Schools with parents on lower incomes get more funding.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Inside Sydney’s new mental health centre where kids will be treated free
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWParenting Inside Sydney’s new mental health centre where kids will be treated free Rachel Rasker October 6, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Families will be able to access walk-in specialist support at Sydney’s first free children’s mental health centre from 2027. The new Medicare Kids Hub will provide free mental health support for zero to 12-year-olds with mild to moderate developmental, emotional, relational or behavioural challenges. They will not need a referral. Thirteen-year-old Logan Smith first developed mental health challenges in year 5. STEVEN SIEWERT “Most mental health conditions in Australia develop before the age of 12, and we know the real difference that earlier identification, intervention and support can make for both children and families,” Emma McBride, federal assistant minister for mental health and suicide prevention, said. The Penrith Kids Hub is the final hub of four NSW centres announced in 2023 as part of a $50.8 million joint investment by the Minns and Albanese governments.



The existing hubs in Wollongong, the Central Coast and Orange have delivered more than 17,000 appointments and support sessions since they opened last year. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Revealed: The NSW children spending years on psychiatry wait lists The new centre is expected to serve families across western Sydney, the Hawkesbury and the Blue Mountains. It will feature play facilities, sensory spaces and six consulting rooms. “There’s a lot of young families here, [and] there’s a lot of disadvantage here,” NSW Minister for Mental Health Rose Jackson said. “We want to make sure we’re locating [these services] in communities where that’s going to have the biggest impact.” But the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists remains concerned that the opening of one hub for Sydney’s population of 5 million people will do little to curb the escalating youth mental health crisis.



“This piecemeal [approach] is really not shifting the dial,” UNSW Sydney child and adolescent psychiatry chair Professor Valsamma Eapen said. “Any investment in the under 12 is always extremely welcome … but it cannot be another fragmented little service with very specific criteria.” Sydney is set to open its first children’s mental health centre. STEVEN SIEWERT Eapen said there had been an underinvestment in services for children, with adolescent centres such as Headspace prioritised: “[If] 75 per cent of adult health problems start before the age of 25, I would say 50 per cent of that starts before the age of 14.” Schofields resident and lived-experience manager at Being Mental Health Consumers Kylie Smith said waiting for her child Logan to turn 12 to access Headspace services was “really frustrating”.



“We need options,” Smith said. “There’s nowhere else to go apart from Headspace [which] is from 12 to 25, and a lot happens before that age.” Logan began to struggle with bullying and anxiety from about year 5, and their mental health gradually deteriorated. Now 13, Logan has only been able to attend school for about three days this year. Kylie said waiting for Logan to age into Headspace was frustrating. STEVEN SIEWERT While support from a school counsellor was helpful, Smith said having access to a service such as Kids Hub at a younger age could potentially have stopped his condition from escalating to self-harm. “Anyone can go through that,” Logan said. “If there’s something that children can go to which [is] easier to access, then you can kind of prevent some things earlier.”



Chief executive of Mental Health Carers NSW Jonathan Harms said the new hub was terrific: “For every dollar invested in child mental health, we know there’s a return of between $9 and $13, which is an incredible investment for the public to make.” Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Deaths of 10 young people put eastern suburbs mental health services on alert However, he said the hubs – of which there are 17 across Australia – had not been well planned, and that questions remained about which identified gap they were designed to cover and how they would work with existing services such as Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) in NSW. “How will both systems work if they’re supporting the same person, and how do they pass people between them as people go up and down in severity and level of need? “Then there’s of course the fact that they never seem to intend to cover 100 per cent of the need for these services.”



Jackson said the government would seek feedback on how the initial hubs were working before looking to expand them in future. Jackson and McBride took the Herald inside the hub site, which is a former GP clinic, on Wednesday. Jackson said once renovated, it would be run by the local health district. “That integration with our district means that those pathways through to our CAMHS team, to our Safeguards team, and later, if needed, to our Adolescent Acute Unit, are really warm,” she said. The ministers inspect the centre, which will open in 2027, following a renovation. STEVEN SIEWERT “There’s no bouncing between services. It’s all run by the district and young people are supported to access whatever point in the system they need to receive support.” Dr Annaliese Finnane, a child and adolescent psychiatrist from Nepean Blue Mountains Local Health District, said poor mental health among children was a growing issue, with about one in seven children affected.



“It’s actually a bigger community issue than we would like to think,” she said. “We need a whole community approach to the difficulties that we’re seeing for our young people, and I think this answer is a first step.” The Penrith site, opposite Nepean Hospital, has sat empty for three years. It will be staffed by a multidisciplinary team including allied health, nurses, Aboriginal health workers, peer workers and specialist medical staff. World.title: Forget New Zealand. This looms as the biggest threat to Australia’s World Cup campaign
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Forget New Zealand. This looms as the biggest threat to Australia’s World Cup campaign Christian Nicolussi October 6, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The biggest threat to Australia’s World Cup defence is not New Zealand, Tonga or Samoa – it will be November 1 when a host of superstars will become free agents. Australia will have 11 players hit the open market midway through the tournament, including Cameron Munster, Harry Grant, Latrell Mitchell and Sam Walker. Many of Australia’s representative players will hit the open market next month, including Jack Bostock (left), Cameron Munster, Bradman Best, Latrell Mitchell, Sam Walker and Harry Grant. Aresna Villanueva Even Australia’s captain Isaah Yeo is yet to officially extend at the Panthers, but said he had no plans to cut and run on the club, and his management was sorting through post-career options. There has been enormous interest in player movement, and knowing what some of Australia’s biggest stars might do with their next career move – especially with the PNG Chiefs officially allowed to enter the market next month with their tax-free incentives – threatens to overshadow the second half of the tournament. The World Cup final will be played on November 15.



Grant will be free to talk to rivals should he fail to take up an option with the Storm for 2028, Munster and a return home to Queensland has persisted in the press, while the Sydney Roosters are eager to lock down Walker who is entitled to hold out for almost $1.5m a season, especially because of his age and now that he has won a premiership. South Sydney have informed Mitchell they are prepared to wait until the start of next season to see how his body is before discussing what happens beyond 2027, while teammate David Fifita also enters the final year of his deal at the Rabbitohs. Premiership winner, Sam Walker after winning Sunday’s grand final. Getty Images Roosters skipper and Clive Churchill Medallist James Tedesco is yet to decide if he plays on beyond next season, and Bradman Best and Jack Bostock will have plenty of suitors should they not extend with Newcastle and the Dolphins respectively. Penrith’s Liam Martin and Manly’s Tom Trbojevic also become fair game, but both have indicated they are eager to stay put.



Yeo said he was keen to secure a two or three-year extension, and if a deal was not official by the start of November, there was no cause for concern. “It’s all pretty close, we’re just trying to tweak a few little things in the background, and how the [post career] might look,” the 31-year-old said. Isaah Yeo is eager to remain at Penrith and hopes to confirm his Getty Images “I love Penrith, it’s where I see my future. “I don’t know if it will [be finalised by November 1]. I also think just because you hit November 1, it’s not like all of a sudden these offers and conversations are had, as much as fans might think that’s the case. It’s not how it looks.



“When you’re in this environment, winning should be your only focus. That will certainly be the case for me. You push things to the side, and you only have to wait two weeks [to resume talks].” Australia coach Kevin Walters has experience dealing with speculation about player movement from his time in charge of the Broncos. He said the mid-tournament free agency period would not be a distraction for his squad. “I feel like the guys are all experienced players and know what they need to do. I don’t see it being an issue in camp. And we’ll make sure it doesn’t become one. “There is a window in there when the open market starts, but it won’t impact us in any way.” Meanwhile, Yeo said he had checked in on Nathan Cleary, the Penrith superstar who underwent surgery on a broken leg, then a second operation on a broken foot, which will sideline him until the start of next season. Yeo said the pair had discussed the NFL rather than any injuries, and it was a shame injuries had denied his good friend another chance to wear the green and gold, after surgeries ruled him out of the Pacific Championships in 2023 and 2024.

World.title: A year after Hastie’s warning, Taylor has a solid migration plan. Hanson has the voters
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalImmigration A year after Hastie’s warning, Taylor has a solid migration plan. Hanson has the voters Natassia Chrysanthos October 6, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s been one year to the week since Liberal MP Andrew Hastie quit Sussan Ley’s frontbench to speak his mind on migration. Hastie thought it was a hot-button issue that required a tough response from the Coalition to appease growing cynicism about the post-pandemic immigration surge. That turned out to be prescient. I don’t need to spell out how much Australia’s political landscape has changed since then, particularly on the right, but the immigration debate has only gotten hotter. Through it all, the Coalition has been looking for its white whale: a credible migration policy that swims with the currents of conservative politics without sinking the economy A year after Hastie quit the front bench to talk immigration, Taylor has a plan to take on Hanson. Illustration: Michael Howard They finally made a go of it on Tuesday, when Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and outgoing home affairs spokesman Jonno Duniam released their plan to reduce immigration levels.



The Coalition have done their homework. Their presentation was far more detailed than the shambles former leader Peter Dutton took to the last election, which crumbled before his eyes during the campaign. Dutton committed to targets on the fly, then ruled visas in and out as questions came thick and fast, until there was no possible way for the arithmetic to make sense. The sensible question for Taylor is whether his policy matches the numbers. The political question is whether it lands in parts of the electorate that have switched to One Nation, or comes too late to assist the opposition’s own political fortunes. The Coalition is promising an overnight cut to net overseas migration, taking it from 292,000 to 100,000. In the fourth year, the target rises to 160,000. Voters seeking quick answers now have three figures to compare. The Albanese government last month announced changes to arrive at net migration forecasts of 225,000. One Nation has decided it will take the country to negative migration levels and potential recession after weeks of backflips, forward flips and flip-outs from the far-right section of its support base.



Related Article Immigration Taylor enters three-way migration battle with 100,000 target as Labor and One Nation fire back The Coalition hopes its pitch strikes middle ground. The number is political, designed to shock and grab attention – the top line of Tuesday’s media release promised “the largest cut to immigration in Australian history”. The policy work is practical, trying to allay business concerns by reconfiguring the inflow towards fewer, higher skilled, higher tax-paying cohorts. The Coalition’s solution is to reduce bridging visas and graduate visas while boosting the number of skilled workers. There are a few measures around the side to cut British backpackers, refugees and foreign students, which will be more contentious. Taylor and co say it is costed and budget-neutral, although they won’t release their calculations until closer to the next election. Labor will do its best to neutralise immigration as a political issue, but it is locked in as a key battleground for 2028. The Coalition is making a genuine play at policy that, in ordinary circumstances, should challenge the government. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has been urging the Coalition to get serious by naming which visas it would cut and the economic impact. The Coalition has now done that.



The two visa classes the Coalition earmarked – temporary graduate visas (with exceptions for regions, health and education) and bridging visas – are fair areas to direct debate. Photo: Matt Golding Temporary graduate visas, held by former students, have tripled from 90,000 before the pandemic to 270,000 today. Bridging visas, held by people waiting for a decision on their status, have more than doubled since. The backlog has gone from 190,000 to a record 440,000 – a clear sign the department is overwhelmed. These issues were largely omitted from Burke’s speech last month, which focused on trimming the backpacker program and curtailing family visas for overseas students. The opposition wants to cut both the bridging and graduate visa categories to next to nothing, to reduce temporary visa places in Australia by about 650,000 within four years. With that wriggle room, it will give out 100,000 more skilled visas.



Easier said than done. Immigration expert Abul Rizvi says it will be impossible to eliminate the bridging visa backlog at the pace the Coalition assumes, while exemptions for graduates will amount to far more than the 10,000 places the Coalition has budgeted to fill crucial roles in health, aged care and the regions. All this makes the 100,000 figure implausible, he says, especially in a strong labour market. Deeper cuts to numbers of international students and Kiwis, who have been flocking across the Tasman, would be required to get close. Related Article Immigration nation ‘You can’t put everything on immigration’: The suburbs at breaking point This brings us back to the politics. Taylor doesn’t need to execute these policies just yet. The 100,000 number is much lower than originally anticipated, at just one-third of the status quo, which demonstrates the Coalition wants to look as tough as possible on migration. Thanks to the policy work, Taylor is much better equipped to answer questions than Dutton ever could. On Tuesday, he handled the heat capably.



But the issue might already be too hot. One Nation last month caved to uproar from its right flank, reverting to a widely panned short-term “net negative migration” policy rather than its more sensible proposal for a 130,000 net figure. There’s a chance Pauline Hanson flames out closer to the election under more scrutiny, but meanwhile, she will continue to outplay Taylor in rhetoric. The opposition’s policies may be fitting for a party of government, but less so for that contest. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: ‘I pretty much made the decision to move out as a five-year-old’: The remarkable family story of North coach Jaymie Graham
World.content:
Jaymie Graham in 2008 with his partner Kasey and their son Hudson, who was then six months old. Jaymie had retired from AFL football to raise his family his younger sister, Candy, who was five at the time.

This story was first published in 2008, when The Age’s Emma Quayle flew to Perth to interview Jaymie Graham. It is the story of how Graham and his partner, Kasey, became legal guardians of his youngest sister, Candy. The decision to take five-year-old Candy into their home - Jaymie and Kasey have two younger children, Hudson and Neve - was a major reason for his retirement from playing at the age of 25. Graham became one of the most respected assistant coaches in the AFL, and on Tuesday was appointed North Melbourne’s senior coach. Candy is now in her 20s. Emma Quayle is a recruiter for GWS.
