World.title: Auckland Council accepts Milldale North rezoning request, moves to deal with unplanned growth
World.content:
Auckland councillors have agreed a request to rezone 145 hectares for housing in North Auckland can proceed to public consultation.

Developer Fulton Hogan wants to build around 2000 homes at Milldale North, near Orewa, beside its existing Milldale development.

The land is currently zoned for development from 2050. If Fulton Hogan's private plan change is approved, housing could be built there much sooner.

At Tuesday's Policy, Planning and Development Committee meeting, chair Richard Hills, said reasons for councillors to reject the request were not as strong as for other developments.

"Our infrastructure providers say it's possible on the timing of when the houses will arrive there. There is already so much connecting infrastructure which is not the case for many private plan changes, but also definitely the fast tracks. It is not outside the rural urban boundary, which is positive."

Auckland Council general manager of planning, John Duguid, said the point of difference for Milldale North, compared to other plan changes the council opposed, was that "it's a logical extension of an existing planned development that has ... infrastructure within the existing development designed in size to cope with this additional development to the north".

That did not mean all the issues were resolved, and advice from Auckland Transport and Watercare was that there were issues to work through, he said.

Later in the meeting, councillors tackled how to deal with the thorny problem of developments being consented in areas not planned for growth.

Hills said the city has a "massive issue" of unanticipated development.

"Fast track has really brought this whole thing to a head, but private plan changes we've tried to reject, we've tried to appeal, 99 percent of the time it gets approved no matter what we do."

With rates capping, the council will "have less and less ability to fund everything everywhere", Hills said.

"Right now, when we see thousands and thousands, up to 50,000 dwellings that we have coming down the track that will be either fast tracked or unanticipated, with about $5b of cost that we do not have any plan to pay for, is a massive issue."

"I think if we don't take a strong stance ... then I think we will continue to have the assumption that we can just pay for everything, everywhere."

Hills said public transport, animal management, and illegal dumping teams would be spread further away from where people were getting up every day to do those jobs.

"It's just becoming pretty impossible and not the way to plan a city."

A recent government change to enable councils to set development contributions for fast tracked schemes left out Delmore and Sunfield, projects which have already been granted consent, and which Auckland Council has appealed.

"That was still a half a billion dollar mistake," Hills said.

"That's $500m we somehow have to find or deal with through this process."

Auckland Council chief advisor growth infrastructure funding and financing, Brigid Duffield, said fast track gives regulatory approval, but does not require the council to provide infrastructure.

World.title: Regional deal formalised for Otago Central Lakes
World.content:
Regional leaders and government officials have pledged to work together on affordable housing solutions, transport projects and better access to healthcare in Queenstown Lakes and Central Otago as part of a regional deal.

The Otago Central Lakes Deal - a 10-year plan to deliver infrastructure and manage rapid growth - was formally signed in Queenstown on Tuesday afternoon.

Queenstown Lakes District Council, Central Otago District Council and Otago Regional Council teamed up in early 2025 to develop a joint proposal.

The deal was initially set to be unveiled in August, but the announcement was scuppered by the National Party's crisis talks.

Speaking at the signing, Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop said he was excited to formalise the deal, and excited about the future of the region.

"It's about the start of a renewed relationship between central government and the councils to try and unlock growth here, but also fix some of the problems that have been built up for too long," he said.

In late August, negotiations were put on hold after the National Party ruled out the idea of a bed tax.

The three councils said they were seeking more clarity, given the deal had included a commitment to explore an accommodation levy in 2027.

Katie Todd

Bishop said the deal ultimately included "a commitment to work together around getting that funding flow."

Queenstown mayor John Glover said discussions over exactly how tourism-related infrastructure should be funded would continue in coming months.

"What we recognise is that we're going into an election, all the parties have different views on how tourism should be supported. So it's probably unreasonable to come up with a form of words this side of the election," he said.

"But when we had a conversation with the ministers we said that what we're looking for is a commitment from the Crown to acknowledge that there is funding impacts on local councils - and a commitment to look at the different ways of bridging that gap."

Transport infrastructure was a core pillar of the plan, Bishop said.

He said the deal would also be accompanied by a new Queenstown Strategic Network Plan - which would explore projects like a replacement Edith Cavell Bridge at Arthurs Point in Queenstown as an early priority, and an additional crossing over the Kawarau River in the long term.

"It's a plan that deliberately looks out over the next 30 years and some of the projects and some of the proposals in the plan are identified in the deal as well. It's not a plan for funding. That's a separate issue. But it is a plan about what we need to do as we build out the network here," he said.

The plain reality was that the region's transport networks had not kept up with growth, he said.

"I think we've under-invested here in the region and we need to step up. And I've been reflecting on that today, just over the course of the conversations, and seeing some of the transport challenges - and frankly getting stuck in traffic on the way here."

The regional deal - while stopping short of specific project announcements - also includes a pledge to look at local councils getting a portion of mining royalties, and a commitment to look at the case for inclusionary housing zoning.

It also built on a previously announced $180 million funding commitment for healthcare, with a commitment to expanded local health services including mental health, maternity, cancer care and radiology, as well as ongoing work to determine whether a new hospital was needed for the Otago Central Lakes region.

As the agreement was being signed on behalf of the Crown, it would remain in place no matter the outcome of the upcoming general election, Bishop said.

World.title: National's path to power narrows in new poll
World.content:
Both National and Labour are stuck in the 20s in a new poll, while the Opportunity Party continues to hold the balance of power.

The 1News Verian results showed the National Party taking the lead, edging up 1 percentage point to 29 percent, while Labour stood still on 28 percent.

The Greens maintained their recent bump in support, holding the line at 16 percent.

New Zealand First was up 1 point to 10 percent, while ACT dropped 2 points to 9 percent.

Opportunity registered 7 percent, up 1 point. Te Pāti Māori remained at 1 percent.

If replicated at the election, that would give National 35 MPs, New Zealand First 12 and ACT 11 - a coalition bloc of 58

On the left, Labour would get 33 MPs, the Greens 20 and Te Pāti Māori just one - 54 together.

Either way, Opportunity's eight MPs would decide the victor.

That assumed all parties were returned to Parliament and allocated MPs roughly in line with their party vote.

The calculations would change if National won more than 35 electorates or Te Pāti Māori won more than one, causing an overhang.

The poll landed ahead of tonight's TVNZ leaders' debate and after an earlier RNZ-Reid Research poll.

Broadly, both polls told a similar story, with the old two-party system squeezed, neither traditional bloc able to govern alone, and Opportunity still pivotal, sitting above 5 percent.

But there were also some striking differences.

RNZ-Reid Research had Labour ahead of National by five points (31 to 26) whereas 1News Verian has National ahead by one (29 to 28).

Both the Greens and Opportunity were also registering stronger in TVNZ's poll.

The 1News Verian poll also had a much higher undecided vote - 11 percent - compared to RNZ-Reid Research's 6 percent.

World.title: Advocate wants longer-term plan for medicines funding
World.content:
Audio player for " National re-commits to failed health promises it failed to deliver this term " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics/1764389%2Fadvocate-wants-longer-term-plan-for-medicines-funding

National re-commits to failed health promises it failed to deliver this term Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

An advocate for better access to medicines says the National party's pledge to invest a further $604 million for Pharmac to fund more new medicines if re-elected is helpful, but that it won't be enough to close the medicines gap.

In the 2023 election, National made a commitment to people with blood cancer, for life-prolonging drugs that are free in Australia to be funded in New Zealand.

In June 2024, Pharmac received a $604m funding increase after backlash when the commitment to blood cancer patients failed to materialise.

Tim Edmonds from the Forbidden Pharmacy campaign group told Checkpoint that National's new commitment will make a difference to New Zealanders waiting for access to medicine, and he's pleased that so far two parties - National and ACT - have costed medicine access in their election pledges.

However, Edmonds said $604m won't be enough to fund all the medicines on Pharmac's recommended list - the Options for Investment list (OFI).

He said these are medicines that Pharmac have evaluated for what they would return to New Zealand.

"These are medicines that Pharmac have said offer value for money for New Zealanders, so it makes our health system more efficient, it helps get people back into work and be productive, and be able to be parents and be part of their communities," he said.

Edmonds said this year Pharmac put out a bid for $800m over four years to fund medicines on the OFI list.

He said his group is calling for a sustainable longer-term view of funding medicines in New Zealand, which he said is already falling behind other OECD countries.

A 2025 report by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research showed that New Zealand spends 4.9 percent of the health and disability budget on medicines, compared to the OECD average of 13.3 percent.

Edmonds said they don't want the issue to be politicised and for his group to have to advocate for what is a right in other countries.

He said he has spoken to patients who held hope when promises, which did not eventuate in reality, were made to myeloma patients in the last election.

"There's a lot of devastated patients out there," said Edmonds.

Edmonds said independent polling by Talbot Mills indicated that 82 percent of New Zealanders across the political spectrum thought it was critically important to fund medicines Pharmac is recommending, and seven out of 10 thought policies in this area would sway how they voted.

Meanwhile, ACT is pledging to increase the share of the health budget spent on medicines by 1 percentage point each year, reaching parity with Australia in 2033.

World.title: Labour rejects Willis' Investment Boost claim, but admits 'small' $90m error
World.content:
Labour says National's Nicola Willis is "wrong" over her calculations for the Investment Boost policy, but has admitted a $90 million error in its fiscal plan.

The Taxpayers Union lobby group this morning warned the plan Labour released on Sunday had listed the reversal of the Income Related Rent Subsidy and Accommodation Supplement changes as a $44.8m saving, when that should have been expressed as a cost.

As a result, the final costings appeared to be $89.6m short.

When RNZ put that to Labour, a spokesperson confirmed the error.

"A cost was incorrectly recorded as a saving, and a saving recorded as a cost. We've checked it and will correct our Fiscal Plan.

"This is a straightforward and small correction, and does not change the fact that we are fully able to pay for our commitments," the spokesperson said.

Labour confirmed its unallocated funding would drop from $10.48b to $10.39b.

However, the party denied another much larger hole National's Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis was claiming to have found.

"Labour claims cancelling Investment Boost will generate $7.7 billion to help pay for its election promises. But based on official Budget costings, the cost of Investment Boost is actually $5.5 billion over the forecast period," she said in a statement on Tuesday morning.

"That leaves a $2.2 billion gap that Chris Hipkins and Barbara Edmonds need to explain."

Labour's own Finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds soon provided that explanation.

"Nicola Willis is wrong. The cost of keeping the policy is a net figure, after accounting for reduced depreciation deductions on existing assets. The revenue from repealing it reflects the new deductions that would stop. Because those are different things being measured, the numbers are different," Edmonds said.

She explained that while the original policy was a net cost, the savings from cancelling it would be a gross figure and larger than the policy's headline cost.

The difference was that headline cost was already reduced by the offset from older assets, while the savings from repealing the policy were based on stopping new deductions.

Willis called a media conference for about an hour later, adamant that Labour's costings stack up and calling Edmonds' explanation "gobbledegook".

"Cancelling investment boost literally means cancelling economic growth and cancelling wage increases," she said.

"People who have already claimed investment boost have made that deduction under tax law, and unless Labour are suggesting that they will punitively go back and retrospectively make those taxpayers pay more tax, then their claims simply do not stack up."

Willis said she was "200 percent" confident that she was right and Edmonds wrong, and refused to accept Edmonds' explanation when reporters put that to her.

"Either what you're saying is they will somehow collect more tax from reversing it than it costs to introduce, or you're just siding with Chris Hipkins and Barbara Edmonds. And my view is that we should look to the Treasury and the IRD as independent modellers."

She said reversing the policy was equal to adding the revenue that would otherwise have been lost, and Labour was claiming it would "get a magic tax dividend from somewhere".

"We're talking about 2.2 billion dollars more in tax revenue being collected ... You don't need to be a modeller at the IRD to know that cancelling something won't generate more revenue than introducing it."

She said she would welcome the Treasury taking an independent look at it, but the Treasury turned down that suggestion.

"As per the Public Service Commission's General Election Guidance 2026, the Treasury does not cost or comment on the policy proposals of political parties," a spokesperson said.

The latest polling from RNZ-Reid Research shows support for National dropping to 25.9 percent.

As a list-only candidate Willis is under particular pressure, as a party vote result that low combined with a high number of National electorate wins could see her out of Parliament.

Asked whether National's polling could be suffering because of the party's attacks on Labour, she said she wanted to be talking about plans for the future but elections were also about choices.

World.title: Loafers Lodge fire trial: Director neglected his duties, prosecutor argues
World.content:
Gregory Mein neglected his duties by "implicitly trusting" that fire safety systems in the Loafers Lodge building were being maintained and operated as they should, according to a prosecution lawyer.

Mein - the director of the lodge - and three others are on trial in the High Court in Wellington for manslaughter after five people died in the building in the 2023 fire.

But a lawyer for the defence says the building had a recent fire safety warrant of fitness that was signed off by council, and that any failings or wrongdoings are at the feet of the agencies tasked with ensuring the boarding house was safe.

The five people died when a fire lit by Esarona Lologa tore through the budget accommodation building - with nearly 100 hundred residents inside - in May 2023.

Last year Lologa was sentenced to life in prison after being found guilty of murder and arson for deliberately lighting the fire that killed Michael Wahrlich, Melvin Parun, Peter O'Sullivan, Kenneth Barnard and Liam Hockings on 16 May 2023.

Gregory Bruce Mein, Barry Charles Collins, Glenn Brendan McAllister, and Marie Louise Murphy each face 10 manslaughter charges over the operation and maintenance of the building.

Jurors were told on the opening day of the trail yesterday that the four defendants faced five charges of gross negligence causing death.

Prosecutor Stephanie Bishop today outlined the five alternative manslaughter charges relating to breaches of health and safety regulations.

The case is set to be a mammoth undertaking with nearly 50 witnesses, made up of emergency service staff and residents, scheduled ahead of further testimony from council and fire safety agencies.

Their testimonies would be supported by tens of thousand of submitted documents.

Mein stepped in to help when owner became ill

Acting for Mein, lawyer Christopher Stevenson KC told the jury Mein had come into the business about 24 months ahead of the fire.

He said he took on the role of temporary director after his friend and former owner Chris Stevenson - no relation - became seriously ill and could not manage his own affairs.

Stevenson died in 2021.

He said Mein was eager to move on from the role, but disputes among Stevenson's family meant it was not possible.

"He did not fail to do anything he was required to do. [Loafers Lodge] wasn't anything to do with Greg Mein," Stevenson said.

The business's practices were well established long before Mein's involvement and the building had received a warrant of fitness that was signed off by Wellington City Council shortly before the fire, he said.

"There were shocking and disturbing failings and wrong doing which was long-standing by agencies that had the responsibility to keep this building safe and to keep the people in it safe," Stevenson said.

A place of last resort

Stephen Winter - counsel for part-time manager Murphy - said the budget accommodation was a "place of last resort" for tenants, many of whom had criminal convictions, drug and alcohol issues or mental health challenges.

He said evidence would show residents would smoke and drink in their rooms and often displayed a "lack of response" when fire alarms were triggered in the building.

Winter said Murphy had little warning of Lologa's mental state and history when she checked him in.

"It was Mr Lologa, in a series of criminal acts, that killed the five victims of this fire.

"Please consider carefully the actions of that man and how easily that could have been planned against," Winter said.

Defendant's victims of arsonist.

Alex Dye - counsel for Glenn McAllister - said his client was a victim of Lologa's actions.

He said McAllister was a tenant in the building who volunteered to assist with the running of the building and was paid "nominal amounts for some but not all of his help".

He said in attempting to charge McAllister for failing to fulfil the duties of the business, the Crown had "invented a job that did not exist".

He said McAllister had lived in the building for nearly 15 years, considered many of the tenants his friends, and had been traumatised by the fire and the manslaughter charges that followed.

Counsel for Barry Collins Val Nisbet said evidence would show Collins was the person who turned off the alarm after the first fire was set by Lologa.

He said Collins - who was also a tenant in the building - was never paid any money to assist with the fire systems and did so in order to protect his place in his home of more than a decade.

"He was asleep and was woken by the alarm. He got up and went downstairs and turned it off. That is what he thought he was supposed to do... It was a favour he was asked to do every now and again," Nisbet said.

He said the fact that Nisbet went back to bed himself was evidence of the regular false alarms and the entrenched response to their occurrence that had become embedded over more than a decade.

Police witness outlines building's layout

Detective Sergeant Olivia Mears was the second in charge of the police investigation following the fire.

She walked the jury through drone footage and photographs of the building showing external damage following the fire.

Mears said, while the building was originally intended as accommodation for students and staff at the nearby hospital, the building's tenancy had changed over time to comprise of "mainly middle aged men" who had trouble finding accommodation elsewhere.

"That may have been due to behavioural problems and other matters," she said.

A three-dimensional architectural model of the building's structure showed the layout of the building, including the fourth floor mezzanine where each of the five victims of the fire lived.

Witnesses photographs, video footage and CCTV showed the development of the fire and the arrival of emergency services.

In a montage of footage smoke can be seen from the building's upper levels and growing in thickness and intensity as the street fills with fire crews and onlookers.

Shortly after 1 am flames from inside the third floor start to overtake the upper part of the building. Debris falls to the street below as the fire billows from the Adelaide Road facing windows. Above the building the sky glows red with the fire on the rooftop.

Accused places 111 call

The jury heard the 111 call placed to emergency services at 12.12 am by McAllister reporting "severe smoke" on level three of the building.

"I'm about to hit the manual firearm," McAllister told dispatchers before another alarm goes off during the call.

Mears said in March 2024 police filed for a warrant to monitor phone calls from Mein and Murphy.

Their home addresses were searched, devices seized and data extracted from each of their phones.

She said Murphy was "very co-operative" in the searches and subsequent dealings with police.

Lawyer for McAllister, Stephen Winter questioned Mears about her knowledge as to what had been communicated to staff at the lodge concerning Lologa's criminal and mental health history.

"He was a man who had contact with corrections and had recently been in a psychiatric facility in Auckland," Winter said.

Mears said she was not aware of those factors being put to the management of the lodge.

World.title: Women's stars call on Cricket Australia to fix scheduling
World.content:
Senior women's players have called on Cricket Australia to push to return some of their games to the peak of summer, fearing the current schedule will hurt the sport's growth among girls.

Australia begin their home summer against Bangladesh on Friday, marking the first of three ODIs in Brisbane before three T20s against New Zealand in Sydney.

All three of the Sydney matches fall on school nights.

They will then not play on home soil until they host New Zealand for ODIs in March, in what looms as a sign of things to come for the world's number one-ranked team.

Australian women's cricket team Upcoming games ODI vs Bangladesh, Brisbane: October 9, 1:50pm AEST

ODI vs Bangladesh, Brisbane: October 11, 1:50pm AEST

ODI vs Bangladesh, Brisbane: October 14, 1:50pm AEST

T20I vs New Zealand, North Sydney: October 18, 6:15pm AEST

T20I vs New Zealand, North Sydney: October 20, 6:15pm AEST

T20I vs New Zealand, North Sydney: October 22, 6:15pm AEST

Under the current ICC schedule, there will be no WBBL or international women's cricket during the school holidays in Australia for at least the next three years, with all fixtures in the shoulder seasons.

"We don't want to be the sport that falls behind because we're just getting it wrong," veteran wicketkeeper-bat Beth Mooney told AAP.

"We're just pushing it uphill, because we're in a bad timeslot and it's a bad time of year for parents.

"They're not dragging their kid out to watch a 7pm T20 on a Tuesday night or whatever it is.

"That's going to stop girls getting into the game, because parents aren't going to take them."

Mooney's comments come after Australia's most-capped player Ellyse Perry expressed similar concerns earlier last month.

Australian players have for a long time had some frustrations over the schedule, particularly around the same consistency in men's cricket.

This summer has been impacted by the ICC moving the Champions' Trophy to India, leaving no international women's games at all in Perth.

But multiple players have also expressed concerns to AAP over India being able to claim the January window for its lucrative WPL, fearing it will only expand into a larger window. This year it runs January 14 to February 7.

Australia wins Women's T20 World Cup Australia has won the ICC Women's T20 World Cup in commanding style, defeating England by seven wickets in the final at Lord's.

They are concerned the national team is at risk of being out of sight and out of mind, stunting momentum after another T20 World Cup win.

One push is for more home matches to be scheduled in December around the Christmas window, with Australia to tour Sri Lanka through that period this year.

"We're not getting crowds, it's not marketed well. There is no big-ticket item where people go, 'The Australian women's team play here [at this time] every year,'" Mooney said.

"We want to be relatable athletes. And if we're not front and centre of the summer it makes it pretty difficult when it's meant to be a summer sport.

"We don't need to compete with the men. They play the day-night Test at some point. We can have T20s before that.

"Or we can play night T20s when there is a men's Test on."

Australia's coach Shelley Nitschke said it was "obviously disappointing" not to play at home in December or January, while captain Sophie Molineux argued home games in December would be "really special" for her team.

"It would also help see fans come through," Molineux said.

"I completely understand that the schedules are getting bigger and busier."

AAP

World.title: Jaymie Graham named new North Melbourne AFL coach
World.content:
North Melbourne has named Fremantle assistant coach Jaymie Graham as the new coach for the AFL side.

A statement from club president Sonja Hood on Tuesday said Graham was the new senior coach, succeeding four-time premiership coach Alastair Clarkson, who was sacked by the Kangaroos earlier this year.

Graham spent five seasons at the Dockers as an assistant to Justin Longmuir.

The Kangaroos finished the 2026 season — Clarkson's fourth season in charge — in 14th spot with nine wins.

Speaking at his first press conference, Graham thanked the club for having faith in him.

Having missed out on a number of coaching opportunities before landing the North Melbourne job, he said he was nervous and proud to take charge of the Kangaroos.

"This opportunity came up, things happen for a reason. I feel I belong here already," he said.

"There's no ceiling on where we want to get to. There's clearly some talent on this list, but there's also some work to do."

Graham described himself as a "systems-based and relationships-based coach".

"People don't care how much you know, until they know how much you care."

Club CEO Jen Watt confirmed the panel tasked with finding the new coach had unanimously picked Grham.

Earlier, in the club statement, Hood told members Graham had "the resilience to handle the relentless toils of the football environment, carrying the exact kind of grit we value at North Melbourne.

"As a coach, Jaymie is a process-driven leader with a quiet, grounded presence, sharp attention to detail, and a clear football vision," she said.

"Outside of his exceptional character, he joins us with a proven skill set. He played a key role in West Coast's 2018 premiership success, and more recently he was the line coach for one of the competition's best forward lines at Fremantle as part of a high-performing program.

"He is widely respected across the industry as a developer of talent and a connector of people — someone who builds strong player relationships instantly and earns respect through his actions."

The announcement marks a change in direction, with a young untested AFL senior coach — who has been a caretaker or interim coach for three games in total at West Coast and Fremantle, after a period in charge of East Perth in the WAFL — after the end of the Clarkson era.

The Kangaroos were criticised for the tone of their press conference in early September announcing Clarkson's departure.

Alastair Clarkson leaves North North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney explain why the club is parting ways with Alastair Clarkson with a year to run on his deal.

At the time, Hood said Clarkson's replacement needed to be "a coach who can coach for the modern game".

"It'll be a coach who knows what they're doing, and it'll be a coach who's the best fit for this football club," she said.

Football manager Todd Viney said in the press conference there were "still some gaping holes in our game plan".

Fremantle paid tribute to Graham in a statement, wishing him well for his new role and thanking him for his "five outstanding seasons" at the club.

"Jaymie has had a significant impact not only on our player group — but the entire football department and broader club," Fremantle executive general manager of football Joe Brierty said.

"It is well documented that Jaymie has had ambitions of becoming a senior coach in his own right one day, and we couldn't be prouder or happier for him to take an opportunity he's worked so hard for."

World.title: Mary Fowler withdraws from Matildas squad for Germany, Haiti games
World.content:
Matildas star Mary Fowler has been withdrawn from the Australian squad for two upcoming internationals, due to personal circumstances.

A release from Football Australia on Tuesday morning said the decision had been taken following discussions between Fowler, Manchester City and Matildas staff.

Fowler has been in solid form, coming on as a sub to spark a comeback win for Manchester City over WSL rivals Arsenal on Monday morning, Australian time.

Fowler's City still perfect in WSL Mary Fowler's landmark 100th game for Manchester City is a bright spot for the beleaguered club, with a big win over Arsenal keeping them with a perfect record on top of the WSL.

There was no talk of injury after the game.

Fowler's partner, Nathan Cleary, is recovering in Sydney after leg surgery.

The Penrith Panthers NRL star went into the preliminary final against Newcastle with a broken foot, before suffering a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle in a hip-drop tackle, requiring emergency surgery.

Fowler has been replaced in the Australian squad by Charlton Athletic midfielder Leah Davidson. Davidson has made four appearances for the Matildas since her international debut in 2024.

The Matildas are playing two international friendlies in Europe as they continue preparations towards next year's FIFA Women's World Cup.

Australia split a two-match series with Mexico in June, with one win each.

Now the Matildas will face Germany in Karlsruhe on Saturday morning, Australian time before taking on Haiti in France on October 13.

World.title: Hawks make King offer official as Tigers swing move for Freo winger
World.content:
Hawthorn has officially lodged the paperwork in its bid to sign Gold Coast forward Ben King as a free agent.

King, who has played 143 games for the Suns, has reportedly been offered a seven-year deal worth $9 million by the Hawks.

As King is a restricted free agent, Gold Coast reserves the right to force Hawthorn into a trade by matching the contract offer to the 26-year-old.

The Suns have a 72-hour window to match the contract offer. If they do not choose to do so, they are expected to receive a band one compensation pick from the AFL in November's draft.

A band one pick would land directly after Gold Coast's first-round selection (currently No.6) in this year's draft, but it remains to be seen whether the Suns will want more in return in exchange for their all-time leading goalkicker.

Hawthorn is limited in what assets it could provide Gold Coast in the way of draft capital in exchange for King after sending multiple picks to Essendon in exchange for Zach Merrett on the opening day of the trade period.

Gold Coast is interested in young Hawthorn forward Aidan Schubert, but is adamant any deal for Schubert would be independent of a deal involving King.

Elsewhere on day two, Richmond bolstered its young list by trading for Fremantle winger Nathan O'Driscoll in exchange for a fourth-round selection (currently No.61) in this year's draft.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all the action from day two of the trade period.

World.title: Demon faces Djokovic in China final after Medvedev disqualified
World.content:
Alex de Minaur will face Novak Djokovic in the China Open final after the Serb's semifinal opponent, Daniil Medvedev, was disqualified ‌for hitting a loose ball into the crowd and causing a spectator to suffer an eye injury.

The Australian number one progressed from his semifinal after Poland's Hubert Hurkacz retired injured when trailing in the second set.

Djokovic was leading 7–5, 5–3 in Beijing and serving for the match when the incident happened.

After a forehand volley winner from Djokovic, the ball bounced off the advertising boards to Medvedev, who smacked a backhand that sailed into the stands.

A male spectator (obscured) was struck in the eye after Daniil Medvedev hit a ball into the stands during his China Open semifinal. (AP: Andy Wong)

It hit a spectator in the front row behind him.

The spectator clutched his left eye and appeared to be in ‌pain as he walked out, assisted by stadium staff.

"Terribly sorry to ‌the spectator, first ⁠of all," Medvedev told reporters. "I'm trying to get in touch with him, if he wants it. Hopefully I can apologise in person and see how he feels."

The Russian world number five said he did not cause the incident intentionally.

"The ball was bouncing back, so I tried to, like, just hit it anywhere, so it doesn't go out from the court. When I saw the result, I mean, I felt horrible because, again, I don't think I was ever close to such a situation."

Medvedev, 30, has a history of on-court behaviour issues. He was fined 6,000 euros ($9,600) after he smashed his racquet seven times during a 6–0, 6–0 loss to Matteo Berrettini at this year's Monte Carlo Masters.

"I was shocked, to be honest … I hope that person is not ‌badly injured," said Djokovic, who was disqualified from the US Open in 2020 under similar circumstances.

"On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil because I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match … ‌I'm sure that Daniil didn't want to do this intentionally."

Alex de Minaur was a set up on Hubert Hurkacz in the China Open semifinal when Hurkacz was forced to withdraw due to injury. (Getty Iimages: Eurasia Sport/Hermann Chu)

De Minaur will be seeking to become the first person to beat Djokovic in 34 matches at the China Open. He has a 1–3 head-to-head record with the Serb.

The winner will leave Beijing ninth in the race to qualify for November's eight-man ATP Finals, with the gap to Medvedev in eighth reduced as the Russian will lose the 200 points he had gained in Beijing.

There are two ATP Masters 1000 events to come, in Shanghai and Paris, but ninth may be enough with Jannik Sinner's availability uncertain.

On Saturday, the world number one, who last played at Wimbledon, pulled out of Shanghai, which begins on Wednesday. The Italian has a knee problem.

De Minaur was up 6–4, 3–2 and 40–0 when Hurkacz retired with an apparent adductor injury after showing mobility problems.

The world number nine had broken a tentative Hurkacz in his opening two service games before holding to lead 4–0, then withstood a comeback to take the first set 6–4.

Another break in the third game of the second set helped de Minaur build a 3–1 lead. Hurkacz fought desperately to hold serve in the following game, surviving four break points and a marathon deuce game, but was unable to battle much longer.

In Tokyo, defending champion Carlos Alcaraz overcame early wobbles on his serve ‌to outclass fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar 5–7, 6–3, 6–1 ‌and reach the Japan Open final.

He will play Jiri Lehecka, who beat Valentin Vacherot 6-4, 6-2.

AAP/AP

World.title: Why NRL grand final 'freak' is making Wallabies lick their lips
World.content:
It was not just the 80,000 spectators crammed inside Sydney's Olympic stadium, nor the millions of TV viewers in Australia, who were left in awe of Mark Nawaqanitawase's performance in the NRL grand final.

Last night, across the Tasman in New Zealand, the Wallabies eagerly watched on as Nawaqanitawase added to his highlight reel by scoring two tries in the Sydney Roosters' nail-biting 19-18 victory over Newcastle.

Roosters win classic NRL grand final A Daly Cherry-Evans field goal proves the difference as the Sydney Roosters beat the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the NRL grand final.

The fact that some of the Wallabies were Nawaqanitawase's ex-teammates helped explain the interest.

But knowing the dual international is switching codes once again, in time for next year's Rugby World Cup, also had Wallabies players licking their lips in anticipation.

"He'll be massive. He's just been a freak," Wallabies prop Allan Alaalatoa told reporters in Auckland today.

"What he's done in the last two years in league is probably unheard of.

"He's gone over there in the space of two years and pretty much done everything, and now he's coming back."

Following the Wallabies' disastrous Rugby World Cup campaign three years ago, Nawaqanitawase announced he would move to the NRL ahead of the 2025 season.

He was given clearance to join the Roosters earlier than scheduled, and made his NRL debut in the final round of the 2024 premiership.

Mark Nawaqanitawase (left) scored twice for the Roosters in the NRL grand final.

To suggest Nawaqanitawase made an impact in rugby league is an understatement.

He took the NRL by storm in his first full season, which was capped off when he debuted for Australia in last year's Ashes series in England.

Nawaqanitawase was selected in NSW's successful State of Origin squad this year and played a crucial role in helping the Roosters capture their first NRL premiership since 2019.

His athleticism and aerial skills on the wing contributed to an astonishing strike rate of 47 tries in as many NRL matches.

Nawaqanitawase has hit the pause button on his NRL career for now, having signed with Japanese rugby club Saitama Wild Knights on a two-year deal.

He will be available for Wallabies selection, although the 26-year-old is unlikely to feature in November's Nations Championship Tests against England, Scotland and Wales.

After impressing for the Wallabies in 11 Test appearances between 2022-23, he is expected to make a smooth transition once he returns to rugby.

Having him play alongside the likes of Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Max Jorgensen in a Wallabies' backline is a tantalising prospect; however, coach Les Kiss says there are "no promises and no guarantees".

Mark Nawaqanitawase played 11 Tests for the Wallabies before switching codes in 2024. (Getty Images: Aurelien Meunier)

Kiss is justified in declaring Nawaqanitawase will not walk straight back into the Wallabies squad.

But his presence will create competitive pressure among candidates for the Wallabies' wing spots ahead of the Rugby World Cup, which Australia is hosting.

"He'll just naturally start demanding more from other people because of the type of competition that is in the squad," said Alaalatoa, as the Wallabies prepare for Saturday's Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park.

"I think that only adds health to the group, and it brings the best out of people in his position because of the type of player that he is and what he's shown on some of the biggest stages in Australia.

"I think that is the type of value he'll add to our group."

Nawaqanitawase is set to debut for Saitama Wild Knights in the Japan Rugby League One competition in December.

Not surprisingly, his immediate focus is helping the Roosters celebrate the club's NRL and NRLW premiership victories.

World.title: Wiradjuri Aboriginal Rivers, Newcastle Yowies claim Koori Knockout glory
World.content:
The Wiradjuri Aboriginal Rivers have defeated the Bourke Warriors, 26-6, to claim their first Koori Knockout men's title.

Despite a nailbiting first half of Sunday's grand final, WAR came back strong in the second half and led their team to victory.

"For this club here, WAR, its more than footy", said WAR player Julian Christian.

"We've been close a couple of times over the years, we've lost against WAC (Walgett Aboriginal Connection) a couple of times in a grand final.

" This is so good, its so worth it. So worth it. "

Fans watch the finals of the Koori Knockout intensely. (ABC Newcastle: Piper Duffy)

As well as winning glory at the Knockout, WAR will now get to choose where the 2027 Knockout is played.

In the women's final, the Newcastle Yowies secured back-to-back titles, defeating the Redfern All Blacks 14-6.

The side featured a mixture of young talent, as well as experienced NRLW players including two-time premiership winner Caitlin Johnston.

She told NITV the win was dedicated to members of their community who recently passed.

"We've lost some very special people to us, so to take it back to back means quite a bit," Johnston said through tears.

" Newy's a community full of footballers ... to host the Knockout is pretty special, and then to win it puts the icing on the cake. "

Game day 'means everything'

About 40,000 fans spent their long weekend on Worimi Country at Raymond Terrace to attend the biggest sporting event of the Indigenous calendar.

Described as a modern-day corroboree, the tournament has been running since 1971, now bringing together almost 180 mens, women's and junior teams from across the state.

Bourke Warriors centre Colby Pellow and his wife Alex travelled more than 700 kilometres to play in the mammoth sporting event.

"Our community, it's only small, but we all get around this time of year," he said.

Colby Pellow and his wife Alex travelled from Bourke to attend the Knockout in Raymond Terrace. (ABC Newcastle: Emma Simkin )

Knockout veteran Josh Toole, who played for WAR, said the annual event brings mob together.

"I've played for a couple of different [Knockout] sides and it doesn't matter which side you go for it's that sense of community," he said.

"Also for Aboriginal people, we're big on footy, we love footy so there's a lot of passion."

Maddi Ireland led her Newcastle team to victory in the under 15s. (ABC Newcastle: Piper Duffy)

Young talent on display

Maddi Ireland spent her childhood watching her father take to the Knockout field year after year.

This year Ms Ireland, a Wiradjuri woman from Dubbo, took out the title for the Under 15's playing for her new team, the Newcastle Yowies.

"[It's] just good to do it for the culture, the mob, and my friends and the families around me," she said.

"'It's surreal honestly playing out on the field with all the crowd and mob around us supporting us.

"It just feels unreal out there," she said.

Ms Ireland said the win had inspired her to pursue bigger rugby league dreams of her own.

"One day I hope I can make NRLW, make my family proud and my culture," she said.

Families from across the state came to watch the annual Koori Knockout in Raymond Terrace. (ABC Newcastle: Piper Duffy)

World.title: Australia's Rugby League World Cup squad is a sign of the changing times
World.content:
The depths of Australia's star power means the Kangaroos will always name squads oozing with class and Kevin Walters's combination for this year's World Cup is no exception.

It's a side with major success stories, young and old and in-between.

James Tedesco's return three years after his last Test caps the 33-year old's resurrection and after he ran the ball to hell and back in the grand final to win the Clive Churchill Medal, there can be no doubt that, at an age where many players best days are only just a memory, he is once again the best fullback in the world.

Walker among six Kangaroos debutants The grand final sides feature in the Kangaroos squad for the Rugby League World Cup, with James Tedesco back in and Sydney's Sam Walker and Newcastle's Bradman Best among six debutants.

The inclusion of Dolphins flyer Jack Bostock, who will almost certainly see a Test debut in the World Cup opener given the side's shortage of wingers, heralds the start of a new generation wearing green and gold.

At 26, David Fifita is no longer a youngster in rugby league terms but his looming Australian debut is both a long time coming and well-earned following his strong finish to the year with Souths.

The one-time prodigy has longed seemed a player of limitless possibilities but only now, eight years after his NRL debut and three years since he last played for Queensland, will he get the chance to be a Kangaroo.

But the Australian squad also reveals the new truths about representative football, that the disconnect between State and Origin and Test matches is wider than ever before and may never be stitched back together again.

The disconnect between Origin and Test football has never been wider. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

It's a process that began with Origin's gradual but unmistakeable rise past Test football as rugby league's biggest stage then continued when a host of players chose to represent Pasifika nations over Australia while retaining their Origin eligibility.

The final change came earlier this year when the NRL allowed players to represent New Zealand or England and still being available for Origin selection.

Both of those eligibility changes reflect the changing face of rugby league and the people who play it and the game is better for them.

But it does require a reset of over a century's worth of thinking that interstate football is the pathway to national selection.

This has not been true for some years now, but there's a reason old habits have a hard time dying.

And while Australia will never be hard up for talent, some of the more eyebrow-raising picks prove this old adage is as antiquated as Kangaroo tours that travel to England by boat.

Robert Toia would have been a walk-up start for Australia but has chosen Tonga. (Getty Images: Izhar Khan)

Not one of the Queensland outside backs is in the side at all. Kalyn Ponga, Robert Toia, Jojo Fifita, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all would be, but they're playing for other nations while Selwyn Cobbo is injured.

That's how we end up with Brisbane's Kotoni Staggs, a fine centre who had a tough year, making the side despite being dropped by New South Wales for the Origin decider after a horror night in Game II at the MCG.

Latrell Mitchell missed the entire series through injury and has only started one match in the past five months but he's made it, while Tom Trbojevic is a likely starter on one wing despite not having played rep football for two years and not playing a match on the flank since 2018.

Tom Trbojevic will play his first Test match in two years. (AAP: Darren England)

Likewise of the 12 men who played in the forwards for New South Wales, only Blayke Brailey, Isaah Yeo, Liam Martin and Cameron Murray have made the squad.

Hudson Young and Payne Haas are both out with injury, but Haumole Olakau'atu and Addin Fonua-Blake will both line up for Tonga while Victor Radley is with England.

So Reuben Cotter makes the squad despite an underwhelming season with the Cowboys and a lacklustre series for Queensland.

His selection over Dolphins hardman Max Plath, who does a similar job with similar attributes whilst offering the same versatility and is coming off a far superior season for club and state, is perhaps the hardest pick to understand.

How Plath became Queensland's newest Origin hero The players who fill the spaces in between the stars are the secret to Queensland's Origin dominance and in Max Plath the Maroons have found yet another player who knows just how to do it.

Plath, along with Newcastle's Fletcher Sharpe and South Sydney's Tallis Duncan can count himself most aggrieved at missing out but it's hard to take up too much issue with Walters's squad, even if it's short of wingers.

This is the hand the Australian coach has been dealt for his final tournament before he departs to take over Super League side St Helens.

The eligibility changes and the fact that Test football misses out on players who pick up injuries during club seasons that are getting longer and longer all the time means sometimes his options are a bit more limited than he would have liked.

Australia are still the pick to win the World Cup and will be warm favourites in every game they play, beginning with their tournament opener against New Zealand next Thursday night in Sydney.

Walters is attempting to solve a puzzle no other Kangaroos coach has ever had to face and there is no one-size-fits-all philosophy in the battle between fitness, function and form when it comes to selecting a player.

But when numbers are scarce, and for the Kangaroos they're a lot shorter than they used to be, the first two are more important than the last.

Tech.title: This remote-controlled wagon is silly but so very useful
Tech.content:
is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Confession: When BougeRV told me about its remote-controlled wagon with animated lighting, I called it in for a laugh, expecting to eviscerate it in a review. It’s ridiculous, to be sure. But the DuneRover also proved very capable, with enough torque to flatten hills even when carrying over 200 pounds of gear. It can also traverse soft sand that defeats conventional wagons.

As someone who regularly uses a variety of wagons to haul all sorts of gear, the DuneRover is an epiphany. But what BougeRV sent me was a Kickstarter prototype — and it shows.

Production units won’t ship until February 2027. So, what follows is less of a review and more a risk assessment for those considering backing the Kickstarter. That way, you can decide whether it makes sense to lock down early-bird pricing at $467, a claimed 48 percent discount off the eventual $899 list price. (Though I’ll wager it’ll always be sold for some kind of discount.)

Nobody needs this, but controlling it with the remote sure was fun.

Frankly, $500 isn’t outlandish for a wagon. Prices start at around $40 for a rickety model that will only last a few months, $300 for something durable from a reputable brand, and closer to $800 at the top end. And none of those wagons provides a motorized assist.

Let’s begin with the dumb stuff. The wagon has LED light bars on the back that are on by default and could come in handy at a campsite after dark. You can turn them off via the app, but you have to do it every time you restart the wagon. The default for a battery-powered device used primarily during the day should obviously be off.

Then there’s the remote control. I think I know what happened here. The product designers had a choice: route a cable through all the folding mechanisms that separate the motor from the handle or make it wireless. Wireless won, and then someone from marketing said, ‘Hey, I’ve got an idea!’

I mean, a remote-controlled wagon is so absurd that it’s kind of fun, and it brought a lot of joyful finger-pointing to onlookers during my testing. Maybe that’s enough?

The DuneRover is no joke for hauling gear. It’s fitted with two brushless geared motors, each producing up to 400W of output and up to 33Nm of torque. The wagon is activated by a trigger embedded in the handle that you press naturally when you pull the cart. Walk faster and the wagon will roll faster. Sometimes the wagon will lurch forward on that initial pull before settling into your walking rhythm. It’s not dangerous, it’s just unexpected. Release the trigger on the handle, and the wagon stops, even on an incline.

The lights are on by default every time you power on the wagon. The handle is also a wireless remote control for some reason. Here the sides are unzipped and the straps loosened for additional capacity. Here the sides are unzipped and folded in to make space for wider loads.

Pulling an oversized load weighing over 200 pounds up a 10 percent grade required a modicum of effort — but just a tenth of what it would have taken without the motor assist. Even on that steep incline, the wagon stops (with an inch or two of rollback) just as soon as I let go of the trigger. Repeated stopping and starting on slopes did, however, seem to confuse the DuneRover, occasionally causing the motors to become jerky as soon as I started walking again. A simple on/off resumed normal operation.

The motors also regulate speed when walking downhill with a heavy load. With the trigger held down, the controller did a good job monitoring changes in acceleration and countering the wagon’s speed to maintain my walking pace. When I stopped, so did the wagon, even on that 10 percent grade with a 200-plus pound load.

The motors aren’t powerful enough to haul that same load through soft sand, however. The oversized beach wheels performed much better in sand with loads weighing about half that, and should be excellent for families carrying a cooler, snacks, beach umbrella, toddler, and toys for a day at the beach.

I like that the DuneRover easily transformed depending on what I needed to haul. The sides can be unzipped and folded flat to convert the wagon into a cart for hauling oversized items or a senior dog. You can also unzip the sides but leave the straps connected to create more volume inside the wagon. I used this configuration a lot. Just know that you’ll want to bring a few bungee cords or cargo nets to keep everything securely in place.

My prototype suffered from intermittent rolling resistance with the motor off. The wagon would roll along fine for five or six feet, but then the wheels attached to the motors would brake, drag along the ground, and then release after a second or two. BougeRV assures me this isn’t something that would be exhibited by its production wagons. I ended up just leaving the motor on throughout my testing, even when I didn’t need it. The 82.14Wh battery was more than up to the challenge.

Previous Next





















1 / 12 A clever trigger under the handle makes powering the wagon intuitive.

I used the DuneRover to move gear out of a beach house along the same route where I tested BougeRV’s original electric wagon. Six times I pulled the DuneRover along a path with 5 percent grade on one end and a 10 percent grade on the other. After six kilometers (3.73 miles) of soft sand, hard asphalt, wooden ramps, and gravel, the battery still showed a 74 percent charge. Not bad.

The removable battery features a bi-directional 100W USB-C port, making it a rather capable power bank. It can also charge from a 100W solar panel plugged into its XT-60 jack, thanks to a built-in MPPT solar controller. The battery in my prototype is not protected against rain, so I tested it in dry conditions, though BougeRV promises “full-vehicle IPX6-rated protection” in the production wagon.

The DuneRover is a beast at 59.5 pounds (27kg) with the battery and wheels installed. It’s also rather chunky when it folds. The quick-release front wheels can be removed if a flatter pack is required.

Dumb fun.

Overall, I’m impressed with the prototype DuneRover I tested — it’s capable, versatile, and proved to be an enormous help over the last few weeks of moving things between a holiday home, home, and adventure van. Like most BougeRV products, it gets the basics right, but not without a few annoyances and inconveniences. I’d expect the same from whatever ships to Kickstarter backers early next year.
